description: Cytosolic AARS1 activates L-alanine with ATP and transfers alanine to tRNA(Ala), producing Ala-tRNA(Ala) for cytoplasmic protein synthesis. This substrate-specific aminoacylation reaction is the enzyme's primary conserved activity.

The embedded AARS1 editing apparatus proofreads mischarged tRNA(Ala) and hydrolyzes the incorrect aminoacyl ester. Ser-tRNA(Ala) deacylation is directly demonstrated with human AARS1; Gly-tRNA(Ala) is a plausible conserved substrate but was not directly tested in the human studies examined here. This post-transfer editing preserves cytoplasmic translational fidelity.

As a conditional secondary activity, AARS1 senses elevated intracellular L-lactate, forms lactoyl-AMP, and transfers lactyl groups to protein lysines. This activity can operate in the cytoplasm and, after lactate-induced nuclear import, in the nucleus on substrates including YAP1, TEAD1, and TP53. It is substrate- and context-dependent; AARS1 depletion did not reduce basal global lysine lactylation in untreated HEK293T cells.

ABCA1 uses ATP binding and hydrolysis to translocate phospholipids across membrane leaflets, with direct support for phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylserine, and sphingomyelin movement and for extracellular phospholipid extraction at the plasma membrane.

ABCA1 binds apoA-I and other exchangeable apolipoproteins, including APOE, to drive cellular cholesterol and phospholipid efflux, nascent HDL particle assembly, and reverse cholesterol transport. This lipidation activity is the ABCA1 function most directly connected to APOE biology.

ABCA1 contributes to cholesterol movement out of cells and away from intracellular pools, limiting cholesterol storage and promoting HDL-associated lipid removal. This cholesterol-efflux role is supported by Tangier/familial HDL-deficiency genetics and cellular efflux assays, although the direct transported lipid substrate is best established for phospholipids.

Uses ATP hydrolysis to flip N-retinylidene-phosphatidylethanolamine from the lumenal to the cytosolic leaflet of photoreceptor disc membranes, facilitating clearance of all-trans and excess 11-cis retinal.
Uses ATP hydrolysis to flip phosphatidylethanolamine from the exoplasmic/lumenal to the cytosolic membrane leaflet. This substrate activity is directly demonstrated alongside NRPE transport.
Uses ATP to flop phosphatidylcholine from the cytosolic to the canalicular-facing leaflet, supplying phospholipid for bile-salt extraction.

ATP-driven export of heme and other porphyrins across the plasma membrane. ABCB6 assembles as a homodimer whose nucleotide-binding domains hydrolyse ATP (Walker A K629) to translocate hemin, coproporphyrin III, protoporphyrin IX and related tetrapyrroles out of the cytoplasm. In red cells this pool carries the Langereis blood group antigen and limits the cytotoxic porphyrin load, which is why hypomorphic ABCB6 alleles aggravate hereditary porphyrias. Glutathione acts as a cofactor for metal-centred porphyrins.

ATP-dependent sequestration of toxic heavy-metal species into the lumen of lysosomes and late endosomes. The N-terminal TMD0 targets ABCB6 to this compartment, where the transporter is oriented with its nucleotide-binding domains in the cytosol and pumps metal complexes inwards. Human ABCB6 substitutes for HMT-1 proteins in fission yeast and nematode mutants, restoring vacuolar cadmium content and cadmium tolerance, and its level sets cadmium sensitivity in human cells. This is the activity shared with the invertebrate HMT-1 proteins of the same PANTHER subfamily, and the vacuolar/lysosomal membrane is the compartment PAINT assigns to the whole opisthokont clade.

Transport across the limiting membrane of early melanosomes, required for formation of the PMEL amyloid matrix on which melanin is deposited. Depletion of ABCB6 in melanocytic cells blocks PMEL fibril formation and produces aberrant multilamellar aggregates in pigmented melanosomes; rescue requires a catalytically active transporter, since neither the Walker A K629M mutant nor the dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria allele G579E restores the matrix. Abcb6 knockout mouse retinal pigment epithelium contains fewer melanosomes.

ATP-dependent organic-anion export by a basolateral ABC transporter. Glutathione conjugates are demonstrated assay substrates; the main endogenous cargo remains unresolved. ABCC6-dependent nucleotide release contributes to extracellular PPi production and prevention of ectopic mineralization, without proving direct ATP translocation.

Regulates Kir6.2 potassium-channel gating by sensing adenine nucleotides and sulfonylurea ligands, coupling metabolism to membrane excitability and insulin secretion. ATP/ADP recognition and sulfonylurea receptor activity are ligand-sensing components of this regulator function. SUR1 provides nucleotide-dependent regulation and channel assembly/surface-expression functions; Kir6.2 supplies the ion-conducting pore. SUR1 has ATPase activity, but channel opening is not a stoichiometric ATP-driven K+ pumping reaction and hydrolysis is not obligatory for every opening under all tested conditions.

ATP hydrolysis is an intrinsic catalytic subactivity of the SUR1 nucleotide-binding machinery, chemically distinct from ATP/ADP recognition. Direct recombinant NBD2 assays and intact human-channel biochemistry support it; nucleotide-dependent gating need not require hydrolysis under every experimental condition.

Bind and allosterically regulate Kir6 potassium channels through SUR2 nucleotide and drug sensing, thereby contributing to ATP-sensitive potassium conductance at the plasma membrane, including the sarcolemma of muscle cells. SUR2 binds inhibitory sulfonylureas such as glibenclamide and activating channel openers; these ligands modulate gating through the regulatory subunit. SUR2A and SUR2B share this role while differing in C-terminal sequence, tissue prevalence and nucleotide/drug responsiveness. Recombinant human SUR2A NBD2 dimers have ATPase activity, a biochemical property distinct from the intact-channel gating readout. Potassium permeates Kir6 rather than an ATP-driven SUR2 transport pathway.

Imports fatty-acyl-CoA-derived substrates into peroxisomes using ATP, principally as an ABCD1 homodimer, supplying beta-oxidation and maintaining fatty-acid homeostasis. Saturated C24/C26 substrates are especially characteristic. The input is recognized as an acyl-CoA ester; whether native membrane crossing retains that ester or includes cleavage and reactivation remains unresolved. Purified human DeltaN1-54 ABCD1 shows C26:0-CoA-stimulated ATPase; mutant-dependent HEK293F lipid measurements provide complementary cellular evidence. These assays do not directly measure purified transmembrane flux.

Exhibits fatty-acyl-CoA hydrolysis in reconstituted preparations, proposed to assist fatty-acid import. This biochemical subactivity is supported by analogue hydrolysis, covalent labeling, substrate competition and chemical perturbation; the native substrate kinetics, catalytic residues and obligatory coupling to each transport cycle remain unresolved. The generic hydrolase term deliberately preserves the measured biochemical scope without claiming that competition with native VLC acyl-CoAs provides a complete chain-specific kinetic demonstration.

ABCD3 is a peroxisomal ABC half-transporter that homodimerizes to form an active ATP-dependent transporter. It catalyzes ATP-driven import of fatty acid substrates (as CoA esters) from the cytosol into the peroxisomal lumen. Cryo-EM structures reveal an alternating-access mechanism: substrate binding to the inward-open state promotes NBD dimerization, ATP binding drives transition to outward-open state for substrate release, and ATP hydrolysis resets the transporter [PMID:39223112, PMID:40501884].

ABCD3 has broad substrate specificity among the peroxisomal ABC transporters, preferentially importing hydrophilic fatty acid substrates including long-chain unsaturated fatty acids, branched-chain fatty acids (pristanic acid), dicarboxylic acids (C14-C18), and bile acid CoA-ester intermediates (DHCA-CoA, THCA-CoA). This contrasts with ABCD1 which preferentially transports the most hydrophobic VLCFAs [PMID:24333844].

ABCD3 is the peroxisomal transporter responsible for import of C27-bile acid CoA-ester intermediates (DHCA-CoA, THCA-CoA) for side-chain shortening to mature C24 bile acids. Loss of ABCD3 causes CBAS5 with accumulation of bile acid intermediates [PMID:25168382]; the substrate assignment rests on these loss-of-function data (published ABCD3 cryo-EM structures are phytanoyl-CoA- and ATP-bound [PMID:39223112]). This represents a unique and non-redundant function of ABCD3 within the ABCD transporter family.

ABCD3 possesses intrinsic thioesterase activity that cleaves fatty acyl-CoAs into free fatty acids and CoA. This may be mechanistically coupled to the transport process, with CoA hydrolysis occurring during or after substrate translocation [PMID:29397936]. The cryo-EM studies suggest substrates may be released either intact or after hydrolysis [PMID:40501884].
ATP-dependent lysosomal cobalamin (vitamin B12) exporter that hydrolyzes ATP to translocate cobalamin from the lysosomal lumen to the cytosol, functioning as a homodimer at the lysosomal membrane.

Intrinsic ATPase / nucleotide-binding activity of the ABC transporter nucleotide-binding domain that energizes cobalamin transport; ATP binding and hydrolysis are coupled to substrate translocation (Walker A K427 is essential).
ABL1 is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that phosphorylates substrates involved in DNA damage response, actin cytoskeleton dynamics, and cell signaling.
ABL1 directly binds F-actin through its C-terminal actin binding domain, enabling localization to and regulation of the actin cytoskeleton.
Nuclear ABL1 binds DNA through its C-terminal DNA binding domain and participates in DNA damage response signaling, promoting apoptosis when damage is irreparable.

Cytosolic, biotin-dependent acetyl-CoA carboxylase: catalyzes the ATP-dependent carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA (acetyl-CoA + HCO3- + ATP = malonyl-CoA + ADP + phosphate), the committed and rate-limiting step of de novo fatty acid biosynthesis. This forms malonyl-CoA, the committed precursor elongated by fatty acid synthase into long-chain fatty acids.

Within the N-terminal biotin carboxylase (BC) / ATP-grasp domain, uses ATP and bicarbonate to carboxylate the biotin cofactor covalently attached to the biotinyl-binding (BCC) domain; this is the first half-reaction of acetyl-CoA carboxylation.

Binds the biotin cofactor, which is covalently attached to the central biotinyl-binding domain and is required for catalytic activity; this biotin carries the activated carboxyl group between the biotin carboxylase and carboxyltransferase active sites.

Catalyzes FAD-dependent oxidation of isobutyryl-CoA to methacrylyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, transferring electrons to electron-transfer flavoprotein during L-valine degradation. The mature enzyme functions as a homotetramer. Lower-efficiency alternate-substrate reactions do not establish an additional physiological pathway.

Catalyzes FAD-dependent, ETF-coupled alpha,beta-dehydrogenation of medium-chain acyl-CoA esters to trans-2-enoyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, performing the first reaction of the beta-oxidation cycle. The active enzyme is a homotetramer with one bound FAD per subunit and a substrate preference centered on C6-C8; overlapping shorter/longer substrate activities do not imply equal physiological contributions.

Catalyzes FAD-dependent dehydrogenation of short-chain acyl-CoAs, including butyryl-CoA to crotonyl-CoA, with electrons passed to electron-transfer flavoprotein. The soluble homotetramer acts in the mitochondrial matrix and binds one FAD per subunit. This reaction supplies the initial oxidation within short-chain acyl-CoA beta-oxidation and butyrate catabolism.

FAD-dependent dehydrogenation of (S)-2-methylbutyryl-CoA to tiglyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, supplying a catalytic step of L-isoleucine degradation. The mature enzyme is homotetrameric and transfers reducing equivalents to electron-transfer flavoprotein. FAD binding and the broader short-chain dehydrogenase activity are aspects of this same enzyme mechanism.

FAD-dependent long-chain fatty acyl-CoA dehydrogenation initiates mitochondrial beta-oxidation of substrates such as palmitoyl-CoA. The homodimeric enzyme operates at the matrix face of the inner membrane and passes reducing equivalents to electron-transfer flavoprotein. FAD binding and membrane-dependent assembly support this catalytic function.

Very-long-chain substrate dehydrogenation extends VLCAD catalysis to C24-CoA within mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation. UniProt records this reaction with experimental attribution to PMID:21237683, and the human structure reveals a cavity accommodating a 24-carbon acyl chain. This activity is carried by the FAD-dependent homodimer at the matrix face of the inner membrane, alongside its long-chain activity toward substrates such as C16-CoA.

Potassium-activated mitochondrial-matrix thiolase acting as a homotetramer. Reversible acetoacetyl-CoA/acetyl-CoA chemistry serves ketone body synthesis and utilization. The same enzyme also cleaves the branched isoleucine intermediate 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA into acetyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA; this additional substrate specificity is described in the evidence and is not encoded by the literal two-acetyl-CoA reaction of GO:0003985.

FAD-dependent acyl-CoA oxidation in the peroxisomal matrix: homodimeric ACOX1 performs the initial beta-oxidation reaction on straight-chain fatty acyl-CoAs, including very-long-chain substrates, producing (2E)-enoyl-CoA and hydrogen peroxide. Substrate breadth and isoform-dependent preferences are integrated within this catalytic function.
ACTA1 polymerizes into the actin backbone of skeletal-muscle thin filaments, contributing their structural integrity and directly participating in thin-filament assembly.

ACTA1 binds ATP and hydrolyzes it during filament assembly. Hydrolysis and subsequent phosphate release influence actin filament dynamics; oriented subunit assembly gives the filament structural polarity.

ACTA1 provides the myosin-binding surface and force-transmitting thin filament used in skeletal-muscle contraction. Myosin heads, rather than actin subunits, couple the power stroke to the myosin ATPase cycle.

Binding to muscle alpha-actinin connects the ACTA1 thin filament to the Z-disc organization machinery. Human patient-muscle actin exhibits altered alpha-actinin affinity, supporting this specific interaction.

Polymerizes into force-bearing actin filaments and dynamic cytoskeletal arrays in smooth-muscle cells and contractile myofibroblast-like cells. This structural activity supports smooth-muscle contraction and cytoskeleton organization; context-dependent replacement by other actin isoforms can preserve some myofibroblast functions.

Binds smooth-muscle myosin through polymerized ACTA2 filaments, providing the actin track and mechanical partner for contractile force generation. Human wild-type ACTA2 supports myosin-driven filament movement in reconstituted assays; disease variants can impair this interaction as well as other aspects of actin behavior.

Hydrolyzes ATP through the conserved conventional-actin nucleotide pocket, supporting the nucleotide-dependent assembly and turnover of cytoskeletal filaments. The conserved biochemical machinery supports transfer of this intrinsic actin activity from pig skeletal actin to human ACTA2.
Assemble into dynamic actin filaments that provide cellular structure, support junctions and generate protrusive force for motility.

Hydrolyze filament-bound ATP as part of the actin nucleotide cycle, with phosphate release changing filament stability and turnover. This intrinsic chemistry is distinct from myosin motor ATPase activity.
Contribute structural support to SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling through the ACTB–ACTL6 module connecting the ATPase module to the complex core. SMARCA2/SMARCA4 supplies the remodeling motor chemistry.

Thin-filament actin of the visceral smooth muscle contractile apparatus. ACTG2 monomers polymerise into the two-stranded helical filament that, anchored at dense bodies and membrane-associated dense plaques, slides against smooth muscle myosin thick filaments to generate contraction in the intestine, bladder and uterus. It contributes the structural integrity of that filament directly: its own cryo-EM reconstructions show a filament architecture indistinguishable from alpha-actin's, with no change in helical twist or rise, and all 38 protomer-interface positions of F-actin are identical in ACTG2. Assembly is nucleated by the smooth-muscle nucleator leiomodin-1 and the filaments are decorated by the smooth muscle tropomyosin isoform Tpm1.4; smooth muscle myosin translocates them at the same velocity as skeletal alpha-actin filaments. The disease variants define the same function negatively, each disabling a different step of it - D-loop intersubunit contacts (R40), the R257-E196 salt bridge holding the two long-pitch helices together (R257), actin-binding protein engagement (R148), or monomer stability (R178).

Nucleotide-hydrolysing engine of its own filament turnover. ACTG2 binds ATP in the cleft of the actin fold and hydrolyses it shortly after a monomer is incorporated, releasing inorganic phosphate to leave an ADP-bound protomer; every protomer of every deposited ACTG2 structure is ADP-Mg bound because hydrolysis and phosphate release ran to completion during sample preparation. This nucleotide cycle is what makes the filament dynamic rather than static, and its measurable consequences - polymerisation rate, depolymerisation rate and critical concentration - are the parameters that every characterised disease variant shifts and that the G-actin/F-actin ratio assays in the knock-in mouse models read out.

Track for smooth muscle myosin. The structural role above is discharged against a motor: ACTG2 filaments are engaged and translocated by smooth muscle myosin, and it is that cyclical, ATP-dependent actomyosin interaction that converts filament integrity into force in the intestine, bladder and uterus. Measured directly on purified human protein - in a gliding assay on surfaces coated with a smooth muscle myosin motor-domain construct, ACTG2 filaments move at a velocity indistinguishable from skeletal alpha-actin, with and without the smooth muscle tropomyosin Tpm1.4, and the same is true of filaments carrying the R40C and R257C disease variants. The myosin-binding surface is independently implicated by disease genetics: R148, one of the recurrent visceral-myopathy residues, lies on it. This is listed as a separate core function rather than folded into the structural one because it is the point at which ACTG2 stops being a scaffold and becomes part of a motor system, and because it is the property that the disease variants conspicuously do not break - the filaments still glide, so the lesion lies elsewhere.

Zinc-dependent hydrolysis of adenosine to inosine supports adenosine breakdown and purine recycling. Cytosolic ADA handles intracellular nucleosides; extracellular membrane-associated ADA also clears adenosine and controls its availability to receptors.

Zinc-dependent hydrolysis of 2'-deoxyadenosine to 2'-deoxyinosine performs a direct step in deoxyadenosine breakdown. This reaction can also act downstream of dAMP dephosphorylation in nucleotide catabolism. Clearance of deoxyadenosine limits toxic deoxynucleotide accumulation and is essential for normal lymphocyte survival.

ADAM10 is a zinc-dependent type I membrane metalloendopeptidase that performs ectodomain shedding and alpha-secretase cleavage of transmembrane substrates at the cell surface and regulated membrane compartments.

Zinc-dependent metalloendopeptidase that cleaves the juxtamembrane stalk regions of transmembrane proteins at the cell surface, releasing their ectodomains; this sheddase activity is the single activity from which essentially all other ADAM17 biology follows.

Conversion of the 26-kDa membrane-anchored TNF precursor into the soluble cytokine, the founding and best-characterised ADAM17 reaction; it sets how much soluble TNF is released and hence the strength of TNF-receptor signalling.

Release of the mature EGF-receptor ligands (amphiregulin, TGF-alpha, HB-EGF, epigen, epiregulin) from their membrane-anchored precursors, which is the step by which GPCR, TGF-beta and stress stimuli are transduced into EGFR activation.

Cleavage of cytokine- and immune-receptor ectodomains - IL-6 receptor alpha (generating the soluble receptor that drives IL-6 trans-signalling), TNF receptors, FcgammaRIIIA/CD16A and CD62L on NK cells, MICA, CXCL16 and TREM2 - which reconfigures the surface receptor repertoire and the pool of soluble immune mediators.

Proteolysis of transmembrane receptors whose signalling output depends on ectodomain removal: regulated (stimulus-induced) alpha-secretase cleavage of the amyloid precursor protein, S2-site cleavage of NOTCH1, cleavage of the DCC/Frazzled guidance receptor, and shedding of vasorin to generate a soluble TGF-beta inhibitor. Note that constitutive neuronal APP alpha-secretase activity and ligand-induced Notch S2 cleavage are attributable mainly to ADAM10; the ADAM17 contribution is the regulated arm.

DNA break-activated NAD+ poly-ADP-ribosyltransferase: PARP1 binds DNA strand breaks, becomes catalytically activated, and synthesises poly(ADP-ribose) on itself and chromatin proteins, recruiting XRCC1 and other factors to repair single-strand breaks/BER intermediates and double-strand breaks; automodification then releases PARP1 from DNA.

HPF1-dependent serine ADP-ribosylation: in complex with HPF1, PARP1 modifies serine residues of histones (H2B Ser6, H3 Ser10) and of itself, the predominant DNA damage-induced ADP-ribosylation, which recruits chromatin remodelers such as ALC1.
DNA strand-break sensing: N-terminal zinc fingers bind and kink single-strand break DNA and drive stepwise assembly of the remaining domains, coupling break recognition to catalytic activation.
Nucleosome binding and chromatin modulation: PARP1 binds nucleosomes specifically and promotes compact chromatin, modulated by NAD+-dependent automodification.
ADRB2 binds catecholamines at the plasma membrane and activates beta-2 adrenergic receptor signaling through Gs/cAMP/PKA, context-dependent Gi, and MAPK-associated signaling branches.
The functional ADSL homotetramer cleaves adenylosuccinate to AMP and fumarate in the cytosol, completing the IMP-to-AMP branch during de novo synthesis and nucleotide recycling.
The functional ADSL homotetramer cleaves SAICAR to AICAR and fumarate in the cytosolic de novo IMP pathway, supplying the shared purine precursor for adenine and guanine nucleotides.

ATP-fueled unfolding, translocation and zinc-dependent endopeptide cleavage of mitochondrial protein substrates by matrix-facing m-AAA protease complexes. This integrated activity removes aberrant or unassembled proteins and supports productive precursor maturation, including AFG3L2 self-maturation and SPG7/paraplegin maturation demonstrated with human proteins expressed in yeast. Human MRPL32 maturation is demonstrated with an engineered soluble protease and recombinant precursor; cellular PINK1 processing implicates AFG3L2 without reconstituting the precise cleavage reaction.

Lysosomal Ntn-hydrolase that cleaves the N-glycosidic GlcNAc-Asn bond joining N-glycans to asparagine in glycoprotein-derived glycopeptides, a late step of lysosomal N-glycoprotein catabolism; activated by autoproteolysis of its precursor.

Hyaluronan binding by the N-terminal G1 region retains aggrecan in extracellular aggregates with hyaluronan and link protein. Its immunoglobulin domain and two Link modules form a structural unit with a hyaluronan-binding groove. Recombinant human G1 binds immobilized hyaluronan with an affinity of about 234 nM and binds pre-existing perineuronal nets in mouse neuron cultures. Residual net binding by hyaluronan-binding-null fragments indicates an additional interaction whose partner remains unresolved.

Compression resistance arises from the fixed negative charge of the glycosaminoglycan-rich central region. Aggrecan retained in hyaluronan aggregates attracts water, generating swelling pressure restrained by the cartilage collagen network. This structural contribution supports cartilage development and load bearing. Severe aggrecan deficiency is lethal in studied animal models; human pathogenic alleles cause distinct skeletal growth and joint disorders.

Binding to extracellular matrix ligands integrates aggrecan into the wider matrix network. G3 binds tenascins and fibulins, and human G3 variants can impair ligand binding and secretion. COMP binding is supported independently and involves aggrecan glycosaminoglycan chains interacting with the COMP signature domain. These are distinct molecular surfaces contributing to extracellular matrix binding.
Transfers a short alpha-1,4-linked glucan segment from a phosphorylase-limit branch to an acceptor chain, exposing the single alpha-1,6-linked glucose for the second debranching reaction.
Hydrolyses the exposed alpha-1,6 branch linkage in glycogen phosphorylase limit dextrin, releasing free glucose and allowing further glycogen degradation.

Acylates lysophosphatidic acid with acyl-CoA at the ER membrane to produce phosphatidic acid. This PA-forming step supplies both the CDP-diacylglycerol branch and the DAG branch leading to triacylglycerols and other glycerophospholipids. Functional association with CDS1/2 supports flux into the CDP-diacylglycerol branch; CDS1/2 perform the cytidylyltransferase reaction, while other enzymes dephosphorylate PA and acylate DAG.

Catalyzes the FAD-dependent exchange of the acyl group of acyl-dihydroxyacetone phosphate for a long-chain fatty alcohol, forming the ether-linked precursor of ether phospholipids and plasmalogens at the luminal surface of the peroxisomal membrane. Oxidized FAD supports covalent catalysis without net substrate oxidation-reduction.
Activates MuSK through LRP4 binding to induce postsynaptic acetylcholine-receptor clustering and organize neuromuscular synapses; activity depends on agrin splice form.
Binds laminin through the N-terminal domain of secreted agrin, anchoring agrin in basal lamina and coupling matrix retention to synaptic receptor organization.
Binds cell-surface dystroglycan through laminin G-like domains, linking extracellular agrin to receptor-associated membrane structures in muscle and non-muscle tissues.

Renin substrate and angiotensin delivery device. Angiotensinogen holds the angiotensin sequence in an ordered 63-residue N-terminal tail with the scissile Leu-Val bond buried, and presents it to renin through a tail-into-mouth conformational change that threads the N terminus into a pocket equivalent to the hormone-binding site of the carrier serpins. Binding is not confined to the catalytic cleft: there is an extensive, largely hydrophobic body-to-body interface with the protease, and mutagenesis and kinetics show that the rate and specificity of angiotensin I release are set by angiotensinogen residues and glycans outside renin's active site. This is the molecular function of the full-length precursor itself, as opposed to that of the peptides cleaved from it, and it is the rate-limiting step of the whole renin-angiotensin cascade.

Source of the angiotensin peptide hormones, and through them the effector of systemic blood pressure and fluid-electrolyte homeostasis. Angiotensin II, released from angiotensinogen by the sequential action of renin and ACE, binds the AGTR1 and AGTR2 G-protein-coupled receptors; through AGTR1 it activates phospholipase C and mobilises calcium, constricts arterioles, drives adrenal aldosterone production and renal sodium retention, and so sets arterial pressure and blood volume. Because angiotensin II has no gene of its own, this activity is recorded on the precursor, which is also what UniProt does. The dependence is absolute and demonstrated in both directions: deleting angiotensinogen abolishes circulating angiotensin I and drops systolic pressure by a third, and restoring it restores angiotensin II and pressure.

Receptor ligand for AGTR1, the pressor limb of the system. The released octapeptide binds the type 1 receptor with high affinity and couples it to phospholipase C and inositol phosphate turnover, and it is through this receptor that the vasoconstrictor, aldosterone-releasing and growth-promoting actions run. UniProt records the interaction on the peptide chain rather than on full-length angiotensinogen (PRO_0000032458 with AGTR1), which is the correct reading of what does the binding.

Receptor ligand for AGTR2, the limb that opposes the AGTR1 output. The same octapeptide binds the type 2 receptor, which engages SHP-1 as its proximal effector, inhibits ERK and can drive apoptosis - the opposite sign to the AGTR1 arm, which is why the two binding functions are recorded separately rather than collapsed into the common parent. UniProt again places the interaction on the peptide chain (PRO_0000032459 with AGTR2) rather than on full-length angiotensinogen. Further processing of the same precursor generates angiotensin-(1-7), which acts through MAS1 and likewise opposes several angiotensin II effects, so a single gene supplies the ligands for both limbs of the system.

PLP-dependent, homodimeric alanine:glyoxylate transaminase converts glyoxylate and L-alanine to glycine and pyruvate in the peroxisomal matrix, limiting glyoxylate availability for oxalate formation. Amino-acid substrate binding supplies recognition within this catalytic cycle.

PLP-dependent serine:pyruvate transaminase converts L-serine and pyruvate to hydroxypyruvate and L-alanine in liver peroxisomes. This reaction contributes substantially to serine breakdown in human liver preparations under the tested quasi-physiological in-vitro conditions.

AHCY hydrolyzes SAH to adenosine and L-homocysteine as a tightly NAD-bound enzyme, normally assembled as a homotetramer. This product-forming step sustains the L-methionine cycle and limits SAH inhibition of methyltransferases. Cytosolic and nuclear pools support the same catalytic chemistry; methyltransferases perform the subsequent methyl transfer.

Primary function. AHR is a ligand-activated intracellular receptor/transcription factor. Ligand binding to cytoplasmic AHR promotes nuclear accumulation, ARNT heterodimerization, binding to AHR response elements, and regulation of xenobiotic/endogenous-ligand response genes.

Activated AHR heterodimerizes with ARNT to form the nuclear DNA-binding transcription-factor complex. This heterodimeric state is required for efficient AHR response element binding and target-gene activation. Crystal structures of ligand-bound AHR:ARNT:DNA complexes show an unconventional assembly with intimate PAS-B to PAS-B association between AHR and ARNT, with the AHR PAS-B domain serving as the principal ligand-binding pocket.

Inactive AHR is maintained in a cytosolic chaperone-associated receptor complex. HSP90/p23/XAP2 interactions support ligand-binding conformation, cytoplasmic retention, and ligand-dependent nuclear import.

AIP/XAP2 binds HSP90 via its C-terminal TPR domain (three TPR motifs plus a terminal alpha-7 helix), serving as a co-chaperone/scaffold in the AHR-HSP90 complex. The TPR domain engages the MEEVD motif at the HSP90 C-terminus (PDB:4APO). Cryo-EM structure of the human agonist-bound HSP90-XAP2-AHR cytosolic complex (DOI:10.1038/s41467-022-34773-w) reveals AIP acting as a structural brace associated with the HSP90 dimer and the AHR client, with the MEEVD motif docked into the TPR domain of AIP, consistent with canonical TPR-mediated recruitment of HSP90 co-chaperones. Disease-causing mutations in the TPR domain disrupt HSP90 binding and are associated with pituitary neuroendocrine tumor predisposition (PitNET/PITA1), consistent with a two-hit tumor suppressor model (loss of heterozygosity in tumors).

AIP/XAP2 is a stoichiometric component of the unliganded AHR 9S core complex (AHR:2xHSP90:AIP:PTGES3), binding directly to the aryl hydrocarbon receptor. It stabilizes the cytosolic AHR-HSP90 complex, enhancing AhR receptivity for ligand and subsequent transcriptional activation. Cryo-EM structural analysis (DOI:10.1038/s41467-022-34773-w) confirms the architectural arrangement of AIP as a brace spanning the HSP90 dimer and AHR client within this complex.

AIP binds to the GAF-B domain of phosphodiesterase 2A (PDE2A), an interaction that inhibits TCDD- and cAMP-induced nuclear translocation of AhR in hepatocytes, providing a regulatory link between cAMP signaling and the AhR pathway. AIP also interacts with PDE4A5, further linking it to localized cAMP regulation (DOI:10.1586/eem.10.42). These phosphodiesterase interactions suggest AIP may modulate pituitary tumor biology through cAMP pathway effects.

AIPL1 binds HSP90 through its TPR region and intact interdomain organization to support the folding, stable assembly and functional maturation of PDE6 in photoreceptors. This co-chaperone activity maintains the PDE6 effector needed for visual signaling. Human interaction and stabilization experiments are complemented by direct PDE6 activity assays using mouse AIPL1.

The AIPL1 FKBP-like domain binds prenyl groups on client proteins, providing a complementary substrate-recognition interaction in the PDE6 chaperone system. Farnesyl-dependent binding is directly supported; mouse and heterologous assays show that productive PDE6 maturation can also occur when the tested prenyl interaction is disabled.

AIRE binds histone H3K4me0 through its zinc-stabilized PHD1 domain and self-associates through CARD to organize nuclear transcriptional assemblies. C-terminal coactivator recruitment coordinates this chromatin engagement with activation of self-antigen genes, supporting central tolerance and negative selection of autoreactive thymocytes.

Catalyzes reversible phosphate transfer between ATP and AMP, forming two ADP molecules in the forward direction and ATP plus AMP in the reverse direction. The mitochondrial intermembrane-space enzyme thereby balances adenine nucleotides; ATP binding, AMP/ATP metabolism and ADP formation are aspects of this single catalytic unit. Both tested human AK2A and AK2B are active. The compartment assignment includes conserved mammalian localization evidence, whereas human enzyme purification directly establishes catalysis.

Uses NADPH to stereospecifically reduce the C4-C5 double bond of 3-oxo-Delta4 steroids in cytosol. Steroid recognition and the Tyr58/Glu120 catalytic environment generate 5beta products with a cis A/B ring junction while preserving the 3-oxo group. Reduction of bile-acid precursors contributes to cholesterol breakdown and primary bile-acid synthesis; the same activity metabolizes androgen and C21 hormone substrates.
Catalyzes ATP-dependent phosphorylation of protein serine and threonine residues within PI3K-AKT signaling, linking receptor activation to downstream growth, metabolic and survival regulators.

Binds phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate through its PH domain to couple PI3K lipid signaling to membrane recruitment and activation of AKT1. The PH domain also recognizes phosphatidylinositol-3,4-bisphosphate.

Porphobilinogen synthase (5-aminolevulinate dehydratase, EC 4.2.1.24): catalyzes the second step of heme biosynthesis, the zinc-dependent asymmetric condensation of two molecules of 5-aminolevulinate into the monopyrrole porphobilinogen, acting as a cytosolic homo-octamer.

Zinc-dependent metallo-catalysis: ALAD binds zinc ions (up to eight per octamer, four required for activity) at its catalytic site; this metal-ion binding is essential for the porphobilinogen synthase reaction and is the site displaced by inhibitory lead.

ALAS2 catalyzes the PLP-dependent condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA to form 5-aminolevulinate, CoA and CO2 in the mitochondrial matrix, initiating the heme-synthesis branch that supplies hemoglobin in erythroid cells. Its homodimer builds each active site from both subunits, with PLP linked to Lys391; the C-terminal extension regulates substrate access and product release. PLP binding is integral to this catalytic unit.

Homodimeric mitochondrial ALDH4A1 catalyzes NAD+-dependent oxidation of L-glutamate gamma-semialdehyde to L-glutamate, completing proline catabolism. Its substrate scope also supports oxidation of the corresponding hydroxylated semialdehyde in trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline degradation. NAD+ binding and the domain-swapped dimer are integral properties of this catalytic unit; ligand-bound structural details were resolved with the highly similar mouse enzyme, whereas human catalytic activity and S352L inactivation were directly measured.

As a homotetramer in the mitochondrial matrix, ALDH5A1 oxidizes succinate semialdehyde with NAD+ to produce succinate and NADH. This catalytic step completes GABA degradation and connects the glutamate/GABA shunt to central carbon metabolism.

Cytosolic class-I fructose-bisphosphate aldolase that catalyzes the reversible aldol cleavage of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate in glycolysis (and the reverse condensation in gluconeogenesis).
In gluconeogenesis, the same cytosolic aldolase reaction runs in reverse, condensing dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

The cytosolic ALDOB homotetramer catalyzes reversible aldol cleavage of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. This single reaction serves glycolysis in the cleavage direction and gluconeogenesis in the condensation direction.

ALDOB cleaves fructose 1-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde in cytosol, enabling dietary fructose catabolism in liver, kidney and intestine. Its substantial F1P activity distinguishes its metabolic role from the other vertebrate aldolase isozymes.

ALK binds extracellular ALKAL cytokines and assembles a signaling receptor complex at the plasma membrane, coupling ligand recognition to ATP-dependent tyrosine autophosphorylation and intracellular signaling. Experimentally tested heparin binding can modulate this receptor mechanism. Human ALKAL2 is a potent activator; ALKAL1 responses depend on ligand preparation and assay conditions. Receptor self-association and kinase activity are integrated here without imposing one universal complex stoichiometry or assigning a separate noncovalent kinase-activator function.

ALMS1 localizes to proximal centrioles and basal bodies and supports centrosome cohesion and normal ciliary architecture. Human depletion reduces centriolar C-Nap1 and produces stunted cilia, without establishing direct C-Nap1 tethering or an autonomous molecular activity. Human fibroblast recycling defects and interactions with actin-associated machinery support a connection to endosomal recycling, while an ALMS1-containing transport scaffold remains a mechanistic model.

TNAP hydrolyzes extracellular inorganic pyrophosphate at mineralizing cell and matrix-vesicle surfaces, removing an inhibitor of hydroxyapatite propagation. Its additional nucleotide phosphatase activities supply local Pi. Mouse vesicle experiments and human TNAP enzymology support this integrated mineralization mechanism; intravesicular crystal initiation also involves other Pi-generating pathways and is not assigned exclusively to TNAP.

TNAP dephosphorylates extracellular pyridoxal 5'-phosphate to pyridoxal at the outward-facing cell surface, making vitamin B6 available for cellular uptake and cofactor metabolism. Human fibroblast and recombinant-enzyme assays establish the reaction; neurological consequences of severe deficiency include disrupted B6-dependent metabolism.

TNAP hydrolyzes extracellular phosphocholine, releasing choline and inorganic phosphate. Purified human enzyme, human serum and human-cell surface assays establish this chemistry. HuH-6 growth rescue is consistent with choline availability; mouse liver/plasma metabolite and lipid phenotypes support hepatic context without establishing direct TNAP transport activity or human VLDL secretion flux.

TNAP hydrolyzes extracellular phosphoethanolamine to ethanolamine and inorganic phosphate. Human fibroblast ectophosphatase assays and purified human TNAP and serum experiments establish this distinct substrate reaction. This supplies ethanolamine for metabolism without assigning membrane transport to TNAP or extending the mouse hepatic choline findings to demonstrated human ethanolamine flux.

Recombinant human TNAP hydrolyzes phosphocreatine to creatine and inorganic phosphate at near-physiological pH. Mouse thermogenic adipocytes use this chemistry in the mitochondrial futile creatine cycle. The human molecular activity is directly measured; a human mitochondrial location or thermogenic process is not asserted by this core entry.

The long alsin protein forms a functional self-associated Rab5 exchange factor. Its VPS9-containing C-terminal region promotes GDP release from Rab5, and regulated recruitment from the cytosol to early endosomal membranes couples this exchange to endosome fusion and membrane transport. Oligomerization supports activity; the core does not require a fixed native subunit count or direct Rac1 exchange catalysis.

Binds sequence-specific regulatory DNA through its homeodomain and regulates nuclear RNA polymerase II transcription. Human DNA-binding measurements and mouse promoter/cofactor experiments support this conserved activity; the tissue-specific human target network remains incompletely defined.

ALX4 binds developmental regulatory DNA and can activate Pol-II transcription. Sequence-dependent dimerization and DNA-associated cooperation with other transcription factors regulate craniofacial mesenchymal programs, skull development and hair-follicle differentiation. Regulatory direction depends on partner, promoter and dosage context; this core does not imply universal activation or a constitutive soluble complex.

Interconverts the (R)- and (S)-epimers of 2-methyl-branched-chain acyl-CoA esters (alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase, EC 5.1.99.4), converting (2R)-methyl-branched acyl-CoAs to the (S)-stereoisomers required by peroxisomal beta-oxidation. Essential for side-chain shortening of the C27 bile-acid intermediates (25R)-THCA-CoA/DHCA-CoA en route to C24 bile acids, and for degradation of the branched-chain fatty acid pristanic acid. Acts as a soluble matrix enzyme in the peroxisome (and a mitochondrial pool).

Secreted TGF-beta family hormone that binds its dedicated type II receptor AMHR2 to activate SMAD signalling, causing Müllerian duct regression in the male fetus and restraining follicle recruitment in the ovary.
Nuclear protein of unknown molecular activity that dimerizes with its paralog AMMECR1L.
Cytosolic AMP deaminase catalysing the hydrolytic deamination of AMP to IMP and ammonia (EC 3.5.4.6), the committed step of the skeletal-muscle purine nucleotide cycle.

By deaminating AMP, AMPD1 drives adenine-nucleotide (AMP) metabolism in muscle, pulling the adenylate kinase equilibrium toward ATP regeneration and buffering the cellular energy charge during intense exercise.
Cytosolic zinc-dependent hydrolytic deamination of AMP to IMP and ammonia, the committed step of the purine nucleotide cycle and AMP catabolism.

Regulation of adenine/guanine nucleotide pools and the adenylate energy charge: by deaminating AMP, AMPD2 relieves feedback inhibition of de novo purine synthesis and thereby sustains the guanine nucleotide (GTP) pool, important for GTP-dependent translation in neurons.

AMT catalyzes transfer of the glycine-derived aminomethyl group from lipoylated GCSH to tetrahydrofolate, releasing ammonia and producing 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate plus reduced lipoyl-GCSH. This is the T-protein reaction within mitochondrial glycine cleavage; GLDC performs the preceding decarboxylation and DLD subsequently reoxidizes the carrier.

ANG is a regulated RNase A-family endoribonuclease whose core function is compartment-dependent RNA metabolism: ribosome-activated cytosolic tRNA cleavage during stress and nucleolar promotion of rRNA transcription under growth conditions, with secreted proangiogenic activity as a major physiological output.

Inhibits extracellular lipases through the N-terminal region: ANGPTL3 cooperates with ANGPTL8 to suppress lipoprotein lipase and also inhibits endothelial lipase. These activities regulate plasma triglyceride turnover and HDL phospholipid/cholesterol homeostasis. Activity depends on oligomer composition and the local lipase-stabilizing environment. Human-protein biophysics supports ATP-independent unfolding of LPL; the later EL mutagenesis predominantly tests mouse ANGPTL3 and is distinguished from human plasma oligomer measurements.

Physically links membrane proteins to the spectrin cytoskeleton and organizes their membrane association. The best-defined example is the native human erythrocyte ankyrin-1 complex; cargo binding also supports selective delivery of proteins to the plasma membrane.

Short muscle isoforms bind obscurin through their cytoplasmic region while associating with SR membranes, supporting a membrane-to-cytoskeleton anchoring model distinct from the large erythroid spectrin linkage. Independent knockdown/rescue demonstrates network-SR maintenance, although the contribution of this particular tether to that phenotype is not fully isolated.

Couples membrane proteins to spectrin-based and associated cytoskeletal assemblies, positioning transporters, channels and dystrophin-associated machinery. This anchoring organizes cardiac calcium-handling proteins and muscle membrane complexes. The giant isoform also organizes Sema3A receptor targeting through a membrane-organizing mechanism separable from its microtubule binding and betaII-spectrin interaction.

The neurospecific giant ankyrin-B domain directly binds and bundles microtubules through tandem repeats and an adjacent conserved segment. Human recombinant fragments establish the molecular activity; human full-length construct rescue in mouse neurons links this activity to restricting microtubule entry into nascent axon branches. This function is distinct from the spectrin-associated membrane-adaptor mechanism.

Calcium-dependent binding to anionic phospholipids (phosphatidylserine, phosphatidic acid, phosphatidylinositol) via the four annexin repeats, mediating peripheral association with plasma membrane, endosomal and vesicle membranes.

Secreted/externalised ANXA1 and its N-terminal peptide Ac2-26 act as agonists of formyl peptide receptors (FPR1, FPR2/ALX, FPR3), triggering GPCR signalling that inhibits neutrophil transendothelial migration and promotes resolution of inflammation as an effector of glucocorticoid action.
Calcium-dependent peripheral phospholipid binding enables regulated association with cellular membranes.

Connects protein-containing ribonucleoprotein granules to lipid membranes through coordinated granule association and phospholipid binding; this membrane-adaptor activity is also demonstrated for sorcin recruitment.
Contributes to the stable midbody matrix during terminal cytokinesis in human cells; its molecular mechanism in this structure remains unresolved.

Beta-adaptins including beta1 directly bind clathrin through their hinge region, recruiting clathrin to form coated vesicles. Core molecular function of the AP-1 complex. PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation of beta1 upon membrane recruitment enables clathrin assembly. Nearly 100% of AP-1 vesicles are clathrin-positive.

AP-1 recruitment to membranes requires coincidence detection of Arf1-GTP and the phosphoinositide PI(4)P. The gamma subunit recognizes PI(4)P through a binding site involving Tyr-45, Arg-48, and Lys-52. This phospholipid binding, together with Arf1 interaction at the beta1 N-terminus, determines TGN localization. AP-1 primarily mediates retrograde trafficking, retrieving proteins from post-Golgi compartments back to the TGN, including recycling of mannose-6-phosphate receptors.

Contributes gamma-1 to the AP-1 clathrin-cargo adaptor: cargo recognition occurs with sigma, while gamma coat/accessory contacts support assembly and regulated membrane recruitment. Human gamma cargo-recognition and ear-structure evidence is distinguished from mouse gamma clathrin and mixed-species core reconstitution; the activity belongs to the assembled adaptor rather than autonomous gamma.

As the small subunit of AP-1, sigma1A forms the gamma1-sigma1A hemicomplex that recognises acidic dileucine sorting signals in the cytosolic tails of transmembrane cargo, thereby selecting cargo into clathrin-coated carriers at the trans-Golgi network and endosomes. The activity belongs to the hemicomplex, not to sigma1A alone -- these signals bind no single AP subunit -- but the cargo-binding pockets are on sigma1A itself, and substituting them abolishes binding.

sigma1A is a structural subunit required for AP-1 to assemble and to associate with TGN and endosomal membranes. In cells lacking all three sigma1 isoforms, wild-type sigma1A restores gamma1 levels and gamma1 membrane staining; the MEDNIK L90P variant, which cannot assemble with gamma1, does not. The complex the subunit completes is recruited by Arf1-GTP and PI-4-P and links cargo to the clathrin coat.

As the small subunit of the heterotetrameric AP-1 clathrin adaptor, AP1S2 pairs with a gamma adaptin to form the gamma/sigma1 hemicomplex that recognises (D/E)XXXL(L/I) dileucine sorting signals in the cytosolic tails of transmembrane cargo, and so contributes to the complex's cargo-adaptor activity at trans-Golgi network and endosomal membranes. The activity belongs to the complex, not to the 157-residue subunit alone, but the cargo-binding site is built jointly from sigma and gamma residues, and human sigma1B assembles into AP-1 and into no other AP complex.

In neurons, the AP-1 complex containing sigma1B rather than sigma1A reforms synaptic vesicles from early endosomes after stimulation. Loss of sigma1B slows and truncates vesicle reformation and leaves clathrin-budding early endosomal intermediates in the presynaptic terminal, with normal targeting and docking of the vesicles that do form - placing the defect at endosomal budding rather than earlier in the secretory pathway. This is the function whose loss plausibly explains the neurological phenotype of AP1S2 deficiency in humans.

sigma1B carries an isoform-private protein interaction that sigma1A lacks: within the gamma1/sigma1 hemicomplex it binds the Rab5 guanine-nucleotide exchange factor Rabex-5 (and the RabGAP5 RUN domain). Sequestering Rabex-5 prevents assembly of the AP-1/sigma1A-ArfGAP1-Rabex-5 complex, lowers endosomal Rabex-5, and so restrains Rab5-GTP-stimulated Vps34 activity and the maturation of early endosomes into multivesicular late endosomes. The two AP-1 sigma isoforms therefore set the balance between recycling a synaptic-vesicle protein and sending it for degradation.

AP2M1 recognizes cytoplasmic sorting sequences in cargo proteins and, as the medium subunit of AP-2, contributes to their coupling to the clathrin coat. Membrane-dependent rearrangement and regulated Thr156 phosphorylation coordinate cargo capture and coat maturation. This supports receptor uptake, endocytic budding and synaptic cargo retrieval; it does not make isolated μ2 the complete clathrin adaptor or a kinase.
AP3B1 is the beta-3A subunit of the heterotetrameric AP-3 adaptor complex. This is the defining structural role - without AP3B1, the AP-3 complex cannot assemble or function properly.

AP-3 recognizes cargo proteins with dileucine or tyrosine-based sorting signals and loads them into coated vesicles for transport to lysosomes and LROs. This cargo selection function is essential for proper protein sorting to melanosomes and platelet dense granules.

AP3B2 functions as the beta subunit of the neuronal AP-3 adaptor complex, a cargo adaptor and vesicle coat that sorts synaptic-vesicle membrane proteins on endosomal membranes. A key role of neuronal AP-3 is generating synaptic vesicles that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation through recruitment of the phospholipid flippase ATP8A1 and its auxiliary subunit TMEM30A. ATP8A1 regulates phosphatidylserine distribution enabling synapsin recruitment to these vesicles. AP-3-derived vesicles contribute specifically to asynchronous neurotransmitter release, which affects the precision of postsynaptic firing. In dopamine neurons, AP-3 has dual functions: targeting VMAT2 to axons, conferring axonal polarity of dopamine release, and producing high-frequency-responsive synaptic vesicles essential for phasic dopamine signaling underlying learning and reward processing.

As the delta subunit of AP-3, contributes to the complex's cargo-adaptor activity: AP-3 binds sorting signals in the cytosolic tails of transmembrane cargo and links them to a self-assembling coat, concentrating the cargo into a carrier. Delta's own contribution is the dileucine-binding surface it forms with sigma-3 and, in the hinge of its disordered linker, a separate receptor that binds the longin domain of VAMP7 when that SNARE is in a cis-SNARE complex.

Binds ARF1-GTP through two interfaces on its N-terminal HEAT-repeat trunk. This is the primary ARF1 contact of the whole complex - the delta-sigma3 hemicomplex binds ARF1 almost as well as intact AP-3, while the beta3-mu3 hemicomplex barely binds at all - and it is what recruits and retains AP-3 on the endosomal membrane. Mutating either interface in human cells sends delta back to the cytosol.

Contributes to assembly of the AP-3 membrane coat. Once two ARF1 molecules are bound and cargo is engaged, AP-3 dimerises and polymerises into spiralling rows of arches cross-linked by ARF1 dimers, tubulating the donor membrane into a carrier. The coat requires no clathrin lattice, which distinguishes AP-3 from AP-1 and AP-2; breaking the lattice interfaces by point mutation abolishes carrier formation and lysosomal cargo delivery in human cells.

Required for the integrity of AP-3 itself, and therefore for both the ubiquitous (beta-3A) and the neuronal (beta-3B) complexes. Loss of delta destabilises the whole heterotetramer in mouse mocha fibroblasts and in HPS10 patient cells, and re-expression of wild-type delta restores complex formation and function. This non-redundancy is why delta loss produces a combined pigmentary, platelet, immune and neurological phenotype while loss of beta-3A alone (HPS2) spares the nervous system.

AP4B1 is the beta-1 subunit (beta4-adaptin) of the heterotetrameric AP-4 adaptor complex. The complex forms a non-clathrin coat on vesicles at the trans-Golgi network to mediate cargo sorting and export to endosomal compartments. Key cargoes include ATG9A (autophagy), APP (Alzheimer disease), DAGLB (endocannabinoid signaling), SERINC proteins (lipid scramblases), Sortilin (lysosomal enzyme trafficking), and AMPA/delta-2 glutamate receptors (neuronal polarity). The beta4 subunit C-terminal ear domain specifically recruits the accessory protein tepsin.

Within AP-4, epsilon contributes the structural and membrane-recruitment side of a cargo-adaptor mechanism. Its trunk assembles into the heterotetramer and directly engages activated ARF1; its ear recruits tepsin. Together these contacts support formation of cytoplasmic carriers at the TGN. Cargo-motif recognition is supplied by mu4, so the cargo-adaptor activity is contributed in the complex rather than attributed to isolated epsilon.
The epsilon trunk binds activated ARF1 and provides a regulated membrane-recruitment contact for AP-4. Epsilon is an ARF effector rather than a GTPase, exchange factor or activating protein.

The cargo-recognition subunit of the AP-4 coat. Within the obligate epsilon-beta4-mu4-sigma4 heterotetramer, mu4 contributes the site that reads short sorting motifs in the cytosolic tails of transmembrane cargo, and it is that recognition event which loads cargo into AP-4-coated vesicles budding from the trans-Golgi network. The specificity is mu4's own rather than the canonical YXXPhi preference of the clathrin-adaptor mu subunits: a combinatorial peptide screen gives a distinct position-by-position profile, the APP motif is YKFFE, the binding site seen crystallographically is at a different location on the domain from other signal-adaptor interactions, and the GluRdelta2 tail engages through motifs that are not tyrosine-based at all. Two residues of the mu homology domain, F255 and R283, are required for the APP interaction. The activity is contributed rather than independently enabled, because a mu4 subunit outside the complex has no coat to load.

Export of ATG9A from the trans-Golgi network, which supplies the peripheral ATG9A pool that autophagosome formation draws on. ATG9A is the only multispanning membrane protein of the core autophagy machinery, and it is the AP-4 cargo identified both by a targeted search and by unbiased organellar proteomics. When AP-4 function is lost, ATG9A is retained at the trans-Golgi network and depleted from the peripheral cytoplasm, LC3B lipidation and preautophagosomal maturation are impaired, and in neurons axons develop swellings and accumulate aggregates. The phenotype is documented in cells whose lesion is in AP4M1 itself, not only in models of the other three subunits.

Export of the amyloid precursor protein from the trans-Golgi network to endosomes, which restrains amyloidogenic processing. The YKFFE motif of the APP cytosolic tail binds mu4 directly; the complex was crystallized, and the mu4 mutations F255A and R283D abolish or strongly reduce the interaction. Disrupting the interaction reduces the endosomal pool of APP and increases gamma-secretase cleavage to amyloid-beta. This is the most completely characterized AP-4 itinerary - signal identified, site solved, point mutations made, and consequences measured for both localization and processing.

Coupling of the AP-4 coat, and of its ATG9A cargo, to microtubule-based positioning. mu4 binds the coiled-coil domains of Hook1 and Hook2 directly, which is how the FTS-Hook-FHIP complex engages AP-4; depleting FHF subunits disperses both AP-4 and ATG9A from the perinuclear region. The FHF complex is an established adaptor for dynein-dynactin, so this is the link between cargo selection at the trans-Golgi network and where the resulting vesicles go.

Architectural subunit of the AP-4 core. Sigma4 is the small subunit that the epsilon trunk wraps around to form the central structural core of the complex, and it is required for the complex to exist at all: the two large adaptins epsilon and beta4 associate with one another only in its presence, and in patient fibroblasts lacking sigma4 every other AP-4 subunit is reduced, neither the hemicomplexes nor the tetramer assemble, and the accessory protein tepsin is no longer recruited to membranes, while AP-1 assembly in the same cells is unaffected. Assembly is chaperoned rather than spontaneous, and AAGAB holds epsilon and sigma4 specifically. This is a subunit-attributable molecular function, distinct from anything the complex does as a whole, and it is the reason a truncating AP4S1 allele phenocopies loss of any other subunit.

As part of AP-4, contributes to a coat adaptor activity that selects transmembrane cargo at the trans-Golgi network and packages it into non-clathrin-coated vesicles bound for peripheral compartments. Recruitment is cooperative: ARF1 and cargo each recruit the complex on their own, and together they do so synergistically, with two ARF1 sites on epsilon and on the mu4 C-terminal domain. Sigma4 contributes to this activity without possessing it - the cargo signals themselves are read by mu4, whether the canonical tyrosine-based motif, the non-canonical YKFFE signal of APP, or the ATG9A peptide - which is what the contributes-to relation expresses. The functional consequence is measurable on AP4S1 itself: bi-allelic loss leaves ATG9A trapped in the TGN and absent from the periphery. GO:0060090 is used rather than its child GO:0140312 cargo adaptor activity because that term's definition is framed as binding the scaffolding elements of a vesicle coat such as clathrin or COPII, and AP-4 uses neither; no scaffold partner for AP-4 is known.
Binds beta-catenin and organizes its recruitment and processing in the cytoplasmic destruction complex, supporting phosphorylation, ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover by the associated enzymes.
Binds and stabilizes microtubules and associates with microtubule-end partners, helping organize cortical and kinetochore microtubules during migration and mitosis.

Binds actin and recruits actin monomers to assemble a filament-nucleation seed. APC remains at the nucleation site while its formin partner can drive barbed-end elongation; this activity is separable from APC microtubule binding.

Binds Asef-family exchange factors through its armadillo region and relieves their autoinhibition. Asef performs nucleotide exchange; APC supplies the activating interaction. The source-specific substrate preferences are not generalized to a single downstream GTPase.
XIAP BIR2/linker and BIR3 regions bind and directly inhibit active apoptotic caspases, restraining downstream executioner caspase activity in the cytosol.
XIAP RING E3 ligase activity ubiquitinates RIPK2 after NOD1/NOD2 activation, producing K63-linked ubiquitin scaffolds that recruit downstream NF-kappaB and MAPK signaling machinery.
Nuclear XIAP uses the same RING E3 activity to monoubiquitylate Groucho/TLE corepressors, weakening their TCF/Lef association and promoting canonical Wnt transcriptional activation.

Survivin is an essential structural component of the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC), forming a triple-helix bundle with INCENP and borealin that anchors and regulates the Aurora B kinase. As a CPC component, survivin is essential for proper chromosome segregation during mitosis and mediates CPC targeting to the midbody for cytokinesis completion.
Through interaction with RAN-GTP, survivin participates in spindle assembly by delivering TPX2 to microtubules.

ApoB is the persistent lipid-binding structural scaffold of apoB-containing lipoproteins, directly contributing to particle assembly and transport. ApoB48 serves intestinal chylomicrons; apoB100 serves hepatic VLDL, IDL and LDL. This carrier role spans chylomicrons and their remnants, VLDL, IDL and LDL; VLDL is the representative complex recorded below.

ApoB100 presents recognition surfaces for LDL receptors, coupling lipid-particle carriage to receptor-mediated clearance. The intestinal apoB48 product lacks the canonical apoB100 LDLR-binding region; remnant uptake can instead use apoE.

APOE is an exchangeable apolipoprotein that binds phospholipids and cholesterol and promotes cholesterol/phospholipid efflux and HDL-like particle formation, including ABCA1-dependent lipidation in peripheral cells and CNS-relevant astrocyte contexts.

APOE acts as a receptor/proteoglycan ligand on triglyceride-rich and cholesterol-rich lipoprotein particles, enabling uptake and clearance of chylomicron remnants, VLDL remnants, IDL/LDL-related particles, and HDL particles by hepatocytes and other cells.

Forms pH-gated membrane cation channels as a direct effector of innate defense against susceptible trypanosomes. Lipid-bilayer association at acidic pH precedes channel opening after neutralization. The membrane location denotes the inserted active pool; circulating HDL-associated APOL1 is a distinct delivery pool, not an assertion of channel activity on HDL.

Full-length APP functions as a cell surface adhesion molecule. APP molecules on neighboring cells engage in trans-dimerization to promote synaptogenesis and cell-cell contact. This is a physiological function of full-length APP at the plasma membrane.

APP regulates axon development through multiple mechanisms. The sAPPalpha ectodomain promotes neurite outgrowth acting as a signaling ligand, while full-length APP interacts with Fe65/Mena to guide axon growth. APP knockout mice show defects in axonogenesis.

APP is highly expressed at synapses and plays physiological roles in synapse formation, maintenance, and plasticity. APP trans-dimerization across the synaptic cleft mediates cell-cell adhesion that contributes to synapse structure. APP knockout models show synaptic deficits.

APP binds copper and zinc ions via its ectodomain (GFLD/copper-binding domain) and participates in copper homeostasis and reduction of Cu(2+) to Cu(+). This is a direct molecular function of the APP ectodomain.
ISOFORM-SPECIFIC: The Kunitz protease inhibitor (KPI) domain in APP751/770 isoforms confers serine protease inhibitor activity (Protease nexin-II function). Absent from the neuronal APP695 isoform.

CLEAVAGE PRODUCT FUNCTION: Abeta peptides (particularly Abeta42) self-assemble into amyloid fibrils via identical protein binding. This is a defining biochemical property of the Abeta cleavage products of APP and is central to Alzheimer disease pathology. Both full-length APP and Abeta cleavage products engage in homodimerization.
APP ectodomain binds heparin and heparan sulfate proteoglycans. This interaction promotes APP dimerization, influences neurite outgrowth, and modulates cell adhesion functions.
Catalyzes the salvage of free adenine by transferring the phosphoribosyl group of PRPP to adenine, producing AMP and diphosphate (EC 2.4.2.7), in the cytosol.
Recycles adenine into the adenine nucleotide pool by producing AMP, constituting the AMP-from-adenine salvage step of purine metabolism.

Full-length AR recognizes and binds androgen through its ligand-binding domain, then combines regulatory-DNA recognition with coregulator recruitment to activate or repress Pol II transcription. This ligand-sensing transcriptional activity supports androgen receptor signaling. Ligand-binding-domain-deficient products can retain distinct constitutive transcriptional behavior. Nuclear/chromatin pools perform DNA-directed transcription; cytosol is a regulated receptor pool preceding or following nuclear entry.

Condensation is a mode of AR assembly associated with transcriptional regulation. Purified human activation-domain fragments establish intrinsic condensate formation under defined solution conditions, while a separate receptor study reports ligand-activated transcriptional condensates. These results do not establish that every nuclear focus is liquid or that every splice product has identical phase behavior.
RAS-activated MAP kinase kinase kinase of the ERK1/2 cascade: at the plasma membrane ARAF, within RAF homo/heterodimers, phosphorylates and activates MEK1/MEK2 (MAP2K1/MAP2K2).
Side-to-side kinase-domain heterodimerization with BRAF (and CRAF), required for ARAF activation and for its contribution to RAS-driven MEK-ERK output.

Retroelement Gag-derived capsid protein. Arc self-assembles, through a seven-residue motif in an N-terminal helical coil and through conserved inter-protomer surfaces on both Gag lobes, into double-shelled virus-like particles roughly 32 nm across. This is the protein's defining structural activity: it contributes to the integrity of a higher-order assembly, and disrupting the interface arrests the protein at the dimer stage. The assembly is RNA-dependent in the same way retroviral Gag assembly is - stripping bound nucleic acid suppresses capsid formation and adding back an unrelated mRNA restores it - and the requirement is quantitative rather than sequence-specific.

RNA capture and intercellular delivery. Arc binds mRNA and packages it inside the capsid, which is then released from neurons in extracellular vesicles, endocytosed by recipient neurons, and delivers its cargo into their cytoplasm where it remains available for activity-dependent translation. RNase treatment of purified capsids does not abolish transfer, showing the cargo is genuinely enclosed, and capsids stripped of RNA fail to be taken up at all. Binding is not transcript-selective: what makes Arc mRNA the dominant cargo is its abundance at the site of Arc synthesis, not recognition of a specific element.

Postsynaptic endocytic adaptor for AMPA receptor removal. Arc bridges the endocytic machinery to the postsynaptic membrane: separate regions of the protein bind endophilin 2/3 and dynamin 2, both interactions are needed for endosome association, and the resulting assembly accelerates internalisation of AMPA-type glutamate receptors into early endosomes. The role is that of an adaptor bringing components together rather than of an enzyme - Arc has no catalytic activity - and it is the same oligomerisation interface that supports capsid formation, since mutating the coil motif blocks Arc-facilitated endocytosis. Membrane attachment is by palmitoylation of an N-terminal cysteine cluster, not by a transmembrane segment. Perturbation works in both directions: losing Arc raises surface AMPA receptors and slows endocytosis, raising Arc blocks the inactivity-induced increase.

Consolidation switch for activity-dependent plasticity and memory. Arc is induced within minutes of plasticity-inducing activity and is then required for changes to persist: blocking its expression leaves LTP induction intact but abolishes maintenance, and leaves task acquisition and short-term memory intact but abolishes consolidation of long-term memory. Arc-null animals show the same dissociation as a biphasic LTP phenotype - enhanced early phase, absent late phase - together with impaired long-term depression. The switch is gated at the oligomerisation interface: CaMKII phosphorylation of the Gag N-lobe disrupts high-order assembly, and a phosphorylation-resistant knock-in alters the magnitude of metabotropic-receptor LTD.

Catalyzes manganese-dependent hydrolysis of L-arginine to ornithine and urea in the cytosol. This reaction supplies the terminal urea-cycle step and directly breaks down L-arginine. Each subunit of the homotrimer binds the binuclear manganese cofactor required for catalysis.

Small GTPase switch (G protein) that is activated in the cilium by its GEF ARL13B and inactivated by its GAP RP2. In the GTP-bound state it binds the lipid-binding carriers PDE6D and UNC119A/B and allosterically releases their farnesylated or myristoylated cargo (e.g. INPP5E, NPHP3) into the ciliary membrane, which sets ciliary membrane composition.
GTP-dependent binding of effectors (PDE6D, UNC119A/B, ARL2BP/BART, CFAP36/BARTL1). For the cargo carriers, this binding is the mechanism of cargo displacement.

ARL6IP1 generates positive membrane curvature through reticulon-like hairpin transmembrane domains, promoting tubular ER formation. The protein oligomerizes (identical protein binding) which is typical for ER-shaping proteins. Overexpression induces extensive ER tubules, and in vitro ARL6IP1 constricts liposomes into tubules (PMID:24262037).

ARPC1B provides a structural subunit of the Arp2/3 complex that coordinates regulated branched actin-network assembly. Human B-cell experiments connect ARPC1B-containing complexes to WASP-stimulated polymerization and cortical organization; reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation shows stronger WASP association with ARPC1B than ARPC1A under the tested cellular conditions.

Remove sulfate from saposin-B-presented sulfatide and related sulfated glycosphingolipids in acidic degradative compartments. Lysosomal localization is established; the endolysosome-lumen activity site also retains the existing curator inference.

Catalyses removal of 4-sulfate groups from N-acetylgalactosamine residues during lysosomal chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate degradation, using a calcium-containing, formylglycine-dependent active site.

Promotes hydrolysis of GalNAc 4-O-sulfate groups in chondroitin sulfate during Golgi proteoglycan maturation. Human rescue and Golgi-fraction evidence support this activity; purified-enzyme substrate range and endo/exo specificity remain unresolved.

Acid ceramidase cleaves ceramide to sphingosine and a free fatty acid in the acidic endolysosomal system. Precursor autocleavage exposes the catalytic beta-subunit N-terminal cysteine. Saposin D enhances access to membrane substrates; an obligatory stable enzyme-saposin complex is not established. This hydrolytic activity is the principal molecular function despite secondary substrate and reverse-reaction activities in particular assays.
ASCL1 is a bHLH transcription factor that binds E-box motifs (CANNTG) as a heterodimer with E-proteins (TCF3, TCF4) and regulates transcription of neuronal target genes.

ASCL1 specifically binds E-box sequences with strong preference for the CAGCTG variant, which is enriched directly beneath 74% of ASCL1 binding peaks (PMID:21536733). This "GC" core E-box preference distinguishes ASCL1 from Neurog2 (which prefers CAGATG), explaining their distinct neuronal subtype outputs. E-proteins enhance ASCL1 binding to CAGSTG sequences through heterodimerization.

ASCL1 functions as a pioneer factor capable of binding nucleosomal DNA and initiating chromatin remodeling at neuronal enhancers. Studies reveal ASCL1 operates through two distinct mechanisms: at ~23.5% of sites it functions as a classical pioneer factor binding closed chromatin independently, while at ~68% of sites it requires cooperation with mSWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes (PMID:36931659). ASCL1 binds chromatin marked by a trivalent signature (H3K9me3, H3K27ac, H3K4me1) and predominantly at distal enhancers (~63%) rather than promoters (~7%) (PMID:25753420).
ASCL1 heterodimerizes with E-proteins (TCF3/E12/E47, TCF4/E2-2) via its HLH domain. This dimerization is essential for DNA binding, transcriptional activity, and protein stability.
ASCL1 forms heterodimers with E-proteins via its HLH domain, which is required for DNA binding and transcriptional function.

Catalyzes the reversible cleavage of argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate as a cytosolic homotetramer, contributing directly to the urea cycle and arginine biosynthesis. Self-association assembles the catalytic sites and is part of this enzyme mechanism.

Contributes a structural scaffold to nitric oxide synthase protein assemblies, supporting utilization of arginine for nitric oxide production independently of its arginine-generating catalytic reaction.

Cytosolic ATPase and TMD chaperone of the GET/TRC pathway that recognizes and binds the C-terminal transmembrane domain of newly synthesized tail-anchored proteins and, in an ATP-driven cycle, carries and delivers them to the ER membrane receptor for insertion.

Soluble protein carrier (TMD chaperone) that shields the hydrophobic tail anchor of TA substrates and, as part of the GET complex docking on the WRB/CAML insertase, delivers them for ER membrane insertion.
Couples N-terminal glutamine hydrolysis and intramolecular nitrogen transfer to ATP-dependent L-asparagine synthesis in the cytosol. The two-domain human enzyme functions as a homodimer.
Zinc-dependent hydrolysis of NAA and other N-acyl-L-aspartates, producing acetate or another carboxylate and L-aspartate.

A cytosolic homotetrameric ligase catalyzing ATP-dependent condensation of citrulline and aspartate into argininosuccinate. This reaction directly contributes to the urea cycle and L-arginine biosynthesis. ATP is consumed to AMP and diphosphate; ASL subsequently produces arginine and fumarate.

ATF4 is a bZIP transcription factor that serves as the central effector of the Integrated Stress Response (ISR). ATF4 binds to cAMP response elements (CRE) and C/EBP-ATF response elements (CARE/AARE) as homo- or heterodimers to activate transcription of stress-responsive genes. Key targets include amino acid metabolism genes (ASNS, PSAT1, PHGDH), amino acid transporters (SLC7A11/xCT, SLC1A5), autophagy genes (MAP1LC3B, BECN1, ATG5, ATG7, ATG12), ER chaperones (GRP78/BiP), and transcription factors (CHOP/DDIT3, ATF3). ATF4 translation is uniquely controlled by upstream open reading frames (uORFs) that enable preferential translation when eIF2alpha is phosphorylated by stress-sensing kinases (PERK, GCN2, PKR, HRI). ATF4 also cooperates with NRF2 as an obligatory metabolic activator of the antioxidant response (PMID:37410595). Neill and Masson (PMID:36825279) catalogued 41 well-validated ATF4 target genes.

ATF4 forms heterodimers with other bZIP transcription factors via its leucine zipper domain, including CHOP/DDIT3, C/EBP family members (CEBPB, CEBPG), CREB1, ATF1, ATF3, and other bZIP partners. The choice of dimerization partner determines target gene specificity and whether the outcome is adaptive or pro-apoptotic. Neill and Masson (PMID:36825279) catalogued 14 direct dimerization partners for ATF4.

The released N-terminal ATF6 transcription factor binds ER-stress response regulatory DNA and activates RNA polymerase II transcription of adaptive unfolded-protein-response genes. Chaperone and quality-control gene induction increases ER folding capacity, while XBP1 transcription coordinates the response with the IRE1 branch. The active DNA-binding product acts in the nucleus after stress-dependent ER-to-Golgi trafficking and proteolytic release of the membrane precursor.

AICAR transformylase (phosphoribosylaminoimidazolecarboxamide formyltransferase, EC 2.1.2.3) that transfers a formyl group from 10-formyltetrahydrofolate to AICAR to form FAICAR -- the penultimate step of de novo IMP biosynthesis. Acts as a cytosolic homodimer.

IMP cyclohydrolase (EC 3.5.4.10) that cyclizes FAICAR to inosine 5'-monophosphate (IMP) plus water -- the final, essentially irreversible step of de novo IMP biosynthesis, which drives the overall AICAR-to-IMP conversion forward. Resides in the N-terminal MGS-like domain; acts as a cytosolic homodimer.

ATM is a PIKK-family protein kinase that executes MRN-linked DNA double-strand-break signaling through SQ/TQ substrate phosphorylation, coordinating checkpoints and DNA repair. Documented oxidative and extranuclear contexts use the same kinase, including a cytosol-facing peroxisomal membrane pool. Nuclear DNA-damage signaling is the dominant defining context. The peroxisomal membrane is a documented ROS-dependent context, not matrix residence or an integral-membrane prediction.
Hydrolyzes ATP to export three sodium ions and import two potassium ions across the plasma membrane, maintaining the gradients used for membrane potential and secondary transport.

Catalyzes ATP-dependent sodium export and potassium import across the plasma membrane as the alpha2 subunit of the sodium/potassium pump, maintaining ion gradients that support cellular excitability and secondary transport.

Hydrolyzes ATP to export sodium and import potassium across the plasma membrane as the catalytic alpha3 subunit of the sodium-potassium pump. This coupled exchange sustains the ion gradients used for membrane potential and neuronal electrical stability.

ATP-coupled calcium export across the plasma membrane lowers cytosolic calcium and helps terminate calcium transients. PMCA2 itself performs the transport step. Splice-dependent targeting and regulation adapt this same activity to specialized cellular environments. In sensory hair cells this export returns calcium from stereocilia to endolymph after mechanotransduction; it is a specialized setting of the same pump mechanism.
