Structural (non-catalytic) subunit of the central stalk of mitochondrial ATP synthase (Complex V): as one of the gamma/delta/epsilon central-stalk subunits it maintains the integrity of, and transmits rotation within, the rotary F1Fo enzyme in the mitochondrial inner membrane, thereby contributing to proton motive force-driven ATP synthesis. It is also required for assembly/biogenesis of the F1 sector.

ATP6V1A is the catalytic A subunit of the V1 domain of V-ATPase, directly hydrolyzing ATP to power proton translocation across organellar membranes. Three copies of subunit A form catalytic AB heterodimers in the V1 hexameric ring.

As the catalytic ATPase subunit, ATP6V1A powers acidification of lysosomal and endosomal lumens, which is essential for protein degradation, receptor-mediated endocytosis, and lysosomal enzyme function.
The lysosomal V-ATPase complex, through the V1 domain, engages Ragulator in an amino acid-sensitive fashion to activate Rag GTPase-mediated mTORC1 recruitment and activation at the lysosomal surface.

Supports assembly and operation of the V1 sector of the V-ATPase, thereby contributing to ATP-hydrolysis-driven proton translocation by the assembled complex. At the apical membrane of renal epithelia this activity supports urinary acidification. B1 is a non-catalytic structural subunit; renal and auditory consequences are contexts of the same pump contribution.

ATP6V1B2 is the non-catalytic B subunit of the V1 domain of V-ATPase. Three B2 subunits alternate with three catalytic A subunits to form the AB heterohexameric ring of V1. B2 is required for V1 complex assembly and enables proton translocation by the holoenzyme.

ATP6V0C is a core structural component of the V-ATPase V0 domain. Nine copies of ATP6V0C assemble with one copy of ATP6V0B to form the c-ring that rotates during proton translocation. The conserved glutamate residue E139 serves as the proton-binding site essential for proton transport.

As part of the V-ATPase complex, ATP6V0C is essential for acidifying intracellular compartments including lysosomes, endosomes, Golgi, and synaptic vesicles. Acidification is required for hydrolase activity, receptor-ligand dissociation, neurotransmitter loading, and protein processing.
ATP6V0A1 is the a1 subunit of the V0 membrane sector of V-ATPase and contributes to rotary ATP-driven proton transport by the assembled complex.

As part of V-ATPase complexes on endolysosomal and synaptic vesicle membranes, ATP6V0A1 supports acidification of lysosomes, endosomes, and synaptic vesicles, with downstream effects on protein degradation, autophagic flux, mTORC1/Notch signaling contexts, and neurotransmitter loading.

ATP6V0A4 is the a4 isoform of the membrane-integral V0 a subunit of the V-ATPase. As part of the V0 sector, it contributes to the assembled V-ATPase rotational proton-pump activity, linking ATP hydrolysis by V1 to proton transfer across membranes.
In kidney, ATP6V0A4-containing V-ATPases are targeted to apical membranes of proton-secreting nephron cells, where they support vectorial acid transport into urine and systemic acid-base homeostasis.

ATP6V0A4 helps couple and regulate the V-ATPase through interactions with V1-sector subunits and glycolytic enzyme PFK-1. These interactions support V1/V0 assembly or functional coupling and explain disease mutations that reduce proton transport without simply removing the subunit from the membrane.

ATP6AP1/Ac45 supports the assembly and stability of the membrane V0 sector through contacts with its c-ring and other subunits, and helps target V-ATPase to functional compartments. It thereby contributes to proton pumping by the assembled complex and to endolysosomal acidification. ER/ERGIC residence in human hepatocytes supports the early assembly/localization context; it does not establish acidification of the ER lumen.
ATP-driven Cu(I) translocation across trans-Golgi and plasma membranes supplies copper to secretory-pathway cuproenzymes and exports excess cellular copper.

ATP-driven copper(I) translocation from the cytosol into Golgi and vesicular compartments supports secretory copper delivery, copper homeostasis and removal of excess cellular copper. Organelle copper import and subsequent vesicular exocytosis describe different boundaries of this route; the export process does not require universal ATP7B residence at the plasma membrane.

NAD+-dependent AASA oxidation to alpha-aminoadipate in L-lysine catabolism. Human purified-enzyme assays, patient biochemistry and neural-progenitor knockout metabolomics establish this catalytic step. The function is conserved, as PAINT places it, with lysine catabolism, at the vertebrate ALDH7A1 node seeded by human, mouse and zebrafish experiments. Matrix placement comes from the curated Reactome catalyst, while mitochondrial and cytosolic pools have independent localization support.

Oxidation of medium-chain and reactive aldehydes, coupled to NADH production. Direct assays with human protein support aldehyde detoxification; membrane reconstitution and human-cell studies establish local NADH generation that inhibits BARS-dependent transport and supports FSP1-dependent ferroptosis protection. ALDH7A1 also consumes reactive aldehydes and assists FSP1 recruitment. The partner proteins retain the carrier-fission and quinone-reduction activities, and the cellular evidence is scoped to the tested conditions.

Full-length ATRX provides the ATP-dependent remodeling motor in an ATRX–DAXX chromatin complex, changing histone–DNA contacts and helping organize histone-variant chromatin at repetitive nuclear regions. DAXX supplies the directly demonstrated isolated H3.3 chaperone activity.

The ADD domain recognizes H3K9-trimethylated histone tails in combination with the H3K4 methylation state, contributing to heterochromatin targeting. Recognition is impaired by H3K4 di- or trimethylation and by tested disease-associated ADD variants.

KIF1A is a neuron-specific kinesin-3 that, as a CC1-FHA-mediated dimer, moves processively toward microtubule plus ends and carries synaptic vesicle precursors and dense core vesicles along axons and dendrites to synapses.

In radial glial progenitors KIF1A acts from the nuclear surface to drive basally directed (G1) interkinetic nuclear migration along uniformly oriented microtubules, the plus-end counterpart of dynein-driven apical nuclear movement.
Catalyzes the hydration of 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA to 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA in mitochondrial leucine degradation. The reaction is reversible; leucine catabolism uses the hydration direction.

Binds AU-rich sequences in transcript 3'-UTRs in vitro. A lysine-rich surface contributes to RNA binding. The interaction is established independently of a proposed transcript-decay role; the physiological RNA targets and relationship to mitochondrial translation remain incompletely resolved. The physiological compartment of the classical AU-rich transcript-binding activity is unresolved; no matrix or cytosolic location is assigned to that specific activity.

THE core function of AXIN1. As the central scaffold of the beta-catenin destruction complex, AXIN1 coordinates CK1 and GSK3B phosphorylation of beta-catenin, leading to its ubiquitination and degradation, thereby suppressing Wnt target gene transcription.
Scaffolds the beta-catenin destruction complex, positioning beta-catenin with its regulatory enzymes to promote turnover and restrain canonical Wnt signaling.

Transfers galactose from UDP-galactose to terminal GlcNAc residues of protein-linked N-glycans in the Golgi, supporting complex N-glycan maturation. Catalysis requires manganese; the enzyme occupies trans cisternae and can occur more broadly across Golgi stacks.
Transfers galactose from UDP-galactose to free N-acetylglucosamine to form N-acetyllactosamine, a substrate-specific facet of the manganese-dependent catalytic activity.

In a 1:1 complex with alpha-lactalbumin in lactating mammary cells, transfers galactose from UDP-galactose to glucose to synthesize lactose. Alpha-lactalbumin promotes glucose binding and changes acceptor preference, enabling this tissue-specific catalytic role at the Golgi.

Catalyzes manganese-dependent transfer of galactose from UDP-galactose to protein-linked xylose, forming the first galactose of the proteoglycan tetrasaccharide linker. The type-II membrane enzyme acts on the luminal side of Golgi cisternae.

Bile acid-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase - the terminal, defining catalytic activity of BAAT. It transfers the bile acid from its CoA thioester (choloyl-CoA, chenodeoxycholoyl-CoA) onto the amino group of glycine (or taurine), producing glyco- and tauro-conjugated bile acids, the final step of bile-acid biosynthesis. A single monomeric enzyme conjugates both amino acids using a Cys-235/Asp-328/His-362 catalytic triad, with Cys-235 forming a covalent bile acid-enzyme intermediate.

Secondary bile-acyl-CoA thioesterase (choloyl-CoA hydrolase) activity carried out by the same catalytic triad; the Cys-235-Ser substitution reduces N-acyltransferase activity but increases thioesterase activity. In vitro the enzyme also hydrolyzes long- and very long-chain fatty-acyl-CoAs, consistent with membership in the type-I acyl-CoA thioesterase family; a physiological role in regulating intracellular acyl-CoA/VLCFA levels is proposed.

BAG3 uses its BAG domain to bind Hsp70-family nucleotide-binding domains and promote nucleotide exchange and client release. This co-chaperone activity regulates productive folding cycles in a concentration- and partner-dependent manner.

BAG3 brings Hsp70 and small heat-shock proteins together through its BAG domain and IPV motifs, coordinating client handling. In muscle, the CASA scaffold connects damaged-protein processing with SYNPO2-associated autophagosome machinery and supports Z-disc maintenance.

BAG3 couples Hsp70-associated misfolded clients to dynein and accompanies them during microtubule-dependent transport to aggresomes, supporting subsequent autophagic disposal. Hsp70 provides client recognition and dynein provides motor activity.

IRSp53 is fundamentally an adaptor that bridges the plasma membrane and the Rho-family GTPases to the actin machinery. The central partial-CRIB and proline-rich region receives activated Cdc42 and Rac1; the C-terminal SH3 domain recruits the actin effectors that do the polymerizing and bundling -- WAVE2, N-WASP, Eps8 and Mena/VASP. IRSp53 itself neither nucleates nor elongates filaments; its contribution is to hold the GTPase signal, the membrane surface and the nucleation-promoting factor in the same place, which is what determines whether a protrusion forms and what shape it takes. The same adaptor logic operates in neurons, where binding to PSD-95/PSD-93 and the Shank family positions IRSp53 in the postsynaptic density and drives dendritic spine morphogenesis.

The N-terminal I-BAR/IMD domain reads negative membrane curvature, and this is what makes IRSp53 a shape sensor rather than a constitutive scaffold. Quiroga et al. compressed fibroblasts to generate bud-shaped plasma membrane evaginations on the ~100 nm scale and found IRSp53 selectively enriched at them, with maximal sorting near 0.05 nm^-1 and roughly twofold enrichment over control. Enrichment creates a local node that couples membrane topography to a transient Rac1/Arp2/3 actin burst, which re-flattens the evagination -- a mechanochemical feedback loop maintaining plasma membrane shape homeostasis.

Direct binding of the IMD/I-BAR domain to PI(4,5)P2 is the membrane-targeting step on which the adaptor and curvature-sensing activities both depend, and it is the feature that distinguishes the I-BAR subfamily mechanically. Mattila et al. mapped the PI(4,5)P2-binding site and showed that its geometry is inverted relative to classical BAR domains, so the domain binds the interior of the tubule and induces curvature of the opposite sign; this is the molecular reason I-BAR proteins generate plasma membrane protrusions where BAR proteins generate invaginations. The same study found the filopodia-forming activity of the IMD to depend on this membrane-deforming activity rather than on the previously proposed F-actin-bundling or GTPase-binding activities -- a point worth carrying, since it means the actin bundling terms this gene carries by IBA are a secondary property of the domain and not the mechanism by which it builds protrusions.

The IMD binds F-actin directly and cross-links filaments into tightly packed parallel bundles, an activity mapped to conserved basic residues at the two extreme ends of the zeppelin-shaped dimer. This is the molecular function underlying the actin filament bundle assembly and actin crosslink formation processes the gene is annotated to, and it had no molecular-function representation in GOA. It is listed last deliberately: Mattila et al. showed the filopodia-forming activity of the domain survives loss of F-actin bundling and tracks membrane deformation instead, so actin binding is a genuine property of the domain rather than the mechanism by which protrusions are built. In cells it operates alongside Eps8, with which IRSp53 synergizes to bundle actin.

BAP1 catalyzes removal of monoubiquitin from histone H2A lysine 119 in nuclear PR-DUB complexes. ASXL proteins activate the enzyme, while contacts with nucleosomal DNA, histones and ubiquitin position the substrate. This chromatin reaction regulates transcription, with activating or repressive outcomes determined by the locus and cellular context.

BAP1 also catalyzes deubiquitination of nonhistone regulatory proteins. Nuclear HCFC1 is an established substrate, whereas an ER-associated BAP1 pool deubiquitinates ITPR3 and supports receptor stability and calcium-dependent cell-death responses. Substrate stabilization is context dependent and is not a universal consequence of BAP1 catalysis.

Recognizes ubiquitin-modified nucleosomes and unmodified H4K20 to recruit BRCA1–BARD1 to damaged post-replicative chromatin and position its H2A ubiquitination machinery. The N-terminal H2A ubiquitin marks recognized by BARD1 are distinct from the C-terminal H2A lysines modified by the heterodimer.

Contributes RAD51-binding and DNA-binding functions that allow the BRCA1–BARD1 heterodimer to stimulate RAD51-dependent synaptic complex formation and strand invasion during homologous recombination. This activity concerns stimulation of the recombinase rather than the strand-exchange reaction itself or BRCA2-like loading onto RPA-coated single-stranded DNA.

Binds active ARL6 through its N-terminal beta-propeller, contributing to recruitment of the BBSome to the ciliary membrane. Human recombinant domain-binding measurements support this interaction; ARL6 supplies the GTPase activity.

Recognizes signaling-receptor cargo as part of the BBSome. Human-cell co-immunoprecipitation and receptor-tail mapping support associations with Smoothened and Patched1. These contacts contribute to the complex's role in controlling receptor localization at cilia; the assays do not establish purified binary affinities for each receptor.

Holds the BBSome core together through distinct contacts with BBS7 and BBS9. A human recombinant subcomplex supports a BBS2-BBS7 coiled-coil interface and a separate BBS2-BBS9 interface; disruption of the latter by the BBS2 R632P substitution impairs association. This establishes a structural contribution without assigning BBS2 the receptor-recognition or ARL6-binding activities of other subunits. In human retinal pigment epithelial cells, BBS2 depletion destabilizes the BBSome and impairs its normal ciliary localization, linking this scaffold role to ciliary protein localization.

Acts as a pericentriolar adaptor through interactions with PCM1 and DCTN1/p150-glued. These interactions support PCM1 positioning and centrosomal microtubule anchoring. Cell experiments support a dynein-associated recruitment model, while allowing that BBS4 also retains PCM1 after transport. Cooperation with DISC1 contributes to PCM1 and ninein localization.

Contributes as a BBSome subunit to protein localization at cilia. Human retinal pigment epithelial cell depletion experiments support a requirement for BBS4 in BBSome ciliary entry, even though much of the remaining complex can remain assembled. The contribution is dependent on cargo and cell context and does not establish autonomous receptor recognition by BBS4.

Binds phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate in recombinant protein-lipid overlay assays. Full-length BBS5 and its N-terminal PH-like domain bind this lipid and phosphatidic acid. This isolated-protein activity does not establish physiological lipid selectivity or an exclusive membrane-anchor mechanism: native BBSome liposome specificity differs, and a recombinant BBS4/BBS8/BBS9/BBIP1 subcomplex also binds lipids without BBS5.

Contributes as a BBSome subunit to cilium formation in human retinal pigment epithelial cells. BBS5 depletion reduces ciliation and impairs normal ciliary entry of the remaining BBSome. Most of the complex can remain assembled after BBS5 depletion, and reducing LZTFL1 restores its ciliary localization. These observations distinguish the BBS5 contribution from an obligatory scaffold for BBSome assembly. Cargo requirements differ: BBS5 depletion does not impair PC1 ciliary trafficking in the reported assay.

Catalyzes PLP-dependent, reversible transamination of leucine, isoleucine and valine with 2-oxoglutarate in the mitochondrial matrix. This homodimer produces the corresponding branched-chain keto acids and glutamate, supplying the first reaction of BCAA catabolism upstream of BCKDH. The same chemistry supports reamination of pre-existing ketoacid skeletons.

Binds the diphosphate portion of thiamine diphosphate at the shared E1 active site and contributes to decarboxylation of branched-chain ketoacids followed by reductive acylation of the DBT lipoyl domain. The activity belongs to the alpha2-beta2 enzyme: BCKDHA helps position the cofactor and the lipoyl-domain recognition loop, while BCKDHB supplies complementary active-site residues. Magnesium supports cofactor binding, and structural potassium sites help organize the enzyme. Acyl-CoA transfer and lipoyl reoxidation are performed subsequently by DBT and DLD within the same multienzyme complex.

Contributes ThDP contacts and catalytic residues to the shared active sites of the alpha2-beta2 E1 enzyme. Together with BCKDHA, it supports branched-chain ketoacid decarboxylation and reductive acylation of the DBT lipoyl domain. A structural potassium site helps organize the beta chain. The subsequent CoA transfer and lipoyl reoxidation are performed by DBT and DLD, respectively. The enzyme is regulated through phosphorylation of its alpha subunit rather than a separate kinase or phosphatase activity of BCKDHB.

Organizes CARD-BCL10-MALT1 signaling assemblies that couple receptor stimulation to NF-kappaB activation. CARD-mediated BCL10 polymerization links upstream CARD proteins to MALT1 and downstream ubiquitin-dependent effector recruitment; BCL10 provides the assembling platform while MALT1, ubiquitin enzymes and kinases perform their respective catalytic steps.
BCL2 recognizes BH3-containing ligands and restrains BAX-dependent mitochondrial permeabilization, maintaining the mitochondrial barrier to cytochrome-c release and caspase activation.
BCL2 inhibits membrane-permeabilizing activity of BAX at mitochondria and IP3-receptor channel opening at the endoplasmic reticulum, linking calcium regulation to cell survival.
BCL2 binding to the BECN1 BH3 region inhibits autophagy; interaction with AMBRA1 supplies an additional mitochondrial route for restraining autophagosome formation.

The CORE molecular function of Bcl-xL (canonical isoform Q07817-1). Bcl-xL contains a BH3-binding groove that binds the BH3 domains of pro-apoptotic proteins including BAX, BAK, BAD, BIM, PUMA, and NOXA. This binding sequesters pro-apoptotic proteins at the mitochondrial outer membrane and prevents their activation of the apoptotic cascade. Structural studies have characterized the BH3-binding groove at atomic resolution (PMID:21199865, PMID:21639858). As established in the foundational paper PMID:8358789, bcl-xL inhibits cell death upon growth factor withdrawal. By preventing BAX/BAK pore formation at the MOM, Bcl-xL inhibits cytochrome c release and blocks apoptosis. CRITICAL ISOFORM NOTE: BCL2L1 produces two antagonistic isoforms through alternative splicing. Bcl-xL (Q07817-1, 233 AA) is ANTI-apoptotic (this core function). Bcl-xS (Q07817-2, 166 AA) lacks the BH1 and BH2 domains and is PRO-apoptotic.

ATP-driven movement of the folded Rieske domain across the mitochondrial inner membrane enables UQCRFS1 incorporation during complex III assembly. The membrane-anchored Bcs1 motor accommodates its client on the matrix side and releases the folded domain toward the intermembrane space.

NAD+-dependent oxidation of (R)-3-hydroxybutyrate to acetoacetate (and the reverse reduction), the reversible dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.30) that interconverts the two ketone bodies at the matrix side of the mitochondrial inner membrane. This activity requires phosphatidylcholine as an allosteric activator and is the enzymatic basis of both ketogenesis and ketolysis.

BECN1 is the central scaffold/adapter of PI3KC3 complexes, assembling VPS34, VPS15, and complex-specific subunits (ATG14L or UVRAG) into functional lipid kinase complexes that generate PI3P for autophagy and endocytic trafficking. As scaffold of PI3KC3-C1 (ATG14L-containing complex), BECN1 is essential for autophagosome nucleation.
BECN1 directly binds VPS34 (PIK3C3), the catalytic subunit of class III PI3K, through its coiled-coil and BARA domains. This binding is essential for PI3KC3 complex formation and function.

The N-BAR region binds lipid membranes and directly bends them into tubular structures. Phospholipid engagement, membrane-bound assembly and curvature-dependent recruitment cooperate in this membrane-shaping activity; muscle splice forms use it in T-tubule organization.

BIN1 binds dynamin through its SH3 domain and recruits the GTPase to membrane tubules. Coupling this partner interaction to BAR-mediated membrane remodeling helps organize endocytic machinery; dynamin supplies GTP hydrolysis, while BIN1 supplies membrane and protein contacts.

BIN1 binds actin and associates with nesprin and the microtubule-associated regulator CLIP170, connecting the nuclear envelope and membrane-associated structures to the cytoskeleton. These structural contacts contribute to nucleus organization, including nuclear position and shape.

BLM couples ATP hydrolysis to 3-prime-to-5-prime DNA strand separation and branched-DNA remodeling. In the BTR complex it supplies the helicase step of double-Holliday-junction dissolution, while TOP3A supplies topoisomerase chemistry. The same DNA motor participates in DNA-end processing, stalled-fork remodeling and telomeric DNA transactions. The recombination-intermediate resolution term denotes participation in BTR dissolution: BLM supplies DNA remodeling and TOP3A supplies transient strand cleavage and rejoining, yielding non-crossover products; it does not assign junction endonuclease activity to BLM.

BLM promotes annealing of complementary DNA strands, a molecular activity distinct from strand separation. Together with unwinding, annealing can contribute to replication-fork regression. The purified catalytic-fragment assay shows concentration-dependent annealing, and does not establish that every cellular BLM assembly or modification has the same balance of activities.
BMP4 acts extracellularly as a growth-factor ligand for BMP receptor complexes, initiating BMP signaling and downstream receptor-mediated SMAD responses.
Realizes extracellular growth-factor activity by binding BMP receptor complexes, initiating BMP signaling and hepcidin-dependent systemic iron regulation.

Forms an experimentally active BMP2/BMP6 heterodimer that contributes extracellular cytokine activity to BMP signaling and hepcidin regulation; this demonstrated recombinant capacity does not establish obligatory endogenous heterodimer assembly.

Recognizes BMP-family ligands at the cell surface and, after activation within a type I/type II receptor complex, uses its intracellular serine/threonine kinase to transmit the signal to R-SMADs. Ligand recognition, receptor assembly and ATP-dependent catalysis form one coupled receptor mechanism.

Binds BMP-family ligands at the cell surface and transmits their signal within a heteromeric receptor complex by phosphorylating type-I receptor components. Ligand recognition, receptor assembly and ATP-dependent receptor-to-receptor phosphorylation form one coupled mechanism; the activated type-I kinase subsequently phosphorylates R-SMADs.

Selective autophagy receptor for mitochondria. BNIP3 in the mitochondrial outer membrane binds LC3/GABARAP via its N-terminal LIR, after homodimerizing through its transmembrane helix. This tethers mitochondria to autophagosomes during hypoxia- and stress-induced mitophagy.
Selective autophagy receptor for the ER. An ER-membrane pool of BNIP3 uses the same LIR to target ER for autophagic degradation (ER-phagy).

Hypoxia-induced promotion of macroautophagy. HIF-induced BNIP3 (redundantly with BNIP3L) is required for hypoxia-induced autophagy, and its atypical BH3 domain can release Beclin 1 from BCL-2 without triggering death.

BNIP3L/NIX functions as a mitophagy receptor at the mitochondrial outer membrane. Anchored by its C-terminal transmembrane helix with an N-terminal cytosolic region containing an LC3-interacting region, it directly binds Atg8-family proteins (LC3 and GABARAP) to tether mitochondria to the forming autophagosome, driving selective autophagic clearance of mitochondria. This is essential for mitochondrial elimination during terminal erythroid/reticulocyte maturation and contributes to developmentally programmed and stress-induced mitochondrial turnover.

Under hypoxia, NIX (a HIF target) promotes pro-survival macroautophagy. Its atypical BH3 domain can disrupt the Bcl-2-Beclin1 complex to initiate autophagy without inducing cell death, and combined loss of BNIP3 and BNIP3L suppresses hypoxia-induced autophagy.

NIX participates in non-canonical mitochondrial quality control via ROS-dependent interaction with SPATA18/MIEAP, acting as an essential mediator of MALM that degrades oxidized mitochondrial proteins; NIX deficiency abolishes MALM.

Dystonin provides product-specific structural links between filament networks and cellular attachment structures. Epithelial BP230 connects keratin intermediate filaments to hemidesmosomal integrin beta4 and collagen XVII contacts. In human keratinocytes, the epithelial product also supports actin organization, front–rear polarity and persistent migration through a beta4-associated Rac1/cofilin pathway whose complete molecular arrangement remains unresolved. Muscle BPAG1-b associates with Z-disc proteins and adjacent intermediate-filament structures.

Microtubule-binding regions of long dystonin products associate with the microtubule lattice and with EB1 at growing ends. Experiments on the BPAG1n4 C-terminal tail demonstrate a calcium-sensitive switch between plus-end tracking and lattice association, dependent on its EF-hand and microtubule-binding regions. These binding properties support microtubule organization; fragment assays do not establish identical regulation in all natural products or a direct calcium-affinity value.

By associating with dynactin p150, the long neuronal BPAG1n4 form helps organize vesicle-associated machinery for retrograde axonal transport. Human brain-derived cDNA underlies the interaction constructs, whereas endogenous localization and transport assays were performed in mice. This adaptor role is distinct from dynein motor catalysis. Exact sequence equivalence between the historical full-length construct and a current human product has not been established.

BRAF is the canonical RAF-family MAP kinase kinase kinase (MAP3K) of the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade. After RAS-GTP-driven membrane recruitment and side-to-side dimerization (BRAF homodimers and the more potent BRAF-RAF1 heterodimers), BRAF phosphorylates and activates MAP2K1/MAP2K2 (MEK1/MEK2) — the committed step that propagates mitogenic signaling to ERK1/ERK2.

BRAF is an ATP-dependent protein serine/threonine kinase. Its intrinsic catalytic activity, demonstrated by direct in vitro kinase assays, phosphorylates substrate serine/threonine residues (most importantly the activation-loop serines of MEK1/MEK2); this enzymatic activity is the molecular basis for its MAP3K function and for its oncogenic activation by the V600E mutation.

The BRCA1 RING engages E2 enzymes in the BRCA1–BARD1 ubiquitin-ligase heterodimer. The complex ubiquitinates nucleosomal H2A C-terminal lysines and other substrates to support repair-associated chromatin regulation. K6-linked autoubiquitination is one experimentally observed product; other E2 partners support different linkages. BARD1 supplies modified-chromatin recognition surfaces, while BRCA1 supplies the E2-engaging RING interface. This is distinct from assigning an intrinsic ubiquitin-modified-histone reader site to BRCA1. The broader ligase term summarizes activity across histone and non-histone substrates, including autoubiquitination; the accepted H2AK127-specific annotation describes one substrate-specific branch of this activity.

The tandem BRCT region recognizes phosphorylated protein motifs, including phosphoserine-containing segments of BRIP1/BACH1, CtIP and Abraxas, and helps organize distinct damage-response assemblies. This protein-recognition activity is separate from direct DNA binding and does not give BRCA1 the helicase or nuclease activity of its partners. Phosphorylated ACCA provides an additional, non-core metabolic context for the same broad recognition chemistry. The broader phosphoprotein-binding term covers the shared recognition chemistry, including phosphorylated ACCA for which the inspected abstract does not resolve the bound residue; source-specific phosphoserine refinements remain explicit in the individual annotation reviews.

A DNA-binding module in the central BRCA1 region cooperates with a separate BARD1 DNA-binding module in the heterodimer. Purified-protein and single-molecule experiments link these modules to stimulation of long-range resection by EXO1 and BLM–DNA2 or WRN–DNA2. BRCA1 helps position and support the resection machinery; it is not the helicase or nuclease. Fragment assays establish BRCA1 DNA affinity, whereas intact-complex and BARD1-mutant experiments establish additional context without making every result a BRCA1-specific mutant assay.

Promotes assembly of productive RAD51-ssDNA nucleofilaments and thereby activates RAD51-catalyzed DNA strand exchange during homologous recombination. Full-length BRCA2 targets RAD51 to ssDNA, overcomes RPA occupancy and stabilizes the filament; RAD51 performs DNA pairing and strand exchange.

Protects the regressed arms of stalled or reversed replication forks from excessive nuclease degradation through BRCA2-dependent RAD51 filament stabilization, a genome-maintenance role separable from double-strand-break repair by homologous recombination. This is the protective contribution to replication fork processing; it does not mean that BRCA2 itself reverses forks or catalyzes fork restart.
Hydrolyses biocytin and related biotin amides to release free biotin for metabolic reuse; the active human enzyme is established in serum and the secretory/extracellular compartment.

ATP-dependent nonreceptor tyrosine phosphorylation transmits immune-receptor signals. BTK activates PLCgamma2 in BCR assemblies and participates in TIRAP-associated innate signaling; direct phosphorylation of NLRP3 supports inflammasome assembly in demonstrated priming/activation settings. B-cell calcium and NF-kappaB responses are downstream consequences of this kinase mechanism, not additional catalytic activities.

Specific PIP3 recognition by the PH domain recruits BTK to the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane, coupling lipid second-messenger production to kinase activation and receptor signaling. Quantitative isolated-domain binding and full-length redistribution studies support this own binding activity; it does not assign phosphoinositide synthesis or hydrolysis to BTK.

Within the mitotic checkpoint complex, BUBR1 contacts CDC20 through degron-like motifs and obstructs APC/C substrate recognition and E2 engagement, delaying anaphase until checkpoint signaling is satisfied.

At mitotic kinetochores, BUBR1 recruits PP2A-B56 through its KARD LxxIxE motif. This adaptor function positions phosphatase activity to oppose excessive Aurora B signaling, stabilize kinetochore–microtubule attachments and support chromosome congression and checkpoint silencing.

Phospho-MELT reader and kinetochore adaptor: in the constitutive BUB1-BUB3 complex, BUB3's WD40 propeller binds MPS1-phosphorylated KNL1 MELT motifs and the BUB1 GLEBS motif, docking BUB1 (and, downstream, BUBR1, MAD1-MAD2 and CDC20) at unattached kinetochores to assemble the SAC signalling platform and to promote efficient end-on kinetochore-microtubule attachment.

Structural subunit of the mitotic checkpoint complex: BUB3 bound to the BUBR1 GLEBS motif is incorporated with closed MAD2 and CDC20 into the diffusible MCC that binds and inhibits APC/C-CDC20, delaying securin and cyclin B degradation and anaphase onset. BUB3 supports BUBR1 engagement rather than contacting the APC/C itself, so it contributes to, but does not independently exert, the ubiquitin ligase inhibitor activity.

An Fe(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent prolyl hydroxylase that modifies HIF-alpha oxygen-dependent degradation domains. Hydroxylation supplies the recognition signal for VHL-dependent ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal turnover, coupling oxygen availability to suppression of HIF signaling. EGLN1 catalyzes the hydroxylation step; the downstream ubiquitin ligase and proteasome carry out targeting and degradation.

Recognizes immunoglobulins through the A-chain globular module and the multivalent C1q head assembly, coupling surface-bound IgG or IgM recognition to C1r/C1s activation in classical complement. The recognition/assembly role is distinct from the proteolytic reactions performed by C1r and C1s.

Contributes the A-chain structural component to phosphatidylserine recognition by the heterotrimeric C1q globular heads on altered-self surfaces. Human C1q and its globular region bind phosphatidylserine, but the principal crystallographic phosphoserine site lies on chain C; autonomous A-chain sufficiency is not established.

Contributes to extracellular receptor-ligand activity of assembled C1q: the globular region binds CD33 and stimulates its inhibitory signaling motifs in human monocytes. This is activation of an inhibitory receptor, not inhibition of ligand-receptor engagement, and neither isolated A-chain sufficiency nor a C1QA kinase activity is implied.

The B-chain globular module binds immunoglobulins, preferentially IgG in the tested isolated-module assays, within the multivalent C1q recognition assembly. Its collagen-like region supplies a C1r/C1s recruitment interface: mature B-chain Lys61 is required for efficient protease-tetramer binding and activation in recombinant human C1q. These recognition and structural activities initiate the classical complement pathway; C1r and C1s perform the proteolysis.

As a structural constituent of the heterotrimeric C1q heads, the B chain contributes to recognition of phosphatidylserine exposed on apoptotic cells. Human C1q and its globular region directly bind this lipid. The principal crystallographically observed phosphoserine pocket lies on the C chain; autonomous phosphatidylserine binding by the B chain has not been established by these experiments.

The B chain contributes to the extracellular C1q ligand assembly that binds inhibitory immunoreceptors. Human whole-C1q experiments demonstrate CD33 binding and ITIM phosphorylation and coordinated engagement of CD33 with LAIR-1 on monocytes. This is a contributed ligand function of the intact protein assembly; the experiments do not establish that an isolated B chain is sufficient for receptor activation.

Associate with the serine/threonine kinase NEK1 in a basal-body and cytoplasmic complex. Local partner association, basal-body clustering and interaction-sensitive ciliation rescue support a nonenzymatic contribution to primary-cilium assembly, while the precise assembly step remains unresolved.

C3b attaches to target surfaces through its exposed thioester and binds complement partners to assemble and regulate convertases. C3b-containing fragments also present recognition ligands that promote phagocytic engulfment. This nonenzymatic complement-effector unit serves several activation pathways, including the GZMK pathway; Bb or activated C2 supplies convertase proteolysis.

Deposited C3d-containing fragments bind CR2/CD21, supplying an extracellular ligand that links complement-tagged antigen to B-cell co-receptor recognition and enhanced activation. This receptor-recognition function is distinct from the larger C3b convertase scaffold and from soluble C3a signaling.

Released C3a binds and activates C3AR1, initiating G-protein and arrestin signaling and context-dependent inflammatory responses. This soluble anaphylatoxin ligand is distinct from C3a-desArg/ASP and does not acquire a chemokine-receptor activity from the structural receptor experiments.

Chaperone / assembly factor that acts during the mid-stage (MCIA-associated) construction of the membrane arm of mitochondrial Complex I. TIMMDC1 transiently binds incompletely assembled Complex I intermediates (including the ~315 kDa subcomplex) together with NDUFAF3, NDUFAF4 and the MCIA machinery (which also engages TMEM70/TMEM242), and dissociates on maturation of the holoenzyme. Its precise molecular activity is unresolved: as a Tim17/Tim22/Tim23-family multi-pass inner-membrane protein it is a candidate membrane scaffold/insertase for the ND (membrane-arm) subunits, but no catalytic insertase or transporter activity has been demonstrated, and it is not a stable structural subunit of the Complex I holoenzyme; therefore no specific molecular_function term is asserted.

Scaffold subunit of the ring-shaped ERLIN1/ERLIN2 SPFH-domain complex that binds inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) tetramers and, with the E3 ligase RNF170, mediates their ER-associated degradation, controlling calcium signaling.

Cholesterol-binding ER membrane protein that restricts SREBP activation by associating with the SREBP-SCAP-Insig machinery and that promotes sterol-accelerated ERAD of HMG-CoA reductase via a gp78/AMFR ubiquitin ligase complex, thereby negatively regulating cholesterol and fatty acid biosynthesis.

ER-membrane adaptor that binds and recruits multiple ER ubiquitin ligases (RNF170, AMFR/gp78, SYVN1, RNF139, RNF185/RNF5) to the ERLIN complex, coupling substrate recognition to ubiquitination during ERAD.

Catalyzes reversible CO2/bicarbonate interconversion through a zinc-dependent active site, supporting cytosolic acid-base equilibration and intracellular pH regulation. Transport proteins move the ions across membranes; CAII performs the associated carbonate chemistry.

Catalyzes zinc-dependent, reversible carbon dioxide/bicarbonate interconversion in the mitochondrial matrix. Bicarbonate production supplies CPS1 and mitochondrial carboxylases, which carry out the downstream nitrogen-disposal and carboxylation reactions.

Binds the cytoplasmic regulatory region of ITPR1 and inhibits IP3-dependent calcium release from intracellular stores. CA8 itself supplies the channel-regulatory activity; ITPR1 forms the calcium-conducting pore. Mouse biochemical mapping, human CA8-fragment interaction assays and receptor-defined HeLa calcium imaging support this mechanism. Exact contact residues and allosteric transmission remain unresolved, and the separate negative Purkinje-culture binding result limits claims of universal interaction across assay conditions. Purkinje-cell enrichment and human loss-of-function phenotypes give neuronal context without proving that every CA8-dependent phenotype is exclusively mediated by ITPR1.

CaBP2 limits CaV1.3 channel inactivation and supports synaptic sound encoding at inner-hair-cell synapses. Calcium sensing and membrane association are features of this regulatory unit. Human genetics and heterologous channel assays complement native mouse IHC/SGN physiology. Sustained synaptic channel availability is the proposed link between channel regulation and sound encoding; peak-current amplitude and synaptic exocytosis are not assumed to change uniformly across assays.

The alpha1B pore converts strong membrane depolarization into calcium entry through neuronal CaV2.2 channels, coupling electrical activity to neurotransmitter release. Beta and alpha2delta subunits support channel expression and gating, and interaction partners regulate this same channel unit. Alpha1B conducts the ion; calcium sensing by release machinery and membrane fusion occur downstream.

The alpha1C pore couples membrane depolarization to calcium entry through L-type CaV1.2 channels. In cardiac muscle, this current contributes to electrical excitation and triggers RyR-mediated stored-calcium release for contraction. Auxiliary subunits and calmodulin regulate this same pore unit, and splice variation changes its gating and surface expression. The channel supplies trigger calcium; the ryanodine receptor performs sarcoplasmic-reticulum release.

CaV1.3 couples membrane depolarization to calcium entry through the alpha1D pore. Relatively negative activation within the L-type family supports sinoatrial pacemaker depolarization and calcium-triggered transmitter release from cochlear inner hair cells. Auxiliary subunits, calmodulin and C-terminal splice variation tune this same channel unit. Human channel reconstitution and SANDD electrophysiology complement native mouse and clinical evidence for these tissue roles.

CaV2.3 couples membrane depolarization to calcium influx through the alpha1E pore. In neuronal membranes this supplies calcium for synaptic signaling and transmitter release. Auxiliary subunits and splice variation modulate the same channel unit; they do not replace its pore-forming activity.

Forms the CaV1.4 L-type calcium pore in a voltage-gated channel complex. Calcium entry across the plasma membrane links retinal voltage changes to transmitter-release signaling and visual perception. Alternative C-terminal splicing and CaBP4 change channel activation and inactivation, so the kinetic behavior depends on the product and its molecular partners.
Opens at relatively negative membrane potentials to conduct calcium into excitable cells across the plasma membrane, contributing to depolarization and firing behavior.

Alpha-2/delta-1 is a constitutive auxiliary subunit of high-voltage-activated calcium channel complexes. Assembled with a CaV1 or CaV2 pore-forming alpha-1 subunit and a cytoplasmic CaV-beta subunit, it is required for the complex to produce a normal calcium current. It contributes no pore of its own - the mature protein is a disulphide-linked extracellular alpha-2 chain plus a membrane-attached delta chain, GPI-anchored on the outer face of the plasma membrane - so its participation in conduction is recorded as a contribution to a complex-level activity rather than an activity it independently enables. Deployed in skeletal and cardiac muscle T-tubules and at neuronal presynaptic terminals.

Separately from being counted as part of the conducting complex, alpha-2/delta-1 modulates that complex. It raises peak calcium-current density and shifts voltage-dependent activation to more negative potentials, and it does so principally by increasing the number of channels delivered to and retained at the plasma membrane rather than by changing the unitary behaviour of the alpha-1 subunit. This trafficking-and-gating modulation is the subunit's own contribution, it is what disease variants perturb, and it is the property the 2025 presynaptic triple knockout confirmed while overturning the synaptogenic claims. It is also the reason gabapentinoids, which bind alpha-2/delta-1, act on neuronal excitability despite having little direct effect on calcium current.

CaVbeta2 is an essential auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated calcium channel complexes. It binds the alpha1 subunit AID with nanomolar affinity (6-20 nM) via its GK domain. PMID:1309651 demonstrated that beta2 is obligatory for functional channel expression and promotes calcium ion transport by enabling channel trafficking to the plasma membrane and modulating channel gating.

PMID:25533460 demonstrated direct CaVbeta-actin interaction using co-sedimentation and FRET experiments. This interaction promotes channel trafficking to the plasma membrane, representing a novel mechanism for beta subunit function.

Carnitine:O-acyl-L-carnitine antiporter of the mitochondrial inner membrane: catalyzes the electroneutral exchange of long-chain O-acyl-L-carnitine for free L-carnitine (and at lower rates carnitine uniport), the translocase step of the carnitine shuttle that delivers long-chain fatty acids into the matrix for beta-oxidation.

Delivery of long-chain fatty acids (as acylcarnitines) into the mitochondrial matrix for fatty acid beta-oxidation; SLC25A20 transports acylcarnitine across the inner membrane so CPT2 can regenerate acyl-CoA for the beta-oxidation spiral.

The CPS II module couples glutamine hydrolysis to ATP-dependent carbamoyl phosphate synthesis in the cytosol, supplying the first chemical intermediate for de novo pyrimidine production. The ammonia-dependent and glutaminase partial activities belong to this coupled function.
The ATCase module transfers carbamoyl phosphate to L-aspartate, producing N-carbamoyl-L-aspartate as the second step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis.
The DHO module catalyzes reversible zinc-dependent cyclization of N-carbamoyl-L-aspartate to (S)-dihydroorotate, completing the three CAD reactions before downstream pyrimidine-nucleotide synthesis.

Calcium-bound calmodulin activates protein serine/threonine kinases, exemplified by human CaMKII, by binding the regulatory segment and relieving autoinhibition. Calcium binding is the sensing mechanism of this regulatory unit; the kinase performs ATP-dependent phosphate transfer. The distinct kinase targets and cellular contexts do not imply that every calmodulin-binding kinase is activated.

Calcium-responsive calmodulin activates calcineurin through direct regulatory association, enabling the phosphatase to dephosphorylate substrates such as NFAT. Calmodulin contributes its own phosphatase-activator activity and does not itself hydrolyze substrate phosphate groups.

Calmodulin regulates calcium-channel activity through target association and calcium sensing. In cardiac channel systems it supports CaV1.2 calcium-dependent inactivation and restrains RyR2-mediated release, contributing to electrical regulation and excitation-contraction coupling. Regulation is target-dependent: other channel contexts, including the curated TRPV4 complex, can be potentiated. The shared calmodulin protein is the regulator, not the channel pore; gene-specific CALM1 disease evidence is distinguished from assays of the shared protein and from mouse RyR2 models.

Calcium-bound calmodulin activates protein serine/threonine kinases such as CaMKII through regulatory association and relief of autoinhibition. Calcium binding is the sensing mechanism of this unit; the kinase performs phosphate transfer. Human CaMKII structural and interaction studies establish the shared-protein mechanism without implying that every calmodulin-binding kinase is activated.

Calmodulin activates calcineurin through calcium-dependent target association, enabling phosphatase signaling. Human calmodulin conformational-lock experiments distinguish this activating function from the phosphatase reaction itself. Cytoplasmic and nuclear calmodulin complexes provide cellular context; the common protein sequence does not identify which CALM gene supplied an individual measured molecule.

Calmodulin regulates calcium channels by sensing calcium and associating with channel regulatory regions. It supports CaV1.2 calcium-dependent inactivation and restrains RyR2-mediated release, coupling calcium sensing to cardiac electrical and excitation-contraction regulation. The broad regulatory unit includes these channel-specific inhibitory mechanisms without making inhibition universal. Human CALM2-associated long-QT evidence is separated from CALM1 and CALM3 variant studies and mouse RyR2 models; calmodulin is an accessory regulator rather than the conducting pore.

Calmodulin binds calcium through its EF-hand sites and couples changing calcium occupancy to conformational changes and target regulation. This calcium-sensor activity is shared by the identical human calmodulin proteins. Direct CALM3 variant affinity measurements and human calmodulin conformational studies support the sensing mechanism; gene-specific expression is a separate question.

Calcium-bound calmodulin activates protein serine/threonine kinases, exemplified by human CaMKII, through regulatory-segment binding and relief of autoinhibition. Calcium binding is the sensing mechanism; the kinase performs phosphate transfer. Shared-protein experiments do not imply that every calmodulin-binding kinase is activated.

Calcium-responsive calmodulin activates calcineurin through direct regulatory association, enabling calcineurin-dependent signaling. Calmodulin supplies its own phosphatase-activator activity, while calcineurin hydrolyzes substrate phosphate groups.

Calmodulin regulates calcium-channel activity through target binding and calcium sensing. In cardiac systems it supports CaV1.2 calcium-dependent inactivation and restrains RyR2-mediated calcium release, coupling its regulatory work to electrical activity and contraction. CALM3 A103V and E141K evidence is distinguished from CALM1 disease variants and mouse RyR2 experiments. Calmodulin is a regulator, not the channel pore.

Calmodulin binds and modulates nitric-oxide synthase, including relief of caveolin-mediated inhibition of endothelial NOS. This is the regulator activity of the shared calmodulin protein; NOS carries out NO synthesis. The biochemical function does not by itself establish CALM3-specific endothelial expression.

Lectin chaperone that binds monoglucosylated N-glycans on nascent glycoproteins in the ER lumen and, with ERp57 and cyclophilin B recruited via its P domain, promotes their folding and oligomeric assembly as part of the calnexin/calreticulin cycle.
Lectin that recognizes monoglucosylated N-glycans, providing the carbohydrate-binding specificity that underlies glycoprotein quality control and retention of incompletely folded clients.
High-capacity calcium-binding protein that buffers ER calcium and regulates intracellular calcium homeostasis and ER calcium storage capacity.

Phosphorylates neuronal targets as a calcium/calmodulin-regulated CaMKII-alpha subunit, coupling calcium signals and intersubunit autophosphorylation to synaptic potentiation and spine development. Target binding and holoenzyme assembly organize this catalytic activity rather than constituting redundant kinase cores.

CAML is a core subunit of the GET (guided entry of tail-anchored proteins) insertase complex. Together with WRB/GET1 it forms the ER membrane receptor for the cytosolic ATPase TRC40/GET3 and mediates post-translational insertion of tail-anchored membrane proteins into the ER membrane.

Catalyzes calcium-dependent endoproteolysis and self processing in the titin-associated muscle environment, supporting muscle-cell maintenance and adaptation. Substrate access and localization change with binding and the extent of autolysis; a complete physiological substrate repertoire is not established.

Selectively binds aldolase A and promotes its recruitment into muscle protein complexes associated with calcium release. This broad adaptor function is supported mainly by mouse null-versus-C129S experiments and controlled recombinant binding. Direct RyR contact, a defined titin-to-triad bridge, exact stoichiometry and precise human subcompartment remain unresolved.

Catalyzes calcium-dependent proteolysis, with self-cleavage directly demonstrated in full-length human CAPN5 assays. Intracellular membrane association promotes activation in these assays. The physiological function of self-cleavage, the activity of its fragments and native substrate specificity remain incompletely established; self-cleavage is not assumed to mature or activate the enzyme.

Binds regulatory DNA through its paired-like homeodomain and regulates RNA polymerase II transcription in the nucleus, contributing to embryonic craniofacial skeletal patterning. Human hCART1 activates selected-site reporters and represses a distinct promoter. Endogenous ALX1 occupancy and ALX1-dependent chromatin and transcriptional changes in human cranial neural crest cells connect this activity to regional facial programs; mouse Alx1 loss establishes corresponding skeletal-patterning defects. The developmental role uses the same transcription-factor mechanism. Long-term perturbations do not identify every affected gene as a direct target, and ALX4 structural measurements are not attributed to ALX1.

Organizes membrane-associated protein assemblies through distinct interaction domains, connecting transmembrane partners to intracellular scaffolds and positioning partner proteins. Human CASK binding assays, mammalian complexes and conserved LIN2/CASK functional evidence support this mechanism; individual interactome hits are not assumed to participate in the same complex.

Catalyzes ATP-dependent protein phosphotransfer through the N-terminal kinase domain, including neurexin-tail phosphorylation promoted by substrate recruitment. Magnesium is not required and inhibits the measured activity; calcium/calmodulin dependence is not implied by the protein name. The separate C-terminal GUK-like region is not assigned GMP kinase catalysis.

Cysteine-type endopeptidase (ICE) activity: the inflammasome effector protease. Procaspase-1 is clustered and autoactivated through CARD-CARD interactions, then cleaves its physiological substrates after an Asp (YVAD consensus) using the His237/Cys285 catalytic dyad.

Maturation of the proinflammatory cytokines IL-1 beta and IL-18: caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1 beta (at Asp116-Ala117) and pro-IL-18 (at Asp36-Tyr37) to their active, secreted, receptor-binding forms. This is the defining physiological output of caspase-1.

Cleavage of gasdermin-D to execute pyroptosis. Autoprocessed caspase-1 engages full-length GSDMD through both its active site and an exosite that binds the GSDMD C-terminal domain, cleaving the interdomain linker to release the pore-forming N-terminal fragment that drives lytic, proinflammatory pyroptotic cell death and IL-1 cytokine release.

CARD-mediated recruitment and self-assembly: the caspase-1 CARD engages activators (directly for NLRC4/CARD8, or via the ASC adaptor for NLRP3/AIM2/pyrin) and polymerizes into a filament, enabling proximity-induced autoprocessing of the zymogen into the active p20/p10 enzyme.
CASP10 tandem death effector domains bind FADD to recruit procaspase-10 to Fas/CD95 and TRAIL death-inducing signaling complexes.
Activated CASP10 cleaves downstream caspase zymogens after Asp residues to propagate apoptotic caspase maturation toward the execution phase.
CASP14 acts as a cysteine-type endopeptidase to cleave filaggrin during cornification, generating natural moisturizing factors essential for skin barrier function

Caspase-3 is a cysteine-type endopeptidase (EC 3.4.22.56) that cleaves substrates after aspartate residues, with a strict requirement for Asp at the P1 and P4 positions of an Asp-X-X-Asp recognition motif. It is synthesized as a zymogen and activated by cleavage by initiator caspases or granzyme B into a p17/p12 heterotetramer.

As the principal executioner caspase, caspase-3 carries out the demolition phase of apoptosis by cleaving many cellular substrates (e.g., PARP1; ICAD/DFF45 to release the CAD/DFF40 DNA-fragmentation nuclease; cytoskeletal, junctional and signaling proteins) and by driving phosphatidylserine exposure through cleavage of XKR scramblases and the ATP11C flippase.

Caspase-3 cleaves and activates gasdermin-E (GSDME/DFNA5), switching apoptotic cells to pyroptosis and permitting IL-1 beta release, coupling the apoptotic protease to a pro-inflammatory lytic cell-death program.

Caspase-3 restrains innate immune and cytokine signaling by cleaving antiviral signaling proteins (cGAS, MAVS, IRF3) and NF-kB subunits (p65/RelA, RelB, c-Rel) and by processing cytokines such as IL-18, dampening cytokine production during apoptosis.

CASQ2 binds and sequesters calcium in the sarcoplasmic-reticulum lumen. Calcium-dependent oligomer and polymer assembly supports a high-capacity calcium reservoir for cardiac contraction. This storage activity is coupled to release-complex regulation but is distinct from modulation of the channel itself.

CASQ2 modulates RyR2 calcium-channel activity through luminal release-complex interactions. Reconstituted channels show inhibition under defined low-luminal-calcium conditions, while human CSQ2–RyR2 association and cell assays support regulation whose observed kinetics also include calcium buffering. The effect depends on luminal calcium and accessory-protein context. CASQ2 performs the regulatory contribution; RyR2 forms the conducting pore.

Senses extracellular calcium through a dimeric class C G protein-coupled receptor and transmits the signal through Gq/11- and Gi-linked pathways. Ligand-dependent extracellular-domain closure and transmembrane rearrangement regulate cellular phosphoinositide, calcium and cyclic-AMP responses, providing a receptor mechanism for endocrine and renal calcium control. Amino acids modulate calcium sensitivity; their agonist versus allosteric classification depends on assay conditions.

CAV1 contributes its own structural contacts to a stable caveolin oligomer and caveolar coat. Human-cell coat isolation, the tightly packed human CAV1 disc and disruption by Arg54Ala support integral structural scaffolding. Membrane reconstitution supports leaflet insertion; the bacterial detergent-purified 11-mer is not assumed to be the universal native stoichiometry. This structural role is distinct from bridging transient signaling partners.

CAV1 organizes contacts and local retention among selected membrane-associated proteins. Human TRPC1 surface retention and recruitment into STIM1-associated domains exemplify this adaptor contribution; CAV1 is not the conducting pore or STIM1 calcium sensor. Relative expression and activation state can alter channel output, so the unit describes organization rather than universal activation. Raft-associated membrane domains are an established location for selected partner organization; detergent fractionation does not identify every such domain as a morphologic caveola.

CAV1 can directly inhibit nitric-oxide synthase through physical interaction, coupling caveolar organization to control of NO production. Peptide and recombinant-enzyme experiments are complemented by full-length cellular coexpression; reductase-linked inhibition and calmodulin reversibility qualify a simple universal motif-competition model. The tested NOS species and isoforms differ, and equivalent native regulation of every NOS isoform is not assumed.

Caveolar coat organization and coordinated protein recruitment at the muscle sarcolemma. CAV3 oligomers and cavin associations organize caveolae; dysferlin/MG53 partnerships link this membrane organization to repair. The resolved molecular-adaptor example recruits NEDD4-2 to hERG and controls mature-channel surface turnover. This does not make CAV3 a ubiquitin ligase, ion-conducting channel, or obligatory stable subunit of the purified dystrophin complex.

Context-dependent regulation of T-type calcium channels. CAV3 associates with CaV3.2 and influences its current and PKA-dependent modulation. Human-construct HEK293 studies and mouse cardiomyocyte experiments distinguish CaV3.2 from CaV3.1 and distinguish altered activity from measured surface abundance; CAV3 is not the channel pore or a calcium-binding sensor.

MICU1 is the calcium sensor of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter. Its two EF-hands face the intermembrane space and bind Ca2+ with high affinity and, in the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer, strong cooperativity, with the transition matching the measured threshold for uniporter disinhibition. Ca2+ binding is transduced into a conformational change of the holocomplex that switches MCU between a blocked and a conducting state, so that matrix Ca2+ tracks cytosolic Ca2+ transients rather than resting Ca2+.

In the Ca2+-free state MICU1 inhibits the uniporter, preventing Ca2+ flux through MCU at resting cytosolic Ca2+ and thereby setting the threshold for mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake. Purified MICU1 suppresses MCU currents in a manner abolished by mutating the MCU-interacting residue K126, and MICU1 restricts cation flux through the uniporter even under divalent-free conditions. Whether this is best described as physical occlusion or as allosteric inhibition has been disputed; current direct evidence favours occlusion.

MICU1 heterodimerises with MICU2 or MICU3 through an intersubunit disulfide; the dimer, not the monomer, is the functional gating unit, and its composition tunes the threshold and cooperativity of the uniporter. MICU2 is inhibitory and MICU1 stimulatory, so the dimer imposes a sigmoidal response of matrix Ca2+ uptake to cytosolic Ca2+. Dimer formation is itself Ca2+-dependent and, unlike gating, does not require MCU.

Independently of its role in the uniporter, MICU1 localises to the inner boundary membrane and cristae junctions, interacts with the MICOS components MIC60 and CHCHD2, and is required for MICOS complex formation and normal cristae organisation. Loss of MICU1 alters mitochondrial ultrastructure, membrane dynamics and cell-death signalling, and Micu1-null lethality is not rescued by deleting MCU or EMRE.

CBL recruits an E2 through its RING domain and promotes ubiquitin transfer to selected receptor and signaling substrates. This activity helps attenuate receptor signaling and directs endocytic sorting; CBL is an E3 rather than an E2 or a HECT-type thioester enzyme. In the LAG3 context, CBL and CBLB can redundantly assemble K63-linked chains that alter signaling-tail membrane association without measurably shortening LAG3 half-life. Substrate fate is therefore context dependent. In human osteoblasts, FGFR2 recruits CBL to plasma-membrane raft microdomains where increased CBL–PI3K association accompanies PI3K ubiquitination and degradation; this is a defined signaling context, not a universal location for every substrate.

The TKB module recognizes selected phosphorylated tyrosine motifs on kinases and regulatory proteins, positioning CBL in substrate or regulatory complexes. Structures and binding measurements establish this recognition independently of whether each intact partner is ultimately ubiquitinated. Positive partner motifs are not generalized to the wild-type FLT1 peptide that failed binding in the tested assay.

CBL supplies proline-rich recognition sequences that engage SH3 domains in recruitment and trafficking adaptors, including CIN85, intersectin and GRB2 in the demonstrated recruitment contexts. This interaction module links CBL to signaling and endocytic complexes. It is CBL binding a domain on its partner; phosphorylation of CBL and recruitment of a phosphotyrosine-binding partner are separate mechanisms.
ER-resident collagen-specific molecular chaperone that binds the folded triple-helical region of procollagen, stabilizing it and preventing premature aggregation during collagen biosynthesis.

Collagen-dedicated chaperone activity within the early secretory pathway; HSP47 escorts procollagen from the ER to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment, where pH-dependent release allows HSP47 to recycle back to the ER.

CBS catalyzes PLP-dependent beta-replacement reactions that convert serine and homocysteine to cystathionine in cytosolic transsulfuration, and can generate H2S when cysteine replaces serine. SAM-dependent allostery, heme-mediated regulation and oligomeric assembly regulate this catalytic unit; they are not separate core occupations.

Rap1 effector: KRIT1 binds GTP-loaded Rap1 through its FERM F1/F2 lobes, which releases it from microtubules and recruits it to junctional plasma membrane, where it stabilizes endothelial cell-cell junctions.

Junctional adaptor of the CCM complex: the KRIT1 FERM domain binds the HEG1 cytoplasmic tail while its NPX(Y/F) motifs bind the CCM2 PTB domain, linking the KRIT1-CCM2-PDCD10 complex to endothelial junctions and restraining RhoA/Rho kinase signaling.
Membrane and microtubule binding that controls KRIT1 availability: KRIT1 binds microtubules through its N and C termini and binds PI(4,5)P2-containing membranes in a Rap1-enhanced manner.
ICAP1 sequestration: KRIT1 binds ICAP1 by a bidentate surface and competes with the beta1 integrin tail, relieving ICAP1-mediated suppression of integrin activation.

Mitogen-responsive regulatory subunit that binds and activates CDK4, forming the cyclin D1-CDK4 holoenzyme that phosphorylates RB-family pocket proteins in the nucleus during G1 and thereby derepresses E2F and drives the G1/S transition.
Binds and activates CDK6 in the alternative cyclin D1-CDK6 holoenzyme, which phosphorylates RB in mid-G1 and links growth-factor stimulation to S-phase entry.

CDK-independent transcriptional corepressor: recruited to promoters by the zinc-finger factor INSM1 via its cyclin box, cyclin D1 bridges INSM1 to HDAC1/HDAC3 and represses NEUROD1 and insulin gene transcription.

Cyclin D2 binds and activates CDK4 or CDK6 as their regulatory cyclin subunit, enabling kinase-dependent control of RB-family proteins and G1/S progression. Complex assembly and redistribution from cytosol to nucleus provide spatial control of this activity.

Cyclin E1 functions as a regulatory subunit that binds and activates CDK2 (cyclin-dependent kinase 2), forming the cyclin E1-CDK2 holoenzyme complex. The cyclin E1-CDK2 complex phosphorylates RB1, releasing E2F transcription factors to activate S-phase gene expression, thereby driving the G1/S transition of the mitotic cell cycle.

Binds monomeric LPS and other acylated microbial ligands (lipopeptides, lipoteichoic acid) handed on by LBP and carries them to the TLR4-MD-2 complex or TLR2 heterodimers, acting as the ligand-delivery component of the LPS receptor complex at the cell surface and, as soluble CD14, in extracellular fluid.
Binds bacterial lipopolysaccharide directly through the amino-terminal hydrophobic pocket of its LRR solenoid.

Organizes a membrane receptor signaling complex through noncatalytic adaptor interactions. Its phosphorylated cytoplasmic tail recruits p85-containing PI3K and other signaling proteins, promoting PI3K activation and adjusting the activation threshold of B lymphocytes.

CD28 is the prototypic T cell coreceptor. It cooperates with the TCR by binding B7 ligands (CD80/CD86) on APCs to provide signal 2 for T cell activation. This is the single most precise molecular function term for CD28.

CD3 delta-epsilon supplies extracellular and transmembrane contacts that organize the TCR-CD3 receptor, while the CD3 delta cytoplasmic ITAM provides a phosphorylation-dependent signaling interface. This is a nonenzymatic structural and signaling contribution to the assembled receptor, including human alpha-beta and gamma-delta complexes. Ligand recognition belongs to the clonotypic TCR chains; in a class-II-restricted alpha-beta complex, CD3D contributes to the complex-level MHC class II receptor activity without itself determining class restriction.

Organizes the TCR-CD3 receptor through extracellular and transmembrane assembly contacts and recruits intracellular signaling proteins through distinct basic, proline-rich and ITAM interfaces. LCK recruitment, SH3-domain recognition and phospho-ITAM kinase docking are own molecular interactions within this adaptor role; phosphorylation is performed by associated kinases.

Phosphorylated CD3E ITAM docks the tandem SH2 domains of the tyrosine kinases ZAP70 and SYK, recruiting them to the engaged TCR. Before ITAM phosphorylation, the membrane-proximal basic residue-rich sequence binds the Unique domain of LCK and the ligation-exposed RK motif binds the LCK SH3 domain, making CD3E the main LCK-recruiting CD3 chain; mono-phosphorylated CD3E ITAMs recruit the inhibitory kinase CSK.

Ligand-induced exposure of the CD3E proline-rich PxxDY sequence recruits NCK1, NCK2 and EPS8L1 SH3 domains. Phosphorylation of the shared Y166 residue switches off SH3 binding in favor of SH2-domain partners.

Recognizes the inhibitory ligand ITPRIPL1 at the cell surface and couples this input to inhibition of TCR-associated signaling. This ligand-recognition role is distinct from the assembly/adaptor contribution to clonotypic antigen recognition; detailed tumor and therapeutic outcomes remain species- and construct-dependent.

CD3 gamma supplies receptor-assembly contacts in the gamma-epsilon module and a cytoplasmic ITAM that recruits signaling effectors after phosphorylation. These activities couple an assembled membrane TCR to intracellular signaling; antigen specificity belongs to the clonotypic receptor chains.

The cytoplasmic dileucine sorting signal binds AP-2 and helps couple the surface TCR to internalization. Phosphoserine-dependent exposure and the surrounding tail context regulate this interaction in the intact receptor; uptake remains possible through other routes.

At the plasma membrane, phosphorylated CD247 ITAMs provide docking sites that organize receptor-proximal kinase signaling complexes. This adaptor activity contributes to the assembled transmembrane receptor response. MHC class II receptor activity is one valid class-II-restricted alpha-beta TCR context, not a specificity intrinsic to CD247. Ligand recognition and kinase catalysis are supplied by the relevant ligand-binding proteins and kinases. Human CD247 also supplies ITAM signaling capacity to selected Fc receptors.

CD247 transmembrane homodimerization supplies a physical assembly module for TCR-CD3 and human CD16A complexes; CD247 can also form mixed dimers with FcRgamma. CD247 itself supplies these organizing transmembrane contacts, thereby participating directly in assembly and surface expression of competent receptors; it is not merely a downstream requirement. Isolated cytoplasmic-domain tetramers at high concentration are not treated as the physiological assembly unit, and human/mouse CD16 compatibility differs.

Binds the membrane-proximal alpha-2/beta-2 concavity of peptide-MHC class II through the D1 immunoglobulin-like domain, acting as the coreceptor that stabilises class II-restricted antigen recognition by the T cell receptor; D4-mediated dimerization is required for stable class II binding.

Carries the Src-family kinase LCK on its cytoplasmic tail through a zinc clasp in which two CD4 cysteines and two cysteines of the LCK unique region co-coordinate one Zn2+ ion, delivering LCK to the peptide-MHC-engaged TCR-CD3 complex so that it can phosphorylate the CD3 ITAMs.

Coreceptor activity: acting with the antigen-engaged T cell receptor as the nearby primary receptor, CD4 raises the sensitivity of class II-restricted recognition and the resulting helper T cell response, a function that requires its cytoplasmic tail and raft localization.

Provides a membrane-tethered adaptor platform within the B-cell antigen receptor. The phosphorylated cytoplasmic ITAM recruits SYK, while a separate phosphorylated non-ITAM site recruits BLNK and couples receptor-proximal signaling to downstream effectors. CD79A also contributes, with CD79B and membrane immunoglobulin, to receptor assembly and transmembrane signal transmission. This receptor-associated unit supports pre-B/B-cell development and activation.

CD79B forms the Ig-alpha/Ig-beta signaling module with CD79A, supporting surface assembly and transmembrane signal transmission by the B-cell antigen receptor. Cooperative Ig-beta-dependent enhancement of Ig-alpha phosphorylation is supported by chimeric-receptor experiments. The paired chains also facilitate receptor-directed antigen delivery to late endosomal processing compartments; this trafficking context is supported at the receptor-complex level.
Sequesters ASF1 histone chaperones through direct binding and occupation of their interaction surfaces, limiting access to histones, downstream partners and the nucleus.

Acts as a noncatalytic activator of the CDIN1 RNA exonuclease. The C-terminal Codanin-1 fragment increases cleavage by purified stabilized CDIN1; the physiological substrates and activity of the unmodified full-length native complex remain unresolved.

Dephosphorylates protein substrates with a strong preference for proline-directed phosphoserine sites. Centrosomal and cytoplasmic pools regulate cilium growth through protein dephosphorylation, including drebrin and centrosomal actin regulation. Cell-cycle substrate regulation is context dependent and does not require an indispensable yeast-like mitotic-exit role.

Ubiquitin ligase activator of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome: CDC20 docks on the mitotically phosphorylated APC/C via its C-box, KILR motif and IR tail, relieves Apc1 auto-inhibition and enhances E2 affinity, converting the APC/C into the active APC/C-CDC20 ligase that polyubiquitinates securin and cyclin B1 to trigger sister-chromatid separation and CDK1 inactivation at the metaphase/anaphase transition.

Substrate adaptor of the APC/C: the CDC20 WD40 beta-propeller recognises D-box, KEN-box and ABBA degrons on substrates (securin, cyclin B1, cyclin A, NEK2A, KIF18A, BUBR1, USP22, FBXO31, AXIN2) and presents them to the APC2-APC11 catalytic module for polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.

Inhibited effector of the spindle assembly checkpoint: at unattached kinetochores CDC20 is captured by C-MAD2 and BUBR1-BUB3 into the mitotic checkpoint complex, which blocks its degron receptor sites and E2 access and can also inhibit a second APC/C-bound CDC20, holding APC/C inactive until chromosome biorientation; APC/C-mediated ubiquitination of MCC-bound CDC20 then reactivates the ligase.

APC/C coactivator in oocyte meiosis I: CDC20 activates the APC/C to drive homologue disjunction and the meiosis I-to-meiosis II transition; biallelic loss-of-function variants cause oocyte maturation arrest and female infertility.

Acts as a membrane-associated GTP-controlled signaling switch that coordinates epithelial polarity through spatially restricted effector engagement. CDC42 hydrolyses GTP, whereas GAPs accelerate hydrolysis and downstream effectors execute their own catalytic activities. Human Caco-2 depletion and constitutive-activation experiments show that balanced CDC42 signaling is required for apical/basolateral organization.

Recognizes GBD/CRIB regions of effectors in a nucleotide-dependent manner, exemplified by WASP binding and release of autoinhibition. This effector engagement connects the CDC42 switch to actin remodeling and positive regulation of filopodium assembly. Human endothelial CDC42 inhibition reduces filopodia-like protrusions; CDC42 does not itself nucleate actin or phosphorylate substrates.

CDC45 binds single-stranded DNA and supplies structural interfaces that organize the nuclear CMG replication helicase. Together with GINS it supports the MCM2–7 motor during genome duplication; ATP-driven unwinding belongs to the assembled complex.

Endosomal sorting scaffold required for constitutive CTLA4 recycling through a Rab11 compartment and protection from lysosomal degradation. This human T-cell mechanism maintains CTLA4-mediated immune homeostasis without requiring LRBA to be a constitutive Rab11-compartment component or stable coat-complex subunit.

ARF-family-dependent trafficking scaffold recruited to the trans-Golgi network and Rab4-positive endosomes, where it supports general intracellular traffic and endolysosome homeostasis. This independently demonstrated route is kept separate from the CTLA4-to-Rab11 recycling mechanism; current evidence does not establish that the TGN/Rab4 pool directly hands CTLA4 to Rab11.

Trafficking factor for delivery of ATG9A-containing vesicles to damaged mitochondria and the phagophore assembly site during PINK1/Parkin mitophagy. The evidence supports a role in phagophore growth but does not establish LRBA as an ATG4 protease, ATG8-processing enzyme, or stable autophagy-complex subunit.

Activation-dependent A-kinase anchoring activity in human B cells through binding to PKA RIIalpha and RIIbeta regulatory subunits. This is a bounded scaffold function and does not imply protein kinase activity or a universal constitutive LRBA-PKA complex.
Cadherin ectodomains engage cadherins on neighboring cells to form homophilic adhesive contacts.

The cytoplasmic tail recruits beta-catenin, with plakoglobin as an alternative catenin partner, to connect cadherin adhesion complexes to the cortical cytoskeleton through associated catenins and actin-binding proteins.
The juxtamembrane cytoplasmic region binds p120-catenin (CTNND1), helping stabilize E-cadherin-containing adhesion complexes at the cell surface.
Calcium binding between extracellular cadherin repeats stabilizes the ectodomain geometry required for adhesive interactions.

Mediates calcium-dependent homophilic adhesion through its extracellular cadherin domains, establishing cohesive cell contacts. The direct human-protein assays include CDH11-bearing mouse L cells binding immobilized human CDH11 ectodomain. These adhesive contacts support cadherin-dependent movement along other cells, without implying a uniform direction of migration regulation.

The canonical cytoplasmic tail recruits beta-catenin into adhesive junctions, coupling CDH11 contacts to catenin-dependent junction organization. The tail-truncated splice isoform does not inherit this canonical linkage.
N-cadherin binds cadherins on apposed cells to supply calcium-dependent intercellular adhesion and organize adherens junctions.
The intracellular N-cadherin tail binds beta-catenin within the catenin complex, coupling the transmembrane adhesion molecule to junctional organization.

N-cadherin coordinates calcium ions at extracellular cadherin-domain interfaces, supporting the conformation used for calcium-dependent cell adhesion. Structural N-cadherin evidence supports this conserved binding activity; the developmental-variant experiments did not directly measure human mutant calcium affinity.

Mediates calcium-dependent homophilic cell-cell adhesion through its extracellular cadherin domains. Human P-cadherin confers adhesion on transfected mouse NIH3T3 cells, and human EC1–2 studies establish specific calcium-dependent self-recognition.

Associates with beta-catenin in adhesive junctions, coupling the membrane cadherin to catenin-containing junction organization.
