Native human co-immunoprecipitation corroborates the specific interaction without establishing a purified binary interface or assigning beta-catenin signaling activity to CDH3.
Cyclin D-dependent serine/threonine protein kinase that phosphorylates retinoblastoma-family pocket proteins (RB1, RBL1, RBL2) in G1 to derepress E2F and drive the G1/S transition.
Binds D-type cyclins (CCND1/2/3); cyclin binding is obligatory for assembly and activation of the CDK4 holoenzyme.
CDK5 is a CDK5R-activated proline-directed serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates neuronal, synaptic, cytoskeletal, stress-response, and autophagy-associated substrates.

In proliferating (non-neuronal) cells CDK5 partners with cyclin B1, rather than its neuronal p35/p39 activators, and is active during mitosis; this CDK5-cyclin B1 complex behaves as a canonical CDK-cyclin kinase that phosphorylates mitotic substrates to safeguard mitotic fidelity and genome stability.
CDK5 phosphorylates MAPT/tau and other microtubule-associated neuronal substrates, contributing to cytoskeletal regulation and neurodegeneration-relevant tau biology.

Stoichiometric inhibitor of nuclear G1/S cyclin-CDK2 complexes: p27 binds cyclin E-CDK2 and cyclin A-CDK2 through its bipartite kinase-inhibitory domain, preventing their activation and inhibiting already-active complexes, thereby keeping Rb hypophosphorylated and restraining the G1/S transition.

Cyclin binding tethers p27 to cell-cycle cyclin–CDK complexes and helps determine its recognition specificity. Sequential folding and kinase contact then form the inhibitory complex; binding to a kinase does not guarantee inhibition of every activating-partner complex.

p27 bridges cyclin D1 and CDK4 and stabilizes their assembly and nuclear targeting. The assembled trimer can be inhibited by unphosphorylated p27; phosphorylation, particularly at Tyr74, weakens the inhibitory kinase contact and permits substrate-dependent CDK4 catalysis while p27 remains associated.

Cytoplasmic p27 binds RhoA and modulates its activation state and downstream actin organization. In the RSK1/phosphorylation context studied, p27 depletion reverses reduced RhoA-GTP and altered motility. The direction of motility effects is cell-context dependent.
Binds and inhibits cyclin-dependent protein kinases, restraining progression through the mitotic cell cycle in the nucleus.

p16INK4A binds and inhibits CDK4/6, limiting productive cyclin D-dependent kinase activity and RB phosphorylation. This restrains G1/S progression and cell population expansion and contributes to stable arrest in senescence contexts. The molecular activity is assigned to the p16 protein; p14ARF has a separate reading frame and mechanism.

Recognizes cis-regulatory DNA through the bZIP dimer and regulates RNA polymerase II transcription, activating lineage-specific genes that establish granulocyte and adipocyte differentiation. Promoter-complex interactions, including E2F repression, couple this program to proliferative restraint. Promoter partners and the N-terminal product context determine output; p30 is not assumed to match p42 potency.

Kinetochore-microtubule coupler: at the outer kinetochore (corona) CENP-F binds microtubules through N- and C-terminal domains, tracks and harnesses force from depolymerizing microtubule ends, and contributes to attachment stability and force transduction (congression defects of CENP-F mutants depend mainly on its NDE1-binding region rather than on the microtubule-binding domains).

Adaptor linking the NudE/NudEL-LIS1-dynein module to cellular platforms: bound to NUP133 at nuclear pores in G2/prophase (centrosome-nucleus tethering; apical interkinetic nuclear migration) and to BUB1/CENP-E at kinetochores in mitosis, CENP-F recruits NDE1 and NDEL1, which in turn bind dynein and LIS1. Dynein recruitment by CENP-F is indirect; at kinetochores the CENP-F-NDE1 link mainly loads LIS1 and restrains dynein-mediated stripping of corona cargoes, while bulk kinetochore dynein recruitment is largely CENP-F-independent.

CEP250/C-Nap1 contributes cohesive structural material at proximal parental centriole ends and anchors linker components. Dynamic contacts between C-Nap1 assemblies and their association with rootlet-fiber termini maintain interphase centriole pairing and organize the centrosomal linker.

Binds actin filaments and severs them, promoting actin turnover and depolymerization in the muscle cytoskeleton. Full-length human protein has direct severing and depolymerization activity; muscle LIM protein modulates the latter. Human muscle studies report Z-disc/I-band localization, whereas neonatal rat cardiomyocytes show enrichment near M-bands. The shared sarcomeric context is represented here without claiming an exclusive subregion or converting the rat result into a human M-band assay.

Conducts chloride through an ATP-gated membrane pore, principally at epithelial apical surfaces. Phosphorylation and ATP-dependent gating control permeability while chloride follows its electrochemical gradient; this is not primary active anion pumping.

Conducts bicarbonate through the same anion pore, contributing to epithelial bicarbonate secretion. Human-protein inside-out patch assays establish direct permeation; dynamic external-chloride selectivity proposed in oocytes is distinguished from invariant selectivity under the later tested conditions.

Hydrolyzes ATP to support channel conformational cycling. Purified reconstituted CFTR ATPase measurements establish catalytic activity separate from passive pore permeation; the nucleotide-binding domains are functionally asymmetric. It is listed separately because nucleotide hydrolysis is a measured chemical reaction, whereas the channel terms describe ion permeation; ATP dependence alone would not establish this catalytic activity.

Catalyses acetyl-CoA-dependent acetylation of choline to supply acetylcholine for cholinergic neurotransmission, including the neuromuscular junction. This is intrinsic enzyme activity; synaptic vesicle loading and transmitter release are performed by other machinery.

Uses ATP hydrolysis to reorganize histone–DNA contacts and assemble or remodel nucleosomes on nuclear chromatin. Purified human CHD2 acts with histones and NAP1 in biochemical reconstitution; cellular chromatin expansion and H3.3 occupancy connect the motor to transcriptional and DNA-repair contexts without assigning autonomous histone-chaperone activity.

CHD3 uses ATP hydrolysis to reposition nucleosomes and alter chromatin accessibility. This motor activity supports context-dependent transcription regulation in CHD3-containing NuRD assemblies; deacetylation is performed by the HDAC subunits. Human purified-protein assays establish the remodeling step directly, while histone recognition and nuclear chromatin localization provide substrate and cellular context.

CHD4 uses ATP hydrolysis to reposition nucleosomes and change chromatin accessibility. Purified human protein assays and nucleosome-bound structures establish its motor work. At DNA lesions, recruited CHD4 supports local chromatin control and homologous recombination; it does not perform RAD51 strand exchange. The motor also operates in transcriptional contexts, including the repressive assemblies described separately.

CHD4 acts as a transcription corepressor by supplying ATP-dependent remodeling within recruited NuRD assemblies. Human erythroid perturbation and rescue experiments establish CHD4-dependent globin repression. ZIP-associated human NuRD purification supplies recruitment context, while its generic Mi-2 binding assays do not uniquely identify every interaction as CHD4. HDAC subunits provide deacetylation. ZNF410 controls CHD4 expression and is not thereby a demonstrated recruiter of CHD4 protein to globin. This is the regulatory role of recruited remodeling, not a claim of a separate ATPase-independent chemistry.
Choline kinase: ATP-dependent phosphorylation of choline to phosphocholine, the first committed step of the CDP-choline (Kennedy) pathway of phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis.

Ethanolamine kinase: ATP-dependent phosphorylation of ethanolamine to phosphoethanolamine, contributing to phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis; a secondary activity of the same active site (choline is preferred).
ATP binding in the nucleotide cleft formed by the N- and C-terminal lobes, providing the phosphate donor for choline/ethanolamine phosphorylation.

REP1 directly binds Rab proteins and escorts prenylated Rab to cellular membranes. It supplies substrate presentation to Rab geranylgeranyltransferase and therefore contributes to that complex activity without independently catalyzing geranylgeranyl transfer. GDP-release inhibition is an experimentally demonstrated property of the Rab-bound escort. Original reconstitution separates human, canine and rat assay contexts; later experiments explicitly use recombinant human REP1. UniProt records P24386-2 as a 110-residue product comprising residues 1-104 of the displayed 653-residue protein followed by RSTLLL; residues 111-653 are absent. This short product lacks most of the full-length escort sequence, so the established Rab-escort activity is not assigned to it. Its endogenous protein expression and possible function remain unresolved. The evidence also does not establish obligatory complex stoichiometry or a universal in-vivo Rab recycling role.

Alpha-chimaerin accelerates GTP hydrolysis on Rac, providing a regulated signaling step that couples guidance-receptor input to axonal cytoskeletal responses. Original purified human alpha2 experiments establish GAP activity; Rho and CDC42 were negative only under the tested assay conditions. Mouse/chick receptor association and GAP/SH2 perturbations establish performed regulation of axon extension and EphA-linked motor-axon guidance. Human-cell Rac-GTP measurements corroborate activity, while WT and mutant overexpression effects are dosage-sensitive. The older constructs were not sequence-aligned to all current products; receptor binding and alpha2 developmental assays do not establish universal all-product function. Human alpha2 C1-dependent diacylglycerol recognition helps position the GAP at membranes; intramolecular autoinhibition and additional inputs make ligand binding distinct from sufficient GAP activation.

Acetylcholine-activated Gq/11-coupled GPCR: acetylcholine binding to M1 at the plasma membrane promotes nucleotide exchange on Gq/G11 alpha subunits, which activate phospholipase C-beta to produce IP3/DAG and a rise in cytosolic calcium.

Postsynaptic modulation of neuronal excitability: in forebrain pyramidal and sympathetic neurons, M1 activation suppresses the M-type K+ current and depolarizes the cell, contributing to hippocampal LTP and memory.

Alpha1 contributes ligand-recognition and pore-gating elements to the muscle acetylcholine receptor heteropentamer, directly converting acetylcholine binding into postsynaptic cation current. Human receptor reconstitution and patient endplate recordings establish the transmission mechanism; two alpha chains act with beta/delta and gamma or epsilon. Calcium conduction is real but the adult calcium fraction is strongly influenced by epsilon, not established as an alpha1-only property. The current displayed P02708-2 functional product must be distinguished from P3A-containing P02708-1; the latter was not incorporated into functional receptors in the original human-product expression study. Existing annotation relations are preserved, while this synthesis explicitly represents subunit contribution.

Alpha4 contributes acetylcholine-recognition interfaces and pore/gating elements to neuronal nicotinic receptor heteropentamers. Human receptor currents and structural studies establish this ionotropic function, with two major alpha4beta2 stoichiometries and accessory-subunit-dependent calcium permeability and desensitization. Presynaptic receptor activity can modulate transmitter release, while receptor activation directly depolarizes the receptor-bearing cell.

Beta1 supplies a pore-lining helix and allosteric gating elements to the muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. In a heteropentamer containing two alpha1 chains, delta and either fetal gamma or adult epsilon, this contribution supports ACh-evoked cation current, endplate depolarization and neuromuscular excitation. In the adult receptor, canonical ligand-binding sites lie at alpha1–delta and alpha1–epsilon interfaces; beta1 gating can change receptor apparent affinity without establishing a direct beta1–ACh contact. Full-length human receptors establish the channel contribution; the function of the N-terminally shortened alternative product remains unresolved.

β2 contributes pore-lining segments and the complementary acetylcholine-binding surface to assembled neuronal nicotinic receptors. Agonist binding gates transmembrane cation flow, including calcium with composition-dependent permeability, coupling cholinergic signaling to membrane depolarization and transmitter-release modulation. Reconstitution and engineered human structures establish the subunit contribution, not an autonomous β2 channel or a universal native stoichiometry.

Gamma contributes pore, gating and complementary acetylcholine-binding elements to the fetal muscle receptor. Agonist-gated cation influx depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane and initiates muscle excitation. Human gamma-containing receptors carry a modest calcium current; native bovine structures resolve the gamma ligand-pocket contribution. Activity of the alternative human product remains unresolved.
CHST3 catalyzes PAPS-dependent GalNAc 6-O-sulfation during chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan biosynthesis in the Golgi.

ClC-5 exchanges chloride and protons across endosomal membranes, supporting proximal-tubule absorption of filtered proteins and solutes. Its proton-transport activity can acidify endosomes under suitable ion gradients; renal uptake also depends on coupled exchange when bulk ATP-driven acidification remains normal. Cytoplasmic adenyl-ribonucleotide recognition and trafficking interactions accompany this transport function.

ClC-7 functions as an electrogenic 2Cl(-)/1H(+) antiporter in the lysosomal membrane, exchanging two chloride ions for one proton and thereby providing the counter-ion conductance that supports V-ATPase-driven luminal acidification and raises luminal chloride concentration.

ClC-7 acts as the alpha-subunit of an obligate heteromeric complex with the beta-subunit OSTM1, which is required for ClC-7 protein stability and transport activity; the assembled CLCN7-OSTM1 complex is the functional transport unit in lysosomes and the osteoclast ruffled border.

ClC-7 transport is tonically inhibited by the lysosome-specific signaling lipid PI(3,5)P2, which binds a site at the transmembrane-cytosolic interface; relief of this inhibition (e.g. on PI(3,5)P2 depletion) activates the antiporter and modulates lysosomal acidification. Gain-of-function HOD variants (Y715C, K285T) line this lipid-binding pocket and reduce PI(3,5)P2 inhibition, causing excess transport. This regulatory lipid-binding function is well established but not currently captured in GOA.

Claudin-14 supplies a polymerizing membrane component of bicellular tight junctions. Homomeric strands and context-dependent copolymers form a barrier to paracellular passage; changes in strand composition couple its abundance to epithelial permeability.

CLN3 conducts chloride across endolysosomal membranes. Human expression, membrane-retargeting and selectivity-changing mutants establish channel activity; endogenous mouse currents additionally show luminal-pH dependence. The tested tagged constructs do not establish identical gating or conductance for all seven products. This ion-conducting role supports lysosomal physiology without assigning CLN3 the hydrolytic reactions performed by luminal enzymes.

A single detailed trafficking study demonstrates direct binding of the CLN3 cytosolic N-terminal fragment to active Rab7 and separate loop-fragment binding to RILP. Cellular associations with motor components and altered late-endosomal redistribution support a trafficking role. This experimentally mapped interaction capability has a narrower, single-study evidence base than the chloride-channel activity; simultaneous adaptor-complex assembly, GEF/GAP chemistry and autonomous motor activity remain unestablished.

CLN5 catalyzes lipid transacylation that produces BMP in the lysosomal compartment and contributes to lysosomal lipid homeostasis. Its measured BMP products and cellular contribution depend on substrate stereochemistry and lipid supply; this capacity is distinct from the PLD3/4 reaction producing S,S-BMP. The glycosylated protein is processed through the secretory pathway and can associate with the luminal lysosomal membrane.

CLN6 cooperates with CLN8 to recruit soluble lysosomal enzyme precursors at the ER. Its luminal-loop region is required for the tested enzyme associations; CLN6 remains in the ER while CLN8 supports subsequent Golgi delivery. CLN6 self-association is integrated into this recruitment role: the luminal-loop deletion retains self-association but loses enzyme association, so self-association alone is insufficient for recruitment. The assays do not resolve a scaffold geometry or simultaneous cargo/coat-adaptor bridging, and equivalent function has not been established for both annotated products.

CLN8 recruits soluble lysosomal enzymes at the ER membrane with CLN6 and couples their export to COPII coat machinery through a cytosolic Sec24-binding motif. CLN8 accompanies cargo out of the ER and cycles back through a C-terminal retrieval signal, maintaining lysosomal enzyme supply.

CLN8 catalyzes acyl-CoA-dependent headgroup acylation of lysophosphatidylglycerol to form BMP. Purified human protein performs this biosynthetic step in vitro, and human-cell loss/rescue links CLN8 to cellular BMP abundance. The tested LPG has a racemic headgroup; these assays do not establish exclusive product stereochemistry or the downstream transformations that produce lysosomal S,S-BMP.

Serine proteolysis within mitochondrial ClpXP. CLPP forms the catalytic chamber and binds the CLPX ATPase, which selects and unfolds substrates and supplies ATP-driven translocation. Direct human reconstitution and mutagenesis establish CLPP cleavage; model-system ERAL1 and respiratory-complex turnover studies place this chemistry in mitochondrial protein quality control. CLPX docking is part of this integrated function, not a second independent catalytic activity of CLPP.

CHC17 is the major structural component of clathrin-coated pits and vesicles at the plasma membrane. It forms triskelia with light chains that polymerize into polyhedral lattices to drive cargo internalization via AP-2 adaptor complexes.

CHC17 assembles with clathrin light chains (CLTA, CLTB) into triskelia, the fundamental building blocks of clathrin coats. The heavy chain provides the structural arms while light chains regulate assembly dynamics.
CHC17 functions at the TGN for lysosomal enzyme sorting and secretory pathway trafficking via AP-1 and GGA adaptor complexes.
CHC17 participates in mitosis through the TACC3/ch-TOG/clathrin complex that stabilizes kinetochore fibers by inter-microtubule bridging. This represents a well-documented moonlighting function.

CNGA1 contributes the cGMP-binding and pore-forming machinery of the rod CNGA1/CNGB1 channel, coupling intracellular ligand recognition to cation conduction. The physiological assembly has three alpha subunits and one beta subunit; experimentally expressed CNGA1 homotetramers also conduct. Human structural preparations use defined N-terminal truncations with full-length functional comparisons, and direct calcium-permeability support additionally comes from bovine recombinant channels. cAMP binding and partial activation remain secondary capabilities within this single channel mechanism.

CNGA3 contributes cGMP-recognition and pore-forming elements to the cone cyclic nucleotide-gated channel. Together with CNGB3 it couples intracellular cGMP to cation flow across outer-segment membranes, supporting the electrical response underlying cone vision. CNGA3 functions within the physiological heteromer and can also form conductive homomeric channels in expression experiments.

Channel-bearing CNGB1 contributes to an assembled intracellular cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channel: rod complexes contain three CNGA1 and one CNGB1, whereas the tested human olfactory complex contains two CNGA2, one CNGA4 and one CNGB1. Rod cGMP gating and olfactory cAMP gating belong to this integrated activity. Human structural preparations use CNGB1 456–1251, with full-length functional comparisons in the rod study; this engineered sequence is not the complete RCNC2A product. Rat native B1b is independently sequence-defined and must not be assigned to a human isoform solely by name. In the tested human olfactory complex, the CNGB1 456–1251 construct binds calmodulin through N- and C-terminal sites and supports calcium-dependent channel inhibition. The interface assignment combines a locally low-resolution map, prediction-assisted modeling, beta-specific cross-links and deletion tests; it is not an all-product binding claim. The shared ciliary-membrane location includes rod outer-segment plasma membrane and olfactory sensory-cilium membrane. Human-beta targeting in Xenopus rods and native rodent localization support these specific contexts; the rod-specific GO:0042622 source assertions remain explicit, without duplicating its GO:0060170 parent in this integrated core.

The soluble human GARP2 product Q14028-3 is inferred to inhibit basal, nonactivated rod PDE6 through orthologous protein interaction. Purified native bovine GARP2/Q28181-5 associates with PDE6 and suppresses basal activity, but does not significantly inhibit the tested transducin- or trypsin-activated enzyme. Human and bovine GARP2 architectures are authenticated but their sequences differ; direct human inhibition, identical kinetics and physiological dark-noise suppression have not been established. This activity is separate from the membrane-channel products. The human outer-segment location is likewise ortholog-inferred from the bovine rod material, not a direct human localization assay in that study.

CNGB3 contributes ligand-binding and pore-forming structures to the CNGA3/CNGB3 cone channel, coupling intracellular cGMP recognition to cation conduction. Direct human structures resolve three CNGA3 subunits and one CNGB3; beta3 alone is not asserted to form a functional channel. cAMP activation is a supported secondary capability. Full-length canonical human CNGB3 and engineered N-terminal truncations provide the structural evidence, whereas natural isoform 2, lacking residues 590–594 in the nucleotide-binding domain, remains functionally unresolved. The human cone outer-segment membrane location is an inference from mouse ortholog and alpha-partner studies together with human surface-channel experiments; direct human outer-segment immunolocalization is not established by those sources.

Binds collagen through the vWFA2 region and associates with extracellular matrix. Sulfated-glycan recognition provides a complementary matrix-binding capability. Human domain and engineered-reporter assays establish these interactions; mouse tendon phenotypes support matrix maintenance without resolving a separate direct tensile or collagen-assembly activity. The alternative product replaces part of vWFA2, so equal full-product activity is untested.

The released LCCL region exhibits chemoattractant activity in an assay with human recombinant reagent and isolated mouse neutrophils. Lower-chamber exposure increases Transwell migration relative to no LCCL; chemokinesis and a responder-derived relay remain unexcluded without checkerboard or receptor tests. Separately, mouse lung infection studies place cochlin upstream of MCP-1/KC production and subsequent recruitment. These routes are distinguished rather than assigning every immune effect to direct attraction. The exact active natural product remains unresolved; other proteases release the LCCL region.

Type X collagen chains assemble through their NC1 domains into homotrimers that contribute extracellular matrix structure and organization, particularly in hypertrophic cartilage. Higher-order networks form in vitro, while fibril-associated arrangements occur in vivo. The isolated human NC1 trimer binds calcium, without an established calcium-driven mineral-nucleation mechanism.

Full-length alpha-2(XI) chains contribute structural integrity and fibril organization as components of collagen-XI heterotrimers in extracellular matrix. Human COL11A2-associated cartilage shows altered fibril diameter and aggregation; targeted mouse Col11a2 disruption separately connects tectorial-fibril disorganization to hearing loss. The tensile-strength term follows the explicit GO convention for ECM collagens, without claiming an isolated human COL11A2 mechanical measurement. Biosynthetic ER residence and downstream skeletal or hearing phenotypes are integrated with this matrix role rather than represented as additional molecular cores. The recorded short product and all splice forms are not assumed to have been tested equivalently.

Provides alpha-1(I) chains for collagen-I trimers and extracellular fibrils that confer tensile strength and organize connective-tissue matrix. C-propeptide-mediated chain selection and self-association enable this integrated structural role; proteolytic processing is performed by other proteins.

As the alpha2 chain of the usual two-alpha1/one-alpha2 type I collagen heterotrimer, COL1A2 contributes the molecular structure that assembles into tensile extracellular fibrils. Its C-propeptide performs intrinsic chain-association work during precursor assembly; subsequent collagen-processing proteases perform the cleavages.

Supplies alpha-1(II) chains for type-II collagen homotrimers and the alpha-3 chain of type-XI collagen, contributing to extracellular fibril assembly and tensile matrix support. Chain association and cross-linked incorporation are parts of this integrated structural role. Propeptide cleavage and other enzymatic processing are performed by other proteins; the short alternative product is not assumed to reproduce full-length fibril function.

Assembles alpha-1(III) chains into type-III collagen homotrimers and extracellular fibrils, contributing matrix architecture and resistance to tensile stress. Interchain association and matrix incorporation are structural work by collagen; modifying enzymes and procollagen peptidases perform the chemical processing. The shorter splice product is not assumed to reproduce all full-length fibril functions.

Acts as an extracellular receptor ligand, with human collagen-III-dependent LAIR1 activation and inhibitory signaling and complementary GPR56-dependent migration-limiting signaling in mouse cortical models. Receptor engagement connects the collagen matrix to cell behavior; the downstream contexts and reagent/product limits differ between assays.

The NC1-containing COL4A1 chain contributes the physical alpha1(IV)2alpha2(IV) network of basement membranes. Human placental NC1 architecture establishes interchain contacts and opposing trimer interfaces; clinical tissue evidence links chain defects to matrix disorganization. This network-forming structural function includes collagen-partner binding and provides mechanical stability. COL4A1 supplies the cross-linked residues, while peroxidasin supplies oxidant-generating catalysis. The short 519-residue alternative product lacks NC1 and is not presumed functionally equivalent.

The COL4A1_ARRESTEN NC1-derived cleavage-product class has an activity distinct from the precursor’s matrix role. Experimentally applied human arresten preparations engage endothelial cell surfaces through a cell-based alpha1beta1-integrin interaction and suppress angiogenic responses. Nonretracted antibody-controlled attachment and alpha1-integrin-null comparisons support this scoped ligand activity; whole-cell binding does not establish purified-integrin affinity. The preparations include tagged/refolded recombinant material and do not test every natural isoform or establish endogenous concentrations. The retracted 2005 signaling study is excluded from positive support.

Assembles with alpha-4 and alpha-5 chains into type-IV collagen protomers and terminal-domain networks, contributing basement-membrane architecture and mechanical integrity. The network-forming role is distinct from fibrillar collagen assembly and from enzymatic hydroxylation, cross-link chemistry or proteolytic processing carried out by other proteins. Alternative C-terminal products are not assumed to reproduce the canonical assembly.

The released NC1-derived tumstatin fragment binds integrins and inhibits pathological angiogenesis through receptor-dependent endothelial effects. Human recombinant fragment rescue and beta3-dependent mouse assays support this receptor-dependent activity. The intact matrix chain and alternative products are not presumed equivalent; MMP-mediated fragment release is a processing step performed by the protease.

The alpha4 chain supplies the collagenous and NC1 structural elements of the alpha3/alpha4/alpha5 type IV network in basement membranes, including the glomerular basement membrane. This network-forming matrix contribution is described by the existing collagen structural term; it does not assign processing or crosslink catalysis to the chain. The recombinant alpha4 NC1 noncanonical crystal is kept distinct from physiological protomer composition.

The alpha5 chain supplies type-IV collagen protomer and terminal-domain interfaces, contributing basement-membrane network architecture and mechanical integrity. Alpha5-containing protomers are distinct from fibrillar collagens. Human recombinant NC1 self-assembly supports intrinsic structural participation without equating its homohexamer crystals to the native alpha3/alpha4/alpha5 network or assigning collagen the enzymes that modify and crosslink it.

Alpha1(V) supplies structural elements of type V collagen and heterotypic fibrils, contributing to fibril initiation, diameter control and extracellular matrix architecture. Human target-dependent deposition/morphology and mouse loss-of-function evidence support performed matrix work. Bovine V/XI hybrids provide additional tissue-specific chain-assembly context, without equating them with the strictly enumerated canonical type XI trimer. N-propeptide interactions and precursor assembly/processing are integrated into this structural role; other proteins perform the proteolytic cleavage.

Contributes the alpha-2(V) chain to type-V collagen heterotrimers and their incorporation into heterotypic extracellular fibrils, organizing matrix architecture and mechanical integrity. Human mutation evidence and mouse alpha2(V)-defective matrix studies support this structural assembly role; altered secretion, stability and assembly are not all experimentally separable in the mouse allele. Processing of the precursor is performed by other proteins.

Alpha1(VI) supplies structural elements of collagen VI trimers and higher-order beaded microfibrils, helping organize the extracellular matrix around cells. Around skeletal muscle fibers, the collagen VI network provides a structural connection to surrounding matrix; this anchoring context is integrated with its matrix role rather than assigned a separate catalytic activity. Canonical alpha1/alpha2/alpha3 assembly is distinct from experimentally secreted alpha1/alpha2/mouse-alpha4 constructs. VWA-domain interactions and chain assembly are integrated into this structural role; the chain is not the enzyme that modifies or degrades collagen. Isolated-chain ligand behavior, growth-factor binding and intracellular cargo observations remain contextual rather than separate universal core activities.

Alpha2(VI) supplies a structural chain of collagen VI assemblies that form extracellular beaded microfibrils and connect matrix structures. Canonical alpha1/alpha2/alpha3 units contribute matrix integrity. The shorter alpha2 C-terminal splice products retain shared structural regions, while their incorporation and matrix-assembly properties remain incompletely established. Collagen-chain contacts support this integrated assembly role: isolated non-triple-helical human major 2C2 alpha2 binds pepsin-collagen VI, while the alpha4 transfection assay demonstrates multichain coassembly; these distinct assays do not establish all splice products as equivalent.

Alpha3(VI) contributes the long structural chain of canonical alpha1/alpha2/alpha3 collagen VI units. N-terminal and C-terminal interfaces support extracellular end-to-end tetramer association and beaded-microfibril deposition. The two short products lacking the collagenous and C-terminal regions have not been shown to substitute for the assembled long chain.

Collagen VII supplies homotrimeric structural units of anchoring fibrils that link epithelial basement membranes to underlying connective tissue. NC1-mediated collagen binding and C-terminal antiparallel assembly are complementary parts of this mechanically stabilizing extracellular connection. Recombinant human full-length and NC1-containing constructs bind collagen I fibrils, while purified NC1 also binds collagen IV; these matrix contacts anchor the structural assembly. Individual splice-product behavior remains incompletely resolved.

Alpha1(IX) supplies structural elements of the alpha1/alpha2/alpha3 type IX heterotrimer at the surface of type II collagen fibrils. Chain assembly and covalent matrix connections support this fibril-associated matrix role. The NC2 structure is an engineered assembly-domain assay, and the chain does not autonomously form the major fibrillar scaffold or catalyze its own processing. Long/short precursor architecture and the severely truncated product are kept distinct.

The alpha1(IX) NC4 domain binds heparin, providing a ligand-binding activity in the extracellular matrix distinct from structural chain assembly. Recombinant human NC4 binding is supported by direct assays, GAG competition and a folding-controlled basic-region mutant; full-length recombinant human collagen IX also binds heparin. Additional binding sites on the intact heterotrimer are not all assigned to alpha1. These experiments do not demonstrate a specific native matrix-bridging mechanism or equivalent activity of all natural splice products, including the NC4-lacking Short product.

Alpha3(IX) contributes structural chain interfaces and covalent matrix connections as part of the alpha1/alpha2/alpha3 collagen IX heterotrimer. Native human cartilage cross-links integrate it with collagen II and neighboring collagen IX molecules, while engineered NC2 structures resolve one chain-selection/stagger interface. This fibril-associated contribution supports matrix integrity and organization; the chain is not itself a modifying enzyme or an autonomous major fibril.

Pentameric COMP supplies a multivalent extracellular matrix platform that associates with collagen and other matrix ligands and promotes early collagen fibril organization. Collagen binding, calcium-dependent conformation and the N-terminal oligomerization region cooperate in this structural work: calcium binding supports the conformation of the ligand-binding signature domain, while collagen engagement and multivalent assembly promote fibril organization. Native bovine pentamer-versus-monomer experiments directly distinguish performed organization from mere presence; human matrix detection and full-length assembly support the conserved tissue role. The isolated human signature-domain crystal is not a physiological trimer, and equal activity of the shorter splice product is not established.

COPG1 functions as a structural subunit of the COPI coatomer complex, mediating retrograde vesicle transport from the Golgi apparatus to the endoplasmic reticulum. As part of the gamma/zeta adaptor subcomplex, COPG1 participates in ARF1-GTP-dependent membrane recruitment, cargo selection through dilysine motif recognition, and vesicle coat assembly.

COQ7 is the carboxylate-bridged di-iron hydroxylase that catalyzes the penultimate step of coenzyme Q biosynthesis, hydroxylating the quinone demethoxyubiquinone (5-methoxy-2-methyl-3-(all-trans-polyprenyl)benzoquinone, DMQ) at the C6 position using NADH and molecular oxygen to give 3-demethylubiquinone. Substrate binding mediates NADH reduction of its two-iron (ferritin-like) center, which then activates O2; the lipid-binding protein COQ9 presents DMQ to COQ7 within the COQ synthome.

CORO1A binds actin filaments and regulates cortical actin-network organization in leukocyte settings. Purified human protein inhibits Arp2/3-dependent nucleation, and human NK-cell evidence connects CORO1A to synaptic meshwork remodeling that permits granule access. Association is context dependent rather than a property of every cellular pool; later native-protein experiments identify substantial actin-independent behavior. The defined Arp2/3-inhibition process describes the purified biochemical result; the human NK meshwork phenotype is not assigned exclusively to that mechanism.
Catalyzes farnesylation of protoheme IX to form heme O at the mitochondrial inner membrane, supplying the first biosynthetic step toward the heme A prosthetic groups of complex IV.

Copper metallochaperone that receives Cu(I) from the intermembrane-space chaperone COX17 and directly inserts copper into the CuB site of the catalytic subunit MT-CO1 during cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) assembly, acting as a single-pass mitochondrial inner-membrane protein with its copper-binding CFCF motif (Cys217/Cys219) exposed to the intermembrane space.

Converts heme O to heme A at the mitochondrial inner membrane, supplying the heme A prosthetic groups needed for cytochrome c oxidase biogenesis. Human complementation directly supports COX15.1; equivalent activity of the alternative C-terminal product is unresolved.

COX4I1 is the principal regulatory supernumerary subunit of cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV). It binds ATP at a matrix-exposed allosteric site and integrates adenine nucleotide and cAMP/PKA signaling to modulate Complex IV catalytic output. As a non-catalytic subunit, COX4I1 contributes_to cytochrome-c oxidase activity while directly participating in regulation of that activity, mitochondrial electron transport from cytochrome c to oxygen, and early Complex IV assembly (MITRAC-associated steps).

Structural (supernumerary) subunit that assembles into and stabilises mitochondrial respiratory chain complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), surrounding the mtDNA-encoded catalytic core; COX5A is non-catalytic and contributes to the complex's cytochrome-c oxidase activity through structural integrity rather than enabling catalysis itself.

COX6A1 is a regulatory/supernumerary subunit of mitochondrial Complex IV. It has enzyme regulator activity in the context of cytochrome c oxidase and contributes to the complex-level cytochrome-c oxidase activity without independently catalyzing electron transfer.

Non-catalytic structural subunit of mitochondrial respiratory Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) that contributes to complex assembly and stability and to the transfer of electrons from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen in the mitochondrial inner membrane.

COX6B1 provides structural support within mitochondrial complex IV, contributing to cytochrome-c oxidase activity and respiratory electron transport. Human structural and complementation evidence supports its integration into the active enzyme. Redox bypass separates an early assembly requirement from the poor catalytic capacity of incomplete complexes; the precise MT-CO2 maturation mechanism remains unresolved.

Structural (non-catalytic) subunit of mitochondrial respiratory Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) that contributes to assembly and stability of the holoenzyme, supporting electron transport from cytochrome c to oxygen in the mitochondrial inner membrane.

Non-catalytic structural subunit that contributes to the assembly and structural integrity of mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), the terminal enzyme of the electron transport chain.

As a subunit of Complex IV, participates in the transfer of electrons from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen in the mitochondrial inner membrane, the reaction that reduces O2 to water during oxidative phosphorylation.
Oxidizes Fe(II) to Fe(III) to support cellular iron homeostasis. Purified human soluble CP provides direct evidence for this extracellular ferroxidase chemistry.

The characterized human CPOX homodimer catalyzes oxygen-dependent oxidative decarboxylation of coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX in the mitochondrial intermembrane-space heme pathway. It performs the chemical step itself; the shorter annotated product has not been shown to retain equivalent catalysis.

CPS1 catalyzes ATP-dependent synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia and bicarbonate in the mitochondrial matrix, providing the first synthetic step of the hepatic urea cycle. N-acetylglutamate allosterically activates the reaction, with magnesium and potassium supporting catalysis. This core describes the established enzyme and does not assert equivalent import or catalytic competence of every alternative product.

Transfers long-chain acyl groups from acyl-CoA to carnitine at the mitochondrial outer membrane, supplying the acylcarnitine-forming step of the malonyl-CoA-regulated carnitine shuttle. The translocase and CPT2 carry out distinct subsequent steps.

Catalyzes succinyl-CoA-dependent peptide-lysine succinylation, directly demonstrated with ENO1 and enzyme/substrate controls. The G710E separation from carnitine transfer and endogenous CPT1A depletion support this distinct activity; the proteomic substrate list is broader than the individually validated direct substrates.

Acts as the reported molecular adaptor recruiting ZDHHC4 to MAVS, enabling MAVS palmitoylation and stabilization and sustaining the type I interferon response. ZDHHC4 performs the palmitoylation chemistry; this recruitment role is distinct from CPT1A acyl-transfer catalysis. This third activity is supported in the reported epigenetic-perturbation and antitumor-immunity setting; its generality across tissues and conditions is unresolved. The complete abstract and curated GO-CAM support the role, while full original Methods were not recovered.

Catalyzes reversible carnitine O-acyl transfer on the matrix face of the mitochondrial inner membrane, regenerating acyl-CoA from imported acylcarnitines to complete the carnitine shuttle and feed fatty acid beta-oxidation. The same enzyme also forms medium- and long-chain acylcarnitines in the reverse direction.

Recognizes C3-derived complement ligands at the B-cell surface and contributes to co-receptor signaling that amplifies B-cell activation. The same complement-receptor activity accommodates C3d, C3dg and iC3b; association with CD19-containing complexes provides signaling context without attributing catalytic kinase activity to CR2.

Bridge processed PIDD1 and caspase-2 through death-domain and CARD interactions, organizing caspase-2 activation in apoptotic signaling. The DD structure defines an assembly interface, not an obligatory intact-cell stoichiometry; stress-induced nucleolar and p53-feedback contexts are described separately.

The canonical CRB1 C-terminal motif binds the PALS1/MPP5 PDZ domain within apical polarity assemblies, contributing to epithelial apicobasal organization and the retinal outer limiting membrane. This describes the experimentally established tail-bearing membrane form; the five official products are not assumed to have equal topology or function.

bZIP transcription factor that binds cAMP response elements (CRE; TGACGTCA) as homo- or heterodimers to activate transcription of target genes. Core defining function of CREB1 supported by extensive structural and functional studies.
Binds the palindromic CRE sequence (TGACGTCA) via its bZIP domain. This is the defining DNA binding specificity that distinguishes CREB family members from other bZIP transcription factors.

Phosphorylation at Ser-119 by PKA and other kinases enables recruitment of CBP/p300 coactivators via the KID-KIX interaction. This coactivator binding is essential for CREB-mediated transcriptional activation.

Acetylates lysine residues on histones and nonhistone proteins, coupling chromatin modification and substrate regulation to transcriptional control. Histone-site specificity is context dependent rather than limited to H3K18/H3K27.
Coactivates sequence-specific transcription factors through promoter-associated protein interactions and recruitment of transcriptional cofactors, increasing RNA polymerase II transcription.

Catalyzes CoA-dependent MRE11 lysine lactylation in the studied DNA-damage response, enhancing MRE11-dependent end resection and homologous-recombination repair. This specifies the measured substrate context rather than assigning all cellular lactylation to CREBBP.

Non-catalytic scaffolding/helper subunit of the ER collagen prolyl 3-hydroxylation complex (with P3H1 and PPIB). CRTAP is required for assembly, stability and activity of the complex that 3-hydroxylates Pro986 of alpha1(I) and alpha1(II) fibrillar procollagen chains; CRTAP contributes to collagen substrate binding but does not itself catalyze hydroxylation.

Collagen-specific molecular chaperone/foldase activity of the complex: CRTAP is required for normal collagen triple-helix folding rate, and its loss causes delayed folding and overmodification of the collagen helix. CRTAP also mutually stabilizes its complex partner P3H1 in the ER.

CRX binds cis-regulatory DNA in the nucleus and integrates partner-dependent activation, including cooperation with NRL, and context-dependent repression to regulate photoreceptor gene expression and development. The mapped NRL interaction supports this integrated transcriptional role; the original domain experiments used human NRL and bovine CRX.
Binds the CLOCK:BMAL1 E-box complex to repress circadian transcription.
Binds FAD as a flavin cofactor.

CRY2 functions as a transcriptional corepressor in the mammalian circadian clock. It partners with PER proteins (PER1/2/3) to form nuclear repressor complexes that inhibit CLOCK:BMAL1-driven transcription of E-box containing genes including Per, Cry, Dec1, Dec2, and other clock-controlled genes. CRY2 also inhibits PP5 phosphatase activity, modulating CKIepsilon-dependent phosphorylation of clock proteins. CRY2 repression and stability are regulated through the FAD pocket, which mediates FBXL3-dependent ubiquitination and degradation.

CRY2 binds FAD as a cofactor in its photolyase homology region. Although FAD occupancy is low in mammalian CRYs, the FAD-binding pocket is functionally critical as a regulatory hub for ubiquitin ligase (FBXL3) recognition, PER2 competitive binding, and small-molecule stabilizer binding.

CRY2 interacts with nuclear receptors including the glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1/GR), androgen receptor (AR), HNF4A, PPARA, PPARD, PPARG, NR1I2, NR1I3, and VDR in a ligand-dependent manner. Through these interactions, CRY2 mediates circadian modulation of nuclear receptor target gene expression, including rhythmic repression of glucocorticoid-responsive genes.

CRYAB (HSPB5) is a small heat shock protein that functions as an ATP-independent holdase chaperone. It binds partially denatured or destabilized proteins to prevent their aggregation, maintaining clients in a refolding-competent state for downstream ATP-dependent chaperone systems such as HSP70, but does NOT actively refold substrates itself. CRYAB forms highly polydisperse oligomers (approximately 10-40 subunits) with rapid subunit exchange dynamics that are important for chaperone activity (DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-54647-7). The canonical architecture comprises a central alpha-crystallin domain (ACD) mediating dimerization, flanked by a variable N-terminal domain (NTD) and a short C-terminal domain (CTD). A conserved N-terminal IXI-like motif (NT-IXI) engages the ACD hydrophobic groove to govern assembly; perturbation of this motif transforms native assemblies into reversible elongated helical fibrils as resolved by cryo-EM (DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-54647-7). Stress-activated phosphorylation (notably p38 MAPK targeting Ser59) modulates oligomeric state and can shift CRYAB condensates toward protective or pathological material states (DOI:10.1016/j.isci.2024.109510, DOI:10.1172/jci163730). Substrates bound by CRYAB can subsequently be refolded by HSP70/HSP40 foldase chaperones, or routed to the ubiquitin-proteasome system for degradation.

CRYAB is one of the major structural proteins of the vertebrate eye lens, contributing to lens transparency and refractive index. In the lens, it serves a dual role as both a structural protein (maintaining lens transparency through high concentration and ordered short-range interactions) and a chaperone (preventing aggregation of damaged crystallins that would cause light-scattering opacification).

CRYAB binds desmin intermediate filaments in a manner dependent on desmin assembly status and subunit organization, acting as a sensor for assembly intermediates. In cardiac and skeletal muscle, CRYAB associates with sarcomeric structures including Z-bands and intercalated disks, and interacts with titin. Mutations in CRYAB (e.g., R120G) cause desmin-related myopathy through aggregation of desmin filaments. Recent work shows that phosphorylation at Ser59 can shift CRYAB condensates toward less dynamic, aggregate-prone states that mislocalize cytoskeletal and sarcomeric client proteins, a pathological mechanism termed condensatopathy; the phosphomimetic S59D behaves similarly to the R120G cardiomyopathy mutant (DOI:10.1172/jci163730).

CSF1R binds CSF1 or IL34 at the plasma membrane and catalyzes ATP-dependent protein-tyrosine phosphorylation, including receptor autophosphorylation. This receptor activity transmits ligand signals that support monocyte, macrophage and osteoclast differentiation and macrophage and microglial proliferation. GO:1990682 specifies the experimentally defined CSF1-bound dimeric receptor assembly; IL34 signaling occurs in a separate ligand-receptor assembly and is not assigned to that CSF1-specific complex.

CSF2RA directly recognizes GM-CSF at the extracellular face of the plasma membrane and contributes to the receptor activity of the cooperative alpha/common-beta complex. Alpha-mediated ligand recognition and productive receptor assembly support GM-CSF signaling and hematopoietic proliferation. The alpha chain participates in activation rather than serving only as a passive ligand tether; the complete transmembrane receptor activity is assigned as a contribution to the complex. This core concerns membrane receptor forms and does not imply intrinsic alpha-chain kinase activity.

Cooperates with the ligand-specific alpha chains to assemble signaling receptors for GM-CSF, IL-3 and IL-5, contributing ligand contacts and affinity conversion and coupling receptor engagement to associated JAK signaling at the plasma membrane. The beta chain is not itself a protein kinase; the alpha chains also contribute to productive signaling. In the 2024 tagged-receptor HeLa recruitment assay, beta associated most strongly with JAK1 FERM–SH2 constructs, with additional JAK2 and TYK2 association; this is not a universal native kinase preference.
Constitutively active protein serine/threonine kinase (ATP- and Mg2+-dependent) that phosphorylates a broad range of substrates, including via primed (phospho-directed) and unprimed mechanisms.

Phosphorylates PER1 and PER2 to control their stability and nuclear transport, acting as a central component of the circadian clock that sets period length; loss-of-function variants cause familial advanced sleep phase syndrome and migraine.
Phosphorylates Dishevelled (DVL2/DVL3) and other components to regulate canonical Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and Wnt-3a-dependent neurite outgrowth.
Acts at the centrosome and Golgi (anchored via AKAP9/AKAP450) to promote microtubule nucleation, Golgi organization and primary (non-motile) ciliogenesis.

Phosphorylates serine and threonine residues in protein substrates, often in acidic sequence contexts, as the catalytic alpha subunit of CK2. Nuclear and cytosolic reactions regulate diverse substrate activities and stability; the compact catalytic role accommodates this breadth without requiring identical downstream effects. Canonical CK2 assembly and free-alpha assays are both positive, while the N-terminally truncated product has unresolved catalytic and assembly competence.

Regulatory (beta) subunit of the protein kinase CK2 holoenzyme - a non-catalytic protein kinase regulatory subunit that dimerizes and bridges the two catalytic subunits (CSNK2A1/CSNK2A2), stabilizing the holoenzyme and modulating its basal activity and substrate selectivity.

Molecular adaptor/scaffold that recruits specific substrates and partner proteins to the CK2 holoenzyme (e.g. via its C-terminal region and the KSSR protein-interaction pocket), redirecting CK2 activity toward selected substrates and bridging interactions such as ARK2N-Jun.

As part of the constitutively active CK2 holoenzyme, contributes to serine/threonine protein phosphorylation of acidic-motif substrates (consensus S/T-X-X-D/E), the biochemical activity underlying CK2's pleiotropic downstream roles.

Full-length MLP binds and cross-links actin filaments and engages Z-disc partners to support muscle-fiber integrity and sarcomere organization. Its actin-regulatory effects depend on the assayed protein preparation and context.

Full-length human MLP directly binds actin filaments and cross-links them in assays using tag-cleaved recombinant protein and purified actin. This supplies a molecular activity underlying its muscle structural role. The result does not assign the same activity to the short splice product, and the differing cofilin effects in tagged versus tag-cleaved preparations remain unresolved.

CSTB binds and inhibits papain-like cysteine proteases, restraining intracellular peptidase activity in the cytosol and nucleus. The measured spectrum includes endopeptidases and cathepsin H/dipeptidyl-peptidase activity, with enzyme- and redox-dependent affinities. Nuclear experiments support restraint of cathepsin L-mediated protein processing, without assigning equal physiological control of every enzyme tested in vitro.

Sequence-specific RNA polymerase II DNA-binding transcription factor that binds NKE (TNAAGTG/TAAG) cis-regulatory elements via its NK-2 homeodomain and activates cardiac target genes such as NPPA/ANF and GATA4 (and context-dependently represses others such as CTNNB1).

Binds partner cardiac DNA-binding transcription factors GATA4 and TBX5 through its homeodomain, forming cooperative complexes on composite promoter elements that synergistically activate targets such as NPPA.

As a cardiac transcription factor, drives heart tube looping, cardiomyocyte (especially ventricular) differentiation, atrial and ventricular septation, and dosage-sensitive development of the atrioventricular node and conduction system.

Transcription factor in splenic mesenchymal progenitors, acting downstream of PBX1 and repressing CDKN2B (p15INK4B) to sustain spleen growth; a heterozygous NKX2-5 missense allele causes isolated congenital asplenia.

CTBP1 functions primarily as a transcriptional corepressor, recruited to target genes by DNA-binding transcription factors via PXDLS motifs. It scaffolds chromatin-modifying complexes containing HDAC1/2, LSD1/KDM1A, and RCOR1/CoREST.
CTBP1 binds diverse DNA-binding transcription factors (ZEB1/2, KLFs, BCL6, MECOM, HIC1, FOXP1, ZNF366, ZNF516) through recognition of PXDLS/PLDLS short linear motifs.
CTBP1 binds NAD+/NADH via its Rossmann fold domain. NADH binding allosterically promotes dimerization and corepressor complex assembly, making CTBP1 a metabolic/redox sensor.
CTBP1 is a functional D-2-hydroxyacid dehydrogenase, though the primary biological role centers on its corepressor/scaffolding function rather than catalytic activity.

Cystathionine gamma-lyase catalysing the final step of the transsulfuration pathway: PLP-dependent cleavage of L,L-cystathionine to L-cysteine, 2-oxobutanoate and ammonia, supplying de novo L-cysteine (cysteine biosynthesis from homocysteine/methionine sulfur).

Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) biosynthesis: using L-cysteine and (at lower rates) L-homocysteine as substrates, CTH is a major enzymatic source of the gasotransmitter H2S, generating H2S together with pyruvate/2-oxobutanoate and ammonia. This is a genuine second physiological function.

Cysteine-protein sulfhydrase / persulfidation activity: via generated H2S, CTH persulfidates target-protein cysteine residues (converting -SH to -SSH) on proteins such as GAPDH, PTP1B/PTPN1 and NF-kB RELA, contributing to redox signaling.
PLP cofactor binding: CTH is a pyridoxal-5'-phosphate-dependent enzyme, binding PLP covalently via a Schiff base to Lys212, which is essential for all of its catalytic activities.

CTLA4 sequesters the CD28 co-stimulatory ligands CD80 and CD86 at the T-cell surface. Its stronger B7 binding than CD28 and dimeric organization favor ligand capture, limiting CD28-dependent costimulation. Transendocytosis removes these ligands from neighboring antigen-presenting cells and directs them toward degradation, thereby suppressing responder T-cell activation. Regulated surface exposure and endocytosis enable this ligand-depleting activity in activated and regulatory T cells.

Full-length alpha-E-catenin anchors cadherin-associated complexes to the cortical actin cytoskeleton. Its N-terminal beta-catenin or plakoglobin binding recruits it to the junctional complex, and force-dependent F-actin engagement by its C-terminal region reinforces the linkage. Recruitment of vinculin and organization of EPLIN- and centralspindlin-associated assemblies support the apical adhesion belt; CAP350 recruitment provides a distinct connection to microtubules at basolateral adherens contacts. These interactions contribute to cell-cell adhesion and apical junction assembly.

Cadherin-free alpha-E-catenin binds and bundles actin filaments. Homodimerization favors filament engagement, and competition for F-actin binding sites can restrain Arp2/3-mediated branched-actin assembly. This actin-organizing activity is distinct from the force-dependent linkage of the cadherin-bound pool; its strength depends on oligomeric state and local concentration.

Alpha-E-catenin directly binds beta-catenin through its N-terminal region. At adherens junctions this interaction recruits alpha-E-catenin to cadherin-containing assemblies. The beta-catenin-binding interface is distinct from C-terminal actin engagement and from cadherin-free homodimeric actin organization.

Wnt-responsive transcriptional coactivation in the nucleus. Beta-catenin binds TCF/LEF factors and participates in chromatin-associated complexes with BCL9/PYGO, CBP/p300 and other coregulators. Its activation regions support transcription without intrinsic sequence-specific DNA-binding activity. It can dock onto preassembled coregulator scaffolds; the composition and recruitment order vary with context.

Cadherin-tail binding and recruitment of alpha-catenin at adherens junctions. Beta-catenin provides a structural connection within the cadherin–catenin complex that supports cadherin retention, junction assembly and cell-cell adhesion. Alpha-catenin supplies the regulated actin-associated interface; beta-catenin is not assigned its partner’s actin-binding activity.

Binding alpha-catenin through the N-terminal region recruits the catenin-complex alpha subunit to the cadherin-associated junctional machinery. This distinct binding activity complements cadherin-tail recognition by the armadillo-repeat region and supports the regulated connection of the junction to the actin cytoskeleton. Alpha-catenin supplies the actin-associated interface; this core does not assign direct actin-binding activity to beta-catenin.

p120-catenin binds intracellular cadherin juxtamembrane tails and protects cadherin surface stability. Regulated occupancy of this interface supports cadherin-dependent cell-cell adhesion and junction maintenance.

Long p120-catenin products are inferred to restrain Rho activation by inhibiting GDP dissociation, based on direct mouse biochemical assays and conservation of the tested regulatory regions in human products. Cadherin-tail competition suppresses the Rho-inhibitory phenotype in the original cellular experiments, distinguishing this activity from simultaneous cadherin-bound junctional stabilization. Phosphorylation and terminal-sequence differences tune Rho regulation.
Proton-coupled export of L-cystine, produced by lysosomal proteolysis, from the lysosomal lumen to the cytosol across the lysosomal membrane.
Couples cystine translocation to proton co-transport (cystine/H+ symport) driven by the lysosomal pH gradient.

CTPS1 couples glutamine hydrolysis to ATP-dependent amination of UTP, producing CTP for nucleotide synthesis. The performed UTP-to-CTP step is stated without assigning an upstream route of precursor production. Homotetramers form regulated filaments; substrate-associated human assemblies have enhanced activity, and phosphorylation tunes catalytic output. Cytosolic CTP production supports the increased nucleotide demand of activated lymphocytes.

CTPS1 deamidates protein asparagine residues in distinct regulatory contexts. At chromatin, histone H1 N76/N77 deamidation enables subsequent EP300 acetylation and chromatin relaxation for DNA repair. IRF3 N85 deamidation reduces promoter binding and interferon induction; human cellular perturbations and mouse genetic experiments support this second substrate context. CTPS1 performs the deamidation, while EP300 performs acetylation and IRF3 carries transcription-factor activity.

Cathepsin D hydrolyzes internal peptide bonds through an aspartic mechanism in acidic endolysosomal compartments, supporting protein turnover. The human precursor is proteolytically matured into active single-chain and light/heavy-chain forms; these chains derive from one precursor rather than alternative splice products.

Mature cathepsin F catalyzes cysteine-dependent internal peptide-bond hydrolysis in acidic lysosomal compartments. Activation removes its long proregion. Its catalytic role encompasses protein degradation and protein processing: measured substrates include blocked synthetic peptides, invariant chain and apoB-100. Invariant-chain cleavage and extracellular LDL degradation are context-dependent applications; the recombinant LDL assay does not establish an intact-cell turnover rate or a universal extracellular role.
Cysteine endopeptidase activity breaks down collagen and other extracellular matrix proteins, linking lysosomal protease production to extracellular matrix turnover.

Non-enzymatic multiligand cargo/endocytic receptor that binds the intrinsic factor-cobalamin (IF-B12) complex via its CUB5-8 domains and, together with AMN (cubam) and megalin, mediates receptor-mediated endocytosis of B12 and reabsorbed proteins.

As the ligand-binding subunit of the cubam receptor at the apical/brush-border membrane, cubilin captures diverse filtered and luminal ligands for receptor-mediated endocytosis, driving intestinal B12 uptake and renal proximal-tubule reabsorption of proteins.

Assemble CRL3 ubiquitin ligases by binding BTB/POZ substrate adaptors through the CUL3 N terminus and RBX1 through its C-terminal region. This scaffold contributes to substrate ubiquitination, including proteasomal targeting in degradative assemblies and non-degradative regulation in other adaptor contexts. It does not independently catalyze ubiquitin transfer, neddylation or proteolysis. BTB/POZ-domain binding is the substrate-adaptor recruitment component of this coordinated assembly function.
CXCR4 recognizes extracellular CXCL12 and activates Gi-coupled signaling, including reduced cellular cAMP, to direct cell chemotaxis.

CYB5A relays electrons through its heme to partner redox enzymes. The ER-anchored form presents its heme domain to cytoplasmic partners, while the mature soluble erythrocyte form supports cytosolic redox metabolism. CYP17A1 17,20-lyase enhancement combines electron donation with substrate-dependent conformational effects.

CYLD is a cysteine-type deubiquitinase that cleaves K63 and Met1 ubiquitin linkages. SPATA2 binds and activates its USP domain and couples it to receptor-associated complexes, allowing CYLD to remodel signaling ubiquitin and regulate canonical NF-kappaB and cell-death responses in a context-dependent manner.

CYLD directly binds HDAC6 and reduces its tubulin deacetylase activity, supporting acetylated microtubules. This N-terminal inhibitory function is distinct from USP catalysis and does not imply inhibition of histone deacetylation. Cytokinesis effects can persist with a DUB-inactive construct, whereas the reported G1/S delay requires both N-terminal and catalytic functions.

The N-terminal CAP-Gly region of CYLD binds polymerized microtubules. Biochemical cosedimentation supports this activity independently of co-immunoprecipitation with tubulin; it does not establish recognition of a unique tubulin isoform. Microtubule binding and HDAC6 inhibition provide complementary mechanisms for regulating the microtubule cytoskeleton, without establishing equivalent activity of both intact CYLD products.

Steroid 11-beta-monooxygenase (11beta-hydroxylase) catalysing the final step of cortisol biosynthesis at the mitochondrial inner membrane, converting 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol (and 11-deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone), using heme and the adrenodoxin electron system.
Heme cofactor binding required for oxygen activation by this heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 (axial cysteine ligand at position 450). Secondary to the catalytic 11-beta-monooxygenase function.

Heme-dependent 11-beta-hydroxylation of deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone supplies the first oxidative step of aldosterone synthesis at the mitochondrial inner membrane, using electrons delivered through adrenodoxin.
Heme-dependent corticosterone 18-hydroxylation produces 18-hydroxycorticosterone, using oxygen and electrons delivered through adrenodoxin at the mitochondrial inner membrane.

The subsequent heme-dependent oxidation of the C18 hydroxymethyl group of 18-hydroxycorticosterone yields aldosterone. This terminal oxidative step uses adrenodoxin-derived electrons and molecular oxygen and is distinct from the preceding corticosterone 18-hydroxylation.

Steroid 17-alpha-hydroxylase activity (EC 1.14.14.19): as a microsomal cytochrome P450 monooxygenase, CYP17A1 hydroxylates the C21 steroids pregnenolone and progesterone at C17 to yield 17-alpha-hydroxypregnenolone and 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone, the obligatory precursors for cortisol (glucocorticoid) biosynthesis, using O2 and electrons from NADPH via cytochrome P450 reductase.

Steroid 17,20-lyase activity (EC 1.14.14.32): CYP17A1 cleaves the C17-C20 bond of the 17-alpha-hydroxy intermediates (17-alpha-hydroxypregnenolone -> dehydroepiandrosterone; 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone -> androstenedione), the committed step generating C19 androgen precursors. This second oxidative activity resides on the same polypeptide as the hydroxylase and requires cytochrome b5 as an allosteric effector (with POR as the electron donor), determining the flux of steroidogenesis toward androgens and estrogens.

Heme binding: CYP17A1 is a heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 whose heme prosthetic group (iron axially coordinated by Cys442) is essential for its monooxygenase/lyase catalysis; heme/iron binding is the supporting cofactor function underpinning both catalytic activities.

Aromatase activity (EC 1.14.14.14): as a microsomal heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 monooxygenase, CYP19A1 catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of estrogen biosynthesis, aromatizing C19 androgens to C18 estrogens (androstenedione -> estrone; testosterone -> 17beta-estradiol) via three sequential O2/NADPH-dependent oxidations (two C19-methyl hydroxylations followed by A-ring aromatization with C10-C19 cleavage and formate release), receiving electrons from cytochrome P450 reductase (POR).

Heme binding: aromatase is a heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 whose heme prosthetic group (iron axially coordinated by Cys437) is essential for O2 activation and catalysis; heme/iron binding is the supporting cofactor function underpinning the monooxygenase reaction.

Heme-dependent estrogen hydroxylation uses electrons supplied through P450 reductase. Human CYP1B1 favors estradiol 4-hydroxylation over 2-hydroxylation in product-resolved enzyme assays, generating catechol estrogens with distinct biological reactivity. The 4-hydroxylase reaction is represented by RHEA:47280; the current steroid-hydroxylase term provides the available activity class while a specific ontology proposal captures the C4 reaction. This human regioselectivity is not inferred from the differently selective rodent enzymes.

POR-supported retinoid oxidation converts all-trans-retinol to retinal and retinal to retinoate. Human enzyme reconstitutions and CYP1B1 Supersomes establish the performed chemistry; these assays do not establish CYP1B1 as the dominant hepatic retinoid enzyme or identify the endogenous substrate responsible for glaucoma. The catalytic class records reduced-flavoprotein-supported oxidation, rather than an NAD(P)-dependent retinol dehydrogenase mechanism.

POR-supported arachidonate oxidation produces hydroxylated fatty acids and epoxyeicosatrienoates. Human reconstituted CYP1B1 and insect-cell Supersomes establish multiple product branches; chiral analysis resolves preferential 8R,9S- and 14R,15S-EET formation and both 11,12-EET enantiomers. This lipid-substrate context is distinct from retinoid oxidation despite sharing the same available donor-class term. Grouped terminal-HETE peaks and heterologous assays do not establish individually resolved terminal hydroxylation rates or dominant flux in human tissues.

Steroid 21-monooxygenase (P450c21) that 21-hydroxylates C21 steroids in adrenal corticosteroid biosynthesis, converting progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone and 17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol, using heme b and electrons from cytochrome P450 reductase, at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane.
Same 21-hydroxylase activity supplying the mineralocorticoid branch of steroidogenesis, converting progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC), the precursor of aldosterone.
Heme-thiolate cofactor binding required for catalysis; the enzyme binds heme b with an axial cysteine iron ligand at the catalytic centre.

Heme-dependent oxidation of the terminal side chain of cholestane intermediates through alcohol and aldehyde to carboxylic acid supplies bile-acid precursors. Adrenodoxin and adrenodoxin reductase deliver the reducing equivalents. The mature enzyme associates peripherally with the matrix face of the mitochondrial inner membrane.

Heme-dependent cholesterol side-chain hydroxylation generates 26(27)-hydroxycholesterol, followed by further oxidation to an aldehyde and cholestenoic acid. This supplies the acidic bile-acid pathway and contributes to cholesterol catabolism. The enzyme acts at the matrix-facing inner-membrane interface; not every oxysterol molecule is assumed to have the same downstream fate.

Mitochondrial 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase producing hormonally active calcitriol from calcidiol, the rate-limiting step of vitamin D activation (renal proximal tubule for circulating hormone; extrarenal cells for local autocrine/paracrine action)

Cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase (cytochrome P450 7A1) catalysing the committed, rate-limiting first step of the classic (neutral) bile-acid biosynthesis pathway - 7-alpha-hydroxylation of cholesterol to 7-alpha-hydroxycholesterol - in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, using heme iron and NADPH-derived electrons.

Contribution of the same cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase activity to cholesterol catabolism - conversion of cholesterol to bile acids is the major route of cholesterol elimination, of which CYP7A1 catalyses the rate-limiting step.
Heme-iron cofactor binding required for the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase catalysis; CYP7A1 is a heme-thiolate P450 with Cys444 as the axial heme-iron ligand.

7-alpha-hydroxylates endogenous steroids, including 25- and 26(27)-hydroxycholesterol, dehydroepiandrosterone and pregnenolone. Oxysterol hydroxylation supplies intermediates for alternative bile-acid synthesis. Formation of 7-alpha,25-dihydroxycholesterol also supplies the EBI2 ligand; the B-cell-guidance physiology is directly established in mice, whereas human enzyme assays establish the ligand-producing reaction.

Sterol 12-alpha-hydroxylase (EC 1.14.14.139): as a microsomal cytochrome P450 monooxygenase, uses O2 and electrons from NADPH--cytochrome P450 reductase to insert a 12-alpha-hydroxyl group onto 7-alpha-hydroxycholest-4-en-3-one and related C27 sterol/bile-acid intermediates (e.g. DHCA; and, in vitro, chenodeoxycholate), the branch-point step that commits the classic bile-acid pathway toward cholic acid rather than chenodeoxycholic acid.

Heme binding: CYP8B1 binds heme (ChEBI:30413) as its obligate prosthetic group, coordinating the catalytic iron through a conserved axial cysteine; substrate binding produces the characteristic type I Soret shift of the ferric heme.

Glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan (DAG1_ALPHA; PRO_0000021065, residues 30–653) binds laminin as the extracellular ligand-binding chain of the alpha/beta dystroglycan receptor. Together with the membrane-anchoring beta chain, it organizes and supports assembly of extracellular matrix and basement membrane. Agrin and perlecan are additional matrix ligands.

Processed beta-dystroglycan (DAG1_BETA; PRO_0000021066, residues 654–895) is the transmembrane cytoskeletal adaptor connecting extracellular alpha-dystroglycan to intracellular dystrophin or utrophin. These contacts provide the intracellular side of the matrix–membrane–cytoskeleton bridge in muscle and non-muscle tissues. In muscle, this linkage contributes to the structural integrity of the sarcolemma. Association with CLASP proteins also connects dystroglycan to microtubule-associated partners.

Transfers isovaleryl, 2-methylbutyryl and isobutyryl groups from its lipoyl arm to coenzyme A in mitochondrial branched-chain ketoacid oxidation. The E2 oligomer organizes the complex and its mobile lipoyl domain channels intermediates between component active sites.
Binds netrin and couples extracellular guidance cues to intracellular signaling that directs axon growth.

At the plasma membrane, DCC recruits components of a ligand-absence, caspase-dependent apoptotic signaling complex. Its intracellular region promotes caspase-9-dependent caspase-3 activation in the presence of additional cytosolic factors.

Secreted SLRP that binds fibrillar collagens through its leucine-rich-repeat core protein, decorating the fibril surface and limiting lateral fibril fusion to control collagen fibril diameter and spacing in skin, tendon and corneal stroma.

Binds TGF-beta1, -2 and -3 and sequesters them in the extracellular matrix, competing with cell-surface receptors and thereby dampening TGF-beta receptor signaling (the basis of decorin's anti-fibrotic activity).
Binds fibronectin through repeat motifs in its core protein, linking decorin to the fibronectin-containing interstitial matrix.

As the dynein-binding subunit of dynactin, p150Glued contributes to activation of cytoplasmic dynein-1 into a processive minus-end-directed motor that transports membranous cargoes and organelles along microtubules.

The p150Glued CAP-Gly and basic domains bind microtubules, tubulin and +TIPs, tethering dynein-dynactin to microtubule plus ends and, in neurons, promoting microtubule nucleation and suppressing catastrophe.
Cortical and spindle-associated dynein-dynactin positions and orients the mitotic spindle; p150Glued localizes asymmetrically to the metaphase cortex under Plk1/NuMA-LGN control.
A pool of p150Glued at mother-centriole subdistal appendages, recruited by KIF3A, anchors microtubules at the centrosome.

Binds and stabilizes the microtubule lattice (between protofilaments, 13-pf selective) in migrating neurons, maintaining the microtubule arrays of the leading process and perinuclear cage needed for neuronal migration.

Damage-sensing subunit of the UV-DDB (DDB1-DDB2) complex that directly binds UV-induced photolesions (CPDs and 6-4PPs) in chromatinized DNA and recruits/hands off the lesion to XPC to initiate global-genome nucleotide excision repair.

Substrate-recognition receptor (DCAF) of the CRL4(DDB2) (DDB1-CUL4A/CUL4B-RBX1) E3 ubiquitin ligase that assembles on UV-damaged chromatin and directs ubiquitination of histones (H2A, H3, H4), of XPC, and of DDB2 itself, helping remodel damaged nucleosomes and couple lesion recognition to repair.
PLP-dependent L-DOPA decarboxylation produces dopamine in the cytosol. The catalytic homodimer uses the same active-site chemistry as the serotonin-producing reaction.
PLP-dependent decarboxylation of 5-hydroxy-L-tryptophan produces serotonin in the cytosol. This is the second major substrate branch of the same DDC enzyme.

Binds the transcription factor CHOP (DDIT3), encoded downstream on the same mRNA, and co-localizes with it mainly in the nucleus. Shown with overexpressed tagged constructs by two independent groups; whether the interaction modulates CHOP activity is unknown.

Recognizes extracellular triple-helical collagen through its discoidin domain and couples collagen recognition to intracellular tyrosine kinase signaling. Src-dependent activation-loop phosphorylation and DDR2-performed autophosphorylation are distinct steps in this receptor mechanism.

ATP-driven 5-prime to 3-prime unwinding of DNA with accessible loading regions, including forked duplexes, D-loops and selected G-quadruplex substrates. At nuclear replication sites, DDX11 supports recovery of stalled forks and establishment of sister-chromatid cohesion.
Uses an ATP-dependent cycle to bind and locally unwind RNA duplexes, enabling RNA remodeling.
Acts as an auxiliary translation initiation factor that promotes formation of functional 80S complexes from mature ribosomal subunits.
Coordinates IKKε and IRF3 recruitment to enhance antiviral type I interferon signaling.
Binds and stimulates casein kinase 1 to support canonical Wnt signaling through Dishevelled phosphorylation.
Self-associates into intermediate filaments and binds cytoskeletal partners to connect and mechanically support muscle myofibrils, Z discs, intercalated discs and the peripheral sarcolemmal network.

Catalyzes the terminal and only committed step of triacylglycerol biosynthesis: transfer of a long-chain acyl group from acyl-CoA to the sn-3 position of 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol, producing triacyl-sn-glycerol and CoA, in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane.

Secondary acyl-CoA:retinol acyltransferase (ARAT) activity: esterifies retinol with a long-chain acyl group to form retinyl esters (EC 2.3.1.76), contributing to retinoid storage/homeostasis, notably in skin.
