Phosphorylates membrane diacylglycerol to phosphatidic acid using ATP, preferentially recycling arachidonoyl-containing diacylglycerol into the phosphatidylinositol cycle. Selectivity is strongest for the sn-2 acyl chain; stearoyl at sn-1 is favored among tested saturated chains, but other sn-1 chains can support substantial activity.
ATP-dependent phosphorylation of deoxyguanosine to dGMP in the mitochondrial matrix initiates purine deoxyribonucleoside salvage and supplies precursors for mitochondrial DNA synthesis.

The same mitochondrial salvage enzyme also phosphorylates deoxyadenosine to dAMP. This is a directly measured substrate activity of DGUOK; the resulting monophosphate supplies the dAMP salvage pathway.
Reduces the C7–C8 double bond of 7-dehydrocholesterol using NADPH, generating cholesterol at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane.
Contributes with EBP to the microsomal conversion of cholesterol-5,6-epoxides into cholestane-3beta,5alpha,6beta-triol at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane.
NADPH-dependent reduction of 7,8-dihydrofolate (and, slowly, folic acid) to tetrahydrofolate in the cytosol, regenerating the THF carrier on which cellular one-carbon metabolism depends.

Within the SHMT1-scaffolded nuclear thymidylate-synthesis complex, reduces the dihydrofolate produced by thymidylate synthase so that de novo dTMP synthesis can continue during DNA replication and repair.

FAD-bound CYB5R3 transfers reducing equivalents from NADH to cytochrome b5. The membrane product supplies this reductase step at the ER and mitochondrial outer membrane; the soluble erythroid product supports methemoglobin reduction. The same electron-delivery chemistry can feed partner enzymes, including mARC, without transferring their terminal substrate chemistry to CYB5R3.
Catalyzes uridine-to-pseudouridine isomerization in RNA. H/ACA guide RNPs support rRNA and snRNA modification, and dyskerin-dependent modification also occurs at human mRNA sites.

Binds the H/ACA region of telomerase RNA and organizes its protein contacts, supporting RNA accumulation and assembly of active telomerase. This structural contribution supports telomere maintenance; TERT performs DNA synthesis.

Receives the extracellular EDA-A1 signal and transmits it across the plasma membrane to intracellular signaling machinery, promoting canonical NF-kappaB signaling. Ligand recognition and signal transmission constitute one cytokine-receptor function.

Dihydrolipoyllysine-residue acetyltransferase (E2) that transfers the acetyl group from the acetyl-dihydrolipoyl-lysine intermediate to coenzyme A, forming acetyl-CoA, as the second catalytic step of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex reaction, acting as the structural and catalytic core of the complex in the mitochondrial matrix.

As a FAD-dependent homodimer, DLD reoxidizes reduced lipoyl groups on E2 or GCSH carrier proteins and reduces NAD+. The same catalytic unit supports several mitochondrial ketoacid-dehydrogenase systems and glycine cleavage; it performs lipoyl regeneration rather than the E1 decarboxylation or E2 acyl-transfer reactions.

Provides a postsynaptic scaffold whose PDZ domains recognize NMDA-receptor C-terminal motifs and whose other interactions link receptor-associated proteins and trafficking machinery, helping position receptors at synaptic sites.

PSD-95 bridges synaptic receptors and downstream signaling/scaffold proteins through PDZ-mediated receptor recognition and SH3–GK partner recruitment. These contacts organize receptor targeting and signaling at excitatory postsynaptic sites.

PSD-95 provides structural elements of the intracellular postsynaptic density that maintain its protein organization and stabilize receptor-associated scaffold assemblies. This architectural role cooperates with its receptor-adaptor activity.

Core transcription factor function - DLX1 binds TAATTA-type DNA motifs at enhancers and promoters to regulate RNA polymerase II transcription, acting as both activator and repressor. Essential for GABAergic interneuron specification in the ventral telencephalon.

Sequence-specific DNA binding function - DLX1 recognizes and binds specific TAAT/ATTA DNA sequences at cis-regulatory regions through its homeodomain. Can modulate chromatin architecture and promoter-enhancer loop topology in a motif-dependent manner.

Long dystrophins provide an integrated cytoskeleton-to-membrane anchor: the N-terminal region binds actin and keratin-19-containing filaments, while the cysteine-rich/C-terminal region engages the sarcolemmal dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex. These complementary contacts support membrane integrity and organization of associated proteins; they are not separate core activities for each binding partner.

Secreted acidic phosphoprotein of bone and dentin matrix that binds calcium through its phosphorylated acidic domains and regulates hydroxyapatite nucleation and growth, contributing directly to mineralization of bone and dentin.

Binds regulatory DNA through the DM domain and forms sequence-dependent homomeric assemblies to activate or repress gonadal gene expression. This nuclear transcription-factor activity supports male differentiation. Mouse promoter occupancy and conditional deletion connect direct Stra8 transcriptional repression to restraint of premature meiotic entry; the separate proliferative outcomes are retained as context-dependent consequences. Regulatory direction depends on the target and cell type.

ATP-driven, minus-end-directed microtubule motor heavy chain of a single-headed inner dynein arm (IDA d). Within the sperm flagellar axoneme it generates sliding force needed for normal flagellar beating, and it is required for the inner dynein arms to assemble there. It also sits along respiratory ciliary axonemes, where its loss reduces beat frequency in mice.

Heavy chain (I1-alpha type) of the two-headed I1/f inner dynein arm, with DNAH2. It is an ATP-driven minus-end-directed microtubule motor that drives axonemal beating in the sperm flagellum and in respiratory and ependymal motile cilia, and it is needed for the inner arms to assemble in sperm.

Beta heavy chain and motor of the proximal (type 1) outer dynein arms of respiratory cilia and of the outer arms of motile embryonic node cilia (as mouse lrd); minus-end-directed microtubule motor whose loss gives a stiff hyperkinetic beat and randomized left-right asymmetry because nodal flow fails.

DNAH12 is an inner dynein arm heavy chain with no microtubule-binding domain. It acts as an assembly hub: it binds DNALI1 and DNAH1 and recruits them into the inner dynein arms of the sperm flagellar axoneme. It also binds the radial spoke head proteins RSPH1, RSPH9 and DNAJB13, which helps keep the central pair stable. Loss of DNAH12 removes the IDAs and the central pair, causing MMAF and asthenoteratozoospermia. The mouse models retain tracheal ciliary beating and morphology; knockout mice also retain tracheal axonemal ultrastructure and comparable DNALI1/DNAH1 abundance and localization in trachea and oviduct. Affected men reported no PCD symptoms. This contrast supports a preferential requirement in sperm flagella, while the human clinical and mouse experimental readouts remain distinct.

Force-generating beta heavy chain of the sperm outer dynein arm. Together with the gamma chain DNAH8, DNAH17 hydrolyses ATP in its AAA1 site and moves towards microtubule minus ends, sliding doublet microtubules to power sperm flagellar beating. It is an essential structural subunit of the sperm ODA: without it the other ODA subunits do not accumulate, and men and mice lacking it have immotile, malformed sperm while motile cilia elsewhere are spared.

Heavy chain of the two-headed I1/f inner dynein arm, with DNAH10. It is an ATP-driven minus-end-directed microtubule motor that drives axonemal beating in the sperm flagellum and in 9+2 motile cilia, and it is needed for the inner dynein arms and normal axonemal organization to form in sperm.

Gamma heavy chain and motor of both proximal and distal outer dynein arms in respiratory, ependymal and nodal motile cilia; hydrolyses ATP to walk towards microtubule minus ends, generating the doublet sliding that drives ciliary beating and the fluid flows of mucociliary clearance and nodal left-right patterning. Required for the outer dynein arm to assemble.

Force-generating gamma heavy chain of the sperm outer dynein arm. Paired with the beta heavy chain DNAH17, DNAH8 uses ATP hydrolysis in its AAA1 site to walk towards microtubule minus ends, producing sliding between doublet microtubules that powers beating of the sperm flagellum. DNAH8 and DNAH17 are required for each other's stable incorporation, and loss of DNAH8 causes MMAF and male infertility while motile cilia are spared.

Beta heavy chain and motor of the distal (type 2) outer dynein arms of respiratory cilia, partnered with DNAH5; minus-end-directed microtubule motor that powers beating of the distal ciliary segment. Its N-terminal tail binds the docking complex subunit ODAD1 (CCDC114), DNAH5 and DNAI2, and it is needed for distal ODAs to assemble. Expressed in nodal pit cells and required for normal left-right patterning.

DNAI1 forms an intermediate-chain interaction unit within outer dynein arms, with conserved contacts to dynein heavy and light chains. As a noncatalytic component it contributes to microtubule motor activity, outer-arm assembly and ciliary or sperm movement. The mature motor pool is axonemal; DNAI1 also occupies cytoplasmic DynAPs during the assembly/deployment stage, whose exact reaction sequence remains unresolved.

DYNC1H1 supplies the ATP-driven minus-end motor activity of the dynein-1 complex. Recombinant human motor preparations establish directionality, and reconstitution with dynactin and an activating adaptor establishes regulated processive transport. The same force-generating activity supports cytoplasmic cargo transport, including retrograde axonal transport, nuclear movement, and spindle organization rather than representing separate molecular activities in each setting. During mitosis, cortical recruitment positions the spindle, while poleward transport contributes to spindle organization and removal of checkpoint proteins. Nuclear-migration evidence includes dynein-complex perturbation in mouse neurons; checkpoint-silencing evidence includes perturbation of an accessory dynein subunit and is not presented as a heavy-chain-specific assay.

The DYNC2H1 heavy chain supplies ATP-driven minus-end-directed movement to the dynein-2 complex during intraciliary retrograde transport. Human recombinant motor measurements establish polarity, and the human holoenzyme structure shows how its heavy-chain tails and accessory subunits organize an inhibited assembly. Conserved retrograde IFT returns transport machinery and cargo during cilium assembly and maintenance; this is a transport contribution, not axonemal polymerization. The 920-residue alternative product lacks the six AAA regions and stalk and is not assigned a complete motor function.

The N-terminal DYNC2H1 tail binds DYNC2LI1/LIC3 within the dynein-2 motor assembly. The recombinant human holoenzyme structure resolves the light-intermediate-chain interface; reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation of human DYNC2H1 residues 1–1650 with DYNC2LI1 independently supports this association. The heavy-chain tails also contact the WDR34/WDR60-associated intermediate-chain block. These complementary subunit interfaces organize the asymmetric assembly of the same motor complex. Full-length and engineered-tail experiments do not establish binding competence of every natural product.

Oligomerizes at membrane necks and couples GTP hydrolysis to membrane remodeling and vesicle scission during endocytosis. PH-domain lipid binding and partner interactions recruit and regulate the machinery. In macroautophagy, SNX18-dependent recruitment supports an early ATG9A membrane-carrier route, whereas LC3-dependent recruitment supports release of nascent autophagosomes from recycling endosomes. The GTPase also supports cortactin-dependent remodeling of actin bundles.

Methylates cytosine at CpG sites using S-adenosyl-L-methionine, preferentially restoring methylation on newly synthesized DNA opposite a methylated template strand. Intramolecular autoinhibition and recognition of ubiquitinated histone H3 help couple catalysis to appropriate substrates. By performing DNA methylation, DNMT1 also contributes to CpG-island silencing and DNA-methylation-dependent constitutive heterochromatin formation. The heterochromatin phenotype does not isolate catalytic from scaffolding effects.

Recognizes the H3K18 ubiquitin mark as part of the RFTS reader module that engages H3 bearing ubiquitin at both K18 and K23. This cooperative recognition regulates maintenance methylation together with hemimethylated DNA; an isolated K18 mark is not asserted to provide full activation.

Recognizes the H3K23 ubiquitin mark in the same cooperative H3K18/K23 reader module. Engagement of the paired ubiquitin marks helps relieve DNMT1 autoinhibition in conjunction with hemimethylated DNA, rather than constituting a separate methylation pathway.

Transfers methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine to the C5 position of DNA cytosines, establishing DNA methylation patterns. Human catalytic-domain assays show a preference for CpG sites while retaining measurable CpA and CpT methylation. Chromatin-associated methylation contributes to silencing at selected CpG-island promoters; histone recognition and regulatory partners help specify genomic targeting.

The ADD domain recognizes the histone H3 amino-terminal tail preferentially when lysine 4 is unmethylated, connecting the local histone state to DNA methyltransferase targeting. Human isolated-domain binding and structural experiments establish this recognition; methylated H3K4 peptides bind more weakly under the tested conditions.

The PWWP domain reads methylated histone H3 lysine 36, including H3K36me3 and H3K36me2, to help target DNA methylation within chromatin. Direct human-domain binding and the altered methylation pattern associated with PWWP substitutions support this recognition function; it is complementary to ADD-mediated recognition of the H3 amino terminus.

Catalytically competent DNMT3B transfers methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine to DNA cytosines, contributing to the establishment of DNA methylation patterns. Human catalytic-domain assays show preferential CpG methylation with measurable CpA and CpT activity. Oligomeric interactions with regulatory partners shape this chemistry; the catalytic activity must not be assigned indiscriminately to truncated or catalytically inactive splice products. This methyl-transfer chemistry contributes to epigenetic gene repression; mouse promoter-methylation experiments and conditional human D4Z4/DUX4 evidence support that role without assigning one silencing mechanism to every genomic locus.

The catalytically inactive DNMT3B3 product binds the nucleosome acidic patch and anchors a DNMT3A-containing methyltransferase complex to chromatin. This positions the active DNMT3A subunits toward linker DNA. Human-protein reconstitution, structural contacts and cellular anchoring-mutant experiments support a targeting role distinct from DNMT3B catalytic chemistry.

DOCK2 promotes guanine-nucleotide exchange on RAC GTPases, connecting upstream signals to actin remodeling and immune-cell motility. Purified human DOCK2–ELMO1 complexes directly exchange nucleotide on RAC1, while human DOCK2 deficiency disrupts receptor-triggered RAC1 activation and chemokine responses. RAC2 is supported as a substrate by the curated RAC2 exchange reaction and human cellular activation studies; these are distinct from the directly measured purified RAC1 assay. ELMO1 regulates substrate access and supports productive cellular signaling, with different N-terminal deletion effects in purified and cellular assays. DOCK2 acts in a cytosolic pool and can undergo regulated membrane recruitment.

DPAGT1 transfers GlcNAc-1-phosphate from UDP-GlcNAc to dolichyl phosphate, forming GlcNAc-PP-dolichol and UMP. This first glycosyl-unit transfer initiates dolichol-linked oligosaccharide assembly on the cytoplasmic face of the ER membrane. The full-length human protein is a ten-pass membrane enzyme whose purified activity is directly demonstrated; subsequent glycan extension and transfer to protein are performed by other enzymes.

DPM1 provides the catalytic component of the endoplasmic-reticulum dolichol-phosphate mannose synthase complex, transferring mannose from GDP-mannose to dolichyl phosphate. DPM3 anchors and stabilizes DPM1, while DPM2 increases activity and stabilizes DPM3. Purified human complexes reconstituted into liposomes produce the lipid-linked mannose donor used by downstream glycosyltransferases. Activity retained without DPM2 when DPM3 is overexpressed distinguishes regulation from an absolute three-subunit requirement; it does not establish activity of an isolated unanchored human protein.

Regulatory (non-catalytic) subunit of the dolichol-phosphate mannose (Dol-P-Man) synthase complex. As an activating regulator, DPM2 stabilizes the complex (required for ER localization/stability of catalytic DPM1 and for DPM3 stability), enhances binding of the dolichyl phosphate substrate, and increases Dol-P-Man synthase activity ~10-fold, thereby driving Dol-P-Man biosynthesis in the ER membrane. Dol-P-Man is the mannosyl donor for N-glycosylation, GPI-anchor synthesis, and protein O-/C-mannosylation.

DPM3 is the membrane-anchoring/adaptor subunit that tethers the catalytic DPM1 subunit (which has no transmembrane domain) to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and bridges it to DPM2, as part of the dolichol-phosphate mannose (DPM) synthase complex.

Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (NADP+) activity: DPD is a cytosolic homodimeric flavoprotein that catalyzes the NADPH-dependent reduction of the pyrimidine bases uracil and thymine to 5,6-dihydrouracil and 5,6-dihydrothymine (EC 1.3.1.2), the initial and rate-limiting step of reductive pyrimidine base catabolism. Catalysis relies on bound FAD, FMN and four [4Fe-4S] clusters per subunit that transfer electrons from NADPH to the substrate, and on binding of NADP and the uracil/thymine substrate.

Zn2+-dependent hydrolytic ring opening of 5,6-dihydrouracil to N-carbamoyl-beta-alanine (and 5,6-dihydrothymine to N-carbamoyl-beta-aminoisobutyrate), the second step of reductive pyrimidine catabolism.
Dihydropyrimidinase activity within the broader pyrimidine nucleobase catabolic pathway, using a binuclear zinc center for catalysis.
Acts as a nuclear transcriptional corepressor, with ETO-enhanced reporter repression and association with nuclear corepressor machinery.

DSC2 is a desmosomal cadherin whose calcium-binding extracellular domains engage cadherins across adjacent cells, while its cytoplasmic tail couples the adhesive interface to the desmosomal plaque. Human ectodomain experiments establish adhesive binding to desmogleins; complementary single-molecule experiments also detect DSC2 self-binding under their assay conditions. These observations support cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion without requiring a universal exclusive homo- or heterophilic arrangement. The two natural splice products share the extracellular and transmembrane regions but have different cytoplasmic tails: human tail constructs associate with plakophilin-2, whereas the longer DSC2a tail additionally supports plakoglobin and desmoplakin-fragment association in lysate-based assays. This integrated adhesive and anchoring role maintains desmosome integrity and contributes to junction assembly in cardiac and epithelial tissues; contextual signaling and repair effects do not establish a separate catalytic activity.

PIGP is a required, non-catalytic accessory subunit of the GPI-GnT complex, an ER-membrane glycosyltransferase that catalyzes the first committed step of GPI-anchor biosynthesis (GlcNAc transfer from UDP-GlcNAc to phosphatidylinositol). PIGP does not independently possess transferase activity (the catalytic subunit is PIGA) but is essential for complex activity: PIG-P-null cells are GPI-anchor negative.

Desmoglein-2 provides a calcium-dependent extracellular adhesive interface at desmosomes. Its cadherin ectodomain binds desmocollins across cell contacts, while its membrane-spanning and cytoplasmic regions connect the adhesive interface to the intracellular plaque and intermediate-filament attachment machinery. These complementary parts supply an adhesive structural component during desmosome assembly and support epithelial and cardiomyocyte cohesion. Purified human ectodomain experiments establish heterophilic binding; separate atomic-force measurements detect homophilic interactions under their assay conditions, so adhesive specificity is not reduced to an exclusive interaction type.

Desmoglein-2 provides a cell-surface attachment receptor for selected species B adenoviruses, including Ad3, Ad7, Ad11 and Ad14/Ad14a. Its extracellular domain engages virus particles, and DSG2 expression enables Ad3 attachment and transduction in receptor-negative human cells. Ad11 can use DSG2 when CD46 is blocked. This receptor role is distinct from cadherin-mediated cell adhesion.

Desmoplakin couples intracellular, plasma-membrane-associated junctional plaques to intermediate-filament networks through complementary N-terminal plaque interactions and C-terminal filament-binding interfaces. This structural linkage organizes desmosomes and the spatial distribution of intermediate filaments, maintaining epithelial and cardiac tissue integrity. Cytoplasmic desmoplakin assembly particles are recruited to cell contacts; cardiac desmoplakin also occupies fascia-adherens-like mixed junctions. Its N-terminal association with EB1 supplies spatial cues for cortical microtubule ends and promotes connexin-43 localization to cell-cell junctions. Human keratinocyte experiments distinguish this EB1-dependent function from generalized loss of adhesion or intermediate-filament attachment. Natural splice products retain the terminal regions while differing in their central rod.

Secreted DSPP-derived proteins contribute to the structural integrity and mineral maturation of dentin. The acidic, phosphorylated DPP region interacts with calcium and collagen, coupling matrix association to mineral deposition; native rat phosphophoryn promotes apatite formation in reconstituted biochemical assays. Mouse null and DPP-truncation experiments establish complementary contributions of the DSP-containing and DPP regions to the amount and uniformity of later circumpulpal dentin mineralization. Initial matrix-vesicle-associated mineral formation can occur without DSPP in that mouse setting.

Thymidylate (dTMP) kinase activity: ATP- and Mg2+-dependent phosphorylation of dTMP to dTDP, the common penultimate step of dTTP synthesis shared by the de novo and salvage routes; essential for supplying dTTP for DNA replication.
Formation of dTDP as the direct reaction product of dTMP phosphorylation, the immediate biosynthetic output of DTYMK en route to dTTP.

ERK1/2-selective dual-specificity MAP kinase phosphatase: removes the phosphates from the activation-loop Thr and Tyr of ERK1/2, inactivating them as an ERK-induced negative-feedback regulator of growth-factor (notably FGF) signalling in the cytoplasm.

Docking of ERK1/2 through the N-terminal kinase-interaction motif, which confers substrate selectivity, allosterically activates the catalytic domain, and together with the nuclear export signal retains ERK in the cytoplasm.

DYRK1A catalyzes ATP-dependent protein phosphorylation. Direct human biochemical studies support serine/threonine substrate phosphorylation and tyrosine autophosphorylation, including weak tyrosine activity of the mature enzyme. Nuclear substrates include the RNA polymerase II CTD and histone H3; Tau and splicing factors extend its substrate repertoire. Phosphorylation-dependent regulation of transcription and alternative exon choice is context-dependent, without a universal positive effect on all transcripts. The histidine-rich region promotes CTD association and hyperphosphorylation; this targeting mechanism is not assigned to natural products lacking that region.

Dysferlin binds acidic membrane phospholipids through its C2 domains. Calcium enhances binding by the tested canonical domains, while basal binding and the alternative exon-1 C2A response show that this activity is not uniformly calcium-dependent across constructs. This membrane interaction underlies its role in muscle membrane maintenance and repair. Surface, T-tubule and endosomal pools are supported, with muscle-specific sarcolemmal localization distinguished from non-muscle plasma membrane. These gene-level activities and locations are not assigned equally to all 15 products, particularly the form lacking the canonical membrane anchor. Human dysferlin also promotes SNARE-dependent lipid mixing in vitro, providing a direct mechanistic contribution to membrane repair.

Calcium binding by dysferlin C2 domains tunes their membrane interactions. Purified human canonical C2A and the seven tested human C2 domains bind calcium directly. The alternative exon-1 C2A fragment behaves differently in solution and on lipid membranes; the observation defines a biochemical construct class rather than proving identical calcium responses of every full-length splice product.

Catalyzes sterol Delta8-to-Delta7 isomerization at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane during cholesterol biosynthesis, including zymostenol-to-lathosterol and zymosterol-to-cholesta-7,24-dien-3beta-ol conversion. Human enzyme assays and the five-transmembrane-helix structure support this catalytic unit.

Thymidine phosphorylase activity - catalyzes the reversible phosphorolysis of thymidine (and 2'-deoxyuridine) to thymine (uracil) + 2-deoxy-alpha-D-ribose 1-phosphate, the defining enzymatic function of TYMP.

Catalyzes mitochondrial enoyl-CoA hydration, including crotonyl-CoA conversion to 3-hydroxybutanoyl-CoA during fatty acid beta-oxidation and methacrylyl-CoA conversion to 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA during valine catabolism. Acryloyl-CoA hydration yields 3-hydroxypropionyl-CoA and is a distinct experimentally supported reaction of the same enzyme.
Delivers aminoacyl-tRNA to the ribosome during translational elongation. GTP binding and hydrolysis are parts of this delivery cycle rather than a separate signaling function.

Binds PI4KB and increases its phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase activity. Direct activation is demonstrated with purified proteins and is supported by endogenous interaction and depletion experiments in MCF7 cells; its contribution in normal tissues remains to be established.

Acts as an extracellular matrix glycoprotein contributing to matrix integrity. Human retinal pigment epithelial knockout and rescue experiments support a role in maintaining collagen VI network formation and extracellular matrix turnover; these experiments do not establish direct collagen binding or intrinsic protease activity.

Associates with the epidermal growth factor receptor and stimulates EGFR-dependent signaling in human pancreatic carcinoma cells. Cellular co-immunoprecipitation and EGF competition support receptor association; purified EFEMP1 treatment activates EGFR and downstream Akt/ERK. The tested product is not assigned to a specific natural splice isoform, and the contribution of this mechanism in normal tissues remains unresolved.

Acts as a plasma-membrane receptor ligand that binds Eph receptors through its extracellular domain and contributes the ligand-engagement step of ephrin receptor signaling at the plasma membrane. Receptor-binding and activation studies support this cell-contact signaling mechanism, with adhesion or repulsion depending on cellular context. Recombinant human ectodomain measurements establish additional Eph receptor interactions without implying that every binding event activates a receptor or that soluble and membrane-bound presentations are equivalent.
EGFR ligand activity that engages EGFR-family receptors at the cell surface and triggers ERBB receptor signaling to downstream MAPK outputs.

The membrane-spanning EGFR receptor binds extracellular growth-factor ligands and couples receptor association to activation of its intracellular tyrosine kinase. Phosphorylation of receptor tails and associated substrates provides docking and signaling sites that connect ligand recognition to downstream cellular responses. Internalized receptor pools can also support kinase signaling on endosomal membranes in defined cellular contexts.

EGR2 binds regulatory DNA through its C2H2 zinc fingers and activates RNA polymerase II transcription in the nucleus. Human-cell promoter, motif-mutagenesis and nuclear-extract binding assays establish direct activation of BNIP3L and BAK. Coactivation by HCF-1 was studied with mouse Krox20 in a heterologous cell system. Its transcriptional program promotes Schwann-cell differentiation and peripheral myelination: mouse loss-of-function studies establish these developmental roles, while human inherited myelinopathies support their conservation.

EGR2 has a conserved SUMO E3-ligase function toward NAB coregulators, recruiting the SUMO-conjugating E2 UBC9 and substrate through distinct interaction regions. Purified mouse Egr2 promotes mouse Nab2 modification in a defined E1/E2/human SUMO1/ATP reaction, supporting catalytic participation; cellular and developmental assays connect NAB sumoylation to transcriptional feedback. This is ortholog evidence for the human function, without a purified human EGR2 assay or equivalence of its natural products.

N-terminal 2-enoyl-CoA hydratase that catalyzes step 2 of the peroxisomal fatty-acid beta-oxidation spiral, hydrating trans-2-enoyl-CoA to L-(3S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA (L stereochemistry, distinguishing it from the D-bifunctional protein HSD17B4). Acts on medium/long-chain and dicarboxylic-acid (omega-oxidation-product) substrates.

C-terminal NAD+-dependent L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase that catalyzes step 3 of the peroxisomal beta-oxidation spiral, oxidizing L-(3S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA to 3-oxoacyl-CoA with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The long-chain-specific activity (GO:0016509) is a precise child.
ER-membrane PERK phosphorylates EIF2S1/eIF2alpha to attenuate translation initiation during ER stress and drive the PERK arm of the integrated stress response.
The PERK luminal domain directly recognizes misfolded proteins, coupling ER protein-folding stress to activation of PERK-mediated UPR signaling.
Contributes to assembly and regulation of the cytosolic eIF2B complex, supporting nucleotide exchange on eIF2 and regeneration of active initiation factor for cytoplasmic translation initiation.

Contributes to the eIF2B nucleotide exchange factor through association with its epsilon subunit and assembly of the cytosolic complex, supporting eIF2 recycling during cytoplasmic translation initiation.
Contributes to assembly and phosphorylation-sensitive regulation of the cytosolic eIF2B nucleotide-exchange complex, supporting regeneration of active eIF2 for cytoplasmic translation initiation.

miRNA-guided AGO2 cleaves sufficiently complementary target mRNAs through its PIWI catalytic site. This is the endonucleolytic mechanism specified by the current GO:0035279 definition; target decay driven by recruited deadenylases is a separate activity.
siRNA-loaded AGO2 recognizes complementary target mRNA and directly cleaves it through the PIWI endoribonuclease active site, executing siRNA-mediated endonucleolytic silencing.

AGO2 binds miRNA guides and target RNAs and recruits TNRC6/GW182-associated effectors to repress translation and promote poly(A)-tail shortening and subsequent decay. AGO2 supplies guide recognition and recruitment; PAN2–PAN3 and CCR4–CAF1 carry out deadenylation. P-body association is supported but visible granules are not obligatory sites for every silencing event.

AGO2 accepts small-RNA duplexes, retains the guide strand and releases or cleaves the passenger during RISC maturation. Reconstituted Dicer/TRBP/AGO2 complexes and cellular pre-RISC assays establish guide loading; canonical Dicer-mediated precursor cleavage is a distinct upstream step.

AGO2 directly cleaves the short pre-miR-451 hairpin to an intermediate in a Dicer-independent maturation pathway. Recombinant human AGO2 supplies this catalytic step; subsequent 3-prime trimming is not attributed to AGO2. RNA endonuclease activity is used here because the substrate is a precursor hairpin, outside the mRNA substrates specified by the two target-slicing molecular functions.
Binds GTP and initiator methionyl-tRNA and hydrolyzes GTP as the catalytic gamma subunit of eIF2, supporting initiator-tRNA delivery during cytoplasmic translation initiation.
Engages initiator methionyl-tRNA through the gamma-centered binding surface of GTP-bound eIF2, supporting ternary-complex formation.
Binds eIF3 subunits, including eIF3H and eIF3M, and contributes to the structural organization and initiation-factor activity of cytosolic eIF3.

Reported deubiquitinase activity includes cleavage of ubiquitin-linked test substrates and DTX1-associated regulation of activated NOTCH1 ubiquitination. The precise NOTCH1 substrate form and human catalytic mechanism remain unresolved.

Catalyzes serine-dependent cleavage of internal peptide bonds in host and microbial proteins, contributing to antibacterial defense and extracellular matrix disassembly. In defined NET-formation pathways, cytosolic actin and nuclear histone cleavage support progression to chromatin decondensation and NET release.
Confers elasticity on extracellular matrix by forming the elastin core of elastic fibers through tropoelastin self-association and matrix incorporation.
Binds fibulin and fibrillin matrix components as tropoelastin, supporting its organization and incorporation during elastic fiber assembly.

Binds microtubule polymers through its N-terminal self-association region together with the adjacent basic region, contributing to organization of the microtubule cytoskeleton. Independently, the concave surface of the TAPE domain associates with soluble alpha/beta-tubulin dimers. The soluble interaction persists after removal of the N-terminal self-association region and is disrupted by the M7 surface mutant without reported loss of the TAPE fold; it does not itself establish an effect on microtubule polymerization.

Cooperates with primary signaling receptors at the plasma membrane. Endoglin potentiates BMP9–ALK1 signaling and modulates TGF-beta receptor responses through receptor association; the effect depends on ligand and cellular context.
Binds BMP9 and BMP10 through its extracellular orphan region, providing ligand recognition for endoglin-associated BMP signaling.

Catalyses the penultimate step of glycolysis, the Mg2+-dependent reversible dehydration of 2-phospho-D-glycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate plus water (EC 4.2.1.11), as the muscle-specific beta subunit of the enolase dimer; the reverse reaction contributes to gluconeogenesis.
The same enolase catalytic activity operating in the hydration (PEP to 2-PG) direction contributes to gluconeogenesis.
Binds magnesium ion, the essential catalytic cofactor required for the enolase reaction and for stabilizing the enolase dimer.
Hydrolyzes extracellular ATP to AMP and inorganic pyrophosphate, supplying a biochemical regulator of mineral deposition in bone and soft tissues.
Hydrolyzes 2′3′-cyclic GMP–AMP to AMP and GMP, limiting availability of this extracellular signaling nucleotide.

Hydrolyzes extracellular ribonucleoside triphosphates and nucleoside diphosphates at the cell surface in a divalent-cation-dependent apyrase reaction. ATP is converted successively through ADP to AMP, releasing inorganic phosphate at each step. Removal of extracellular ADP contributes to endothelial inhibition of platelet aggregation. Conversion of AMP to adenosine is a separate reaction performed by ecto-5'-nucleotidase/CD73.
Acetylates internal lysine residues in histones and nonhistone proteins using acetyl-CoA, modifying chromatin and regulatory-protein function.
Coactivates transcription by recruiting and stabilizing assemblies of DNA-binding transcription factors and other transcriptional regulators.

Binds transmembrane ephrin-B2 at the plasma membrane and transduces cell-contact signals through receptor tyrosine kinase activity. EphB4–ephrin-B2 interactions participate in angiogenic vessel patterning and endothelial organization through both EphB4 forward signaling and reciprocal ephrin-B2 signaling; the vascular role is not attributed exclusively to receptor catalysis. The receptor molecular activity applies to the canonical membrane- and kinase-containing product; equivalent functions have not been established for the three shorter natural splice products.

Laforin binds glucan substrates through its carbohydrate-binding and phosphatase domains and hydrolyzes phosphate esters on glycogen, directly contributing to glycogen metabolism. Human recombinant-protein assays establish glycogen dephosphorylation, while structure-guided mutations distinguish substrate binding from catalytic efficiency. The tested long laforin products are not assumed to confer the same activity on all alternative products. These biochemical results do not establish that every effect on glycogen architecture or disease prevention requires phosphatase activity.

Laforin acts as an adaptor that permits malin-dependent ubiquitination of protein targeting to glycogen (PTG/PPP1R3C). The reconstituted reaction requires laforin and an interaction-competent malin protein, distinguishing this coordinated substrate–ligase role from association alone. Malin supplies the ubiquitin-ligase activity; laforin supplies the adaptor contribution. Cellular PTG regulation can persist with catalytically inactive laforin, separating this role from glucan phosphate hydrolysis.

ERBB-family receptor tyrosine kinase coreceptor activity in plasma-membrane signaling receptor dimers, phosphorylating tyrosine residues that couple ERBB2-containing receptors to MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling.

Canonical full-length XPD uses ATP to unwind DNA in the 5′–3′ direction within TFIIH, contributing DNA opening during nucleotide-excision repair. Human XPD-dependent motor and repair assays establish this catalytic role separately from XPB translocation and the downstream incision reactions.

As an integral TFIIH subunit, full-length XPD provides a protein-complex scaffold that connects the p44-associated core and the CAK module in an assembly competent for RNA-polymerase-II transcription initiation. This structural contribution is distinct from its repair helicase activity; CDK7 supplies the associated protein-kinase chemistry.

XPB couples ATP hydrolysis to movement along duplex DNA within the TFIIH core, promoting DNA opening during nucleotide-excision repair and RNA polymerase II transcription initiation, and contributing to the transition through promoter clearance. The motor acts in regulated multiprotein assemblies; its transcriptional impact varies among promoters and experimental conditions.
Hydrolyzes ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate at the XPB active site within TFIIH, supplying chemical energy to its coupled DNA-translocation motor during repair and transcription.

ERCC4 provides the catalytic nuclease subunit of ERCC1–XPF, cleaving duplex DNA near a double-strand/single-strand junction during nucleotide-excision repair and interstrand cross-link repair. NER uses this activity for the incision on the 5′ side of the lesion. The broader ICL term includes SLX4-associated repair contexts as well as NER-associated crosslink incision; it does not restrict all ICL repair to the GO:1901255 branch or impose one universal recruitment and incision sequence.

The same ERCC1–XPF nuclease processes junctions bearing nonhomologous 3′ tails during single-strand-annealing repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Human RAD52 binds XPF and can stimulate junction incision under defined order-of-addition conditions; ERCC4 performs the cleavage step rather than the annealing reaction.

Full-length XPG recognizes single-strand/double-strand DNA junctions and catalyzes the 3′ incision of the damaged strand during nucleotide-excision repair, acting in repair assemblies in the nucleoplasm in both global-genome and transcription-coupled pathways. Its DNA endonuclease activity also cleaves covalently closed single-stranded DNA in purified-protein assays. The repair-complex context does not imply a permanently preassembled complex or constitutive TFIIH membership. These activities are established for the canonical 1,186-residue protein; the functions of the natural 419- and 232-residue products remain unresolved.

Site-specific endoribonuclease (KEN domain) that excises the 26-nt intron from XBP1 mRNA during ER stress, initiating unconventional cytoplasmic splicing that produces the XBP1s transcription factor; also cleaves ER-associated mRNAs (RIDD).
Serine/threonine kinase that trans-autophosphorylates upon stress-induced dimerization of the luminal sensor domain; autophosphorylation and nucleotide occupancy activate the RNase domain.
Luminal-domain homodimerization (opposed in unstressed cells by BiP bound via ERdj4) that couples the ER protein-folding state to activation of the cytosolic effector domains.

Electron transfer (electron-carrier) activity: the ETFA/ETFB heterodimer accepts electrons from multiple mitochondrial matrix FAD-dependent primary dehydrogenases and passes them to ETF-ubiquinone oxidoreductase (ETFDH), feeding the respiratory chain.
FAD binding: ETFA coordinates most of the single FAD cofactor of the ETF heterodimer, which transiently stores the electrons transferred between dehydrogenases and ETFDH.

As the common electron acceptor for the beta-oxidation acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, ETF is required for mitochondrial fatty-acid beta-oxidation flux; its loss produces a functional block in this pathway (MADD).
As the electron acceptor for amino-acid-catabolic dehydrogenases (e.g. glutaryl-CoA and isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenases), ETF is required for normal amino-acid catabolism.

Beta subunit of the electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF) heterodimer; together with ETFA it accepts electrons from matrix FAD-dependent dehydrogenases and relays them to ETF-ubiquinone oxidoreductase, functioning as a mobile electron carrier.

As part of ETF, accepts electrons from acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of mitochondrial fatty-acid beta-oxidation (e.g. medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase), coupling beta-oxidation to the respiratory chain; the ETFB recognition loop docks these dehydrogenases.

Electron-transferring-flavoprotein dehydrogenase (ETF-QO, EC 1.5.5.1): oxidizes reduced electron-transfer flavoprotein and reduces ubiquinone in the mitochondrial inner membrane, using bound FAD and a [4Fe-4S] cluster as redox relays.
Ubiquinone binding at a single hydrophobic site per monomer, positioning the physiological electron acceptor for reduction to ubiquinol.
FAD cofactor binding; the flavin is a core redox center that shuttles electrons from reduced ETF toward ubiquinone.
[4Fe-4S] cluster binding; a single iron-sulfur cluster serves as the second redox center of ETF-QO.

Links fatty-acid beta-oxidation (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase branch) to the respiratory chain by accepting the electrons generated during acyl-CoA dehydrogenation via ETF; loss of ETFDH blocks this flux and causes multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.

Transcriptional coactivator recruited to target genes by SIX homeodomain transcription factors (SIX1/2/4/5); SIX supplies DNA binding and EYA1 supplies transactivation, and EYA phosphatase activity converts SIX1-DACH from repressor to activator, driving inner ear, kidney and branchial arch development.

HAD-family non-thiol protein tyrosine phosphatase (substrates include itself and histone H2AX pTyr-142, GO:0140793); after DNA damage it dephosphorylates H2AX Tyr-142 at gamma-H2AX foci, promoting repair-factor recruitment and survival rather than apoptosis.

Mg2+/ATP-dependent long-chain fatty acid-CoA ligase that thioesterifies long-chain fatty acids (preferentially palmitoleate, oleate, linoleate; also palmitate and arachidonate) with CoA on the cytosolic face of the outer mitochondrial membrane, generating the acyl-CoAs that are channelled into carnitine-dependent mitochondrial beta-oxidation.

At the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, the same long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase activity supplies acyl-CoA donors for glycerolipid synthesis, notably triacylglycerol, which underlies ACSL1-dependent neutral lipid storage (lipid droplet accumulation is a downstream consequence; ACSL1 protein itself has not been shown to reside on lipid droplets).

Activates long-chain fatty acids, especially arachidonate and other highly unsaturated C20 and C22 substrates, to acyl-CoA thioesters using ATP and CoA. This supplies lipid synthesis/remodeling and promotes ferroptosis susceptibility by enabling accumulation of peroxidation-sensitive membrane lipids. ER and mitochondrial pools are supported in human cells; their relative contributions depend on cellular context.
FADD bridges death-domain receptor platforms to CASP8/CASP10-containing DED assemblies to form death-inducing signaling complexes that initiate extrinsic apoptotic signaling.
Fumarylacetoacetase catalyzing the terminal step of cytosolic tyrosine/phenylalanine catabolism: hydrolysis of 4-fumarylacetoacetate to fumarate and acetoacetate.

The bromodomain-proximal PHD finger recognizes H3K4me3 and helps recruit or stabilize NURF on chromatin. This is the H3-recognition arm of a coupled PHD–bromodomain mechanism. BPTF contributes targeting and regulation to NURF remodeling; the associated ISWI motor supplies ATP hydrolysis.

The adjacent bromodomain recognizes H4K16ac as the acetyl-histone arm of the same coupled NURF-recruitment mechanism. In the tested mononucleosomes, H4K16ac enhances engagement alongside PHD recognition of H3K4me3, and intact reader pockets support full-length BPTF recruitment at HOXA9. Peptide binding to other acetyl-H4 sites limits claims of universal H4K16ac exclusivity.

As an essential, non-catalytic structural subunit and protein-interaction hub of the multiprotein Fanconi anemia (FA) core complex, FANCA acts as a scaffold/adaptor that binds FANCG and FANCF and directly anchors FAAP20, promoting assembly, stability, nuclear accumulation and chromatin loading of the core complex so that it can monoubiquitinate the FANCD2-FANCI complex during replication-coupled repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks.

Central scaffold and dimerization subunit of the FANCB-FANCL-FAAP100 (BL100) catalytic module of the Fanconi anemia core complex. FANCB bridges and dimerizes two BL100 heterotrimers, templating assembly of the symmetric core complex and stimulating the FANCL RING E3 ligase to monoubiquitinate the FANCD2-FANCI complex during replication-coupled interstrand crosslink repair.

Non-catalytic substrate-recognition subunit of the Fanconi anemia (FA) core complex E3 ubiquitin ligase; FANCC binds FANCE (and, via complex assembly, FANCA) to form, with FANCF, the module that recruits and positions the FANCD2-FANCI substrate for monoubiquitination, thereby contributing to the ubiquitin-ligase activity of the complex.

With its paralog FANCI, FANCD2 forms the ID2 DNA-repair complex that binds DNA and, upon FANCL/UBE2T-catalyzed monoubiquitination at Lys561, is remodeled into a closed sliding clamp encircling duplex DNA. FANCD2 itself preferentially binds single-stranded DNA. This chromatin-loaded, DNA-binding clamp scaffold coordinates the core steps of replication-coupled interstrand crosslink repair (nucleolytic incision, translesion synthesis) and homologous recombination, and recruits downstream factors such as the nuclease FAN1.

Molecular adaptor within the Fanconi anemia core complex: FANCE directly binds FANCC (bridging into the assembled FA core complex) and directly binds the substrate FANCD2, physically linking the core complex to its downstream substrate and thereby promoting DNA-damage-induced FANCD2 monoubiquitination and interstrand crosslink repair. FANCE is also required for the nuclear accumulation of FANCC.

Acts as a flexible molecular adaptor/scaffold within the Fanconi anemia nuclear core complex, bridging the FANCA:FANCG and FANCC:FANCE subcomplexes to assemble and stabilize the complex; this scaffolding is required for the complex's monoubiquitination of FANCD2-FANCI and thus for replication-coupled DNA interstrand cross-link repair and chromosome stability.

FANCG is a tetratricopeptide-repeat (TPR) scaffold subunit of the nuclear Fanconi anemia core complex. It binds FANCA directly and, as a protein-protein adaptor, is required for the assembly, stability and nuclear accumulation of the eight-subunit core complex. The intact core complex acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase (catalyzed by the FANCL RING subunit) that monoubiquitinates the FANCD2-FANCI heterodimer on chromatin in response to DNA damage/replication stress, thereby driving replication-coupled DNA interstrand crosslink repair (and coordinating downstream translesion synthesis and homologous recombination). FANCG has no intrinsic catalytic or DNA-binding activity; whether it contributes more than structural stabilization (e.g. substrate presentation) to the E3 ligase reaction is unresolved.

Mg2+-dependent hydrolysis of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate to fructose 6-phosphate in the cytosol, the irreversible, AMP- and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate-regulated step of gluconeogenesis in liver and kidney.

Squalene synthase: catalyses the NAD(P)H- and Mg2+-dependent reductive condensation of two molecules of farnesyl diphosphate to squalene (via presqualene diphosphate), the first committed step of sterol biosynthesis, at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane.

Second condensation step of farnesyl diphosphate synthase: Mg(2+)-dependent head-to-tail condensation of isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) with geranyl diphosphate (GPP) to form (2E,6E)-farnesyl diphosphate (FPP), EC 2.5.1.10. This is the defining activity of FDPS and the committed step producing the FPP branch-point metabolite of the isoprenoid pathway.

First condensation step of farnesyl diphosphate synthase: Mg(2+)-dependent head-to-tail condensation of isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) with the allylic primer dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) to form geranyl diphosphate (GPP), EC 2.5.1.1. GPP is the substrate for the subsequent FPP-forming step catalyzed by the same enzyme.

FECH is ferrochelatase, catalysing the terminal, committed step of heme biosynthesis: insertion of ferrous iron (Fe2+) into protoporphyrin IX to form protoheme (heme b). It acts as a homodimer on the matrix face of the mitochondrial inner membrane.

Each FECH subunit coordinates a [2Fe-2S] cluster (via three C-terminal cysteines plus one additional ligand) that is required for enzyme activity and stability, and binds the ferrous iron substrate; these metal-binding activities support, but are secondary to, the catalytic ferrochelatase function.

Secreted, mesenchyme-derived FGF10 binds selectively to the epithelial IIIb isoform of FGFR2 (and FGFR1b) in heparan-sulfate-stabilized complexes, activating receptor tyrosine kinase signalling including the RAS-ERK cascade in adjacent epithelium.
FGF10 acts as a paracrine growth factor stimulating proliferation of FGFR2b-expressing epithelial cells, including embryonic pancreatic epithelium, urothelium and keratinocytes.
FGF10 is the mesenchymal chemoattractant and inductive signal that directs epithelial bud outgrowth and branching morphogenesis of lung, salivary and lacrimal glands.

Secreted endocrine FGFR ligand: FGF19 binds FGFR4 in complex with the beta-Klotho co-receptor on hepatocytes, activating FGFR signaling (FRS2/ERK1/2) that represses CYP7A1 and bile acid biosynthesis as the intestinal arm of the bile acid feedback loop.

Postprandial, insulin-independent hepatic signal: FGF19 acting through hepatic FGFR (KLB-FGFR4) and Ras-ERK-p90RSK signaling increases glycogen synthase activity and hepatic glycogen and protein synthesis.

Endocrine ligand that binds FGFR1c in a ternary complex with the co-receptor alpha-Klotho, initiating FGFR signalling (FRS2 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation) in Klotho-expressing target cells of kidney and parathyroid.

Bone-derived phosphaturic hormone that lowers serum phosphate by suppressing renal sodium-dependent phosphate reabsorption, lowers 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D by suppressing renal 1alpha-hydroxylase, and suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion.

Secreted FGF8 binds FGFR1-FGFR4 in receptor-splice-selective, heparan-sulfate-assisted complexes and activates receptor tyrosine kinase signaling. Isoform-dependent receptor affinity tunes the strength, range, and duration of mitogenic and morphogenetic outputs.

Ligand-activated receptor tyrosine kinase for FGFs at the plasma membrane: binds FGF (with heparan sulfate or Klotho co-receptors), dimerizes, trans-autophosphorylates and phosphorylates FRS2 and PLC-gamma1 to initiate FGF receptor signalling.
Binding of FGF ligands (paracrine FGF1/FGF2 and others; endocrine FGF23 in a Klotho-dependent ternary complex) via Ig-like domains D2-D3, with isoform-specific (IIIb/IIIc) selectivity.
Heparin/heparan sulfate binding by the D2 domain, stabilizing the 2:2:2 FGF:FGFR:heparin signalling dimer.
Protein tyrosine kinase activity toward downstream substrates (FRS2, PLC-gamma1, SHC1), driving RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and PLC-gamma branches.

Ligand-activated transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase for FGFs at the plasma membrane: FGF and heparan sulfate binding drives dimerization, trans-autophosphorylation and phosphorylation of effectors (FRS2, PLCG1), activating ERK1/2 and other FGFR signalling branches.

FGFR3 receptor signalling in growth-plate chondrocytes restrains proliferation (STAT1 arm) and hypertrophic differentiation (ERK arm), acting as a negative regulator of endochondral bone growth; this is the paralog-distinguishing physiological role.
Recognition of FGF ligands via the D2-D3 ectodomain, with heparin/heparan sulfate as co-receptor; D1 and the acid-box linker autoinhibit binding.

Plasma membrane FGF receptor tyrosine kinase: binds FGF ligands (with heparan sulfate), dimerizes and trans-autophosphorylates, then phosphorylates FRS2/PLCG1 to activate ERK1/2 and other FGFR outputs.
In hepatocytes, FGFR4 with the coreceptor beta-Klotho is the receptor for intestinal FGF19 (FGF15), transducing the enterohepatic signal that represses CYP7A1 and bile acid synthesis.
Ligand recognition: binds paracrine FGFs and, with beta-Klotho and sulfated glycosaminoglycans, the endocrine FGF19.
Mitochondrial matrix fumarate hydratase catalysing hydration of fumarate to L-malate in the TCA cycle, as a homotetramer whose active sites are built from three subunits.

Cytosolic fumarase (MTS-lacking product of alternative transcription initiation) interconverting fumarate and malate in the cytosol, consuming fumarate generated by argininosuccinate lyase and amino-acid catabolism.

Damage-induced nuclear FH, phosphorylated by DNA-PK at Thr236, binds H2A.Z at double-strand breaks and makes fumarate locally. The fumarate inhibits KDM2B, raising H3K36me2 and promoting Ku70/DNA-PK accumulation and NHEJ.
Peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (rotamase, EC 5.2.1.8), the catalytic activity of the FKBP domain, inhibited by FK506 and rapamycin.

HSP90 co-chaperone that binds HSP90 via its TPR domain and is part of unligated steroid hormone receptor heterocomplexes; negative regulator of glucocorticoid and progesterone receptor signaling (antagonist of FKBP4).
Scaffold/adaptor that promotes the AKT1-PHLPP1 interaction, enhancing PHLPP1-mediated AKT1 dephosphorylation and thereby negatively regulating PI3K/AKT signaling.

The phase-separating species is profilaggrin, not the mature monomer: its tandem array of intrinsically disordered, histidine- and arginine-rich repeats scaffolds keratohyalin granules as liquid-liquid phase-separated condensates, and profilaggrin is the major component of those granules. The critical concentration for phase separation scales with repeat number - repeat-truncating FLG variants raise it steeply, which is how they cause disease - and the N-terminal S100 domain lowers it further by dimerising while it is still attached, before being cleaved during terminal differentiation. The condensates and the keratin filament bundles that surround them are reciprocally organising. Granule dissolution at the granular-to-corneum transition releases the free monomers whose keratin-binding activity is the next core function; whether condensate scaffolding and keratin bundling are one physical activity at two scales or two separable ones is an open question (see suggested_questions), so GO's two molecular function terms are recorded here as two core functions.

Keratin filament binding is the founding, directly demonstrated activity of the filaggrin repeat and the one the protein is named for. The repeat monomer associates specifically with intermediate filaments and not with other cytoskeletal proteins, at roughly two filaggrin molecules per three-chain filament building block, and aggregates keratin filaments into macrofibrillar bundles in vitro and in vivo. The mechanism is a charge-complementary "ionic zipper" between cationic beta-turns of the repeat and the packed rod domains of the filament, and it is sequence-degenerate enough that a short synthetic peptide reproduces it. In vitro the repeat also binds type III vimentin and desmin filaments; in vivo the partner is keratin. This is the activity that GO:0005198 (structural molecule activity, IEA from IPR003303) should be repointed to. It acts on the cytoplasmic keratin network rather than inside the granule: the monomers are liberated by proteolysis of profilaggrin and by granule dissolution, so this activity is downstream in time of the condensate scaffolding recorded above. No core location is asserted - the relevant compartment is the cytoplasm of granular and transition-layer keratinocytes, which this review keeps only as the non-core GO:0005829 cytosol rows.

A fraction of filaggrin is covalently isodipeptide cross-linked by transglutaminases into the cornified envelope, where it becomes a permanent structural constituent and anchors the subjacent keratin-filaggrin network to the developing envelope. Unlike the transient keratin-condensing activity, this pool is not degraded to natural moisturising factor.

The N-terminal S100 "A" domain of profilaggrin is a calcium-binding module - a canonical EF-hand plus an S100-type pseudo-EF-hand - that dimerises and, together with the adjacent B domain, binds partner proteins including annexin II, stratifin/14-3-3 sigma and HSP27 in a partly calcium-dependent manner. After proteolytic release this fragment translocates to the keratinocyte nucleus via a functional NLS in the B domain; that nuclear pool is transient and is treated here as a non-core location rather than a site of this core activity. This is a regulatory activity of the precursor and its cleaved N-terminus, entirely separate from the repeat unit's barrier-forming activity.

Fibronectin binds integrins (alpha5beta1, alpha4beta1, alphaVbeta3, alphaVbeta1, alphaVbeta6, alpha8beta1) via the RGD motif in FN-III10 domain, mediating cell adhesion, migration, and signaling at the cell-matrix interface. This is the primary molecular function enabling fibronectin's role as a major cell adhesion molecule.

Fibronectin binds collagen types I-V and VII through FN-I modules, organizing the ECM architecture and coordinating fibrillar network assembly. This interaction is essential for ECM structural integrity.

Fibronectin binds fibrinogen through N-terminal and C-terminal sites (FN-I modules), playing critical roles in provisional matrix formation during wound healing and hemostasis. This allows rapid assembly of a temporary scaffold supporting cell migration and tissue repair.

FOXO1 is a sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factor that binds to insulin response elements (IRE; 5'-TT[G/A]TTTTG-3') and DAF-16 binding elements (DBE; 5'-TT[G/A]TTTAC-3') via its conserved forkhead/winged-helix domain to regulate transcription of target genes.

FOXO1 is the main downstream effector of insulin signaling through the PI3K-AKT pathway. Insulin-activated AKT phosphorylates FOXO1 at T24/S256/S319, promoting 14-3-3 binding, nuclear export, and transcriptional inactivation. This represents FOXO1's role as the transcriptional switch for insulin signaling.

FOXO1 mediates cellular adaptation to oxidative stress by translocating to the nucleus and activating transcription of antioxidant and stress resistance genes. This represents one of FOXO1's primary evolved functions alongside metabolic regulation.

FXN binds Fe2+ and delivers it to the ISC assembly complex for [2Fe-2S] cluster synthesis. Iron is released from FXN only when the cysteine desulfurase is activated by L-cysteine and reductant, demonstrating regulated iron delivery. FXN also delivers iron to ferrochelatase for the terminal step of heme biosynthesis.

FXN functions as an allosteric activator of the cysteine desulfurase NFS1, accelerating persulfide formation and sulfur transfer to ISCU. Recent cryo-EM structures show FXN optimally positions ISCU assembly-site residues to enable rapid sulfur transfer.

FXN binds ferrous iron (Fe2+) with high affinity but does not bind ferric iron (Fe3+). The iron-binding site is located on the alpha1-beta1 face of the protein. Iron binding is essential for FXN's iron chaperone function.

The ferroxidase activity of FTH1 catalyzes oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ at the dinuclear center within the four-helix bundle (EC 1.16.3.1). This is the defining enzymatic function of the ferritin heavy chain that enables safe iron storage within the ferritin mineral core.
FTH1 sequesters intracellular iron by storing it within the ferritin nanocage as an inert ferrihydrite mineral, buffering the labile iron pool and preventing iron-mediated oxidative damage.
FTH1 binds ferrous iron (Fe2+) at the dinuclear ferroxidase center as the first step in the ferroxidase catalytic cycle, with sequential binding at sites A then B.

Lumenal lysosomal exoglycosidase that hydrolyses terminal alpha-L-fucose residues, including the alpha1,6-linked core fucose of N-glycans, from glycoproteins, glycolipids and oligosaccharides; core defucosylation enables AGA to complete N-glycoprotein degradation.

NADPH-dependent 3-ketodihydrosphingosine (3-dehydrosphinganine) reductase that catalyses the second step of de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis, reducing 3-ketodihydrosphingosine to dihydrosphingosine (sphinganine) at the cytosolic face of the ER membrane.

Catalyzes the hydrolysis of D-glucose-6-phosphate to D-glucose and inorganic phosphate (EC 3.1.3.9) at the luminal face of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, the terminal and committed step of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.

NADP+-dependent oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phospho-D-glucono-1,5-lactone, the committed, rate-limiting first step of the oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway, generating NADPH.
Provision of NADPH reducing power for antioxidant defense, most critically regeneration of reduced glutathione, protecting cells (especially erythrocytes) from oxidative stress.
NADP+ binding, both as catalytic cosubstrate and as a tightly bound structural cofactor required for stability of the active homodimer/homotetramer.

Glucose-6-phosphate:inorganic-phosphate antiport across the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, moving cytosolic glucose-6-phosphate into the ER lumen in exchange for luminal inorganic phosphate. This delivers substrate to the luminal active site of the glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunits (G6PC1 in liver, kidney and intestine; G6PC3 in neutrophils and other cells), and with G6PC1 constitutes the terminal step of hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis that maintains interprandial blood glucose.

Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase; GH31): at acidic lysosomal pH, hydrolyses terminal alpha-1,4-glucosidic bonds (and, more slowly, alpha-1,6 branch linkages) of glycogen, releasing glucose. This is the terminal step of lysosomal glycogen degradation (glycophagy), degrading glycogen delivered to the lysosome by autophagy; it is distinct from cytosolic glycogenolysis. Loss of this activity causes Pompe disease.

Pyridoxal-5'-phosphate-dependent decarboxylation of L-glutamate to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) plus CO2 in the cytosol, providing constitutive (basal) synthesis of the major inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA. GAD67 uses PLP covalently bound at an active-site lysine and functions as a homodimer.
Binding of the cofactor pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), which is essential for the decarboxylase catalytic mechanism; PLP forms a Schiff base with the active-site lysine (Lys405) of GAD67.

Lysosomal galactosylceramidase (galactocerebrosidase, EC 3.2.1.46): a soluble GH59 acid hydrolase that removes the terminal galactose from galactosylceramide (galactocerebroside) to yield ceramide and D-galactose, and also hydrolyzes galactosylsphingosine (psychosine) and related galactolipids. It thereby carries out the lysosomal galactosylceramide catabolic step of glycosphingolipid degradation, acting on membrane-embedded substrate presented by saposin A (from PSAP). Galactosylceramide is a major myelin lipid, and loss of this activity causes Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy).

NAD+-dependent UDP-glucose 4-epimerase catalysing the reversible interconversion of UDP-glucose and UDP-galactose, the recycling step of the Leloir pathway of galactose catabolism, acting as a cytosolic homodimer.

Bifunctional UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 4-epimerase activity interconverting UDP-GlcNAc and UDP-GalNAc, supplying UDP-GalNAc for glycoprotein and glycolipid biosynthesis; a cytosolic activity specific to the human enzyme.

At the Golgi membrane, B4GALNT1 transfers N-acetylgalactosamine from UDP-GalNAc onto glycolipid acceptors in beta-1,4 linkage. Its GM3-to-GM2 and GD3-to-GD2 reactions produce gangliosides that can be further elaborated; substrate availability also supports the neutral LacCer-to-GA2 branch.

GALK1 is the cytosolic galactokinase that catalyzes the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of alpha-D-galactose to alpha-D-galactose 1-phosphate (EC 2.7.1.6), the first committed step of galactose catabolism in the Leloir pathway.

Lysosomal N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase (galactose-6-sulfate sulfatase, EC 3.1.6.4) that hydrolytically removes the 6-O-sulfate group from terminal N-acetyl-D-galactosamine-6-sulfate (chondroitin-6-sulfate) and D-galactose-6-sulfate (keratan sulfate) residues, using a Ca2+/formylglycine active site, during glycosaminoglycan degradation.
Same lysosomal 6-sulfatase activity acting on chondroitin-6-sulfate, contributing to chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan degradation in the lysosome.

Golgi-resident polypeptide N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase that initiates mucin-type O-glycosylation; its non-redundant physiological role is O-glycosylation of FGF23 at Thr178 in the proprotein convertase site, which protects FGF23 from furin cleavage and permits secretion of intact hormone.

Third, committed step of the Leloir pathway of galactose catabolism: transfer of a uridylyl (UMP) group from UDP-alpha-D-glucose to alpha-D-galactose 1-phosphate to form alpha-D-glucose 1-phosphate and UDP-alpha-D-galactose, via a covalent uridylyl-His186 enzyme intermediate.

GAMT catalyzes the SAM-dependent methylation of guanidinoacetate to creatine, the terminal step of endogenous creatine biosynthesis, consuming S-adenosyl-L-methionine and releasing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine.
Binds to WGATAR consensus sequences in cis-regulatory regions via two C4-type zinc finger domains to regulate RNA polymerase II transcription
Activates transcription of Th2 cytokine genes (IL4, IL5, IL13) through direct promoter/enhancer binding and coactivator recruitment

Functions as a pioneer transcription factor that binds to nucleosomal DNA and recruits chromatin remodeling complexes to establish enhancers; CHD4/NuRD counterbalances inappropriate pioneer activity via nucleosome positioning over GATA3 motifs

Acts as master regulator of Th2 cell differentiation by activating Th2-specific genes and repressing Th1 lineage genes; requires a distal enhancer ~900 kb downstream of GATA3 that loops to the Gata3 TSS in Th2 cells for in vivo differentiation and allergic airway inflammation
Physically interacts with T-bet to mutually antagonize each other's transcriptional programs during Th1/Th2 lineage decisions
Regulates CD4+ T cell development in the thymus by inducing ThPOK and promoting CD4 lineage commitment
Forms transcriptional complexes with c-Myb, Menin, and MLL to maintain Th2 cell identity through histone modifications

Sequence-specific RNA polymerase II DNA-binding transcription factor that binds GATA motifs in cis-regulatory regions (including within compacted chromatin) and activates target genes such as NPPA, AMH and ID2; with TBX5 it also represses non-cardiac genes in cardiomyocytes.

Binds partner DNA-binding transcription factors (NKX2-5, TBX5, SMAD4, NR5A1) through its zinc fingers, forming cooperative complexes that synergistically activate cardiac and gonadal target promoters; disease mutations selectively disrupt these interactions.

As a cardiac transcription factor, drives heart development: cardiomyocyte proliferation, right ventricle and atrioventricular canal/endocardial cushion morphogenesis, and atrial septation (dosage-sensitive; human haploinsufficiency causes septal defects).
With its cofactor ZFPM2/FOG2 and partner NR5A1, activates Sertoli-cell genes (SRY, SOX9, AMH) required for testis determination and differentiation.

Glycine amidinotransferase activity: transfers the amidino group of L-arginine to glycine, producing guanidinoacetate and L-ornithine - the committed, rate-limiting step of creatine biosynthesis - acting in the mitochondrial intermembrane space.

Broader amidinotransferase activity reflecting the enzyme's substrate promiscuity: in addition to glycine, GATM amidinates GABA, beta-alanine and taurine to form guanidinobutyrate, guanidinopropionate and taurocyamine, respectively.
Lysosomal acid glucosylceramidase activity that hydrolyzes glucosylceramide to ceramide and glucose, maintaining glycosphingolipid turnover and lysosomal lipid homeostasis.

Catalyzes the formation of alpha-1,6-glucosidic branch points during glycogen biosynthesis by cleaving a segment from the non-reducing end of an alpha-1,4-linked glucan chain and transferring it to an internal glucose, increasing glycogen solubility and the number of non-reducing ends.

GBX2 acts in the nucleus and on chromatin as a homeodomain sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factor. It binds RNA polymerase II cis-regulatory regions and regulates target transcription, producing activation or repression according to promoter context and cofactors. This molecular activity underlies its conserved roles in anterior-hindbrain identity, isthmic-organizer positioning and maintenance, and cerebellar territory patterning.

FAD-dependent glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase that oxidatively decarboxylates glutaryl-CoA to crotonyl-CoA and CO2, transferring electrons to ETF. This step degrades lysine-pathway intermediates while producing the short-chain fatty-acyl-CoA crotonyl-CoA.

The primary molecular function of GCH1 is GTP cyclohydrolase I activity (EC 3.5.4.16), catalyzing the conversion of GTP to 7,8-dihydroneopterin triphosphate as the first and rate-limiting step in de novo tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) biosynthesis. GTPCH1 is primarily localized in the cytosol and requires zinc for catalytic activity. BH4 is a critical cofactor for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases (PAH, TH, TPH) and all nitric oxide synthase isoforms.

ATP-dependent phosphorylation of D-glucose to D-glucose 6-phosphate, the committed first step of glucose utilization, catalyzed by a low-affinity (high-KM), cooperative, product-inhibition-resistant enzyme that thereby functions as the cellular glucose sensor.

In the pancreatic beta cell, glucokinase acts as the glucose sensor that sets the threshold for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion; the low glucose affinity ensures its activity tracks glucose across the physiological range, so it is the flux-controlling determinant coupling glycolytic glucose metabolism to insulin release.

Glucokinase is a central determinant of whole-body glucose homeostasis; in the liver it drives glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis and restrains gluconeogenesis, and its loss (MODY2/PNDM) or gain (hyperinsulinism) of function shifts the glucose set-point.

Maintains the BLOC-1 trafficking assembly as an integral structural subunit, including its pallidin-Cappuccino-BLOS1 trimer. Stable subcomplex reconstitution and loss of complex components after BLOS1 depletion support a scaffolding role that enables endosomal cargo trafficking and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis.

Helps maintain the BORC assembly on the cytoplasmic face of lysosomes, enabling ARL8 recruitment and outward lysosome positioning. BLOS1 knockdown destabilizes the complex and disrupts ARL8 localization; kinesins perform the motor step, while BLOS1 supplies part of the supporting protein assembly.

Promotes mitochondrial respiratory-protein acetylation and restrains respiratory activity in the tested human cell system, counteracting SIRT3-associated deacetylation. The mitochondrial regulatory role is supported, while the precise molecular activity of GCN5L1 within the acetylation machinery remains unresolved.

Lipoyl-carrier (H-protein) function in the glycine cleavage system: GCSH bears a covalently attached lipoyl cofactor whose swinging arm shuttles the aminomethyl reaction intermediate between the P-, T- and L-proteins, making GCSH essential to glycine decarboxylation via the glycine cleavage complex in the mitochondrial matrix.

Rate-limiting, first and committed step of the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway: transfers the amido nitrogen of L-glutamine to D-fructose 6-phosphate to produce D-glucosamine 6-phosphate and L-glutamate, feedback inhibited by the downstream product UDP-GlcNAc.

Cytosolic geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase: catalyzes the Mg2+-dependent condensation of isopentenyl diphosphate with farnesyl diphosphate (and the upstream elongation steps from dimethylallyl/geranyl diphosphate) to synthesize the C20 isoprenoid geranylgeranyl diphosphate, the lipid donor for protein geranylgeranylation.

Cleaves the gamma-glutamyl amide bond of extracellular glutathione (gamma-Glu-Cys-Gly) as the first, rate-limiting step of extracellular glutathione catabolism / the gamma-glutamyl cycle. The gamma-glutamyl group is transferred either to water (hydrolysis, the predominant physiologic reaction, yielding L-glutamate + L-cysteinylglycine) or, when a suitable acceptor amino acid/dipeptide is present at high concentration, to that acceptor (transpeptidation, EC 2.3.2.2, the classic gamma-glutamyltransferase reaction). GO directs the obsolete gamma-glutamyltransferase term to this glutathione hydrolase term, so both reactions are represented here.

Hydrolyzes the cysteinyl leukotriene C4 (LTC4) to leukotriene D4 (LTD4) plus glutamate (EC 3.4.19.14), a step in cysteinyl-leukotriene metabolism; also cleaves other glutathione S-conjugates (drug mercapturates, lipid-mediator conjugates).

Binds dietary cobalamin (vitamin B12) as a secreted carrier and functions as the ligand recognized by the ileal cubam (CUBN/AMN) cargo receptor, thereby mediating receptor-dependent intestinal absorption of cobalamin.

Acts as the cargo ligand for the ileal endocytic cubam receptor: the cobalamin-loaded CBLIF complex is recognized by CUBN/AMN and internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis, coupling cobalamin binding to its cellular uptake.

Hydrolyzes terminal alpha-D-galactose residues from lysosomal glycosphingolipids, especially globotriaosylceramide (Gb3Cer) and Gal2Cer, as a saposin-B-dependent homodimeric alpha-galactosidase A in the lysosomal lumen.

Lysosomal acid beta-galactosidase that hydrolyzes terminal non-reducing beta-D-galactose residues from beta-D-galactosides, acting in the lysosomal lumen as part of a multienzyme complex with CTSA/PPCA and NEU1.

Lysosomal acid beta-galactosidase that degrades the glycosaminoglycan keratan sulfate (and galactose-terminated glycoprotein/oligosaccharide glycans) by removing terminal beta-galactose residues in the lysosome.

GCLC is the catalytic subunit of glutamate-cysteine ligase, catalyzing the ATP-dependent ligation of L-glutamate and L-cysteine to form gamma-L-glutamyl-L-cysteine. This is the rate-limiting step in de novo glutathione biosynthesis. The enzyme requires Mg2+ as a cofactor and is feedback inhibited by GSH. Km values are 1.8 mM for glutamate, 0.1 mM for cysteine, and 0.4 mM for ATP.

Regulatory (modifier) subunit of glutamate-cysteine ligase: binds the catalytic subunit GCLC and modulates the holoenzyme to increase glutathione synthesis efficiency (lowers Km for glutamate/ATP, raises Ki for GSH feedback inhibition).

As part of the GCL heterodimer, GCLM contributes to catalysis of the first, rate-limiting step of glutathione biosynthesis (ATP-dependent ligation of L-glutamate and L-cysteine to gamma-glutamylcysteine); the catalytic activity is a property of the holoenzyme, to which the non-catalytic modifier subunit contributes.
Functions in the glutathione biosynthetic process as the regulatory subunit of the rate-limiting enzyme, supporting cellular antioxidant defense.

Pyridoxal-5'-phosphate-dependent decarboxylation of glycine as the P protein of the mitochondrial glycine cleavage system: releases CO2 from glycine and transfers the residual aminomethyl group to the lipoamide arm of the H protein (GCSH).
Binds the pyridoxal 5'-phosphate cofactor (covalently attached as a Schiff base at Lys754) required for glycine decarboxylation.

GLI2 is the activator-forming effector of Hedgehog signaling. Once Smoothened activation releases it from Suppressor of fused and it enters the nucleus, GLI2 binds GLI consensus sites in target promoters and activates RNA polymerase II transcription, converting the amount and duration of Hedgehog ligand exposure into target-gene output. GLI1 is a direct target, establishing the amplifying feedback loop that sustains the response.

The five tandem C2H2 zinc fingers of GLI2 recognise the GLI consensus sequence in RNA polymerase II cis-regulatory regions. This has been shown on naked DNA by band shift and EMSA at the GLI1 and FAM38B promoters and in chromatin by ChIP, and it is the DNA-binding capability that both the activating and the repressing outputs of GLI2 depend on.

Sequence-specific occupancy of GLI consensus elements in RNA polymerase II cis-regulatory regions. The five C2H2 zinc fingers lie in the N-terminal half of the protein and are therefore retained by both the full-length activator and the processed repressor, which is why the same DNA-binding activity underlies both outputs.

Repression of Hedgehog target genes by the proteolytically processed N-terminal form GLI3R (UniProtKB:P10071-PRO_0000406137).
