IFT122 is required for primary cilium assembly; its loss abolishes ciliogenesis, consistent with IFT trains building and maintaining the axoneme.

Recognizes acetylated H4 and H3 in regulatory chromatin and brings together histones with transcriptional effectors. H4 recognition is supported across biochemical and cellular studies; H3K9ac and H3K27ac recognition is linked to bromodomain-dependent chromatin recruitment. The coupled recognition and recruitment mechanism supports transcription at active regulatory regions.

Coactivates transcription through physical engagement of DNA-binding transcription factors, including acetylated RelA and regulated p53, and recruitment of P-TEFb or ET-domain-associated regulatory proteins. This non-histone interaction arm cooperates with histone reading. The long product recruits P-TEFb, whose CDK9 subunit performs the phosphorylation assigned to it in this mechanism; ET-dependent effector recruitment provides a separable P-TEFb-independent route.

Substrate-recognition (F-box) adaptor of the SCF(FBXO7) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex (CUL1-SKP1-RBX1-FBXO7) that recruits substrates (e.g. DLGAP5/HURP, BIRC2/cIAP1, TRAF2, UXT-V2, SIRT7) via its proline-rich region and Ubl/FP regions and bridges them to the catalytic cullin-RING core for K48-linked polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.

SCF-independent regulator of mitophagy that relocates from the cytosol to depolarized mitochondria downstream of PINK1, interacts with PINK1 and PRKN/Parkin via its N-terminal Ubl region, and promotes Parkin recruitment to mitochondria and mitofusin ubiquitination to drive selective autophagic clearance of damaged mitochondria.

Negative regulator of canonical NF-kappa-B signaling, achieved by SCF(FBXO7)-mediated K48/K63 polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the NF-kappa-B cofactor UXT isoform 2 (and ubiquitination of TRAF2 and cIAP1/BIRC2).

Proteasome-associated regulator of proteostasis that, through FP-domain heterodimerization with the proteasome inhibitor PSMF1/PI31 and ubiquitin signaling on proteasomal components, tunes 26S proteasome assembly/activity; loss of FBXO7 reduces proteasome activity and models a parkinsonism-like phenotype, indicating a role in neuronal proteostasis.

Substrate-recognition subunit of the mitochondrial outer membrane SCF-FBXL4 E3 ubiquitin ligase, which recruits the mitophagy receptors BNIP3 and BNIP3L/NIX (assisted by the PPTC7 adaptor) for constitutive ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, thereby restraining basal mitophagy and maintaining mitochondrial mass.

ALADIN is a scaffold nucleoporin of the nuclear pore complex at the nuclear envelope. Its NDC1-dependent NPC anchoring supports normal NPC-associated nucleocytoplasmic transport; disease-associated variants commonly fail to target to NPCs, linking loss of NPC integration to triple-A syndrome biology.
During mitosis, ALADIN acts as a spatial regulator of Aurora A localization and associated spindle factors, supporting robust mitotic spindle formation and timely chromosome alignment.

Sequence-specific CTCF binding anchors chromatin loops and organizes regulatory contacts in the nucleus, including contacts between enhancers and promoters. Its architectural contribution is distinct from the ATP-dependent extrusion motor supplied by SMC complexes.

CTCF binds regulatory DNA to modulate transcription by RNA polymerase II. It can repress or activate transcription according to the promoter and cellular context, as shown by MYC repression and APP activation assays.

Binds extracellular cadherin partners through calcium-stabilized repeats. CDH23-PCDH15 links connect stereocilia within a sensory hair bundle and transmit mechanical force, whereas separate homophilic contacts can mediate adhesion between cells. These are distinct contact contexts of the same broad cadherin-binding activity.

Binds harmonin PDZ domains through the CDH23 cytoplasmic tail, contributing to sensory stereociliary anchoring assemblies. The directly resolved PDZ2 interaction is separate from harmonin N-terminal-domain recognition and exon68-dependent CDH23 self-association; harmonin supplies the actin-binding activity.

CYFIP2 is a Rac-binding regulatory component of the SCAR/WAVE complex that balances WAVE restraint and activation, connecting small-GTPase signaling to regulated actin assembly and cell morphogenesis. This unit also contributes to neuronal projection and synaptic organization, with soluble and particulate cytoplasmic pools. Mouse CYFIP2-R87C rescue increases lamellipodia formation under reduced Rac; human patient fibroblasts show disturbed actin remodeling. These results support regulated WRC output without implying that all variants have the same effect. WAVE and ARP2/3 execute downstream actin nucleation. Purified CYFIP1 studies provide family context; activation need not entail complex disassembly.
Tether that retains GLUT4 storage vesicles intracellularly until insulin-stimulated cleavage releases them for translocation.
p97/VCP adaptor that binds through an extended UBX domain and disassembles p97 hexamers at the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment.
Cofactor that stimulates VCP lysine trimethylation by VCPKMT.

Secreted LOXL3 catalyzes copper- and lysine-tyrosylquinone-dependent oxidative deamination of peptidyl lysine residues to allysine in extracellular collagen and elastin precursors. This core chemistry is supported for recombinant human full-length LOXL3 and P58215-2/LOXL3-sv1, with isoform-dependent substrate preferences; the exon-4/exon-5-deleted sv2 form corresponding structurally to P58215-3 also retains collagen-I-directed activity.

ABCG5 assembles with ABCG8 to export neutral sterols using ATP. Its membrane domain and nucleotide-binding domain are integral parts of the heterodimer, with the ABCG5 Walker motifs contributing to the active composite ATPase site. At hepatocyte and enterocyte apical membranes, this activity promotes biliary sterol secretion and restricts net absorption and accumulation of dietary cholesterol and plant sterols.

As the ABCG8 half of the ABCG5–ABCG8 heterodimer, contributes transmembrane structure and a signature region of the active composite nucleotide site to MgATP-powered neutral-sterol export. The transporter operates at apical enterocyte and hepatocyte membranes, supporting cholesterol/phytosterol elimination into the lumen and bile and limiting net dietary sterol absorption. ATP binding, ATP hydrolysis and heterodimer formation are integrated parts of this transport mechanism, rather than separate autonomous ABCG8 activities.

HDAC4 functions primarily as a transcriptional corepressor by bridging DNA-binding transcription factors (especially MEF2) to the enzymatically active HDAC3/NCoR/SMRT complex. Due to a Tyr->His substitution in the active site (H803), HDAC4 has very weak intrinsic deacetylase activity and relies on the HDAC3/NCoR/SMRT complex for catalytic function.

HDAC4 binds to DNA-binding transcription factors including MEF2 family members (MEF2A, MEF2C, MEF2D), HIF-1alpha, Sp1, and others. This binding is central to its function as a transcriptional coregulator.

HDAC4 functions as a molecular scaffold/adaptor bridging transcription factors to the HDAC3/NCoR/SMRT corepressor complex. Class II HDACs regulate transcription by bridging enzymatically active complexes to transcription factors independently of intrinsic HDAC activity.

HDAC4 binds 14-3-3 proteins at phosphorylated serine residues (S246, S467, S632), which sequesters HDAC4 in the cytoplasm. This interaction regulates HDAC4 nucleocytoplasmic shuttling and is critical for its transcriptional regulatory function.
HDAC6 deacetylates alpha-tubulin at K40, regulating microtubule stability and dynamics. This is one of the best-characterized functions of HDAC6.

HDAC6 is a Zn2+-dependent deacetylase that removes acetyl groups from lysine residues of various non-histone substrates including tubulin, HSP90, cortactin, peroxiredoxins, and other cytoplasmic proteins.
HDAC6 binds and deacetylates HSP90, regulating its chaperone activity. This affects client protein maturation including steroid hormone receptors.
HDAC6 binds ubiquitin via its C-terminal ZnF-UBP domain. This is essential for recognizing polyubiquitinated misfolded proteins and transporting them to aggresomes.
HDAC6 is essential for aggresome formation. It binds polyubiquitinated misfolded proteins via its ZnF-UBP domain and recruits dynein motors for retrograde transport to the MTOC.
HDAC6 promotes cilium disassembly through deacetylation of alpha-tubulin and cortactin at the ciliary basal body. This is regulated by Aurora A phosphorylation.

BACH2 functions primarily as a sequence-specific DNA-binding transcriptional repressor. It heterodimerizes with small MAF proteins (MAFK, MAFG, MAFF) via its bZIP domain to bind MARE elements and repress target gene transcription. In B cells, it represses PRDM1/Blimp-1 to maintain germinal center identity. In T cells, it represses effector gene programs (Prdm1, Gata3, Irf4, Gzmb) to stabilize Treg identity and promote memory/stem-like CD8+ T cell states. It also represses HMOX1 in the context of oxidative stress responses.

BACH2 heterodimerizes with small MAF proteins (MAFF, MAFG, MAFK) and other bZIP family members (BATF3, FOSL2) via its bZIP leucine zipper domain. Heterodimerization with small MAFs is essential for DNA binding and transcriptional repression at MARE elements. BACH2 also homodimerizes via its BTB/POZ domain (residues 37-103), forming a disulfide-linked dimer through Cys-20.
Contractile-ring scaffold that binds actin filaments, active RhoA and septins and links them to the furrow membrane, keeping the ring organized through ingression and abscission.
Membrane anchor and RhoA effector scaffold: the C2, Rho-binding and PH domains bind active RhoA and PI(4,5)P2 at the equatorial cortex, retaining RhoA at the membrane to recruit effectors.
PH-domain binding of PI(4,5)P2, which targets anillin to the furrow membrane and recruits septins there.

Non-catalytic subunit of the GPI-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (GPI-GnT) complex, contributing to the first committed step of GPI-anchor biosynthesis (transfer of GlcNAc from UDP-GlcNAc to phosphatidylinositol) at the ER membrane; PIGQ stabilises the complex rather than performing catalysis itself (the catalytic subunit is PIGA).
Cleaves 3′ trailers from precursor tRNAs during nuclear and mitochondrial tRNA maturation.

BLNK provides noncatalytic docking sites that assemble B-cell receptor signaling effectors. SYK-dependent phosphorylation enables recruitment of SH2-containing proteins, while proline-rich motifs bind SH3-domain adaptors. The resulting complexes couple receptor activation to PLCgamma-dependent calcium signaling and other downstream responses. BLNK supplies the organizing scaffold; SYK, BTK and PLCgamma supply their respective catalytic reactions.

BLNK combines multivalent CIN85 binding with amino-terminal lipid-vesicle attachment to organize signaling condensates. Reconstitution with purified human SLP65 fragments, CIN85 and vesicles establishes the physical scaffold mechanism, while human SLP65 mutant complementation in chicken DT40 cells links granule formation to B-cell receptor responses. This evidence supports a condensate-organizing activity without asserting that every endogenous human granule has the identical reconstructed ultrastructure.

CIC recognizes regulatory DNA through its HMG-box and C1 domains and represses RNA polymerase II transcription. Human GFP-tagged CIC-S links promoter occupancy to reduced reporter expression; human HMG–C1 fragments independently establish direct motif recognition. The human construct accession NP_055940.3 maps to Q96RK0-2. Engineered min18/min31 structures do not establish equivalent regulation or affinity of both complete products.

Sphingoid-base N-acyltransferase (ceramide synthase) that N-acylates sphinganine (and sphingosine in the salvage pathway) using acyl-CoA, with high selectivity for stearoyl-CoA (C18:0-CoA), to produce C18-(dihydro)ceramide in de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis.

Assembles and activates MOZ/MORF acetyltransferase complexes by bridging KAT6A or KAT6B with ING5 and MEAF6, promoting nucleosomal H3 acetylation and context-dependent transcriptional coactivation. BRPF1 also forms alternative KAT7/HBO1 complexes and helps determine their H3 substrate preference; the KAT subunits perform acetyl transfer. Through complex assembly and activation, BRPF1 contributes to the histone-modification component of chromatin remodeling; this does not imply ATP-dependent nucleosome repositioning.

Recognizes histone states and couples them to chromatin engagement by acetyltransferase complexes. The PZP module binds the H3 amino terminus preferentially when Lys4 is unmethylated and supports nucleosomal engagement; the bromodomain recognizes acetylated histone peptides including H2AK5ac and H4K12ac. ING5 can redirect the assembled complex toward H3K4me3-rich chromatin without changing intrinsic BRPF1 PZP specificity. Reader-dependent substrate engagement enables the assembled complex to acetylate nucleosomal histones, providing the mechanistic link to chromatin remodeling without assigning catalytic or ATPase activity to BRPF1.

CD2AP uses distinct SH3 and proline-rich interaction regions to organize selected membrane-associated and junctional protein assemblies. It binds SH3-containing partners through its own proline-rich regions and recognizes other proline-rich partners through its SH3 domains. In epithelial complexes it helps position actin regulators, including SH3BP1 and CapZ; SH3BP1 supplies GAP catalysis. These dynamic organizing interactions do not imply one invariant complex stoichiometry.

CD2AP directly binds actin filaments. Full-length human recombinant protein caps barbed ends and suppresses both addition and loss of actin subunits, whereas the 351–639 C-terminal construct retains filament binding without full capping activity. This provides a direct stabilization mechanism; epithelial depletion and mechanical-stress experiments connect CD2AP with junctional actin integrity. A human disease-associated C-terminal truncation also shows reduced F-actin binding in the reported in vitro assay.

The CD2AP CPI region directly binds heterodimeric actin-capping protein and reduces its barbed-end capping activity without covalent modification. Human CD23 and extended CD30 peptides demonstrate inhibition in reconstitution with chicken CP; inhibition depends on construct boundaries and is partial. CPI-region fragments can promote release of prebound CP in uncapping assays. These fragment-level regulatory activities are distinct from full-length CD2AP acting directly on filament ends; the balance at native junctions depends on context.

With IFT74, IFT81 forms the tubulin-binding module of IFT-B: its CH domain binds tubulin so that anterograde trains can deliver tubulin for axoneme extension; tubulin binding is required for ciliogenesis.

Regulatory component of cullin-RING/SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes that binds directly to the RING domain of RBX1 and inhibits RBX1-dependent E3 ubiquitin ligase activity by masking its E2 (CDC34)-binding surface, thereby controlling CRL activity and the assembly/turnover of SCF components such as FBXW7.

Binds the RBX1 RING-domain E3 ligase subunit, an interaction that stabilizes CRL/SCF components (FBXW7, RBX1, cullins) and blocks RBX1-mediated neddylation of CUL1, thereby regulating cullin-RING ligase-dependent proteasomal turnover of substrates including FBXW7 (and downstream Cyclin E and c-Myc).
Catalyzes acyl-CoA/malonyl-CoA condensation at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, initiating two-carbon extensions during synthesis of very long-chain fatty acids.

Very-long-chain 3-oxoacyl-CoA synthase / fatty acid elongase (EC 2.3.1.199): catalyzes the first, rate-limiting condensation step of the ER VLCFA elongation cycle, condensing a saturated or monounsaturated very-long-chain acyl-CoA with malonyl-CoA to yield a very-long-chain 3-oxoacyl-CoA plus CO2 and CoA, thereby extending the acyl chain by two carbons per cycle.

Principal elongase producing saturated and monounsaturated very-long-chain fatty acids (extending C22 to C24 to C26); the single elongase making C26:0 and C26:1, supplying the >=C24 VLCFAs used for sphingolipid, ceramide and membrane-lipid synthesis.

NADPH-dependent all-trans-retinol dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.300) acting in the reductive direction: it reduces all-trans-retinal (released from photobleached rhodopsin) to all-trans-retinol using NADPH, the first step of all-trans-retinal clearance from photoreceptor outer segments. RDH8 has a clear preference for NADP.
Binds the NADP(H) cofactor via an N-terminal Rossmann-fold NAD(P)-binding region, providing the reducing equivalents (NADPH) used to reduce all-trans-retinal to all-trans-retinol.

Integral multi-pass membrane protein of the photoreceptor (rod and cone) outer segment, where it is tightly associated with the outer segment membranes and acts at the membrane on retinoids of the visual cycle.

Catalyzes magnesium-dependent hydrolysis of phosphatidic acid to 1,2-diacylglycerol and orthophosphate. This PA-specific PAP1 reaction is the best-supported core activity of LPIN2 and supplies diacylglycerol for triacylglycerol and major glycerophospholipid synthesis. LPIN2 partitions between soluble and tightly membrane-associated pools; its catalytic state is modeled at the ER membrane, while stable ER association is less directly demonstrated for LPIN2 than for LPIN1. Human-cell knockdown induces LPIN1 compensation, so total cellular PAP1 activity can rise after LPIN2 loss and must not be interpreted as the intrinsic direction of LPIN2 catalysis.

Acts in the nucleus as a noncatalytic transcriptional coactivator for PPAR-response-element-dependent gene expression. Mutation studies separate this coactivator output from phosphatidate phosphatase catalysis. This is a conserved lipin-family activity supported for mouse lipin-2 and by phylogenetic transfer; endogenous human LPIN2 occupancy, partners, and target-gene programs remain less directly established than its phosphatidate phosphatase activity.
Apical chloride/oxalate exchange in intestinal epithelium mediating oxalate secretion into the gut lumen, which limits net intestinal oxalate absorption and urinary oxalate
Apical chloride/bicarbonate exchange in intestinal, pancreatic duct and proximal tubule epithelia, supporting bicarbonate secretion and intracellular pH regulation
Promotes CDC42 activation through guanine-nucleotide exchange-factor activity, regulating the CDC42 signaling switch from a supported cytosolic pool.

Recruits gephyrin to postsynaptic membrane phosphoinositides, regulating assembly of the inhibitory postsynaptic scaffold. This conserved adaptor function is separable from nucleotide-exchange activity.

Damage-sensing ubiquitin and Parkin kinase. On depolarized or import-defective mitochondria, full-length PINK1 is stabilized at the outer-membrane TOM complex and phosphorylates Ser65 of ubiquitin (free and chain-incorporated) and of the Parkin Ubl domain. This recruits and activates Parkin and drives a feed-forward phospho-ubiquitin signal that initiates mitophagy.

Phosphorylation of additional mitochondrial-quality-control substrates. PINK1 phosphorylates Miro (triggering its Parkin-dependent degradation and arresting mitochondrial movement), DRP1 Ser616 (promoting fission) and TRAP1 (protecting against oxidative-stress-induced cytochrome c release).
J-domain co-chaperone that stimulates the ATPase activity of HSP70 (HSPA1A/HSPA1B), driving HSP70-mediated folding, refolding and disaggregation of client proteins.
Binds the HSP70 chaperone and misfolded/aggregation-prone client proteins, recruiting clients to HSP70 for folding; in striated muscle this supports myofibril and Z-disc proteostasis.

Suppresses aggregation and inclusion formation by aggregation-prone client proteins. The well-characterized DNAJB6b product can act independently of added HSP70 in purified antiaggregation assays; nuclear client suppression is also supported for the historical long a construct.

Interacts with HSP70 through its J-domain as a regulated co-chaperone. The adjacent GF region masks the HSP70-binding surface in the tested WT protein. Exposed-domain and disease-mutant constructs can activate HSP70 ATPase, while native relief of this inhibition remains unresolved; that conditional activation is retained separately as non-core evidence.
Binds keratin intermediate filaments and contributes to organization of the K8/K18 network.
ER-lumenal J-domain co-chaperone of BiP (HSPA5) that stimulates BiP's ATPase activity via its J domain, coupling substrate delivery to BiP's ATP-dependent folding cycle.

Binds unfolded and misfolded substrate proteins directly (ATP-independent holdase via its cysteine-rich domain), recruiting BiP to nascent and ERAD substrates to promote folding, maturation, trafficking and degradation in the ER.
Required for the maturation and correct trafficking of secretory/membrane clients including polycystin-1 (PKD1); loss causes ADPKD (PKD6).
Interleukin-22 receptor binding activates JAK-STAT signaling in epithelial cells to induce antimicrobial peptide production
Cytokine activity stimulates hepatocyte acute phase protein synthesis through STAT3 activation
Interleukin-22 receptor binding promotes epithelial cell proliferation and tissue repair at barrier surfaces

Primary enzymatic function of SIRT1. Catalyzes NAD-dependent removal of acetyl groups from lysine residues of histones and numerous non-histone proteins. The reaction couples NAD+ cleavage to lysine deacetylation, producing nicotinamide and 2-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose.
Preferential histone substrate. Deacetylation of H4K16 is a major activity of SIRT1 critical for heterochromatin formation and transcriptional silencing.
Major histone substrate. H3K9 deacetylation is linked to heterochromatin formation at rDNA and telomeric regions.
SIRT1 functions as a transcriptional corepressor through histone deacetylation and deacetylation of transcription factors.

PIGS is a required, non-catalytic subunit of the ER membrane GPI-anchor transamidase (GPI-T) complex, which post-translationally attaches a pre-assembled GPI anchor to the C-terminus of GPI-anchored proteins, replacing their C-terminal GPI-attachment signal peptide. PIGS is indispensable for complex activity but does not itself catalyze the reaction (PIGK is catalytic; GPAA1 forms the amide bond).

As a required structural subunit of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane GPI-anchor transamidase (GPI-T) complex, PIGT binds the GPI lipid substrate and, by forming an interchain disulfide bond with the catalytic subunit PIGK/GPI8 and stabilising the complex, contributes to attachment of pre-assembled GPI anchors to the C-terminus of GPI-anchored proteins during GPI anchor biosynthesis.
GPR101 functions as an orphan class A GPCR at the plasma membrane, with receptor-family evidence supporting GPCR signaling while ligand identity and exact coupling specificity remain unresolved.

POFUT1 catalyzes transfer of L-fucose from GDP-beta-L-fucose to the hydroxyl of a Ser/Thr residue in the consensus C2-X(4,5)-S/T-C3 of a properly folded, disulfide-bonded EGF-like repeat, producing O-linked fucose (EC 2.4.1.221). This is the defining catalytic activity of the gene.

Intramembrane zinc metalloendopeptidase that performs the second, membrane-embedded cleavage in regulated intramembrane proteolysis of S1P-trimmed membrane-bound bZIP transcription factors, releasing their cytosolic domains; principal substrates are SREBP-1/-2 (sterol-regulated lipid synthesis) and ATF6/ATF6B (ER unfolded protein response), with CREB3-family factors (OASIS/CREB3L1, CREB3L2, CREB3L3) as further substrates.

Golgi-resident subtilisin-like serine endopeptidase that performs the first (lumenal, RxxL-directed) cleavage in regulated intramembrane proteolysis of membrane-bound bZIP transcription factors, principally SREBP-1/-2 (sterol-regulated lipid synthesis) and ATF6/ATF6B (ER unfolded protein response), as well as CREB3-family transducers; the cleaved intermediates are then substrates for site-2 protease (MBTPS2).

Proprotein convertase-type processing of non-transcription-factor substrates in the Golgi, notably cleavage of the GNPTAB alpha/beta precursor that activates GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase for mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal enzymes, and removal of the FAM20C propeptide required for FAM20C secretion and kinase activity.

Secreted LEKTI and its furin-generated single- and multidomain fragments act as tight-binding inhibitors of serine endopeptidases. Their main physiological targets are the epidermal kallikreins KLK5, KLK7 and KLK14 in the extracellular space of the upper epidermis, where inhibition of KLK5 is released at the acidic pH of the outer stratum corneum. The activity is established by direct assays with native and recombinant human protein; the PAINT inference places it at the Theria node, so it is shared by mammalian orthologs but not by invertebrate members of PTHR10913.
Molybdopterin adenylyltransferase (G domain): adenylylates molybdopterin using ATP to form adenylyl-molybdopterin, the first of the two gephyrin-catalysed steps of molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis.

Molybdopterin molybdotransferase / molybdenum insertase (E domain): inserts molybdenum into adenylyl-molybdopterin to form the mature molybdenum cofactor with release of AMP, the final step of MoCo biosynthesis.

Inhibitory postsynaptic scaffold: acts as a protein-macromolecule adaptor that clusters glycine receptors and major subsets of GABA type A receptors at the postsynaptic membrane and anchors them to the cytoskeleton, organizing the inhibitory postsynapse.

Glycine receptor clustering at glycinergic postsynapses: the classical, deeply conserved scaffolding function by which gephyrin localizes and immobilizes glycine receptors at the inhibitory postsynaptic membrane.

Clathrin-uncoating co-chaperone that binds the clathrin heavy chain and clathrin cages and, via its J domain, recruits HSPA8/HSC70 and stimulates its ATPase activity to drive ATP-dependent disassembly of the clathrin coat.
HSP70/HSC70 co-chaperone activity, recruiting and stimulating the ATPase of HSPA8/HSC70 through its J domain to power clathrin coat disassembly.
Drives clathrin coat disassembly / synaptic vesicle uncoating during clathrin-mediated endocytosis, supporting synaptic vesicle recycling at nerve terminals.

DIAPH3 binds actin and promotes filament assembly through its FH1–FH2 region. N-terminal and C-terminal regulatory regions restrain this activity. An activated human construct lacking the C-terminal regulatory segment promotes filopodia and concentrates at their tips. The actin-binding, filament-growth and regulatory properties form one integrated mechanism.

DIAPH3 has a microtubule-associated function distinct from actin assembly. Purified mDia2 fragments bind microtubule polymers and protect them against depolymerization even when their actin-assembly activity is impaired. Endogenous human DIAPH3 localizes to the microtubule-rich central spindle. The fragment biochemistry and human localization support this function together; they do not establish identical activity for every natural product.

Acts at the plasma membrane as an LPA-activated GPCR. Direct ligand-binding and receptor-deorphanization studies establish LPA recognition, with greater activity of 2-acyl-LPA than 1-acyl-LPA in a heterologous assay. The strongest recurring proximal output is G12/13-G13-dependent Rho activation; Gi-dependent calcium and ERK signaling and direct Gq coupling are supported in specified expression systems. LPA-bound LPAR6-mini-G13 and LPAR6-mini-Gq structures and functional mutagenesis define activated coupling states, not constitutive stable complexes. Human hair-follicle expression and recessive loss-of-function genetics connect this receptor activity to maintenance of hair growth and texture, but the follicular branch weights and downstream effectors remain unresolved.

At the plasma membrane, KLB acts as the extracellular ligand-recognition and coreceptor component of endocrine-FGF receptor complexes. Its repurposed tandem GH-like domains bind FGF19 and FGF21, and KLB association with FGFR4 or FGFR1-family receptors permits ligand-dependent receptor activation. In the liver, the FGF19-KLB-FGFR4 arm represses CYP7A1 and limits bile-acid synthesis.

Inducible negative-feedback inhibitor of RTK-Ras-ERK signalling (notably downstream of FGFR). SPRY4 binds RAF1 through its C-terminal cysteine-rich Sprouty domain and blocks Ras-independent RAF1 activation, and (Tyr75-dependent) limits Ras activation upstream of Ras by associating with SOS1 and reducing GRB2-SOS1 recruitment to FRS2. The kinase-inhibitor MF captures the RAF1 arm; the SOS1/GRB2 arm is better described as sequestration and has weaker (co-IP) support. SPRY4 lacks the C-terminal PxxPxR GRB2 SH3-binding motif that is unique to SPRY2 (OpenScientist ortholog scan; grafting the motif onto SPRY4 confers GRB2-dependent inhibition), so any GRB2 effect of SPRY4 is not via direct SH3 binding, while the RAF1-binding cysteine-rich domain is conserved in all paralogs. Direct kinase-inhibition evidence is strongest for TESK1.

Direct inhibition of the cofilin kinase TESK1 via the C-terminal cysteine-rich region, suppressing integrin-mediated cofilin phosphorylation and cell spreading independently of ERK and of Tyr75 phosphorylation.

CHCHD10 binds CHCHD2 to form heterodimers in human cells in the mitochondrial intermembrane-space/cristae environment, within partly redundant roles in mitochondrial membrane organization and respiratory homeostasis. Human loss/re-expression experiments link the pair to OMA1-dependent OPA1 processing; a direct protease-inhibitory, chaperoning or membrane-scaffolding mechanism remains unresolved. Heterodimers coexist with higher-order complex populations: control human fibroblasts contain CHCHD10 in 170 and 220 kDa complexes (PMID:29121267, Fig. 6A), while differentiated mouse tissues contain approximately 100–140 kDa complexes and retain CHCHD10 oligomerization without CHCHD2 (PMID:41053020). These sizes are electrophoretic complex estimates, not exact stoichiometry or proof of one invariant assembly. MICOS membership remains disputed. Positive COX stimulation is retained as biological context, but the CHCHD2-dependent, potentially indirect association does not yet define a direct enzyme-activator MF or a specific respiratory step performed by CHCHD10; neither is added as a core term.

In the tested human HEK293 nuclear context, CHCHD10 acts as a transcriptional corepressor through CXXC5-dependent recruitment to an oxygen-responsive COX4I2 promoter complex. Intact-versus-mutant reporter and CHCHD10 perturbations resolve repression, while CXXC5 depletion prevents endogenous ORE recruitment. This is a secondary, experimentally defined activity; its wider tissue relevance remains unresolved and it does not imply that CHCHD10 itself binds DNA directly.

Antagonist binding to IL-36 receptor (IL-36R/IL1RL2, an IL-1 receptor family member) with high affinity (Kd ~5-6 nM) to competitively block IL-36 agonist cytokines from activating the receptor. Unlike agonists, IL-36Ra binding prevents recruitment of IL-1RAcP co-receptor, thereby blocking MyD88/NF-κB/MAPK signaling cascade. IL-36Ra's defining molecular activity is antagonism, not generic receptor binding (PR

TLR7 is the recognition receptor of the endolysosomal TLR7 signalling pathway. Its leucine-rich-repeat ectodomain binds RNA catabolites in the lumen of the endolysosome and its cytoplasmic TIR domain transduces the event: occupancy of both ligand sites locks two protomers into an activated m-shaped dimer whose apposed TIR domains recruit MyD88, assembling the IRAK4-IRAK1/2-TRAF6 myddosome that activates canonical NF-kappaB and IRF7. Because the ligands are generic RNA degradation products rather than a foreign-specific chemistry, discrimination of self from non-self rests on where the receptor is: it signals only from acidified endolysosomes reached via UNC93B1.

The first ligand-binding site of TLR7, at the interface between the two protomers and conserved with TLR8, binds a guanosine moiety, and this is the occupancy that is essential for activation. Guanosine, deoxyguanosine and C8-substituted guanosine analogues act as RNA-independent agonists through this pocket; physiologically it is filled by the guanosine 2',3'-cyclic monophosphate that PLD3 and PLD4 release from RNase T2-cleaved RNA. The lupus variant Y264H lies in this site and selectively increases sensing of guanosine and 2',3'-cGMP. GO has no term for the cyclic-phosphate form, so guanosine binding is the closest available description of the activity.

The second ligand-binding site, on the concave face of the TLR7 horseshoe and absent from TLR8, binds short single-stranded uridine-containing RNA fragments and raises the affinity of the first site for its guanosine ligand. This is how TLR7 reads viral RNA genomes: endosomal recognition of influenza genomic RNA and of other single-stranded RNAs drives MyD88-dependent interferon and cytokine induction, and nucleoside modifications that occur in host RNA abolish the response.

TLR8 is the recognition receptor of the endosomal TLR8 signalling pathway. Its ectodomain reads RNA degradation products in the endosomal lumen at two sites - uridine at the interface between protomers and a short oligonucleotide on the concave leucine-rich-repeat surface - and both must be occupied for activation. The receptor is a pre-formed dimer that is held inactive until endosomal furin-like convertases and cathepsins cleave its Z-loop, which otherwise blocks the two protomers from approaching each other; ligand binding then reorganises the dimer so that the two C-termini and their TIR domains come together, recruiting MyD88 and assembling the IRAK4-IRAK1/2-TRAF6 myddosome that activates canonical NF-kappaB and IRF7. Because the ligands are ordinary RNA catabolites, specificity for microbial RNA rests on compartment and on the local supply of RNase T2 cleavage products.

The second TLR8 ligand-binding site, on the concave face of the leucine-rich-repeat horseshoe, binds short single-stranded oligoribonucleotides - the purine-2',3'-cyclophosphate-terminated fragments left by RNase T2 cleavage - and this is how TLR8 reads viral RNA. GU-rich single-stranded sequences from HIV-1, SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2, and endogenous RNAs such as microRNAs, act through this recognition to drive proinflammatory cytokine and type I interferon output from human myeloid cells. The requirement extends to the first site: single-stranded RNA activates TLR8 only when uridine also occupies the interface pocket, so RNA sensing by TLR8 is the joint occupancy of both sites by products of the same cleavage reaction.

Endolysosomal pattern recognition receptor for microbial CpG DNA. After UNC93B1-dependent transport and ectodomain cleavage in the endolysosome, ligand-bound TLR9 dimerizes and recruits MyD88 through its TIR domain, initiating the TLR9 signalling pathway that activates NF-kappaB and type I interferon production.

Direct binding of DNA containing unmethylated CpG motifs, allowing discrimination of microbial DNA from largely methylated, CpG-poor host DNA. Agonistic CpG DNA is bound across two protomers in a 2:2 complex, whereas inhibitory DNA binds a monomer.

UGGT1 catalyzes the reglucosylation of N-glycans on misfolded glycoproteins in the ER lumen, serving as the central folding sensor and checkpoint of the calnexin/calreticulin quality control cycle. Its seven-domain architecture (TRXL1-4, betaS1-2, GT24 catalytic domain) provides interdomain conformational flexibility that enables recognition of diverse molten-globule-like folding intermediates and glucosylation of glycans at variable distances from misfolded regions (DOI:10.1073/pnas.1703682114). UGGT1 writes a site-selective "glyco-code" that programs which ER chaperones engage substrates at specific glycosylation sites (DOI:10.1016/j.molcel.2023.11.006). This reglucosylation competes with EDEM-family mannose trimming in a "tug-of-war" that determines substrate fate between refolding and ERAD commitment (DOI:10.1101/2023.10.18.562958). UGGT1 also promotes substrate solubility by maintaining misfolded glycoproteins in the lectin-chaperone cycle, reducing insoluble aggregation (DOI:10.1091/mbc.e13-02-0101). Activity is modulated by the partner selenoprotein SELENOF/SEP15, which affects a subset of UGGT1 clients (DOI:10.1073/pnas.2315009121).

ALG9 transfers the seventh mannose from dolichyl-phosphate-mannose to the Man6 lipid-linked N-glycan precursor at the luminal face of the ER membrane. This completes the B branch before the intervening ALG12 addition.

ALG9 transfers the ninth mannose from dolichyl-phosphate-mannose to the Man8 lipid-linked N-glycan precursor at the luminal face of the ER membrane. This completes the C branch after ALG12 adds the eighth mannose.
Mitochondrial mRNA stabilization via suppression of PNPase/SUV3-mediated 3'-5' decay. LRPPRC-SLIRP complex binds mt-mRNAs and protects them from degradation.
Promotion of mitochondrial mRNA polyadenylation via MTPAP. LRPPRC enhances MTPAP-mediated addition of poly(A) tails to mt-mRNAs.
mRNA delivery to the mitoribosome. LRPPRC docks on small subunit via mS39/mS31, forming a corridor with SLIRP for mRNA handoff to the decoding center.
mRNA holdase activity maintaining proper mt-mRNA folding for efficient translation.

HID1 is recruited from the cytosol to the cytoplasmic face of the trans-Golgi network, where it is required for the biogenesis of large dense core vesicles (secretory granules) in neuroendocrine and endocrine cells, including cargo sorting into nascent granules and dense core formation. The evidence is genetic and structure-function work with the rat ortholog in PC12 and INS-1 cells, including the human DEE105 patient frameshift modelled in rat HID1; the human protein itself has been shown only to localize to the TGN. Its molecular activity is unknown, so no molecular function is asserted.

HID1 is required for maturation of immature secretory granules by homotypic fusion, and so for proinsulin processing, in pancreatic beta cells. This rests on conditional knockout of the mouse ortholog (same PANTHER subfamily, about 96% identical) and is a metazoan-level inference for the human protein.

Recognizes regulatory DNA motifs and controls Pol II gene expression as the sequence-specific component of ChAHP. Complex-dependent restriction of chromatin accessibility regulates lineage genes and can constrain CTCF occupancy at overlapping sites.

Recruits CHD4-containing chromatin-remodeling activity to sequence-selected sites through ChAHP assembly. This targeting supports repression of gene expression, including a mechanistically defined Pol III SINE pathway in mouse cells; CHD4 supplies the remodeling enzyme activity.

Binds HP1 chromoshadow domains through a conserved interaction motif. This association supports ADNP recruitment to H3K9me3-marked heterochromatin, complementary to sequence-directed ChAHP targeting of euchromatic sites.
Seipin binds anionic phospholipids through its lumenal domain. This lipid-recognition activity helps organize the ER membrane environment in which seipin and LDAF1 assemble nascent lipid droplets.

Oligomeric seipin tethers growing lipid droplets to the ER, organizes their membrane contacts and supports lipid and protein exchange during droplet growth. Together with LDAF1, it defines productive assembly sites. This contact activity cooperates with seipin’s lipid recognition within the same droplet-formation mechanism.

Catalyses guanine-nucleotide exchange on class I ADP-ribosylation factors, converting ARF1 and ARF3 to their GTP-bound active forms through its Sec7 domain, in a reaction inhibited by brefeldin A. This is the protein's defining activity and the step that licenses coat and adaptor recruitment to donor membranes.

Maintains the structural integrity of the recycling endosome and drives the return of internalised receptors from it to the plasma membrane, a function it does not share with its paralog BIG1. This entry carries the same molecular function as the first because it is the same catalytic activity acting at a different compartment on a different process set - class I ARF exchange on recycling endosomes rather than at the trans-Golgi network - and the E738K mutant separates the two phenotypes without separating the activity.

Acts as an A-kinase anchoring protein, tethering PKA regulatory subunits through three amphipathic regions in its N-terminal half and assembling a local cAMP module that also contains phosphodiesterase PDE3A. This couples cAMP signalling to ARF activation and is structurally separate from the Sec7 catalytic domain.

FAD-dependent oxidation of the free polyamine spermine to spermidine, with production of 3-aminopropanal and hydrogen peroxide (spermine oxidase activity; EC 1.5.3.16), the direct back-conversion step of polyamine catabolism.
Binding of the FAD cofactor required for the amine-oxidase catalytic cycle; SMOX binds one FAD per subunit as a member of the flavin monoamine oxidase family.

Hydrolyzes the sn-1 acyl ester of lysophosphatidylserine, controlling a bioactive lipid pool at the endoplasmic reticulum. Human assays establish this reaction; patient cells and mouse studies connect its loss to disrupted lipid homeostasis.

Hydrolyzes oxidized sn-2 acyl chains of phosphatidylserine to fatty acid and lysoPS, limiting oxidized lipid accumulation during oxidative/inflammatory stress. The demonstrated chemistry is distinct from hydrolysis of unoxidized diacyl phosphatidylserine.

CFAP61 functions as a structural scaffold within the calmodulin- and spoke-associated complex (CSC), providing the structural basis for radial spoke 3 (RS3) assembly and contributing to RS2 base stability. Through the CSC, CFAP61 mediates the connection between radial spokes and the nexin-dynein regulatory complex (N-DRC), enabling mechanochemical signal transduction that coordinates dynein motor activity and ciliary beating. The protein contains a Rossmann-like FAD/NAD(P)-binding fold that serves as a structural scaffold rather than an enzyme active site, an N-terminal axoneme-targeting domain, and a C-terminal dimerisation domain.

In sperm, CFAP61 is essential for flagellum morphogenesis and motility. Loss of CFAP61 function causes multiple morphological abnormalities of the flagella (MMAF) and male infertility (SPGF84). CFAP61 interacts with intraflagellar transport proteins (IFT22, IFT81, WDR35) and its loss disrupts IFT protein distribution during spermiogenesis.

Pantothenate kinase that catalyzes the first, committed and rate-limiting step of coenzyme A biosynthesis, phosphorylating pantothenate (vitamin B5) using ATP to produce (R)-4'-phosphopantothenate. The mitochondrial (intermembrane space) human enzyme is feedback-inhibited by acetyl-CoA and activated by palmitoylcarnitine.

IFT52 is a structural hub of the IFT-B complex that bridges the two IFT-B1 subcomplexes and links IFT-B1 to IFT-B2; it is required for IFT-B integrity, anterograde IFT and ciliogenesis. No specific molecular-function term beyond complex scaffolding is established.

Negative regulation of serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) activity as a ceramide-sensitive regulatory subunit of the SPT holoenzyme complex. ORMDL3 physically occludes the SPT substrate entry tunnel through its N-terminus, competing with substrate binding (PMID:33558761). Ceramide binding to the ORMDL3 N-terminus (Asn13-dependent) stabilizes this inhibitory conformation, implementing homeostatic feedback control of de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis (PMID:37308477).

Ceramide binding at the N-terminus enabling homeostatic feedback regulation of sphingolipid de novo biosynthesis. ORMDL3 senses cellular ceramide levels and translates this into inhibition of SPT activity. Asn13 is a critical residue for ceramide sensing (PMID:37308477). This molecular sensing function is integral to the sphingolipid homeostatic feedback loop.

Obligate ER-membrane-anchored cofactor/substrate-adaptor of the UFM1 E3 ligase that binds the E3 ligase UFL1 (and CDK5RAP3) to form the UREL complex, tethering ufmylation activity to ER-docked ribosomes and stabilizing UFL1.

UFM1-modified protein reader that, via its UFM1-interacting motif (UFIM), specifically binds ufmylated RPL26/uL24 on the 60S ribosome, producing stable association of the 60S subunit with the UREL complex and promoting release/recycling of the large subunit from the ER translocon.

Riboflavin (vitamin B2) transmembrane transporter that mediates cellular uptake of riboflavin across the plasma membrane, directly demonstrated by saturable, riboflavin-selective [3H]riboflavin uptake in transfected cells and by knockdown experiments.

Apically (brush-border) localized riboflavin transporter that drives intestinal absorption of dietary riboflavin. RFVT3 is expressed at the apical membrane of polarized intestinal epithelial cells and is the principal transporter for riboflavin uptake at that surface; loss of RFVT3 function impairs intestinal riboflavin absorption.

COX4I2 is the tissue-biased COX4 isoform used as a non-catalytic, supernumerary subunit of mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex IV. It contributes to cytochrome-c oxidase activity only in the context of the assembled complex and directly participates in electron transport from cytochrome c to oxygen as part of that complex. Distinct from the ubiquitous COX4I1 isoform, COX4I2 acts as a regulatory/kinetic tuning subunit that lowers Complex IV oxygen affinity (a COX4I2-containing complex has ~2-fold higher p50 than a COX4I1-containing complex) and is required for acute oxygen sensing in specialized tissues — COX4I2-null mice show selectively impaired hypoxic ventilatory response, and conditional Cox4i2 knockout strongly inhibits hypoxic L-type Ca2+ channel modulation in arterial smooth muscle. COX4I2 expression is enriched in lung, carotid body, and pulmonary/arterial smooth muscle — canonical O2-sensing cell types — making oxygen-affinity tuning and acute O2 sensing its defining functional distinction from COX4I1.

Membrane-anchored HSC70/HSP70 co-chaperone that, via its J domain, recruits and stimulates HSC70/HSPA8 to chaperone the presynaptic SNARE machinery (SNAP-25), maintaining release-competent synaptic vesicles.
General chaperone of regulated/synaptic-vesicle exocytosis that supports calcium-dependent neurotransmitter release at nerve endings and protects synapses against activity-dependent degeneration.

Hippo-regulated transcriptional coactivator of TEAD transcription factors. Unphosphorylated YAP1 enters the nucleus, binds TEAD1-4 through its TEAD-binding domain, and supplies the transactivation function for TEAD-dependent genes such as CTGF. LATS1/2 phosphorylation causes 14-3-3-mediated cytoplasmic retention and degradation. Ancestral: the Capsaspora ortholog binds Capsaspora TEAD and activates Hippo-responsive transcription.

Binding of DNA-binding transcription factors that recruit YAP1 to chromatin: TEADs through the N-terminal TEAD-binding domain, and p73/p63 and other PPxY-containing factors through the WW domains. Which partner is bound selects the target-gene program, e.g. p73 proapoptotic genes after c-Abl phosphorylation of Y357 following DNA damage.

WW domain-mediated binding of PPxY (proline-rich) motifs. This is how YAP1 engages its upstream regulators (LATS1/2, angiomotins, PTPN14), which hold it in the cytoplasm or at junctions, as well as some transcription-factor partners. The tandem WW domains are conserved in the Capsaspora ortholog.

High-affinity thiamine (vitamin B1) uptake across the plasma membrane, coupled to proton antiport (thiamine-in / H+-out), enabling cellular thiamine utilization; specific for vitamin B1 and does not transport folate.

NFU1 is a late-acting [4Fe-4S] cluster chaperone that receives [2Fe-2S] clusters from upstream donors ISCU2 and ISCA1, assembles them into [4Fe-4S] clusters, and delivers these to target proteins. This chaperone function is demonstrated by biochemical reconstitution, spectroscopic analysis, and functional complementation studies (PMID:12886008, PMID:27538573, PMID:28906594).

NFU1 dimerizes and ligates a bridging [4Fe-4S] cluster. Mossbauer spectroscopy and UV-visible absorption studies demonstrate approximately one [4Fe-4S] cluster per two NFU1 monomers (PMID:12886008). The cluster-binding cysteines (C210 and C213) are essential for function and are disrupted by pathogenic mutations (PMID:28906594).

MRM2 is the SAM-dependent 2'-O-ribose methyltransferase that installs Um1369 (U3039) in the A-loop of 16S mitochondrial LSU rRNA. The activity is established in human cells by site assignment and catalytic-dead mutants, and it is inherited from the FtsJ/RlmE clade (PANTHER PTHR10920:SF18; PAINT node PTN000100455).

Independently of its catalytic activity, MRM2 binds late mtLSU assembly intermediates near the A-loop and is required for folding of 16S rRNA domains IV and V and for release from the MALSU1:L0R8F8:mtACP-bound state. Catalytically dead MRM2 rescues translation in knock-out cells. This assembly role is established for human MRM2. The mitochondrial-specific details should not be transferred to orthologs without evidence.

Acting as the protein-macromolecule adaptor of the upper tip-link density, holding the myosin VIIa motor against the harmonin/cadherin-23 anchor through a bipartite SAM / C-terminal PDZ-binding-motif interface with harmonin and a central-region interface with the MYO7A MyTH4-FERM cassette, so that resting tension is maintained on the stereociliary tip link during hair-cell mechanotransduction.

Acting as a scaffold/adaptor at the photoreceptor ciliary base and periciliary membrane compartment: binding intraflagellar transport complex B proteins IFT52 and IFT57 through its ankyrin repeats and central domain to position IFT-B for cargo delivery into the sensory cilium, and engaging MAGI2 through its CK2-phosphorylated SAM domain to control clathrin-dependent endocytosis at the periciliary membrane, both required for outer-segment renewal and photoreceptor survival.

Acting in the nucleus as an adaptor that couples U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP particles to spliceosomal and nuclear-body components (SF3B1, SON, PRPF6, PRPF31), mediating their transfer from Cajal bodies to nuclear speckles and thereby setting the kinetics of pre-catalytic spliceosome assembly and the pattern of constitutive and alternative splicing.

PDZ-domain protein-macromolecule adaptor activity of the long whirlin isoform within the transient ankle-link/USH2 complex at the base of developing stereocilia, where whirlin binds the cytoplasmic PDZ-binding motifs of the transmembrane proteins usherin (USH2A) and ADGRV1 and heterodimerizes with PDZD7 to assemble the quaternary USH2 complex (multivalent, condensate-forming interactions), anchoring the ankle links that maintain hair-bundle cohesion during morphogenesis; loss of this function causes the deafness of Usher syndrome type 2D.

Scaffolding/adaptor activity of the short (C-terminal) whirlin isoform at stereocilia tips, where whirlin is delivered by the motor MYO15A and, together with the actin regulator EPS8, forms the tip complex that drives stereocilium elongation and establishes the staircase architecture of the hair bundle required for hearing; disruption of this tip module underlies DFNB31 nonsyndromic deafness.

PDZ adaptor activity of long-isoform whirlin at the photoreceptor periciliary membrane compartment, at the apex of the inner segment adjacent to the connecting cilium, where whirlin recruits and retains USH2A and ADGRV1 as the USH2 complex, organizing the periciliary membrane region that supports protein trafficking toward the outer segment and long-term photoreceptor maintenance; loss of this function causes the retinitis pigmentosa of Usher syndrome type 2D.

GSH-independent glyoxalase that converts methylglyoxal to lactate and glyoxal to glycolate, providing cellular detoxification of reactive dicarbonyl species. This is the best-supported enzymatic activity of DJ-1, though catalytic efficiency is low (kcat ~0.02 sec-1; PMID:31653696).

Redox-dependent molecular chaperone that inhibits alpha-synuclein aggregation and protects against oxidative stress. Cys-106 oxidation to sulfinic acid activates chaperone function and serves as a cellular oxidative stress sensor. Stabilizes NFE2L2/Nrf2 by preventing Keap1-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, thereby upregulating antioxidant gene expression.

Copper chaperone that delivers copper to SOD1, facilitating SOD1 activation. Binds both Cu(I) and Cu(II) ions. This activity links DJ-1 to both metal homeostasis and antioxidant defense via SOD1 maturation.

CARD11 converts receptor-dependent activation into a BCL10-nucleating assembly and recruits MALT1 and ubiquitin-signaling components. This physical organization advances canonical NF-kappaB signaling, including bringing BCL10 together with the HOIP enzyme. Plasma-membrane and lipid-raft association provide established functional contexts for this regulated adaptor; a fixed native oligomer size is not assumed.

NLRP3 nucleates the inflammasome that activates caspase-1. Its N-terminal pyrin domains stack into a filament on the activated oligomer, and that filament seeds unidirectional polymerisation of the adaptor ASC, which recruits procaspase-1 and permits proximity-induced autoprocessing. NLRP3 has no catalytic activity of its own in this step: it supplies the geometry.

Through the assembled inflammasome NLRP3 activates procaspase-1, which matures pro-interleukin-1 beta and pro-interleukin-18 and cleaves gasdermin D to execute pyroptosis. This is the physiological output of NLRP3 and the step that CAPS gain-of-function mutations render constitutive.

A conserved polybasic region of NLRP3 binds phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate on the dispersed trans-Golgi network through ionic interaction, and this is what recruits and concentrates NLRP3 at the membrane scaffold on which it aggregates. It is the one well-established direct binding event in NLRP3 activation, and the reason the protein can respond to structurally unrelated agonists without binding any of them: diverse stimuli converge on trans-Golgi disassembly. Charge neutralisation of the same linker by BTK phosphorylation tunes the interaction.

The central NACHT domain binds and hydrolyses ATP, and the nucleotide state is the conformational switch of the protein: the resting oligomer is ADP-bound with the pyrin domains sequestered, while the active disc holds an ATP-bound NACHT whose subdomains have rotated by about 85 degrees. Nucleotide binding is required for caspase-1 activation and for the constitutive activity of disease-associated mutants, and the ATP-hydrolysis motif is where the clinical inhibitor MCC950 acts.

NLRP3 scaffolds a biomolecular condensate at the pericentriolar material of the microtubule organising centre, into which microtubule-dependent transport delivers both NLRP3 and the licensing kinase NEK7, and within which the inflammasome assembles. Priming, microtubule transport, NEK7 and NLRP3 abundance all converge on making this environment permissive, which sets the activation threshold. This route is important but not obligatory: low-molecular-weight, non-cage NLRP3 species support a slower trans-Golgi- and MTOC-distal pathway that dominates in human neutrophils.
Transiently supports selective turnover and replacement of N-module subunits during repair of assembled mitochondrial complex I. The precise biochemical step is unresolved.

Binds mitochondrial ATP synthase through contacts with its subunits, including MT-ATP6 and ATP5MC2, and contributes to regulation of mitochondrial ATP production. Mouse neuronal and mitochondrial ATP-output phenotypes complement human complex-association evidence. The causal route from this association to ATP-output regulation remains unresolved; direct complex-V catalytic modulation and a universal effect across tissues are not established.

Sequestration of the GLI transcription factors. SUFU binds full-length GLI1, GLI2 and GLI3 through a bipartite interface that clamps the conserved SYGHL motif, holding them in the cytoplasm, blocking their nuclear import, repressing their transcriptional output and shielding them from proteasomal degradation. These are readouts of one binding event: mutating the interface abolishes all of them together. The activity is relieved when GLI is phosphorylated by Fused-family, DYRK2 or MAP kinases, or when SUFU itself is ubiquitylated by SCF(FBXL17).

Adaptor activity that promotes conversion of GLI3 into its repressor form. In the pathway-off state SUFU bridges GLI3 to the enzymes that process it, recruiting GSK3B to GLI3 and linking GLI to the Slimb/BTRC-dependent degradation machinery, so that full-length GLI3 is efficiently cleaved into GLI3R. This happens on the SUFU-GLI3 complex delivered to the primary cilium, where the processing kinases act at the ciliary base. It is the one SUFU function separable from sequestration: here SUFU contributes positioning and recruitment to a proteolytic step carried out by other enzymes.

Phosphoinositide-stimulated GTPase-activating protein for ARF6, acting on the cytoplasmic face of tubular recycling endosomes to terminate ARF6 signalling. Recombinant ACAP1 accelerates GTP hydrolysis on ARF6 in preference to ARF1 and ARF5; activity requires phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate together with phosphatidic acid, and is abolished by mutation of the arginine-finger residue Arg-448. Recruitment to the membrane is itself ARF6-GTP dependent, so the GAP is delivered to its own substrate, and the catalytically dead mutant is the one form absent from the endosomal tubules. Substrate specificity cannot be stated in the term because the ARF-specific GAP term was merged into the generic one, so an annotation of this function should carry has_input UniProtKB:P62330 (ARF6).

Cargo-selective adaptor within an ARF6-regulated clathrin coat that packages transmembrane cargo for return from recycling endosomes to the cell surface. ACAP1 bridges the three elements a coat adaptor must connect: it binds clathrin heavy chain directly, it reads a sorting signal in the cytoplasmic tail of integrin beta-1 and the third cytoplasmic loop of SLC2A4/GLUT4, and it deforms the membrane itself. Cargo capture is gated rather than constitutive - Akt phosphorylation of Ser-554 relieves a local autoinhibition, S554A abolishes both ITGB1 binding and integrin-dependent migration while the phosphomimetic S554D enhances binding - which makes this the step at which growth-factor signalling is coupled to the recycling route. The two physiological outputs are integrin-dependent cell migration and insulin-stimulated GLUT4 delivery.

Membrane deformation, carried out by the PH domain rather than by the BAR domain that would normally do it. ACAP1's BAR domain can neither bind membrane nor impart curvature on its own; specific PH-domain residues perform both, while the BAR domain instead binds the BAR domains of neighbouring ACAP1 dimers to build the lattice that deforms the bilayer. Banana-shaped homodimers assemble laterally into tetramers that pack helically onto the membrane, with only one PH domain per dimer inserting. The bending element is Loop1 of the PH domain, between strands beta-1 and beta-2, whose distal aromatic residue Phe-280 inserts into a single leaflet: purified protein binds and tubulates liposomes in vitro, F280A reduces both binding and tubulation, F280E effectively abolishes binding, and the conservative F280W preserves both. In the cryoEM reconstruction of a coated tubule the BAR domain makes no significant contact with the bilayer at all. In cells, tubulation of endosomal membranes requires both domains and is greatly enhanced when phosphoinositide supply is raised by co-expressing PIP5K1C.

Phosphoinositide recognition by the PH domain, which is the input that couples both the GAP activity and the membrane binding to local lipid composition. The PH domain binds phosphatidic acid, PI3P, PI(3,5)P2 and PIP3, and the single substitution K274N abolishes PIP2 and PIP3 binding and, with it, association with endosomal tubules. This is a regulatory activity rather than an output in its own right, but it is the reason ACAP1's catalysis is restricted to membranes of the right composition.

Binds ClC-Ka/ClC-Kb and regulates their activation and surface organization, contributing to chloride conductance by the heteromeric complex without forming the conducting pore. Electrophysiological studies distinguish trafficking from modulation of permeation and cooperative common gating. Barttin favors an open common-gate configuration; Cys54/Cys56 palmitoylation supports channel activation without requiring increased membrane insertion in the tested systems. This accessory mechanism supports renal chloride transport and inner-ear ionic homeostasis.

ASC is the bipartite adaptor that links an activated inflammasome sensor to procaspase-1. Its pyrin domain is nucleated into a filament by the sensor (NLRP3, NLRP1, AIM2, NLRP6, IFI16 or pyrin), and the clustered CARDs then recruit procaspase-1; this is the defining molecular function of the protein and it is purely a connectivity/geometry role with no catalytic activity.

Through its clustered CARD filament ASC nucleates procaspase-1 CARD filaments, driving proximity-induced autoactivation of caspase-1 that matures IL-1 beta and IL-18 and drives gasdermin-D-dependent pyroptosis. This is the catalytic output ASC enables (without itself being an enzyme).

ASC self-associates through homotypic PYD-PYD and CARD-CARD contacts, polymerizing into filaments that condense into the single perinuclear speck/pyroptosome. This self-oligomerization is what converts a localized sensor signal into the large caspase-1-activating platform.

CHEK2 transfers phosphate from ATP to protein serine/threonine residues. Regulated self-association and autophosphorylation couple activation to DNA-damage checkpoint and apoptotic signaling, principally in nuclear compartments. Substrate phosphorylation regulates downstream repair and transcriptional responses rather than executing their chemistry.

Captures extracellular transcobalamin carrying cobalamin and mediates its uptake by endocytosis. The calcium-coordinating extracellular domains recognize the carrier protein, providing cobalamin for later intracellular metabolism.

Binds newly synthesized membrane-protein clients and helps direct their disposition. BAP31 associates with CFTR F508del, Sec61/TRAM and Derlin-1 machinery; depletion reduces mutant-CFTR degradation and permits some protein to reach the cell surface. These observations support client delivery and positive regulation of ERAD. The inspected PAINT node PTN000294723 also carries GO:0140388, dated 20260603 and seeded by human BCAP31 (UniProtKB:P51572), a genuine curator judgment based on target evidence. The broader carrier activity here states the experimentally supported binding-and-delivery function; the narrower ATP-coupled translocation mechanism remains an explicit question rather than a claim that the curator made a circular inference.

Participates with FIS1 in a platform at the ER-mitochondria interface that recruits procaspase-8 during apoptotic signaling. Deletion of the BAP31 cytoplasmic region historically called a variant death effector domain disrupts procaspase-8 recruitment. Following cleavage, ER-localized p20 contributes to calcium release and downstream mitochondrial responses. The recruitment function belongs to the intact platform and is distinct from BAP31 merely serving as a caspase substrate.

Supports localization of selected complex I proteins to mitochondria from ER-mitochondria contact sites. In human U2OS cells, BAP31 associates with TOMM40 and NDUFS4 in crosslinked co-immunoprecipitation experiments, while BAP31 depletion alters the mitochondrial distribution and turnover of NDUFS4 and NDUFB11. These experiments support a contribution to protein localization without assigning BAP31 the catalytic or channel activity of the mitochondrial import machinery.

Substrate-recognition (F-box/WD40) subunit of the SCF(FBXW7) E3 ubiquitin ligase that recruits phosphodegron-bearing substrates to the CUL1-RBX1 catalytic core for polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.

Phosphodegron recognition by the WD40 beta-propeller (phosphothreonine residue binding), which provides the substrate selectivity underlying FBXW7-directed degradation of cyclin E, MYC, NOTCH ICD and other targets.

DHX30 uses ATP to unwind RNA and has cytosolic and mitochondrial populations. Its mitochondrial RNA-granule-associated activity supports large ribosomal subunit assembly. RNA binding and ATP hydrolysis are components of this helicase mechanism. The specific endogenous RNA substrates and the molecular remodeling step during assembly remain unresolved.

Facilitates cytoplasmic assembly and correct axonemal incorporation of outer and inner dynein arms that power motile cilia and sperm flagella. In human airway multiciliated cells, DNAAF11 associates with dynein-containing DynAPs alongside other assembly factors.

Methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase (racemase) activity: reversible interconversion of (2R)- and (2S)-methylmalonyl-CoA (D-/L-methylmalonyl-CoA), the epimerisation step that provides methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMUT) with the isomer it requires.
In the mitochondrial matrix, MCEE performs the epimerase step of propionyl-CoA catabolism, feeding the mutase reaction that produces succinyl-CoA for the citric acid cycle.

Associates with RNA polymerase II in PAF1C and helps couple productive transcription elongation to recruitment of mRNA 3′-end processing factors. Human coimmunoprecipitation establishes complex-associated binding, without isolating a binary CDC73–PolII interface or a CDC73 catalytic processing activity.

Binds beta-catenin and connects the nuclear Wnt transcription complex to PAF1C-dependent transcription. Human parafibromin and Drosophila Hyrax experiments support this conserved coactivator role; direct beta-catenin engagement distinguishes it from a nonspecific consequence of altered transcription or cell proliferation.

Calcium-dependent alpha-1,2-mannosidase that catalyzes the downstream ER mannose-trimming step from Man8GlcNAc2 to Man7GlcNAc2 (and further toward Man5GlcNAc2 isomers), accelerating glycoprotein ERAD by generating the demannosylated glycan recognized by the downstream lectin OS-9.

Accelerates ubiquitin-dependent ER-associated degradation of misfolded glycoproteins by trimming their N-glycans within the gpERAD pathway, acting downstream of EDEM2 and in association with the HRD1 adaptor SEL1L.

Catalyzes the central adenylyl-transfer step of NAD+ biosynthesis: condensation of nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) with ATP to yield NAD+ and pyrophosphate (EC 2.7.7.1). This Mg2+-dependent reaction, shared by the NAD+ salvage and de novo routes, is the primary evolved function of NMNAT2.

Also condenses nicotinate mononucleotide (NaMN) with ATP to yield deamido-NAD+ (NaAD) and pyrophosphate (EC 2.7.7.18), the same adenylyltransferase chemistry acting on the deamidated substrate with lower efficiency; feeds the deamido-NAD+ branch of NAD+ biosynthesis.

ATP-binding activity: COQ8A binds adenine nucleotides via its atypical protein-kinase-like fold, with an unusual selectivity for ADP over ATP conferred by the alanine-rich (AAAS) nucleotide-binding loop. This nucleotide binding is required to relieve autoinhibition and is essential for the protein's role in coenzyme Q biosynthesis.

ATP hydrolysis (ATPase) activity: rather than canonical protein-kinase phosphotransfer, the demonstrated catalytic activity of COQ8/COQ8A is ATP hydrolysis (a small-molecule "water kinase" activity) that is enhanced by the UbiB-specific KxGQ motif and by coenzyme-Q head-group intermediates. Mutations that abolish this activity eliminate CoQ production in vivo, linking the ATPase to the endogenous function; canonical protein-kinase activity in trans is not exhibited.

Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) biosynthesis: COQ8A is essential for CoQ10 biosynthesis, acting as a member and stabilizer of the multi-subunit CoQ biosynthetic complex (the COQ synthome / complex Q; COQ3-COQ7, COQ9) at the matrix face of the inner mitochondrial membrane. Loss of COQ8A destabilizes complex Q and causes CoQ deficiency (ARCA2/COQ10D4).
GTPase of the mitochondrial outer membrane that, with MFN1, tethers apposed mitochondria and drives outer-membrane fusion using GTP hydrolysis.
Phosphorylates BCKDHA within the matrix-associated branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase system, inhibiting the complex and limiting branched-chain amino acid breakdown.

Phosphorylates ATP-citrate lyase at human Ser455. This distinct substrate reaction is supported by purified human-protein assays; cytosolic localization and increased lipogenesis were investigated in rodent liver and cell systems. Human UniProt records the cytosolic localization by similarity to rat Q00972 (ECO:0000250), rather than as direct human localization evidence.

ATG7 is the E1-like activating enzyme for ATG12. It adenylates ATG12's C-terminal glycine, forms a thioester intermediate via Cys572, and transfers ATG12 to the E2 enzyme ATG10 for subsequent conjugation to ATG5.

ATG7 is the E1-like activating enzyme for ATG8 family proteins (LC3, GABARAP, GATE-16). It adenylates the C-terminal glycine of processed ATG8 proteins, forms a thioester intermediate, and transfers ATG8 to the E2 enzyme ATG3 for lipidation with phosphatidylethanolamine.
ATG7 forms a functional homodimer required for trans-thioester transfer of activated ubiquitin-like substrates (ATG12, ATG8) to their cognate E2 enzymes.

Diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase catalyzing the terminal, committed step of triacylglycerol biosynthesis: acyl transfer from long-chain acyl-CoA to the sn-3 position of 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol to form triacylglycerol + CoA (EC 2.3.1.20), at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and lipid-droplet surface.

Secondary acyl-CoA:retinol O-fatty-acyltransferase (ARAT, EC 2.3.1.76) activity of the DGAT2/MOGAT-family fold, esterifying retinol to retinyl esters; a genuine but minor side activity relative to DGAT catalysis.

Scaffold subunit of the ring-shaped ERLIN1/ERLIN2 SPFH-domain complex that binds inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) tetramers and, with the E3 ligase RNF170, mediates their ER-associated degradation, controlling calcium signaling.

Cholesterol-binding ER membrane protein that restricts SREBP activation by associating with and stabilizing the SREBP-SCAP-Insig complex, thereby negatively regulating cholesterol and fatty acid biosynthesis and contributing to cellular cholesterol homeostasis.
Cytoplasmic R3H-domain protein that binds uridine-rich 3' UTR sequences and promotes expression of target mRNAs, opposing miR-128 to support dendritic branching.

As the outer-nuclear-membrane KASH subunit of LINC complexes, nesprin-2 links the cytoskeleton to the nucleus: its KASH peptide binds SUN1/SUN2 in the perinuclear space while its cytoplasmic domains bind F-actin (TAN lines) or recruit dynein-dynactin (via BICD2) and kinesin-1 (via a LEWD motif), allowing force-driven nuclear movement and positioning.
The N-terminal calponin-homology domains of giant nesprin-2 bind F-actin, tethering the nucleus to dorsal actin cables.

KASH-domain outer-nuclear-membrane component of LINC complexes: binds SUN1/SUN2 in the perinuclear space and the actin cytoskeleton (and motor/MTOC partners) in the cytoplasm, anchoring the cytoskeleton to the nuclear envelope and transmitting force for nuclear positioning and migration.
N-terminal calponin-homology domains of giant nesprin-1 bind F-actin, providing the cytoskeletal attachment of the LINC bridge.

NCSTN is an essential non-catalytic gamma-secretase subunit that helps assemble and position the substrate-recognition extracellular domain of the complex, enabling presenilin-dependent intramembrane cleavage of APP, Notch receptors, and related substrates.

Cleaves double-stranded RNA and pre-miRNA hairpins into small regulatory RNAs and performs precursor-processing work during assembly and guide loading of Argonaute silencing complexes with TARBP2 or PRKRA.

Acts as a selective autophagy receptor by simultaneously binding polyubiquitin chains on cargo (via the UBAN motif) and ATG8/LC3/GABARAP-family modifiers on the autophagosomal membrane (via the LIR motif), thereby bridging ubiquitinated cargo to the nascent autophagosome; TBK1-mediated phosphorylation at Ser177 enhances LC3 binding.

Binds K63-linked and linear polyubiquitin chains via the UBAN domain, the molecular basis for recognizing ubiquitin-coated cargo (damaged mitochondria, cytosolic bacteria) and for engaging polyubiquitinated components of inflammatory/innate-immune signaling complexes.

Functions in antibacterial autophagy (xenophagy), serving as the cell-autonomous defense receptor that targets ubiquitin-coated cytosolic Gram-negative bacteria such as Salmonella for autophagic clearance, acting downstream of TBK1 and alongside SQSTM1/p62 and CALCOCO2/NDP52.

Serves as a receptor for PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy, recognizing ubiquitinated outer-membrane proteins on depolarized/damaged mitochondria and recruiting LC3 to drive autophagosome formation around them; this function is disrupted by the ALS-linked UBAN mutant E478G.
Regulate small GTPases by cooperating with ARL13B in ARL3 nucleotide exchange and stabilizing GTP-bound ARL3 and ARL2.
Bind STAT3 and support its retention in the nucleus, sustaining cytokine-dependent transcriptional responses.

PLD3 is a 5'-3' exonuclease that degrades ssDNA and ssRNA from the 5' end in lysosomes at acidic pH. This has been demonstrated by multiple biochemical, structural, and genetic studies. The enzyme releases nucleoside 3'-monophosphates as products.

PLD3 synthesizes (S,S)-bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP) via a transphosphatidylation reaction. This activity is important for lysosomal lipid catabolism. BMP is a key phospholipid in lysosomal intralumenal vesicles essential for lipid degradation.

The C-terminal GT7 domain of CHSY1 transfers GalNAc from UDP-GalNAc to the terminal GlcA of a chondroitin acceptor, creating a beta1,4 linkage. This is one of two coupled catalytic steps in Golgi chondroitin backbone elongation. CHPF or CHPF2 supports the polymerase complex, while CHSY1 supplies the sugar-transfer chemistry.

The N-terminal GT31 domain of CHSY1 transfers GlcA from UDP-GlcA to the terminal GalNAc of a chondroitin acceptor, creating a beta1,3 linkage. Alternation with its GalNAc-transfer reaction extends the same proteoglycan chain within the Golgi. This backbone synthesis precedes modification by sulfotransferases.

Hydrolyzes terminal alpha-linked glutamate residues from tubulin C termini and polyglutamate side chains, controlling the glutamylation state of the cytoplasmic microtubule system. On the tested tubulin substrates it shortens side chains without cleaving their gamma-linked branch point. Tubulin recognition and zinc-dependent carboxypeptidase chemistry form one integrated activity; non-tubulin deglutamylation is an extension of substrate scope rather than a separate catalytic mechanism.

Binds tubulin and coordinates its controlled incorporation into centriolar microtubules during centriole replication and elongation. PN2-3-mediated tubulin recognition acts with assembly-partner interactions in building the centriole/basal-body system. Engineered fragments and larger constructs can have different effects on growth, so this core does not assign universal polymerase or depolymerase activity.

Radical-generating small subunit of ribonucleotide reductase; with the large catalytic subunit RRM1 it catalyzes the de novo reduction of ribonucleoside diphosphates to 2'-deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (EC 1.17.4.1) via a diiron-tyrosyl free radical center, using thioredoxin/glutaredoxin as reductant.

p53/TP53-inducible provider of deoxyribonucleotide precursors for mitochondrial DNA synthesis. In quiescent and post-mitotic cells that lack RRM2, the RRM1/RRM2B complex supplies the dNTPs required for mtDNA replication; loss of RRM2B causes mitochondrial DNA depletion (MTDPS8).

Dysbindin is a structural subunit of BLOC-1, a complex that deforms endosomal membranes into tubular transport carriers. Recombinant human BLOC-1 containing dysbindin residues 1–259 bends negatively charged membranes; this establishes a contribution to the complex activity, not autonomous membrane bending by isolated dysbindin. The complex coordinates carrier formation and selective cargo trafficking, supporting melanosome and platelet dense-granule biogenesis and neuronal anterograde vesicle trafficking.

Dysbindin regulates synaptic vesicle exocytosis and dopamine D2 receptor trafficking. Mouse acute-protein rescue distinguishes effects on fusion kinetics and quantal size from slower changes in release probability, while human neuronal-cell and rat-neuron studies link dysbindin to D2 internalization and downstream signaling. These results establish trafficking and release regulation without identifying an autonomous fusion, motor or receptor-binding activity.

BRWD3 participates in nuclear chromatin-associated regulation of RNA polymerase II transcription. In mouse preadipocytes, BRWD3 binds DDB1 through its WD-repeat region and recruits it to immediate-early gene promoters, supporting transcriptional activation. This mammalian mechanism connects chromatin association to recruitment of transcription-regulatory machinery.
TPR subunit of the APC/C that binds the coactivator C-termini and is essential for stable substrate recruitment and ubiquitination; needed for APC/C-CDH1 degradation of Ki-67 in neurons.

G protein-coupled receptor signaling through the seven-transmembrane region. Human VLGR1a and engineered C-terminal constructs show context-dependent Gs/Gq/Gi coupling; mouse beta-subunit assays support a Gi-dependent adenylate cyclase-inhibiting pathway. These experiments establish signaling capacity at the cell surface, while the coupling and activation state of intact VLGR1b in native sensory cells remain unresolved.

The ADGRV1 ectodomain supplies a structural constituent of transient stereocilia ankle links in developing cochlear hair bundles. Together with its membrane anchor and intracellular partners, it maintains cohesive bundle geometry and supports directional mechanotransduction. Mouse mutants show altered organization and reduced excitatory transduction currents in outer hair cells, while inner hair cells retain current amplitude at the examined stage. Calcium binding is directly measured for isolated repeat fragments, not all 35 repeats in the intact fiber.

The cytoplasmic C-terminal PDZ-binding motif docks ADGRV1 onto whirlin and PDZD7 in the USH2 protein network. Physical docking to this membrane receptor supports the retention of sensory-complex partners, complementing the observed loss of partners from the stereocilia base in mouse mutants. This anchoring contribution supports establishment of protein localization without assigning transport-motor activity.
