Human AHI1 self-associates and interacts with ciliary partners, but its native stoichiometry and exact physical contribution to the transition-zone assembly remain unresolved. Its loss can reduce cilium formation or alter the composition of cilia that remain, including ARL13B and neuronal receptor localization. Outcomes vary with the model and allele: in human hTERT-RPE1 cells, tested WD40-domain variants reduce basal-body enrichment without significantly changing cilium frequency or length, and fibroblasts from one patient with retinitis pigmentosa retain ciliation. Similar localization defects in the tested RP and Joubert variants do not explain their different clinical phenotypes.

Jouberin associates with beta-catenin and promotes its nuclear accumulation, potentiating an already stimulated canonical Wnt response. Ciliary sequestration can constrain this activity. The pathway effect is supported by cell-based interaction, localization and reporter experiments and by mouse kidney/cerebellar studies; its magnitude and developmental consequences depend on the tissue and signaling state.

In immune signaling, Jouberin recruits OTUD1 to TYK2, enabling OTUD1-dependent deubiquitination and stabilization of the kinase and thereby maintaining type I interferon responsiveness. The specific bridging dependency is demonstrated in mouse macrophages, with human-cell interaction and stability evidence supporting conservation. Jouberin acts as the adaptor, while OTUD1 performs the deubiquitination.

CEP85L associates with CDK5 and supports its localization at the proximal mother-centriole region. This organizational role connects centrosomal migration-associated proteins to the microtubule organization used during cortical neuronal migration. Human cultured-cell association and recruitment assays complement mouse cortical knockdown/rescue evidence. The observed CDK5 phosphorylation changes support an activation model, while the direct molecular route and any purified binary interface remain unresolved.
TOMM7 is a regulatory/structural small TOM subunit that modulates TOM complex assembly, stability, and oligomeric organization at the mitochondrial outer membrane.
TOMM7 links the TOM complex to mitochondrial quality control by enabling PINK1 stabilization/activation at TOM and downstream PINK1-Parkin mitophagy signaling after mitochondrial damage.

The human CERKLa product binds mRNA through its N-terminal region and associates with cytoplasmic compact messenger ribonucleoprotein particles. Direct binding was established with purified His-MBP-tagged Q49MI3-2 protein; cellular shuttling and granule associations supply context, while specific transcript selection, cap recognition and transport remain unresolved.

CERKL supports resistance to oxidative-stress-induced apoptosis. Human CERKLa reduces PARP cleavage in a 300 micromolar hydrogen-peroxide challenge over 12-24 hours; thioredoxin association and SIRT1 stability are reported regulatory connections. This protective role has no established intrinsic antioxidant or caspase-inhibitor molecular activity, and direct mRNA binding has not been shown to cause the survival effect.

BRAT1 occupies the INTS11 active site through its conserved C-terminal motif, inhibiting premature endoribonuclease activity while stabilizing an INTS9–INTS11 assembly intermediate. This assembly-factor activity supports formation and nuclear delivery of the Integrator cleavage module; BRAT1 is released during maturation rather than retained as a catalytic subunit of mature Integrator.

CCM2 organizes signaling partners through its noncatalytic adaptor activity. Its interactions with KRIT1 and MEKK3 support endothelial junctional organization and constrain MEKK3-KLF2/4 and RhoA-ROCK signaling. These coordinated interactions support the endothelial lumen-formation context; distinct SMURF1 localization experiments also connect CCM2 to regulation of RhoA abundance.

DYNC2I1 binds the TCTEX1D2–DYNLT1/DYNLT3 light-chain module and organizes the dynein-2 intermediate/light-chain assembly. Its complementary heavy-chain and DYNC2I2 contacts connect this scaffold to the two motor tails. Through these structural interfaces it contributes to minus-end-directed motor activity during retrograde IFT and the return of components used in cilium formation and maintenance. The ciliary base and the modeled tip-turnaround state are complementary locations in this transport cycle.

Within the same asymmetric dynein-2 assembly, the C-terminal WD-repeat propeller of DYNC2I1 contacts a DYNC2H1 heavy-chain tail and links the intermediate/light-chain block to that motor tail. This is a subunit-binding interface of the assembled motor.

DYNC2I1 associates with the complementary DYNC2I2 intermediate chain in the dynein-2 intermediate/light-chain block that connects the two heavy-chain tails. This records the partner-class interaction within the same assembly; complex capture does not by itself establish an isolated binary affinity.
Phosphorylates monoacylglycerols with ATP to produce lysophosphatidic acid in mitochondrial glycerolipid metabolism.
Phosphorylates diacylglycerol with ATP to produce phosphatidic acid in mitochondrial glycerolipid metabolism.
Supports TIM22 complex integrity and the import and assembly of multipass mitochondrial carrier proteins, independently of AGK lipid-kinase activity.

AP5Z1 supplies the zeta structural subunit of the AP-5 complex, which associates with SPG11 and SPG15 on endolysosomal membranes. Its stable assembly supports endosomal transport and lysosome organization. Native complexes associate with cargo receptors, while the molecular cargo-to-coat connection remains unresolved.

MED13L functions as a structural tether within the Mediator CDK8 kinase module (CKM), linking the CKM to core Mediator and regulating RNA polymerase II engagement at promoters through its intrinsically disordered regions.

Lysosomal-membrane escort/chaperone that targets and stabilizes the ABC transporter ABCD4 at the lysosomal membrane (translocating it from the ER), thereby enabling assembly of the lysosomal cobalamin export machinery.

As a subunit of the lysosomal LMBD1:ABCD4 complex (handing off to cytosolic MMACHC), participates in the export of cobalamin (vitamin B12) from the lysosomal lumen to the cytosol. LMBD1 has no intrinsic transport activity; the catalytic transport is performed by ABCD4. Loss of LMBD1 causes lysosomal cobalamin accumulation (cblF).

PDSS2 is a subunit of the human all-trans-decaprenyl-diphosphate synthase, a heterotetramer of two PDSS1 and two PDSS2 subunits that condenses (2E,6E)-farnesyl diphosphate with seven isopentenyl diphosphate units to form all-trans-decaprenyl diphosphate, the C50 polyprenyl side chain of ubiquinone-10. The catalytic activity is a property of the assembled complex; PDSS2 contributes to this activity (rather than enabling it alone) and, together with PDSS1, determines the isoprenoid chain length. The reaction is the first committed step of the ubiquinone side chain and occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.

Transfers mannose from Dol-P-Man to Man5GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol in an alpha-1,3 linkage at the lumenal face of the ER membrane, producing the Man6 intermediate during assembly of the lipid-linked precursor used for protein N-linked glycosylation.

Golgi-membrane solute carrier of the bile acid:sodium symporter fold that acts as a negative regulator of cellular calcium entry, a function conserved from its fungal orthologs Rch1p and CaRch1p. Loss of the protein increases Ca2+ influx into human cells. The transported species is unidentified - SLC10A7 transports neither bile acids nor steroid sulfates, and no other substrate has been tested, so the activity is asserted only at the level of transmembrane transporter activity rather than as a specific ion or solute transport. Through this activity SLC10A7 maintains the lumenal conditions the secretory pathway needs, which is why its loss reduces the number of heparan sulfate chains, perturbs N-glycosylation and blocks post-Golgi delivery of glycoproteins.

Catalyzes the first glucose addition to the dolichol-linked N-glycan precursor on the lumenal side of the ER membrane, using Dol-P-Glc to convert Man9GlcNAc2-PP-Dol into Glc1Man9GlcNAc2-PP-Dol. This substrate-producing catalytic step participates directly in LLO biosynthesis and the protein N-glycosylation pathway.

Adds the second mannose of the LLO precursor in an alpha-1,3 linkage: transfers mannose from GDP-mannose onto Man1GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol to form Man(alpha1,3)Man1GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol (EC 2.4.1.132), on the cytoplasmic face of the ER membrane during dolichol-linked oligosaccharide biosynthesis.

Adds the third mannose of the LLO precursor in an alpha-1,6 linkage: transfers mannose from GDP-mannose onto Man2GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol to complete the branched Man3GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol core (EC 2.4.1.257), on the cytoplasmic face of the ER membrane. This branched product is the substrate for ALG11.

Through LLO biosynthesis, ALG2 acts upstream of protein N-linked glycosylation, providing the mannosylated dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor that is ultimately transferred to asparagine residues of nascent glycoproteins.

Transfers the second glucose from dolichyl-phosphate-glucose to Glc1Man9GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol on the lumenal face of the ER membrane, forming the diglucosylated lipid-linked precursor for N-linked glycosylation.

ATP-dependent DNA translocase that binds branched DNA and catalyzes ATP-driven branch migration of stalled/regressed replication forks and Holliday junctions, remodeling branched replication/recombination intermediates; this activity is stimulated by the MHF1-MHF2 (CENPS-CENPX) histone-fold dimer and is required for replication fork protection and ICL repair.

Chromatin-binding scaffold that, together with FAAP24 and the MHF dimer, anchors the Fanconi anemia core complex to chromatin at stalled replication forks and interstrand crosslinks, enabling efficient DNA damage-induced monoubiquitination of the FANCD2-FANCI complex and activation of the FA pathway.

KEAP1 functions as the substrate-recognition component (substrate adaptor) of the CUL3-RBX1 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. It binds CUL3 via its BTB domain and recruits substrates (primarily NRF2) via its Kelch domain.

KEAP1 inhibits NRF2 (NFE2L2), a master transcription factor regulating antioxidant and cytoprotective gene expression. Under basal conditions, KEAP1 targets NRF2 for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, thereby inhibiting NRF2-mediated transcription.

Heme-dependent terminal hydroxylation of long-chain fatty acids, including myristate, palmitate, EPA and DHA, uses P450 reductase to deliver NADPH-derived electrons and produces omega-hydroxy fatty acids. The physiological retinal substrate balance remains unresolved.
Terminal hydroxylation of the C12 medium-chain substrate laurate produces 12-hydroxydodecanoate through the same heme/P450-reductase oxygenation system.

A secondary catalytic outcome is penultimate-carbon hydroxylation of EPA and DHA, giving 19-hydroxy-EPA and 21-hydroxy-DHA in recombinant assays. These smaller products were identified but not quantified separately; their physiological contribution and efficiency relative to terminal hydroxylation are not established.

GPI inositol acyltransferase that transfers an acyl group (usually palmitate) from acyl-CoA to the 2-OH of the inositol ring of glucosaminyl-phosphatidylinositol (GlcN-PI), forming 2-acyl-GlcN-PI (GlcN-(acyl)PI) during GPI-anchor biosynthesis in the ER membrane.

Catalytic subunit of GPI ethanolamine phosphate transferase III (GPI-ET-III); transfers the bridging ethanolamine phosphate from phosphatidylethanolamine onto the third mannose of the GPI intermediate (the protein-attachment EtNP), acting with the accessory subunit PIGF.

UBA5 is the E1-activating enzyme of the ufmylation cascade. As a homodimer it adenylates the C-terminal glycine of mature UFM1 with ATP and forms a high-energy thioester between that glycine and its catalytic Cys250 (releasing AMP), then transfers activated UFM1 to the E2 enzyme UFC1.

UBA5 homodimerization is an integral part of its catalytic mechanism. The two subunits cooperate in a trans-binding mechanism in which UFM1 contacts distinct sites on both protomers, and dimerization is required for UFM1 activation.

As an essential subunit of the MCTS1-DENR heterodimer (an eIF2D-like non-canonical factor), binds the 40S small ribosomal subunit and (via its PUA domain) mRNA/the cap region, recruits DENR, and delivers initiator tRNA to the 40S P-site in an eIF2-independent manner to drive translation reinitiation after short uORFs.
Binds the 40S small ribosomal subunit, the structural basis for the MCTS1-DENR complex's action in delivering tRNA and recycling post-termination 40S subunits.

At the melanosome limiting membrane, LRMDA bridges active RAB32-family GTPases to the Retriever subcomplex and thereby recruits a distinct Commander assembly during melanosome biogenesis. In human melanocytic cells, LRMDA loss perturbs PMEL processing, fibril and striation formation, organelle pH, melanosome maturation, and melanin content. Direct RAB32/RAB38-binding, localization, and Commander interaction experiments used a longer 226-residue human proteoform, whereas the reviewed target is 198 residues. The available sources do not establish their sequence relationship or functional equivalence.

LRMDA is required for normal vertebrate melanocyte differentiation. Human biallelic loss causes oculocutaneous albinism, while zebrafish orthologue knockdown reduces pigmentation and the apparent number of pigmented melanocytes; wild-type but not disease-mutant human C10orf11 rescues the morphant phenotype. This developmental role is retained separately from the later melanosome-organelle mechanism because their causal relationship remains unresolved.

DOLK phosphorylates dolichol using CTP to produce dolichyl monophosphate at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. This reaction completes de novo synthesis of the lipid carrier needed by several glycosylation pathways. The human protein has a cytoplasm-facing nucleotide-binding region; glycosyl-chain assembly is performed by downstream enzymes.

DHTKD1 supplies the ThDP-dependent E1 reaction of mitochondrial oxoadipate dehydrogenase: decarboxylation of 2-oxoadipate and reductive transfer of its glutaryl intermediate to the lipoyl group on DLST. This catalytic step participates in the convergent lysine and tryptophan catabolic pathway. DLST and DLD carry out the subsequent CoA transfer and lipoamide reoxidation; cofactor binding and homodimer formation are features of this one catalytic core.

MORC3 is a MORC-family GHKL/HATPase chromatin-associated ATPase. Its ATPase cycle works with its CW zinc-finger chromatin-reader module and SUMOylation to support repressive chromatin organization at foreign or deleterious DNA templates.
The MORC3 CW-type zinc finger recognizes methylated H3K4, connecting MORC3 to chromatin-reader activity in nuclear chromatin contexts.

MORC3 acts as a SUMO-regulated PML-body scaffold/adaptor that recruits and maintains nuclear restriction factors at PML bodies and incoming viral genomes, contributing to antiviral restriction and interferon-beta regulatory programs.

Associates with nuclear chromatin and replication factors to regulate DNA synthesis and G1/S cell-cycle progression. The direct molecular step controlling PCNA loading remains unresolved; ANKRD17 is a cyclin E/CDK2 substrate rather than a demonstrated kinase or clamp loader.

Coordinates RIG-I/MDA5 association with MAVS to promote antiviral signaling. ANKRD17 also binds NOD2 and supports bacterial innate responses, although the NOD mechanism and cell-context dependence are distinct from the demonstrated receptor–MAVS coordination.

TIMM50 is the inner-membrane TIM23 presequence receptor and gatekeeper that captures transit peptide-containing mitochondrial precursors on the intermembrane-space side, coordinates TIM23 channel gating, and supports import into the matrix or IMM sorting pathway.

UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase activity of the N-terminal domain, converting UDP-N-acetyl-alpha-D-glucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) and water to N-acetyl-D-mannosamine (ManNAc), UDP and a proton (a hydrolyzing 2-epimerase, EC 3.2.1.183); the first and rate-limiting step of sialic acid biosynthesis, allosterically feedback-inhibited by the pathway end product CMP-Neu5Ac.

N-acetylmannosamine kinase activity of the C-terminal ROK-family domain, phosphorylating N-acetyl-D-mannosamine (ManNAc) with ATP to ManNAc-6-phosphate (EC 2.7.1.60); the second committed step of sialic acid biosynthesis, requiring a divalent metal ion.

Gasdermin-B is an autoinhibited cytosolic protein that cytotoxic lymphocytes convert into a pore. Granzyme A, which must dimerize and engage an exosite on the GSDMB C-terminal domain, cleaves the interdomain linker at Lys244; the released N-terminal fragment binds inner-leaflet phosphoinositides of the target-cell plasma membrane and oligomerizes into a 27-subunit transmembrane pore, permeabilizing the cell and causing pyroptosis. This activity is gated by alternative splicing rather than by cleavage - granzyme A cleaves every isoform, but only isoforms translating exon 6 provide the belt elements the oligomer needs, so Q8TAX9-4 (GSDMB3) and Q8TAX9-6 (GSDMB4) are pore-competent while Q8TAX9-1, Q8TAX9-2 (GSDMB2), Q8TAX9-3 (GSDMB1) and Q8TAX9-5 are not, and the non-competent fragments inhibit the competent ones dominant-negatively. Cleavage by neutrophil elastase or caspases yields shorter, non-cytotoxic fragments and is inhibitory. Interferon-gamma raises GSDMB expression.

A second, membrane-target-switched activity of GSDMB that distinguishes it from the rest of the gasdermin family. Isoform Q8TAX9-1 does not recognize host inner-leaflet phosphoinositides and does not lyse the host cell; instead its granzyme-A-released N-terminal fragment binds cardiolipin, phosphatidylglycerol and lipid A - lipids of Gram-negative bacterial membranes - and forms pores directly in the bacterium, killing intracellular Shigella. The lipid requirement is strict enough that the fragment cannot insert into a plasma-membrane-mimetic bilayer unless cardiolipin is added. Shigella flexneri counters the pathway with the secreted E3 ligase IpaH7.8, which ubiquitinates GSDMB for proteasomal degradation and thereby shields the bacterium from natural killer cells; the same effector targets human but not mouse GSDMD.

Constitutive, ligand-independent G(s)-coupled receptor activity that sustains a high local cAMP concentration. An ECL2 beta hairpin occupies the orthosteric pocket and a sterol bound between TM6 and TM7 stabilises the active state, so GPR161 engages heterotrimeric G(s)/GNAS without any agonist and drives adenylate cyclase. In the resting primary cilium this keeps cAMP high and PKA active, sustaining conversion of GLI2 and GLI3 into repressors; pools of the receptor in the plasma membrane and the periciliary recycling endosome, where accessible sterol is more abundant than in the ciliary membrane, contribute to the same output. Mutating the sterol site ablates cAMP production and G protein recruitment but leaves repression of ciliary GLI2 intact, so this arm is the dispensable one for the ciliary brake.

A-kinase anchoring: tethering the type I PKA holoenzyme to the ciliary membrane. An amphipathic helix in the GPR161 cytoplasmic tail binds PKA type I regulatory subunits directly - the only such element in any GPCR - positioning the kinase where it phosphorylates GLI2 and GLI3 and drives their processing into repressors. This arm, not cAMP production, is what suppression of GLI2 accumulation at the ciliary tip requires: a receptor that cannot couple to G(s) still represses ciliary GLI2, whereas one carrying the helix-breaking L465P substitution does not. Hedgehog-induced export of GPR161 removes the anchored PKA from the cilium together with the receptor, which is how pathway activation lifts the brake.

GPI-specific phospholipase A2 that hydrolyzes the ester bond linking the unsaturated (sn-2) fatty acyl chain to the inositol phospholipid of the mature GPI anchor, generating a lyso-GPI intermediate - the first step of Golgi GPI fatty-acid remodeling (before PGAP2 reacylation with a saturated stearoyl chain).

In the nuclear trimeric PTF1 transcription-regulator complex, PTF1A forms the sequence-specific bHLH component with a class A E protein and RBPJ or RBPJL. The complex binds composite cis-regulatory sites and activates RNA polymerase II transcription. The RBPJ-containing PTF1-J and RBPJL-containing PTF1-L forms deploy this same molecular activity in different developmental and differentiated-cell contexts.

Ceramide synthase (sphingosine N-acyltransferase) that catalyzes the N-acylation step of de novo ceramide biosynthesis at the ER membrane, transferring a very-long/ultra-long-chain fatty acyl group from acyl-CoA onto a sphingoid base (sphinganine) to form (dihydro)ceramide, producing the ultra-long-chain ceramides required for the epidermal permeability barrier.

Phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate 5-kinase: PIKfyve converts PI3P to PI(3,5)P2 on early/late endosome and phagosome membranes, recruited by its PI3P-binding FYVE finger, as the kinase subunit of the PIKfyve-VAC14-FIG4 complex. The PI(3,5)P2 it produces drives endosome fission and endosome-to-TGN retrograde transport and endolysosome maturation. Established experimentally for the human protein.

Phosphatidylinositol 5-kinase: PIKfyve phosphorylates PI to PI5P and is the principal cellular source of PI5P, a lipid that regulates actin remodelling and VPS34-independent autophagosome biogenesis. Established experimentally in vitro and in human and rodent cells; the share made directly versus via PI(3,5)P2 dephosphorylation is unresolved.

Protein serine kinase (autophosphorylation): PIKfyve phosphorylates serines on itself, including the activation-loop Ser2053. This represses its lipid kinase activity and stimulates FIG4 lipid phosphatase activity, and FIG4 reverses the phosphorylation, forming a feedback loop that sets PI(3,5)P2 levels. Shown for human PIKfyve in the reconstituted complex; no trans substrates are established.

ASXL2 binds BAP1 through its DEUBAD regulatory region and stimulates BAP1-mediated deubiquitination of histone H2A at lysine 119. As a regulatory subunit of nuclear PR-DUB, it promotes substrate recognition and helps maintain the complex. BAP1 supplies the hydrolytic activity; ASXL2 supplies the activating interaction. Its PHD-dependent MBD5/6 interactions support complex assembly and chromatin association within this integrated regulatory role.
ASXL2 supports transcriptional coactivation through association with transcription factors and chromatin-associated partners. PPARgamma is an experimentally established receptor context.

Molecular adaptor/scaffold that assembles structure-specific endonucleases — SLX1, XPF-ERCC1 (ERCC4-ERCC1) and MUS81-EME1 — into a modular DNA-repair toolkit (the SLX-MUS complex), physically bridging the catalytic nucleases and positioning them on branched DNA intermediates during interstrand crosslink repair and homologous-recombination-mediated double-strand break repair. SLX4 itself is nuclease-dead and provides the docking platform, not the catalysis.

Regulatory (enzyme-activator) subunit that stimulates the nucleolytic activity of its bound structure-specific endonucleases, enhancing SLX1-, MUS81- and XPF-catalyzed cleavage of branched DNA; through the SLX1-SLX4 module it contributes to symmetrical Holliday-junction resolution (crossover-junction endodeoxyribonuclease activity of the complex), which SLX4 activates but does not itself catalyze.

NDUFA12 (B17.2) is a non-catalytic accessory (supernumerary) structural subunit of the peripheral (matrix) arm of mitochondrial Complex I, near the N/Q-module junction. It does not independently catalyze NADH oxidation, quinone reduction, or proton translocation; instead it provides a structural molecule activity that stabilizes the mature holoenzyme and thereby contributes to the complex-level NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase activity, supporting electron transfer from NADH to ubiquinone within a fully assembled, functional Complex I. The two complex-level assertions it does carry are split deliberately. Electron transport from NADH to ubiquinone (GO:0006120) is asserted as a direct involvement: NDUFA12 catalyzes no redox step itself - the chemistry belongs to the FMN- and Fe-S-cluster-bearing core subunits - but it is a structural subunit of the mature complex that performs the activity, which is the same structural contribution recorded by contributes_to GO:0008137, of which GO:0006120 is the process counterpart; GO:0006120 is also the Complex I-specific descendant of GO:0042775, which GOA already carries for NDUFA12 by IMP, so this direct involvement refines an existing experimental process assertion rather than introducing an unanchored one. Complex I assembly (GO:0032981) is deliberately NOT asserted, and this is what distinguishes NDUFA12 from the other accessory subunits: UniProt records that complex I assembly is unaffected in NDUFA12-knockout cells because the NDUFAF2 paralog substitutes at the same site, so NDUFA12 is dispensable for assembly per se while still being required for a fully mature, correctly functioning complex. The broader complex-level processes (proton translocation, proton motive force-driven ATP synthesis, aerobic respiration) are held as non-core, since those steps are performed by the antiporter-like membrane-arm subunits rather than by this peripheral-arm subunit.

Central structural subunit of the calmodulin- and spoke-associated complex that spans the bases of radial spokes 2 and 3 on axonemal doublet microtubules, binding the RS3 base subunits CFAP251 and CFAP61 and the spoke-base protein RSP3; it scaffolds radial spoke 3 assembly and relays regulatory signals from the spokes to the dynein arms, supporting normal beating of motile cilia and formation of the sperm flagellum. The accepted cilium movement annotation (Chlamydomonas, Tetrahymena and Trypanosoma evidence) is not listed separately because sperm flagellum assembly entails it: GO:0120316 is part_of flagellated sperm motility, which is_a cilium movement involved in cell motility, which is_a cilium movement. CFAP91 also extends into the base of radial spoke 2 (GO:0120341 radial spoke base 2, proposed in the radial spoke stalk MODIFY row); because in_complex holds a single term and radial spoke base terms are protein-containing complexes rather than locations, the RS3 base, where its scaffolding role in spoke assembly is documented, is recorded here.
AFAP1 functions as an actin-binding adaptor protein that links Src kinase and PKC to the actin cytoskeleton, regulating cytoskeletal dynamics and signal transduction.
AFAP1 acts as a molecular adaptor linking Src and PKC to cytoskeletal structures, facilitating signal transduction at sites of cell-matrix adhesion.
P-type ATPase-mediated polyamine transport supports cellular polyamine uptake, with cellular evidence favoring release from endosomal compartments into the cytosol.

B9D1 assembles with B9D2 and MKS1 within the MKS transition-zone complex. It contributes to formation and organization of the ciliary gate, including interdependent localization of gate proteins, thereby supporting ciliogenesis and the distinct protein composition of the cilium.

The cytosolic CDGSH domain binds a [2Fe-2S] cluster and can deliver it to an apo-protein acceptor. Recombinant human soluble NAF-1 establishes this molecular capacity; physiological acceptor identity and the extent of intact-cluster transfer in cells remain unresolved. The stable homodimer supports the cluster-bearing fold. Human localization experiments support the ER pool; endogenous mouse fractionation shows a predominantly mitochondrial pool enriched at the outer membrane and a smaller ER pool.

CISD2 binds the BCL2 BH4 region and supports BCL2-mediated restraint of Beclin 1-dependent autophagy at the ER. Direct domain/peptide binding and cellular complex and flux experiments establish complementary molecular and regulatory evidence. BH3-region interaction is also observed, while BCLXL site mapping and a universal direction of calcium regulation are not established.

DRC1 is an integral structural subunit of the axonemal nexin-dynein regulatory complex. Its conserved coiled-coil architecture with DRC2 and DRC4 provides the scaffold supporting other N-DRC subunits. Detailed scaffold contacts are resolved in the algal complex; human respiratory-axoneme models place the human homologues in the corresponding complex using cryo-EM density and predicted subcomplex structures. Human loss-of-function and ortholog experiments establish a requirement for N-DRC integrity, coordinated ciliary beating and sperm-axoneme organization. DRC1 loss causes later disorganization of initially formed mouse sperm axonemes, whereas respiratory cilia can retain the gross dynein-arm and radial-spoke arrangements. The scaffold role does not imply autonomous dynein motor activity, and the specific requirement for human IDAe docking remains unresolved.

Interphase TRAPPC12 contributes a TRAPP/TRAPPIII-associated subunit to complex-level RAB1 GEF trafficking between ER, ERGIC, and Golgi. This is the proteostasis-network TRAPP-component role and should be modeled as complex contribution rather than independent GEF activity or COPII coat assembly.

TACO1 binds the mitochondrial ribosome and acts as a translational activator of the mitochondrially-encoded MT-CO1 (COX1) mRNA, promoting mitochondrial translation of COX1 (and the other polyproline-rich subunit COX3) and thereby enabling assembly of respiratory chain complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). It functions in the mitochondrial matrix as the mitochondrial counterpart of EF-P/eIF5A, alleviating mitoribosome stalling at polyproline stretches.

C1GALT1 catalyses the committed step of mucin-type O-glycan elongation, transferring galactose from UDP-galactose in a beta-1,3 linkage onto the alpha-GalNAc that polypeptide GalNAc-transferases have attached to serine or threonine, to form the core 1 disaccharide (T antigen). It acts as a type II membrane enzyme in the Golgi, and its activity determines whether O-glycans remain as the truncated Tn antigen or are elaborated into core 1-derived extended structures. Attaining this active state requires co-translational folding by its dedicated ER chaperone Cosmc.

C1GALT1C1 (Cosmc) acts in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane as the dedicated co-translational folding chaperone for core 1 beta-1,3-galactosyltransferase (C1GALT1). It engages the nascent T-synthase polypeptide during translation, prevents its aggregation and enables it to reach a stable, active conformation. It has no catalytic activity of its own, and no client other than C1GALT1 is known, so its molecular function is exercised entirely in the service of core 1 mucin-type O-glycan biosynthesis. It is retained in the ER by a determinant within its own 18-residue transmembrane domain, and although it belongs to the GT31 glycosyltransferase family it has no transferase activity of its own. Its contribution to mucin-type O-glycan biosynthesis is exercised entirely through that client: it catalyses no step of the pathway and contributes neither structure nor cofactor activity to the glycosyl transfer itself, so no direct involvement in the process is asserted here even though the GOA process rows are accepted.

BOLA3 binds an Fe-S cluster in a GLRX5 heterocomplex and contributes to late mitochondrial Fe-S protein assembly. Reconstituted human complexes support cluster transfer to NFU1, while genetic evidence connects mitochondrial Bol function to lipoic acid synthase maturation, protein lipoylation and succinate dehydrogenase function. Complex formation and stability depend on biochemical conditions.

CHST14 catalyzes PAPS-dependent GalNAc 4-O-sulfation during dermatan sulfate proteoglycan biosynthesis. Human full-length recombinant enzyme assays establish the chemical specificity, and a purified human 61–376 construct cooperates with DS-epi1 to form extended sulfated iduronic-acid blocks. Endogenous human-cell microscopy supports a Golgi location; type-II membrane topology remains sequence-based. Cellular FRET/co-immunoprecipitation supports enzyme association, without assigning epimerase activity or a defined complex stoichiometry to CHST14.

Reductive decyanation of cyanocobalamin: cleaves the Co-CN bond of dietary cyanocob(III)alamin using FAD/FMN and NADPH to produce cob(II)alamin plus cyanide, generating the common intermediate for downstream active-cofactor synthesis (EC 1.16.1.6).

Glutathione-dependent dealkylation of alkylcobalamins: transfers the alkyl group (methyl from methylcobalamin, adenosyl from adenosylcobalamin) to the thiolate of glutathione by nucleophilic displacement, yielding cob(I)alamin and an S-alkylglutathione (EC 2.5.1.151), so incoming alkylcobalamins are converted to a common intermediate for both cofactor pools.

Cobalamin binding: binds incoming cob(III)alamin derivatives in the base-off configuration (dimethylbenzimidazole displaced from the cobalt), positioning the substrate for decyanation or dealkylation.
Glutathione binding: an arginine-rich pocket adjacent to the cobalamin site binds glutathione, the co-substrate required for the alkylcobalamin dealkylase reaction.
FAD binding: binds the flavin prosthetic group (FAD or FMN) required for NADPH-dependent reductive decyanation of cyanocobalamin.

CHMP2B performs membrane-deforming structural work in dynamic ESCRT-III assemblies. Human full-length WT/C-terminal-tag cellular tubulation and purified activated 1–154 protein after CHMP4B provide direct evidence, with tag, lipid, activation and geometry limits. The C-terminal MIM recruits VPS4 rather than supplying ATP hydrolysis. One structural activity contributes to endosomal sorting, abscission, cooperative nuclear-envelope reassembly and later stages of membrane repair; the evidence does not establish autonomous universal scission, direct phagophore closure, or a membrane-fenestration grommet. PMID:33832485 is condition-dependent countercontext: CHMP2B coats stiffen membranes under its tested conditions, so it is not used as affirmative evidence of bending. The 2021 full-length 1–222 numbering does not match current 213-aa Q9UQN3 and is not silently assigned to an isoform.

C2CD3 contributes structural organization at the distal centriole, positioning a radial luminal network that supports centriole elongation and recruitment or retention of distal ciliogenesis machinery. This integrates appendage maturation and primary-cilium formation; it does not assign C2CD3 to every ring node or hook, require loss of initial procentriole formation, or infer catalytic activity from recruited partners.
Binds chromatin and recruits MCM2–7 with ORC and CDC6 to assemble licensed pre-replicative complexes.

Restrains early-S-phase DNA synthesis by inhibiting CMG-dependent fork progression through its MCM-contacting domains. Purified human replication and Pol-epsilon controls support the inhibitory target; isolated CMG-alone unwinding and an inhibitory structure were not established, and altered helicase–polymerase coupling remains an explicit alternative.
Binds microtubules and associates with Hec1/NDC80 at mitotic kinetochores to support stable spindle attachment.

CIB2 binds intracellular regions of TMC channels and regulates the hair-cell mechanotransduction complex at stereocilia. Calcium and magnesium binding shape its conformation and partner interactions. Its auxiliary role includes control of channel localization and opening, with the exact coupling between metal occupancy and gating remaining unresolved.

CIB2 binds the small GTPase RHEB and participates in Raptor-associated signaling complexes that restrain mTORC1 activity. This provides a molecular interaction context for its contribution to lysosomal and retinal pigment epithelial homeostasis; the precise nucleotide-regulatory mechanism remains unresolved.

CIB2 binds calcium and magnesium through its EF-hand region, with metal-dependent changes in conformation and partner binding. Purified human protein supports both ligand classes, and human CIB2–TMC1 assays resolve magnesium occupancy and calcium-sensitive interactions. CIB2 also attenuates ATP-evoked cytosolic calcium responses in transfected cells; buffering versus effects on calcium-release machinery remains unresolved.

Non-catalytic light intermediate chain of cytoplasmic dynein-2. It binds and stabilises the heavy-chain (DYNC2H1) tails, which is required for dynein-2 integrity. It contributes to the minus-end-directed motor activity that drives retrograde IFT from the ciliary tip to the base.
Direct binding to the dynein-2 heavy-chain tail, forming the heavy-chain/LIC ("H1") subcomplex that the intermediate-chain/light-chain block then bridges into the asymmetric holoenzyme.

As part of the IFT motor, it is needed for intraciliary transport during cilium assembly and maintenance. Loss causes IFT-B accumulation in cilia, loss of cilium length control and abnormal Hedgehog signalling (ciliary SMO, GLI3 processing).

Selenocysteine-specific translation elongation factor: a GTP-dependent translational GTPase that binds selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec) and, together with SECISBP2/SECIS, delivers Sec-tRNA(Sec) to the ribosomal A-site to decode in-frame UGA codons as selenocysteine during selenoprotein synthesis.

GTP hydrolysis: eEFSec is an active translational GTPase (catalytic His96) whose ribosome-stimulated GTP hydrolysis drives the conformational change that releases Sec-tRNA(Sec) for accommodation and peptide-bond formation.

Selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec) binding: eEFSec uses all four of its domains to clasp tRNA(Sec) (acceptor-TYC arm by D1-D3, variable arm by the D3-D4 linker and D4), recognizing Sec-tRNA(Sec) with high affinity and stringent specificity.

EHMT1 catalyzes histone H3K9 methylation and cooperates with EHMT2/G9a in chromatin-mediated repression at selected gene loci. Conserved complex activity supports euchromatic H3K9 mono- and dimethylation. The complex also supports locus-specific DNA methylation through a contribution separable from histone methyltransferase activity in mouse embryonic stem cells.

EHMT1 also methylates the nonhistone substrate p53 at lysine 373. Purified human GLP assays and cellular coexpression support formation of the dimethylated product in this substrate context. This catalytic function is distinct from histone H3K9 methylation; its physiological effects depend on the cellular setting and are not assigned to every natural splice product.
FMN adenylyltransferase (FAD synthase) catalyzing the final step of FAD cofactor biosynthesis: adenylylation of FMN by ATP to form FAD plus diphosphate, requiring a divalent metal (Mg2+).

FAD diphosphatase / FAD hydrolase activity of the N-terminal molybdopterin-binding (MPTb) plus KH domains, cleaving FAD to FMN and AMP (and hydrolyzing other ADP-containing dinucleotides), providing control over the cellular FAD/FMN balance.
ATP binding at the C-terminal catalytic (PAPS-reductase) domain, providing the adenylyl donor for FMN adenylylation.
Magnesium ion binding required for FMN adenylyltransferase (FAD synthase) catalysis.

Fe(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxidative removal of methyl groups from adenosine residues in single-stranded RNA. The best-established cellular substrates are N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) at the transcription-start nucleotide of snRNAs and of capped mRNAs, and N6-methyladenosine in U6 snRNA; FTO also oxidizes internal m6A in mRNA in vitro, though whether mRNA m6A is a physiological substrate is disputed. An active-site loop restricts FTO to single-stranded substrates. Recent chemistry indicates the isolated enzyme stops at the hemiaminal N6-hydroxymethyladenosine, with release of formaldehyde occurring by slow non-enzymatic fragmentation, so the demethylated product may form off-enzyme.

Removal of N1-methyladenosine from tRNA. FTO acts on both nuclear and cytoplasmic tRNA pools; loss of FTO raises tRNA m1A in human knockdown cells and in Fto-knockout mouse cells, and the effect size is substantially larger than the changes seen for m6A or cap m6Am in polyadenylated RNA. Demethylation of tRNA m1A by FTO directly represses translation, making this the FTO activity with the clearest cellular consequence.

The catalytic identity of FTO, and the one molecular-function statement untouched by either current dispute. FTO couples oxidation of a methyl group on a single-stranded nucleic acid to decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate at a mononuclear Fe(II) centre, releasing succinate and CO2. This holds whether the enzymatic product is the demethylated base or the hemiaminal, and whatever the physiological substrate turns out to be. Homozygous loss of this activity in humans (R316Q) causes a lethal polymalformation syndrome.

At rod and cone photoreceptor terminals, LRIT3 acts presynaptically to organize the opposing depolarizing-bipolar-cell postsynaptic specialization. Mouse knockout, photoreceptor-specific rescue, endogenous tagging, and domain-deletion rescue show that LRIT3 is required for nyctalopin and TRPM1 assembly at bipolar-cell dendritic tips and for normal ON-pathway transmission; loss also alters downstream OFF- pathway responses. Human biallelic loss causes complete congenital stationary night blindness, connecting this conserved organizer mechanism to disease. The evidence supports a trans-synaptic organizing role but does not yet define a purified direct human binding interface or obligate stable complex.

Substrate receptor of the APC/C: the FZR1 WD40 propeller recognises D-box, KEN-box and ABBA degrons on cell-cycle proteins (mitotic cyclins, PLK1, AURKA, CDC20, SKP2, CDC6, geminin, TK1, RRM2, claspin, cyclin F, HECW2, SASS6) and, with APC10, forms the bipartite D-box receptor that presents them to the APC2-APC11 catalytic module for K11-linked polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.

APC/C coactivator: unphosphorylated FZR1 binds the APC/C through its C-box and IR tail from late anaphase through G1 (replacing CDC20 as CDK1 activity falls), repositioning the catalytic module and increasing APC/C affinity for its E2 enzymes, so that mitotic regulators are cleared, mitotic exit is completed and G1 is maintained; the interaction is blocked by cyclin A/CDK2 phosphorylation and EMI1, and promoted by CDC14B dephosphorylation, SIRT2 deacetylation and nuclear PTEN.

G2 DNA-damage checkpoint effector: after genotoxic stress in G2, CDC14B-mediated dephosphorylation re-engages FZR1 with the APC/C and the reactivated APC/C-Cdh1 degrades PLK1, stabilising claspin and WEE1 and preventing entry into mitosis; FZR1-directed turnover of RAD17 and claspin then contributes to checkpoint termination and recovery.
Outer-membrane receptor/adaptor that binds cytosolic DNM1L (DRP1) and recruits it to mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission sites.

Glucose-6-phosphatase activity: hydrolysis of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose and inorganic phosphate at the luminal face of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, via a covalent phosphohistidine (His167) intermediate, contributing to glucose 6-phosphate metabolism and intracellular glucose production in concert with the ER G6P transporter SLC37A4.

Stabilizes microtubule plus ends by limiting tubulin loss and growth. Ciliary partners recruit CEP104 and tune its TOG-dependent activity within the tip-protein network. Mapped TOG-function rescue links this microtubule-regulatory machinery to ciliary elongation, without establishing an initiating role.

Binds tubulin through its TOG domain. Human TOG-domain SEC-MALS and interface-mutant experiments establish soluble-tubulin binding; independent full-length human reconstitution demonstrates microtubule-end engagement. These construct-specific observations support the binding component of the ciliary-tip activity without assigning isolated-domain polymerization kinetics to full-length CEP104.

VPS37A is an ESCRT-I subunit that organizes endosomal MVB cargo sorting and, through its PUEV-containing phagophore-targeting function, coordinates recruitment of VPS28 and ESCRT-III machinery for autophagosome completion.

Non-catalytic complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) assembly factor that, as a core component of the MITRAC complex with COX14, associates with and stabilises newly synthesised MT-CO1 in an early COX1-COA3-COX14 assembly intermediate and coordinates its progression into complex IV assembly. As a MITRAC component it also couples MT-CO1 translation to assembly (positive regulation of mitochondrial translation). No molecular function is asserted because COA3 has no catalytic activity and only binding/chaperone-type molecular functions.

E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme of the Fanconi anemia pathway: accepts ubiquitin from the E1 activating enzyme via active-site Cys86 and, partnered with the cognate RING E3 ligase FANCL, catalyzes the DNA-damage-induced, site-specific monoubiquitination of FANCD2 (and FANCI) on chromatin, the central activating step of interstrand cross-link repair.

Membrane component of the MKS module of the ciliary transition zone; with other core MKS membrane proteins it is mutually required for MKS-module localization at the TZ, contributing to the ciliary diffusion barrier.

Required for primary cilium assembly, including apical docking of the centrosome/basal body in polarized epithelial cells; the resulting cilium supports Hedgehog and other cilium-dependent signalling.

Functions as a RING-type E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase that recognizes cytosolic intracellular bacteria (e.g. Salmonella) via its leucine-rich repeats and generates the bacteria-associated polyubiquitin signal via its RING domain, marking the bacteria for antibacterial autophagy (xenophagy) and lysosomal degradation.

Acts as a TSG101-specific E3 ligase (Tal) that monoubiquitinates the ESCRT-I component TSG101, inactivating its ability to sort endocytic (EGFR) and exocytic (HIV-1) cargo, thereby regulating receptor endocytosis and retroviral budding.

Catalyzes the terminal step of the mitochondrial 4-hydroxyproline degradation pathway, the retro-aldol cleavage of 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate (HOG) into glyoxylate and pyruvate, via a Schiff-base (type I aldolase) mechanism using Lys196 as the catalytic nucleophile.

SLC25A46 acts as an outer-mitochondrial-membrane scaffold/adaptor that regulates mitochondrial membrane dynamics in a pro-fission (anti-fusion) manner. Although a member of the SLC25 mitochondrial carrier family, it lacks the conserved carrier pore residues and does not function as a metabolite transporter; instead it physically bridges the outer-membrane fusion GTPases (MFN2, OPA1) and the inner membrane MICOS complex (MIC60/IMMT, MIC19). Loss of SLC25A46 causes mitochondrial hyperfusion and its overexpression causes fragmentation, and this activity is essential for normal mitochondrial network morphology.

Through its interactions with the MICOS complex and, via the ER membrane protein complex (EMC), with ER-mitochondria contact sites, SLC25A46 organizes cristae architecture and helps distribute mitochondrial phospholipids. It functions upstream of MICOS and is required for maintaining normal cristae; its loss disrupts MICOS, shortens cristae, alters mitochondrial phospholipid composition, and secondarily impairs respiration.

Cobalamin-trafficking branch-point/adaptor activity: acting downstream of MMACHC (cblC) in the cytosol, MMADHC receives the common cob(II)alamin intermediate and partitions it between the cytosolic methylcobalamin (MeCbl) branch supplying methionine synthase (MTR) and the mitochondrial adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl) branch supplying methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMUT).

4-hydroxybenzoate polyprenyltransferase (PHB:polyprenyltransferase, EC 2.5.1.39): catalyzes the Mg2+-dependent transfer of an all-trans polyprenyl tail (decaprenyl in humans) from all-trans-polyprenyl diphosphate onto 4-hydroxybenzoate, producing a 4-hydroxy-3-(all-trans-polyprenyl)benzoate. This is the committed prenylation step of coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis, carried out as a multi-pass protein of the mitochondrial inner membrane.
CCDC39 and CCDC40 form an extended axonemal scaffold that organizes the 96-nm repeat and positions inner dynein-arm and associated regulatory structures, enabling effective motile-cilium beating.

Binds membrane phospholipids and lipophilic aromatic-isoprene CoQ-pathway intermediates (including 5-demethoxyubiquinone) within a hydrophobic TetR/FadR-like pocket, as a non-catalytic accessory subunit of the mitochondrial CoQ biosynthetic complex (CoQ synthome).

Selectively binds aromatic-isoprene CoQ intermediates and presents the 5-demethoxyubiquinone substrate directly to the hydroxylase COQ7, thereby activating the penultimate C6-hydroxylation step of coenzyme Q biosynthesis (COQ9 increases COQ7 catalytic efficiency but is itself non-catalytic).

CFAP65 is a structural component at the base of the C2a projection of the axonemal central apparatus. Together with CFAP70 and MYCBPAP it holds the projection together on the C2 microtubule, which stabilizes the central apparatus and the axoneme of motile cilia and flagella. This structural role is essential for assembling an organized sperm axoneme and for sperm motility, and it supports ependymal ciliary flow. Respiratory cilia tolerate its loss better.

ER-membrane RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates the activated inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (ITPR1/IP3R) to drive its ERAD-mediated degradation, acting as the catalytic partner of the ERLIN1/ERLIN2 complex to control IP3R abundance and ER calcium signaling.

ER-membrane ubiquitin ligase that builds K48-linked polyubiquitin chains on Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3) to promote its proteasomal degradation, negatively regulating TLR3-triggered innate immune signaling.
Hydrolyze GTP under stimulating conditions; strong autonomous intrinsic turnover is not established.
Promote nucleotide exchange on ARL3, with ARL2BP/BART enhancing exchange and active-state maintenance under the tested conditions.
Bind tubulin and contribute to ciliary membrane–axoneme organization during primary-cilium assembly and maintenance.

Supports adipocyte lipid turnover and mitochondrial utilization of long-chain fatty acids at lipid droplet–mitochondrial contact regions. C19orf12 associates with mitochondrial import machinery in human adipocyte models; the molecular activity coupling this association to fatty-acid metabolism remains unresolved.
Catalyzes pseudouridine formation at positions 38 and 39 in tRNA anticodon loops as a homodimeric stand-alone enzyme
Redistributes phospholipids between the leaflets of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane; calcium and membrane lipid composition modulate this scrambling activity.

Catalyzes ATP-dependent attachment of L-aspartate to mitochondrial tRNA(Asp), supplying charged tRNA for mitochondrial protein synthesis. The active enzyme is homodimeric; its matrix placement reflects the established mitochondrial translation context rather than a compartment-resolved measurement of charging flux.

RING-type E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase that is recruited via its C-terminal WD40 domain to RPA-coated single-stranded DNA at stalled replication forks and sites of DNA damage, where (following ATM/ATR phosphorylation) it polyubiquitinates the RPA complex and RAD51 to drive their VCP/p97-dependent turnover and timely removal, enabling homologous recombination and interstrand crosslink repair to progress.

DNA-binding subunit of the FANCI-FANCD2 (ID2) complex: binds duplex DNA (preferring branched replication-fork/junction structures) and, upon FANCL/UBE2T-catalyzed monoubiquitination on Lys523, converts the complex into a closed sliding clamp that encircles DNA at stalled forks and interstrand crosslinks, coordinating downstream ICL repair; FANCI is itself required to promote FANCD2 monoubiquitination that activates the pathway.

CFAP44 is a non-catalytic structural subunit of the axonemal tether/tether-head complex, built with CFAP43. Its N-terminal beta-propellers engage the motor domain of inner dynein arm f, and its C-terminal helices dock onto the doublet microtubule. This anchors and stabilizes the I1 dynein motor and supports coordinated inner-arm activity during beating. In the sperm flagellum this structural contribution is needed for an organized axoneme, central pair and peri-axonemal structures, and for progressive motility.

UFM1-specific cysteine (thiol-dependent) protease that removes UFM1 from conjugated substrates (deUFMylation), most prominently RPL26/uL24 on ER-associated 60S ribosomal subunits, and also processes pro-UFM1; catalytic residue Cys302.

deUFMylation of RPL26/uL24 releases the UFM1 E3 ligase from UFMylated 60S subunits, enabling recycling of 60S ribosomal subunits after ribosome-associated quality control of ribosomes that stall during co-translational ER translocation.
As the distal subunit of the IFT-A peripheral subcomplex, TTC21B is required for retrograde intraflagellar transport, returning IFT-A, IFT-B and ciliary GPCRs from the ciliary tip.
Through IFT-A-mediated trafficking, TTC21B contributes to correct ciliary localization of membrane proteins such as Smoothened and GPR161.

Assembly chaperone for AP-type membrane coat adaptor complexes. AAGAB binds folded but unassembled adaptor subunits - the small sigma subunits via its N-terminal type I pseudoGTPase domain, and the AP-1 gamma and AP-2 alpha subunits via a shared surface on its C-terminal dimerisation domain - protecting them from degradation and enforcing an ordered assembly sequence. It is required for assembly of AP-1, AP-2 and AP-4, but specifically not AP-3. AAGAB is a homodimer that becomes monomeric on client binding, and it leaves before the tetramer is finished: for AP-2 the alpha/sigma2 intermediate is handed off to CCDC32. This is assembly chaperoning, not protein folding - the clients are already folded. The molecular_function term below is a partial stand-in on two counts: it is AP-2-specific while the client set spans AP-1, AP-2 and AP-4, and it names the assembled complex while AAGAB in fact binds the free subunits. The accurate term would be the subunit-binding term filed under proposed_new_terms.

CHMP6 is a myristoylated Vps20/ESCRT-III component that links ESCRT-II to ESCRT-III on endosomal membranes. By binding ESCRT-II, CHMP4-family ESCRT-III subunits, and VPS4 through its MIM2 element, CHMP6 supports ESCRT-III assembly/remodeling, MVB formation and sorting of ubiquitinated/endocytosed membrane cargo, and downstream late-endosome-to-lysosome degradation of cargo such as EGFR and ferroportin.
Second step of coenzyme A biosynthesis: cytosolic ATP-preferring ligation of L-cysteine to (R)-4'-phosphopantothenate to form N-[(R)-4-phosphopantothenoyl]-L-cysteine.
Assembly into an obligate catalytic homodimer, with the active site formed at the dimer interface, required for ligase activity.

Pore-forming activity of the caspase-cleaved N-terminal fragment (GSDMD-NT). After inflammatory-caspase cleavage releases GSDMD-NT from autoinhibition, the fragment oligomerizes in the plasma membrane and forms large ring-shaped transmembrane pores (10-15 nm inner diameter). These non-selective wide pores conduct mature IL-1 family cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and drive pyroptotic, lytic cell death, providing host defense against infection and danger signals.

Acidic-phospholipid binding that targets GSDMD-NT to the cytoplasmic leaflet of membranes. GSDMD-NT selectively binds inner-leaflet phosphoinositides (including phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate), phosphatidylserine and the bacterial/mitochondrial lipid cardiolipin, but not the outer-leaflet lipids phosphatidylcholine or phosphatidylethanolamine. This specificity localizes pore formation to the inner leaflet and underlies both pyroptosis of the host cell and the direct bactericidal activity of secreted GSDMD-NT.

Innate antibacterial effector activity. GSDMD-NT released from pyroptotic cells, and GSDMD-NT acting at intracellular membranes, forms pores that kill both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, contributing to defense against bacterial infection. This effector role is a direct consequence of the same pore-forming/lipid-binding activities and their preference for bacterial (cardiolipin-rich) membranes.

GPI inositol-deacylase that hydrolyzes and removes the acyl chain linked to the 2-OH of the inositol ring of the GPI anchor of a GPI-anchored protein in the ER, the first step of post-attachment GPI-anchor remodeling.

The inositol-deacylation performed by PGAP1 is required for efficient ER-to-Golgi transport of GPI-anchored proteins, enabling recognition of the remodeled anchor by p24-family cargo receptors that load GPI-APs into COPII vesicles.

TRAPPC11 contributes a metazoan TRAPP/TRAPPIII-associated subunit needed for stable TRAPP architecture, early secretory pathway traffic between ER, ERGIC, and Golgi, and autophagosome maturation/sealing in variant-sensitive mammalian cell contexts. It should be modeled as contributing to complex-level TRAPP/RAB1 GEF activity and TRAPP stability rather than independently enabling GEF activity or COPII coat assembly.

Structural transmembrane component of the MKS module at the ciliary transition zone; required for TZ localization of neighbouring MKS-module proteins (TMEM67, MKS1) and hence for building the MKS part of the transition zone.
As part of the TZ diffusion barrier, maintains ciliary membrane composition and supports (tissue-specific) cilium assembly, which in turn is required for Smoothened-dependent Hedgehog signalling.
BTB substrate receptor of CRL3-ARMC5 that ubiquitinates excess and defective RNA polymerase II, and full-length SREBF, for proteasomal degradation.
DCAF17 associates with cullin-containing DDB1 assemblies as a component of CUL4 complexes.

Hydrolyzes GTP during the SBDS-assisted release of eIF6 from late cytosolic 60S ribosomal subunits. Human-protein biochemistry establishes ribosome-stimulated GTP hydrolysis and factor release, while structures with human EFL1 and SBDS on Dictyostelium subunits support a conformational mechanism in which accommodated EFL1 competes with eIF6 for an overlapping ribosomal site. The exact temporal relationship between hydrolysis and eIF6 displacement remains unresolved by these experiments.

Supports cilium assembly at the ciliary base by promoting recruitment of selected CPLANE components and peripheral IFT-A subunits. Mouse transition-zone localization and Xenopus basal-body recruitment/rescue experiments complement human fibroblast ciliogenesis evidence. The molecular activity coupling CPLANE1 interactions to recruitment remains unresolved.

NADPH-dependent polyprenal reductase acting in the terminal steps of de novo dolichol biosynthesis, reducing the alpha-isoprene unit of di-trans,poly-cis-polyprenal to the corresponding dolichal en route to dolichol
Supplies dolichol/dolichol-phosphate, the lipid carrier used to build the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor, thereby enabling protein N-linked glycosylation
ATAD1 is an ATP-dependent membrane protein dislocase that extracts mistargeted tail-anchored proteins from the mitochondrial outer membrane. This is the main conserved molecular role of the protein.
ATAD1 hydrolyzes ATP through its AAA+ ATPase domain to power extraction of membrane protein substrates and disassembly of selected protein complexes.

Sequence-specific binding, via its RRM domains, of GU-rich/UGG-containing cis-elements in intronic and exonic regions of target pre-mRNAs (e.g. FGFR2 ISE/ISS-3), through which ESRP1 enhances or silences alternative exons in a position-dependent manner in the nucleoplasm of epithelial cells. Established experimentally for human ESRP1 (endogenous-protein pulldown, knockdown/rescue, genome-wide splicing profiling).
Binding of intronic auxiliary splicing elements in pre-mRNA, the binding mode underlying exon inclusion when ESRP1 binds downstream of a regulated exon.

LYR-motif subunit of the MALSU1-AltMIEF1-mt-ACP anti-association module, which binds late-stage mitoribosomal large-subunit assembly intermediates in the mitochondrial matrix next to uL14m. Through its LYR motif, AltMIEF1 docks the 4'-phosphopantetheine arm of mt-ACP (NDUFAB1), and the module sterically prevents premature joining of the small subunit until mt-LSU maturation is complete. Loss of AltMIEF1 impairs mt-LSU assembly and lowers the rate of mitochondrial translation.

Catalytic subunit of the GPI ethanolamine phosphate transferase II complex that transfers ethanolamine phosphate (from phosphatidylethanolamine) onto the second mannose of the GPI intermediate during GPI-anchor biosynthesis in the ER, acting together with the stabilizing subunit PIGF.

NSUN2 is the human Trm4 orthologue and the principal RNA m5C writer of the cell. Using SAM and a motif VI catalytic cysteine, it methylates C34 of intron-containing pre-tRNA-Leu(CAA) and C47-C50 in the variable loop of many cytoplasmic tRNAs, and the same enzyme, imported into the mitochondrial matrix, makes m5C at positions 48-50 of several mitochondrial tRNAs. The activity has been reconstituted in vitro with purified protein and mapped product positions, and the corresponding modifications are lost in NSUN2-null mouse tissue, NSUN2 knockout human cells and cells from patients with biallelic NSUN2 variants. The methylation stabilises tRNA against stress-induced endonucleolytic cleavage.

Substrate recognition by NSUN2 extends beyond tRNA. It is the only enzyme that methylates C69 of the vault RNA VTRNA1.1, and that single modification determines how VTRNA1.1 is processed into small vault RNAs, so NSUN2 binding and methylation of a structured non-coding RNA has a defined downstream consequence. NSUN2 is also recovered in mRNA interactome capture and recognises a specific structural motif in exosome-enriched transcripts. This binding function is listed separately from the catalytic function because in several of these contexts the binding, rather than the chemistry, is what has been directly demonstrated.

Mitochondrial inner-membrane tetratricopeptide-repeat assembly/maintenance factor for respiratory Complex III (cytochrome bc1); required for turnover of UQCRFS1 (Rieske) N-terminal fragments to preserve Complex III integrity. Non-catalytic scaffold protein.
DNAAF5 associates with dynein intermediate-chain and early assembly machinery to support cytoplasmic preassembly of outer and inner axonemal dynein arms.

Catalytic subunit of the MRPP1-MRPP2 (TRMT10C-HSD17B10) tRNA methyltransferase subcomplex, transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to N1 of purine 9 (m1G9 and m1A9) in mitochondrial tRNAs, which is important for correct folding of the non-canonical mitochondrial tRNAs.
Catalytic subunit for m1G9 formation in mitochondrial tRNAs, the guanosine counterpart of the same position-9 N1-methylation reaction.

Essential non-catalytic subunit of proteinaceous mitochondrial RNase P (with HSD17B10 and the PRORP nuclease) that binds pre-tRNA and enables 5'-end cleavage of tRNAs from polycistronic mitochondrial transcripts; the MRPP1-MRPP2 subcomplex then retains the tRNA to support ELAC2 3'-end processing and CCA addition.

Alpha-1,6-mannosyltransferase (GPI-MT-II) that transfers the second mannose from dolichyl-phosphate-mannose (Dol-P-Man) onto the Man1-GlcN-(acyl)PI GPI intermediate, forming the alpha-1,6 mannosyl linkage, during GPI-anchor biosynthesis on the lumenal face of the ER membrane.

Acts as a dedicated chaperone/assembly factor for succinate dehydrogenase (respiratory Complex II): binds the flavoprotein subunit SDHA and, together with a dicarboxylate cofactor, remodels and orients its flavin and capping domains to license covalent attachment of FAD (flavinylation) to SDHA. This maturation of SDHA is required for assembly of a functional Complex II. SDHAF2 has no catalytic activity of its own and is not a subunit of the mature enzyme.

TMEM70 acts as a scaffold/adaptor protein that brings together subunit c molecules during c8-ring assembly. It forms oligomeric complexes that interact with subunit c and promote its membrane insertion and oligomerization. UniProt describes TMEM70 as a "Scaffold protein that participates in the c-ring assembly of mitochondrial ATP synthase" (PMID:32275929, PMID:31652072, PMID:33359711).

TMEM70 directly binds to ATP synthase subunit c (ATP5MC1/ATP5MC3) during the assembly process. This interaction is essential for facilitating c-ring formation and membrane insertion. Multiple studies have demonstrated direct interaction between TMEM70 and subunit c using immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry (PMID:31652072, PMID:33359711, PMID:33753518).

tRNA(His) guanylyltransferase: catalyzes the post-transcriptional 3'-5' addition of a single guanylate (G-1) to the 5' end of tRNA(His) after RNase P cleavage, using GTP as the guanylyl donor, ATP to activate the monophosphorylated tRNA 5' end, and two catalytic Mg2+ ions. The active enzyme is a homotetramer. This ancestral activity is required for tRNA(His) identity and translational fidelity.

Mitofusin guanine-nucleotide exchange factor: at the mitochondrial outer membrane, THG1L/IHG-1 binds MFN1 and MFN2 and enhances MFN2 GTP loading, acting as a GEF that promotes mitochondrial fusion and protects cells from oxidative-stress-induced apoptosis. This moonlighting function is disease-relevant (the SCAR28 p.Val55Ala variant impairs mitochondrial fusion).

CCDC40 contributes the coiled-coil structural scaffold of the motile axoneme with CCDC39, organizing the 96-nm repeat and the docking or retention of inner dynein-arm and regulatory components. This physical organization supports effective ciliary movement. Human structures and mutant respiratory epithelia establish the target role; mouse localization and algal structural guidance are complementary rather than interchangeable evidence. The scaffold is not itself a dynein motor or an established active transporter.

CFAP69 is required during spermiogenesis for building a normal sperm flagellum. It is concentrated in the flagellar midpiece of human sperm, and without it all flagellar components, including the axoneme, outer dense fibres and mitochondrial sheath, are disorganized, SPEF2 is lost from the flagellum and sperm are immotile. Its molecular activity is not defined. The armadillo-repeat fold and the Tetrahymena data, in which Cfap69 forms part of the SPEF2-containing C1b central-apparatus projection, suggest a structural or scaffolding role, but this has not been shown for the mammalian protein.

Component of the MKS/tectonic transition-zone complex. It is required for MKS1 and TMEM67 to localize to the transition zone, for tissue-specific ciliogenesis, and for the diffusion barrier that keeps membrane proteins in or out of the cilium. No specific molecular activity has been defined.

Molecular adaptor/scaffold that physically bridges BRCA1 (via its N-terminal coiled-coil) and BRCA2 (via its C-terminal WD40 β-propeller), forming the BRCA1-PALB2-BRCA2 complex that localizes and stabilizes BRCA2 at damaged chromatin and promotes RAD51 loading for homologous recombination.

DNA-binding activity of the intrinsically disordered N-terminal domain (preference D-loop > dsDNA > ssDNA) that stimulates RAD51-mediated strand invasion and D-loop formation, promoting homologous recombination; the domain also has intrinsic strand-exchange activity and cooperates with RAD51AP1. The MF term is GO:0000217 DNA secondary structure binding rather than the bare GO:0003677 DNA binding, because the quoted evidence is a documented structural preference (D-loop over duplex over single-stranded) rather than sequence-independent DNA binding - the same reasoning applied to FANCI in this cohort.

CTC1 contacts single-stranded DNA within CST and organizes the template with polymerase alpha–primase for telomeric C-strand synthesis. DNA substrate sequestration limits telomerase initiation. CTC1-containing CST also enhances new origin firing during recovery from replication stress; this regulatory effect is distinct from the DNA-binding cofactor contribution and does not assign polymerase or primase chemistry to CTC1.

Binds and stabilizes microtubule ends and damaged lattices, limiting catastrophe and depolymerization and promoting pauses followed by regrowth. Reconstitution establishes luminal action of CSPP-L, while cellular experiments support control of microtubule-end dynamics. CSPP-L also localizes to primary cilia in human cells; the purified singlet-microtubule assays establish activity without directly reconstituting human axonemes.

Promotes cytokinesis through recruitment or organization of MyoGEF at the central spindle in the tested human CSPP-L context. Depletion disrupts MyoGEF localization and produces furrow regression despite largely preserved central-spindle formation. This role does not establish CSPP1 as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor or show that its luminal stabilization activity causes MyoGEF recruitment.

NADPH-dependent reduction of long-chain (C16/C18) fatty acyl-CoA to the corresponding primary fatty alcohol (EC 1.2.1.84), the committed step that supplies fatty alcohols for ether-lipid biosynthesis.
As the rate-limiting enzyme supplying fatty alcohols, FAR1 drives ether-lipid (plasmalogen) biosynthesis, acting at the peroxisomal membrane; its product is used by AGPS to form the ether bond.

Multivalent PDZ-domain protein-macromolecule adaptor of the stereocilia ankle-link (USH2) complex. Acting at the ankle region just above the tapered base of developing cochlear hair-cell stereocilia, PDZD7 binds the short cytoplasmic PDZ-binding motifs of the transmembrane adhesion receptors usherin (USH2A, via PDZ1/PDZ2) and ADGRV1 (via PDZ2), heterodimerizes with the paralogous scaffold whirlin (whirlin PDZ1-PDZD7 PDZ2) to bridge the two receptors into one quaternary complex, and homodimerizes through PDZ2, providing the multivalency that condenses the complex at this membrane subdomain. By recruiting, positioning and retaining USH2A, ADGRV1 and whirlin at the ankle region during the first postnatal window of hair-bundle maturation, this adaptor activity organizes stereocilium architecture and cohesion; its loss splays and disorganizes hair bundles, eliminates short-row stereocilia, reduces mechanotransduction and abolishes hearing (mouse knockouts; human DFNB57).

Facilitates BBSome assembly through association with BBS proteins and regulation of the BBS-chaperonin machinery. The primary process is chaperone-mediated BBSome assembly; BBS10 also regulates formation of the machinery that performs it, as shown by opposing knockdown and overexpression effects on BBS6-CCT association. The molecular step performed by BBS10 within this machinery remains unresolved.

Pseudosubstrate inhibition of protein kinase A. ARHGAP36's N-terminal arginine-rich region is a pseudosubstrate motif that occupies the acidic active-site cleft of the PKA catalytic subunit, the same site the regulatory subunits and the PKI family use, and blocks catalysis with a potency the discovering laboratory measured as comparable to PKI in the same assay. The binding requires R153 and R154 on ARHGAP36 and is reciprocally disrupted by mutating E127, E170 and E230 in the PKAC cleft. The interaction has been shown by coimmunoprecipitation of the endogenous kinase, by FRET with acceptor photobleaching, and by isothermal titration calorimetry on a synthesised 25-residue peptide, and the inhibition by an in vitro kinase assay on recombinant PKAC and by a genetically encoded FRET biosensor in cells. A second, separable activity of the same region routes PKAC into a ubiquitin-dependent lysosomal degradation pathway, which full-length PKI does not do, so ARHGAP36 both blocks and depletes the kinase. The activity takes place at the plasma membrane, where the protein concentrates and from which it recruits cytosolic PKAC onto endosomal and lysosomal vesicles. Because PKA generates the GLI repressor forms, the downstream consequence is a shift of the GLI pool towards full-length activator and a rise in Hedgehog target gene expression that needs neither ligand nor Smoothened.

A second, spatially distinct role at the centrosome, currently characterised only in mouse. A pool of ARHGAP36 is held at the mother centriole by Patched1 and keeps centrosomal PKA activity low; activation of the Shh pathway displaces it, centrosomal PKA accumulates, Inversin is phosphorylated, and Smoothened translocates into the cilium. Knockdown raises both PKAc and phosphorylated Inversin, so the sign of the relationship is established by loss of function and not only by overexpression. This places ARHGAP36 inside the ciliary trafficking step of the pathway as well as downstream of it, and it is the one context in which ARHGAP36 restrains rather than promotes a Hedgehog step. The detailed centrosomal evidence comes from mouse cells and provides an ortholog-based mechanistic model for the human protein.

Mitochondrial NAD(+) kinase activity - NADK2 phosphorylates NAD(+) using ATP (or inorganic polyphosphate in vitro) to yield NADP(+), generating the mitochondrial NADP(H) pool. This is the sole known route of mitochondrial NADP(+) biosynthesis in human cells.
ATP binding - NADK2 binds ATP as the phosphoryl donor for the NAD kinase reaction (Km for ATP 1.7 mM), and can alternatively use inorganic polyphosphate.

Structural component of the mother-centriole distal appendage blades that acts downstream of CEP83 to recruit FBF1 and CEP164 (and LRRC45), enabling membrane docking of the mother centriole and initiation of primary cilium assembly.

Extended structural element bound along the axonemal doublet microtubule that interconnects inner dynein arms with regulatory complexes and targets or stabilizes the docking of a subset of single-headed inner dynein arms (dyneins g and d in Chlamydomonas) in the 96-nm repeat, supporting normal ciliary and sperm flagellar beating; the long isoform is required in sperm flagella.

Transmembrane dynein activating adaptor of the outer nuclear membrane: the N-terminal EF-hand pair binds the dynein light intermediate chain and, with the coiled coil, assembles dynein-dynactin-LIS1 into processive motors that pull on telomere attachment sites to drive meiotic telomere clustering and homologue pairing.

KASH subunit of the meiotic LINC complex: the C-terminal KASH peptide binds SUN1 (and SUN2) SUN-domain trimers in the perinuclear space, forming SUN-KASH 6:6 assemblies that anchor KASH5 and its dynein cargo at telomere attachment sites, transmitting microtubule force across the nuclear envelope to telomeres.

LOXHD1 acts at the stereociliary membrane of mature auditory hair cells to maintain the mechanotransduction apparatus required for detection of sound. Human genetics establishes its requirement for hearing, and mouse hair-cell studies show that Loxhd1 preserves mechanotransduction currents and maintains TMC1 near the lower tip-link force-reception site. This is represented as a conserved biological role without assigning a molecular function: no catalytic activity or direct binding mechanism has been demonstrated. Heterologous co-immunoprecipitation supports selective association with TMC1, not membership in a defined stable complex. The responsible human cochlear isoform is unknown, so the function is not restricted to any one of Q8IVV2-1, Q8IVV2-3, Q8IVV2-4, or Q8IVV2-5.

Lysosomal-membrane acetyl-CoA:alpha-glucosaminide N-acetyltransferase: transfers an acetyl group from cytosolic acetyl-CoA onto the free amino group of the terminal non-reducing alpha-glucosamine residue of intralysosomal heparan sulfate, producing N-acetyl-alpha-glucosamine. This transmembrane acetylation is an obligatory step in the stepwise lysosomal catabolism of heparan sulfate: it converts the terminal residue into a substrate for the exoglycosidase NAGLU so degradation can continue. The enzyme is a polytopic (11-TM) lysosomal membrane protein and is the only membrane-bound, transferase member of the heparan sulfate degradation pathway.

DZIP1L binds SEPTIN2 through its N-terminal region and occupies centriolar, basal-body and ciliary transition-zone compartments. Endogenous human association and altered PC1/PC2 ciliary distribution support a role in organizing ciliary proteins. Combined human DZIP1/DZIP1L depletion and mouse Dzip1l studies support cilium assembly, with the mouse experiments resolving Cby positioning and ciliary-bud formation. SEPTIN2 binding is a measured partner activity; its contribution to each downstream outcome remains unresolved, and DZIP1L is not assigned SEPTIN2 GTP hydrolysis or universal control of cilium number.

DOK7 activates MUSK by binding its phosphorylated juxtamembrane region and promoting receptor dimerization, which supports MUSK trans-autophosphorylation and neuromuscular junction assembly. Human PH-PTB fragments form complexes with the MUSK cytoplasmic domain; direct kinase-stimulation and cellular tests in the structural study used mouse Dok7.

DOK7 couples activated MUSK to downstream signaling by using its phosphorylated C-terminal tail to recruit CRK and CRKL. Mouse myotube experiments separate this recruitment and acetylcholine-receptor clustering function from the stronger PH-PTB-mediated kinase-activation mechanism. The corresponding human adaptor role is supported by orthology.

MLKL is the terminal effector of necroptosis. Once RIPK3 phosphorylates its pseudokinase domain, MLKL oligomerizes, and its N-terminal four-helix bundle engages plasma-membrane phosphatidylinositol phosphates, preferentially PI(4,5)P2, then permeabilizes the membrane. The pseudokinase domain binds ATP but has no catalytic activity; it acts as a phosphorylation-controlled switch.
The N-terminal four-helix bundle binds phosphatidylinositol phosphates, with PI(4,5)P2 the preferred partner, which targets activated MLKL to the plasma membrane.

Activation: binding of highly phosphorylated soluble inositol phosphates (IP6 and related) to the N-terminal region of cytosolic MLKL is required, together with RIPK3 phosphorylation, for MLKL oligomerization and plasma membrane recruitment.

Participates in BBSome assembly through the BBS-chaperonin machinery. Association with MKKS/BBS6, BBS7 and CCT proteins, together with BBS12 depletion experiments, links BBS12 to stabilization of assembly intermediates and subsequent incorporation of BBSome subunits. BBS12 is released as assembly proceeds. These experiments establish an assembly role but do not resolve an independent folding activity or the contribution of nucleotide binding by BBS12 itself.

Flagellar coiled-coil protein, concentrated in the sperm midpiece, that is required during spermiogenesis for assembly of the sperm axoneme (central pair and radial spoke integrity) and of the midpiece mitochondrial sheath; loss causes MMAF and male infertility (SPGF49). Its molecular activity and exact structural position within the flagellum are unknown.
